title: Probabilistic Residual Learning for Online Recommendations
comment: Accepted at the 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys 2026)
summary: Modern recommender systems are typically based on deep learning (DL) models, where a dense encoder learns representations of users and items. As a result, these systems often suffer from the black-box nature and computational complexity of the underlying models, making it difficult to systematically enhance their recommendation capabilities. To address this problem, we propose Probabilistic Residual Learning (PRL), a causal Bayesian recommendation model that models the residual between ground-truth and base predictions, enabling targeted refinement of existing systems. Specifically, PRL (1) probabilistically groups users for localized residual modeling, (2) models domain-level confounders that influence user and item representations, and (3) aggregates cluster-specific residual predictions over the confounders using do-calculus. Experiments demonstrate that our plug-and-play PRL is compatible with various base deep learning recommender systems, improving their performance while automatically discovering meaningful user clusters.

AI.tldr: PRL is a plug-and-play causal Bayesian framework that improves existing deep learning recommenders by modeling prediction residuals through probabilistic user clustering and confounder adjustment via do-calculus.
AI.motivation: Deep learning-based recommender systems suffer from opacity (black-box nature) and high computational complexity, which obstructs systematic performance improvements. The authors aim to provide a principled, interpretable way to refine existing systems without redesigning them from scratch.
AI.method: PRL models the residual between ground-truth ratings and base model predictions using three components: (1) probabilistic user clustering via a Gaussian mixture model for localized residual modeling; (2) identification and modeling of domain-level confounders affecting user/item representations; and (3) do-calculus-based aggregation of cluster-specific residual predictions over confounders to estimate causal effects.
AI.result: Experiments show PRL is compatible with multiple base DL recommender systems, consistently improving their recommendation performance while automatically discovering meaningful user clusters.
AI.conclusion: PRL offers an effective, model-agnostic, and causally grounded approach to enhancing black-box recommender systems through targeted residual correction, with the added benefit of interpretable user segmentation.

title: LO-FAR: A Cost-Aware Local Filter for Sparse Feature Ranking in Industrial Ad Recommendation
summary: Industrial ad recommendation models rely heavily on sparse, high-cardinality ID-list features that encode user histories and contextual identifiers. Each is backed by a dedicated embedding table, so these features dominate storage, training, and serving cost and must be revisited as traffic and downstream models evolve. Therefore, sparse feature ranking is not just an offline modeling problem but also a recurrent systems decision limited by compute budgets and iteration cadence. We present Localized Feature Ranking (LO-FAR), a CPU-only, model-agnostic workflow that ranks each candidate feature from its stand-alone held-out predictive signal using lightweight local estimators rather than the GPU-bound retraining loops of permutation- and stochastic-gate-based methods. On a production dataset of more than one million logged interactions and 475 sparse ID-list features, LO-FAR completes ranking in approximately two CPU-hours and preserves downstream Normalized Entropy gains on CTR and CVR tasks that are competitive with shuffle-based importance, Binary Stochastic Neurons, and a coverage-based heuristic across budgets of 100--400 retained features. The contribution is a deployable workflow showing that, when cost and turnaround constraints are binding, a simple local filter can be a practical production choice over heavier interaction-aware alternatives.

AI.tldr: LO-FAR is a CPU-only, model-agnostic sparse feature ranking method that uses lightweight local estimators to rank ID-list features, completing in ~2 CPU-hours on a million-interaction dataset while matching the downstream CTR/CVR performance of GPU-bound alternatives like permutation importance and Binary Stochastic Neurons across retention budgets of 100–400 features.
AI.motivation: Industrial recommendation systems are dominated by high-cardinality sparse ID-list features with dedicated embedding tables that drive storage, training, and serving costs. Ranking and pruning these features is a recurring systems problem constrained by limited compute budgets and tight iteration cycles, yet existing methods (permutation importance, stochastic gates) require expensive GPU retraining loops, making them impractical for frequent redeployment.
AI.method: LO-FAR (Localized Feature Ranking) evaluates each candidate feature independently using a stand-alone held-out predictive signal computed via lightweight local estimators. The ranking is performed entirely on CPU without any GPU-bound retraining, making it model-agnostic and computationally inexpensive. Each feature's importance is scored in isolation from its held-out signal, and features are ranked globally based on these scores for budget-constrained selection.
AI.result: On a production dataset with over one million logged interactions and 475 sparse ID-list features, LO-FAR completes ranking in approximately two CPU-hours. Downstream Normalized Entropy gains on both CTR and CVR tasks are competitive with shuffle-based importance, Binary Stochastic Neurons, and a coverage-based heuristic across retention budgets ranging from 100 to 400 features.
AI.conclusion: When cost and turnaround constraints are binding, a simple local filter like LO-FAR offers a practical and deployable alternative to heavier interaction-aware feature selection methods, delivering comparable predictive performance with dramatically lower computational overhead.

title: Controllable and Content-Based Recommendations
summary: Traditional recommendation systems rely on latent (dense) representations, making them difficult to interpret and control. We propose the Controllable and Content-Based Recommendations (CCBR) framework, which builds its recommendations from textual user profile representations. CCBR plugs into collaborative filtering models and introduces controllability via text bottlenecks. We show that CCBR enables text-based and multimodal interventions, allowing users to steer the model towards the directions they prefer. Different from existing controllable recommendation systems, CCBR infers the text summaries directly from item contents (images, audio or video). Across image-, audio-, and video-based datasets, we demonstrate that the proposed framework obtains competitive model performance with standard (latent-representation) models while providing controllable model summaries via text. The model also outperforms TEARS, a recent baseline for controllable recommendation systems. Through systematic interventions, we demonstrate the efficacy of the user steering mechanism.

AI.tldr: CCBR is a controllable recommendation framework that uses textual user profiles as bottlenecks, enabling interpretable, multimodal interventions while maintaining competitive performance against latent-representation models.
AI.motivation: Traditional collaborative filtering models use opaque latent (dense) representations, which are inherently difficult to interpret and provide no mechanism for users to control or steer recommendations. Existing controllable systems often lack the ability to derive text explanations directly from item content (images, audio, video), limiting their applicability across modalities.
AI.method: The CCBR framework integrates with collaborative filtering models by introducing a text bottleneck: it infers textual user profile summaries directly from item contents (images, audio, or video) and uses these text representations to generate recommendations. This design allows both text-based and multimodal interventions, giving users direct steering capability over the model's behavior.
AI.result: CCBR achieves competitive performance compared to standard latent-representation models across image-, audio-, and video-based datasets. It also outperforms TEARS, a recent controllable recommendation baseline. Systematic intervention experiments confirm the effectiveness of the user steering mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Controllable recommendation systems can be built by grounding user profiles in interpretable text derived from item content, without sacrificing predictive performance. The text bottleneck approach enables effective user steering and broad applicability across multiple modalities.

title: Fast and Efficient Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search for High-Dimensional LLM Embeddings
summary:
The annual SISAP Indexing Challenge benchmarks Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) algorithms under rigorous constraints. This paper presents our submissions for the 2026 edition, addressing both $k$-Nearest Neighbor Graph (kNNG) construction on 1024-dimensional BGE-M3 embeddings (Task 1) and Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) on unnormalized Llama-3.2-8B features (Task 2). To optimize construction speed, we utilize Equi-Voronoi Polytopes (EVP) for efficient quantization, supplemented by targeted reranking strategies to maintain high recall. For MIPS, we transform the asymmetric inner product problem into a Euclidean search space via dimensionality augmentation. To reduce query latency and optimize memory access, we introduce a 1D presorting mechanism via Fast Linear Assignment Sorting (FLAS) prior to graph construction. This significantly improves spatial locality and cache hit rates during subsequent graph traversal.
  Source Code: https://github.com/Visual-Computing/sisap26-deglib

AI.tldr: Submission to SISAP 2026 Indexing Challenge: uses Equi-Voronoi Polytopes (EVP) quantization with reranking for fast kNNG construction (Task 1), and dimensionality augmentation plus Fast Linear Assignment Sorting (FLAS) for efficient MIPS via graph-based Euclidean search (Task 2).
AI.motivation: The SISAP Indexing Challenge imposes strict performance constraints for ANNS. The authors aim to accelerate kNNG construction on high-dimensional BGE-M3 embeddings and reduce query latency in MIPS over unnormalized Llama-3.2-8B features, where naive inner product search is costly and graph traversal suffers from poor memory locality.
AI.method: For Task 1 (kNNG construction, 1024-d): EVP-based efficient quantization is used to speed up graph building, with targeted reranking to recover recall lost during quantization. For Task 2 (MIPS, Llama-3.2-8B): the asymmetric inner product problem is converted to Euclidean nearest neighbor search via dimensionality augmentation (adding an extra dimension). A 1D presorting step using Fast Linear Assignment Sorting (FLAS) is applied before graph construction to improve spatial locality and cache hit rates during traversal.
AI.result: Not explicitly stated in the abstract; the paper reports submissions to the 2026 challenge and presumably competitive recall-speed trade-offs on both tasks, with open-sourced code provided.
AI.conclusion: EVP quantization with reranking and FLAS-based presorting are effective techniques for accelerating ANNS index construction and querying under challenge constraints. The approach is made reproducible via public source code.

title: Verifier-First Evaluation of Agentic LLMs for Infrastructure-as-Code Generation
comment: 26 pages, 3 figures, 17 tables. Benchmark dataset available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/iac-eval-v2/iac-eval-v2
summary:
Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) generation from natural language requires satisfying provider schemas, dependency planning, and organizational policy constraints, not merely producing syntactically plausible configurations. We present a verifier-first empirical study of seven agentic strategies for Terraform generation evaluated on IaC-Eval v2, a modernized 186-task AWS/Terraform benchmark with Rego v1 intent policies. Our evaluation separates failures into three verifier stages (terraform validate, terraform plan, opa eval) and applies McNemar's test with Wilson confidence intervals on all pairwise comparisons (n=186, alpha=0.05).
  We report five principal findings. (1) Active retrieval via ReAct agents with MCP or ChromaDB-backed RAG raises Qwen2.5-Coder 7B from 14.0% to 45.7% pass@1 (p<0.0001), primarily by reducing VALIDATE_FAIL from 144 to 66 tasks. (2) Iterative refinement with verifier feedback achieves 62.9% (Qwen 7B) and 84.4% (GPT-4o) pass@1, exhibiting binary convergence -- tasks either resolve in one retry or exhaust the budget. (3) GEPA reflective instruction optimization raises the Active RAG baseline by +7.5 pp (p=0.026) using only 80 verifier-guided rollouts, providing evidence that prompt optimizers can improve verifiable IaC generation without weight updates. (4) SIMBA teacher-free demonstration injection achieves performance equivalent to Active RAG (p=1.0) without retrieval infrastructure, but fails to address the dominant SELF_DEFINED_PROPERTY error class (50% of failures). (5) A diagnostic Rego-injection experiment shows that 79% of post-refinement OPA failures are information-gap failures resolvable when policy text is visible (p=0.016), motivating policy

AI.tldr: A verifier-first empirical study evaluating seven agentic strategies for generating Terraform configurations from natural language, tested on 186 AWS tasks. Iterative refinement with verifier feedback achieves up to 84.4% pass@1 with GPT-4o, while active retrieval lifts a small model from 14% to 45.7%. Key failure modes are identified across three verifier stages, with policy information gaps being the dominant unresolved issue.
AI.motivation: IaC generation from natural language is not just a syntax problem — it requires satisfying cloud provider schemas, dependency planning, and organizational policy constraints. Existing approaches lack systematic evaluation across these dimensions, motivating a rigorous, verifier-first empirical study that disentangles failure modes across validation, planning, and policy compliance stages.
AI.method: The authors evaluate seven agentic strategies (Active RAG via ReAct+MCP/ChromaDB, iterative refinement with verifier feedback, GEPA reflective instruction optimization, SIMBA teacher-free demonstration injection, and Rego-injection) on IaC-Eval v2, a 186-task AWS/Terraform benchmark with Rego v1 intent policies. Failures are categorized into three verifier stages: terraform validate, terraform plan, and opa eval. All pairwise comparisons use McNemar's test with Wilson confidence intervals (n=186, α=0.05).
AI.result: (1) Active RAG raises Qwen2.5-Coder 7B from 14.0% to 45.7% pass@1 (p<0.0001), cutting VALIDATE_FAIL from 144 to 66 tasks. (2) Iterative refinement achieves 62.9% (Qwen 7B) and 84.4% (GPT-4o) pass@1 with binary convergence. (3) GEPA instruction optimization adds +7.5 pp over Active RAG (p=0.026) using only 80 rollouts. (4) SIMBA matches Active RAG performance (p=1.0) without retrieval but fails on SELF_DEFINED_PROPERTY errors (50% of failures). (5) 79% of post-refinement OPA failures are information-gap failures resolvable when policy text is visible (p=0.016).
AI.conclusion: Verifier-feedback loops and retrieval-augmented generation are highly effective for IaC generation, with iterative refinement producing the strongest results. Policy information gaps represent the dominant remaining failure mode, motivating tighter integration of policy text into generation pipelines. The study provides robust statistical evidence across all strategy comparisons.

title: HARP: The Human--AI Research Platform
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, SAP Academic Community Conference North America, 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shifted human--computer interaction from `traditional'' interface journeys toward more conversational exchanges. Researchers studying HCI and UI use moderated usability sessions, interviews, surveys, transcript analysis, and static prototypes. However, static prototypes provide limited opportunities to study interaction with live AI systems or systematically control how an LLM behaves across participants and scenarios. Conversation transcripts reveal little about how users formulate, revise, and hesitate over prompts before submission. We designed the Human--AI Research Platform (HARP) for researchers, designers, and anyone who has ever wondered, `What if AI did this?' HARP places participants in controlled mock scenarios with live, configurable AI agents. Researchers can control agent prompts, model parameters, response characteristics, and experimental conditions; trigger surveys at predefined moments; and record prompt composition time, response latency, deletions, and keystroke pauses. Planned capabilities include voice, facial expression, gesture, and, where legally and ethically appropriate, emotion analysis. We illustrate HARP through a study examining how technical specificity and response length affect retention of LLM output. By pairing controllable live agents with behavioral and self-report measures, HARP enables systematic testing of how AI design choices affect users.

AI.tldr: HARP is a research platform enabling systematic human-AI interaction studies with live, configurable LLM agents, capturing behavioral metrics (keystroke dynamics, response latency, prompt composition) alongside surveys, surpassing the limitations of static prototypes and transcript analysis.
AI.motivation: Traditional HCI/UI research methods—moderated usability sessions, interviews, static prototypes, and transcript analysis—fail to capture how users compose, revise, and hesitate over prompts before submitting them to live AI systems, and offer no systematic control over LLM behavior across participants and scenarios.
AI.method: HARP provides a platform where researchers place participants in controlled mock scenarios with live, configurable AI agents. Researchers can manipulate agent prompts, model parameters, response characteristics, and experimental conditions; trigger surveys at predefined moments; and record fine-grained behavioral data including prompt composition time, response latency, deletions, and keystroke pauses. Planned extensions include voice, facial expression, gesture, and emotion analysis.
AI.result: The authors demonstrate HARP through a study investigating how technical specificity and response length affect user retention of LLM-generated output, illustrating the platform's capacity to pair controllable live agents with both behavioral and self-report measures.
AI.conclusion: HARP bridges a critical methodological gap by enabling reproducible, ecologically valid experiments that systematically test how AI design choices affect user behavior and experience, moving beyond the constraints of static prototyping and post-hoc transcript analysis.

title: pAI-Econ-claude: A Gated Human-in-the-Loop Multi-Agent Architecture for AI-Assisted Economic Theory Development
summary: In many social-science research tasks, such as economics, LLM-based agents must produce outputs for which no cheap, task-complete, machine-readable correctness signal exists. This creates a distinctive reliability problem for multi-agent systems: how should generation, critique, coordination, and human judgment be organized when no component can certify the final result? We address this problem through pAI-Econ-claude, a gated, human-in-the-loop multi-agent architecture for AI-assisted economic theory development. Agents coordinate through a shared workspace of inspectable intermediate records; specialized gates diagnose targeted failure modes and recommend loopbacks without certifying correctness; and human checkpoints retain authority over decisions that are costly to reverse. We evaluate the architecture on five matched economic-theory tasks against an ungated baseline. Two evaluators blinded to configuration agreed on all five pairwise rankings, preferring the gated architecture in four tasks and the baseline in one. Mean failure severity fell from 1.58 to 1.16, while overall usefulness rose from 2.60 to 3.10. The largest observed gain occurred when a reality check rejected a false market-structure premise and a proof review prompted revision of a false welfare claim. The negative case shows that scaffolding can also compress an economically important mechanism too aggressively. The results support a bounded claim: gated oversight improves the auditability of AI-assisted economic theory without substituting for formal verification, and the allocation of irreversible human judgment is a more informative design variable than pure agent autonomy. The workflow is publicly available at https://github.com/maxwell2732/pAI-Econ-claude.

AI.tldr: pAI-Econ-claude is a gated, human-in-the-loop multi-agent architecture for AI-assisted economic theory development where no cheap correctness signal exists. It uses inspectable records, specialized diagnostic gates, and human checkpoints. In a five-task evaluation, the gated architecture outperformed an ungated baseline on four of five tasks, reducing failure severity and increasing usefulness, with the largest gains from reality checks and proof reviews.
AI.motivation: In social-science domains like economics, LLM-based agents produce outputs that lack cheap, task-complete, machine-readable correctness signals. This creates a reliability problem for multi-agent systems: standard approaches to generation, critique, and coordination break down when no component can certify the final result. The paper addresses how to organize these processes under such uncertainty.
AI.method: The authors propose pAI-Econ-claude, a gated, human-in-the-loop multi-agent architecture. Agents coordinate through a shared workspace of inspectable intermediate records. Specialized gates diagnose targeted failure modes and recommend loopbacks without certifying correctness. Human checkpoints retain authority over decisions costly to reverse. The architecture is evaluated on five matched economic-theory tasks against an ungated baseline, with two blinded evaluators providing pairwise rankings, failure severity scores, and usefulness ratings.
AI.result: Blinded evaluators agreed on all five pairwise rankings: gated architecture preferred in four tasks, baseline in one. Mean failure severity dropped from 1.58 (baseline) to 1.16 (gated). Overall usefulness rose from 2.60 to 3.10. The largest gain came from a reality check rejecting a false market-structure premise and a proof review prompting revision of a false welfare claim. The negative case showed scaffolding can overly compress an economically important mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Gated oversight improves the auditability of AI-assisted economic theory without substituting for formal verification. The allocation of irreversible human judgment is a more informative design variable than pure agent autonomy. The claims are bounded and the workflow is publicly available.

title: PhantomSeal: Proactive Deepfakes Defense with Identity/Context Protection and Forensic Tracing
summary: Deepfakes, especially face-swapping attacks, pose significant challenges to authenticity, security, and ethics across science, engineering, and society. While most existing detection/tracing approaches operate post hoc, proactive defenses that aim to intervene before deepfake generation remain limited in terms of real-world effectiveness. In this paper, we present PhantomSeal, the first proactive defense to simultaneously protect both the identity and the context of users' images from being used in face-swapping attacks, while supporting forensic tracing. We present a novel cloaking technique that embeds a selected identity as a stealthy identifier. This mechanism steers the deepfake generation process toward producing content that resembles the chosen cloak identity, thereby preventing successful face-swapping while enabling effective feature-based forensic analysis. The effectiveness and robustness of PhantomSeal is demonstrated in extensive experiments across different face-swapping architectures and models. For example, it reduces the attack success rate of SimSwap, an advanced deepfake model, to 0.30%, and correctly identifies 97.97% of manipulated content. Codes can be found at https://github.com/LiangqinRen/PhantomSeal

AI.tldr: PhantomSeal is the first proactive defense against face-swapping deepfakes that simultaneously protects both identity and context by embedding a stealthy cloaked identifier. This identifier redirects deepfake generation to produce outputs resembling a chosen cloak identity, thwarting attacks and enabling forensic tracing with high accuracy (e.g., reducing SimSwap attack success to 0.30% and identifying 97.97% of manipulations).
AI.motivation: Existing deepfake defenses are predominantly post-hoc (detection or tracing after generation), while proactive defenses that intervene before generation remain limited in practical, real-world effectiveness. There is a need for a unified proactive approach that can protect both the identity and contextual integrity of images while also supporting forensic traceability.
AI.method: PhantomSeal introduces a novel cloaking technique that embeds a stealthy identifier — a selected "cloak identity" — into users' images. This embedded identifier steers the face-swapping generation process so that the output converges toward the cloak identity rather than the attacker's intended target. This simultaneously prevents successful identity theft and enables feature-based forensic analysis to trace manipulated content back to its origin.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple face-swapping architectures demonstrate PhantomSeal's effectiveness: it reduces the attack success rate of SimSwap to 0.30% and correctly identifies 97.97% of manipulated content via forensic tracing.
AI.conclusion: PhantomSeal represents a significant advance in proactive deepfake defense, offering the first method that simultaneously protects identity and context before attacks occur while enabling reliable forensic tracing. Its strong empirical results across diverse models suggest practical viability for real-world deployment.

title: What is Good? Extracting and Testing Implicit Theories of Literary Quality from LLM Reasoning Traces
summary:
What makes writing "good" remains a persistent question in literary studies and computational linguistics. We present a two-study investigation of how reasoning-enabled LLMs evaluate literary quality.
  In Study 1, we construct a benchmark of 30 real texts spanning six quality tiers, from canonical literature to anonymous forum posts, and extract the model's implicit theory of quality from its reasoning traces. Across five DeepSeek replications, the model achieves 79.3% mean tier-classification accuracy. The traces reveal a consistent stated theory: the model values intentionality over correctness, prioritizing craft, depth, and distinctive voice. A familiarity experiment with style-matched but unrecognizable passages suggests that source recognition may inflate scores, although this is confounded by genuine quality differences between canonical originals and researcher-written pastiches.
  In Study 2, we probe this theory through systematic degradation of five canonical prose passages. We apply six manipulations - vocabulary simplification, rhythm flattening, imagery removal, voice genericization, structure simplification, and combined degradation - and reevaluate each version. Vocabulary simplification causes the smallest quality loss (0.41 +/- 0.46 points), far below structure (2.78) or voice (2.34) loss. Combined degradation is devastating (-5.64) but subadditive. An exploratory comparison with Qwen QwQ shows the same broad qualitative pattern.
  Together, these studies suggest that LLM judgments of writing quality are holistic, author-specific, and more sensitive to structural than lexical features, with implications for automated writing feedback and computational aesthetics.

AI.tldr: Two studies examine how reasoning-enabled LLMs evaluate literary quality. Study 1 uses a 30-text benchmark across six quality tiers and finds that DeepSeek models achieve 79.3% classification accuracy, with reasoning traces revealing a stated theory prioritizing intentionality, craft, depth, and voice over mere correctness. Study 2 systematically degrades canonical prose across six dimensions, finding that structural and voice manipulations cause the greatest quality loss, while vocabulary simplification has minimal impact. Results suggest LLM quality judgments are holistic, author-specific, and more sensitive to structural than lexical features.
AI.motivation: The persistent question of what makes writing "good" remains unresolved in literary studies and computational linguistics. The authors aim to understand how modern reasoning-enabled LLMs implicitly theorize and evaluate literary quality, moving beyond surface-level metrics to examine the underlying criteria models actually employ.
AI.method: Study 1: Constructed a benchmark of 30 real texts across six quality tiers (canonical literature to anonymous forum posts). Extracted the model's implicit theory of quality from reasoning traces across five DeepSeek replications. Included a familiarity experiment using style-matched but unrecognizable passages to test source recognition bias. Study 2: Applied six systematic degradations (vocabulary simplification, rhythm flattening, imagery removal, voice genericization, structure simplification, combined degradation) to five canonical prose passages and reevaluated. Included an exploratory comparison with Qwen QwQ.
AI.result: Study 1: DeepSeek achieved 79.3% mean tier-classification accuracy. Reasoning traces revealed the model values intentionality over correctness, prioritizing craft, depth, and distinctive voice. The familiarity experiment suggested source recognition may inflate scores, though confounded by genuine quality differences. Study 2: Vocabulary simplification caused the smallest quality loss (0.41 ± 0.46 pts), far below structure (2.78) and voice (2.34) loss. Combined degradation was devastating (-5.64) but subadditive. Qwen QwQ showed qualitatively similar patterns.
AI.conclusion: LLM judgments of writing quality are holistic, author-specific, and more sensitive to structural than lexical features. These findings carry implications for automated writing feedback and computational aesthetics.

title: DataPrep-Bench: Benchmarking LLMs as Training Data Preparators
summary: The quality of training data fundamentally determines the capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet no unified benchmark exists to measure how well LLMs, agents, and data-centric workflows actually prepare training data end to end. We view LLM-driven data preparation as comprising two complementary capabilities: data construction, which transforms raw sources into supervised training data, and data quality evaluation, which predicts the training value of candidate datasets before downstream training; throughout, "quality" refers to downstream training utility rather than surface-level textual properties. We introduce DataPrep-Bench, the first unified benchmark that jointly evaluates both capabilities under a shared downstream-grounded protocol over six domains and multiple base models. For data construction, methods consume identical raw sources and are scored by fine-tuning a base model on their outputs jointly with Dolly-15k; alongside this track we release Data-Construction-Skill, a skill-guided agent that lifts the Dolly-only baseline by nearly 20 points absolute on Llama-3.1-8B Finance and is competitive with the strongest agent- and DataFlow-based methods in knowledge-extraction-dense domains. For data quality evaluation, scoring functions are scored by Pearson correlation with downstream performance on a shared candidate pool; we release the Distributional Alignment Score (DAS), a distribution-based evaluator that uses MMD between a candidate dataset and a domain proxy. DAS attains the strongest cross-model correlation in four of six domains and is the only metric clearing r > 0.70 simultaneously in Math, Science, and Medical, outperforming existing quality-, diversity-, and heuristic-based evaluators. DataPrep-Bench provides a unified, downstream-grounded framework for measuring progress on both capabilities as co-equal targets of LLM-driven data preparation.

AI.tldr: DataPrep-Bench is a unified benchmark that jointly evaluates LLM-driven data construction and data quality evaluation using downstream training utility as the quality metric. It introduces Data-Construction-Skill (a skill-guided agent) and the Distributional Alignment Score (DAS), with DAS achieving superior cross-model correlation across multiple domains.
AI.motivation: No unified benchmark exists for end-to-end evaluation of LLM-driven training data preparation. Existing efforts conflate data construction and quality evaluation, and "quality" is often measured by surface-level textual properties rather than downstream training utility—the metric that truly matters.
AI.method: The benchmark covers six domains and evaluates two capabilities: (1) Data construction — methods consume identical raw sources and are scored by fine-tuning a base model on their outputs jointly with Dolly-15k; (2) Data quality evaluation — scoring functions are evaluated via Pearson correlation with downstream performance on a shared candidate pool. Authors also release Data-Construction-Skill (a skill-guided agent) and DAS (a distribution-based evaluator using Maximum Mean Discrepancy between candidate and domain-proxy distributions).
AI.result: Data-Construction-Skill lifts the Dolly-only baseline by ~20 absolute points on Llama-3.1-8B Finance and is competitive with strongest agent/DataFlow methods in knowledge-extraction-dense domains. DAS achieves the strongest cross-model correlation in 4/6 domains and is the only metric clearing r > 0.70 simultaneously in Math, Science, and Medical, outperforming existing quality-, diversity-, and heuristic-based evaluators.
AI.conclusion: DataPrep-Bench establishes a downstream-grounded, unified framework treating data construction and quality evaluation as co-equal targets, enabling systematic progress measurement in LLM-driven data preparation.

title: AINTMA: Agentic AI Architecture for Autonomous Test Management with Generative Intelligence, Secure Cloud Communication and Adaptive Quality Analytics
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables, Submitted to AICCONS (AIP Conference Proceedings format)
summary: Modern software quality assurance demands intelligent, autonomous systems capable of adaptive decision-making across distributed cloud environments. This paper presents AINTMA (Agentic Intelligent Test Management Architecture), a multi-agent agentic AI system that transforms traditional test management into an autonomous quality intelligence ecosystem. AINTMA deploys six specialized AI agents (Test Discovery, Risk Assessment, Reinforcement Learning Prioritization, Execution Orchestration, Generative Quality Intelligence, and Cloud Security Monitor) coordinated through a secure multi-agent communication framework over a cloud-native microservices infrastructure. The Generative Quality Intelligence agent employs large language models to produce plain language quality narratives, defect risk summaries, and data-augmented test recommendations. The RL Prioritization agent models test selection as a Markov Decision Process, learning contextual policies from large-scale historical test execution data (47 features, rolling 36-month window). Secure cloud communication is enforced through a zero-trust API gateway with OAuth2/JWT authentication, encrypted inter-agent messaging, and multi-tenant isolation. Evaluation across 12 heterogeneous software projects over 18 months demonstrates: 88.4% test prioritization accuracy (APFD, vs. 51.2% random, 82.1% best commercial baseline); 43% test cycle time reduction; defect escape rate reduced from 8.3% to 2.1%; 340% ROI at 9-month payback. The agentic architecture scales to 50,000+ test cases with sub-400ms response time, and the generative intelligence module achieves 4.3/5.0 developer usefulness rating. AINTMA demonstrates that agentic AI, combining autonomous multi-agent coordination, generative intelligence and secure smart connectivity, can fundamentally advance software quality management in cloud-scale enterprise environments.

AI.tldr: AINTMA is a multi-agent AI system for autonomous test management that deploys six specialized agents to handle test discovery, risk assessment, RL-based prioritization, execution orchestration, generative quality reporting, and cloud security. Evaluated over 18 months across 12 projects, it achieves 88.4% APFD accuracy, 43% cycle time reduction, and defect escape rate reduction from 8.3% to 2.1%.
AI.motivation: Modern software quality assurance requires intelligent, autonomous systems capable of adaptive decision-making across distributed cloud environments. Traditional test management lacks the coordination, intelligence, and scalability needed for cloud-scale enterprise systems.
AI.method: AINTMA deploys six specialized AI agents (Test Discovery, Risk Assessment, RL Prioritization, Execution Orchestration, Generative Quality Intelligence, Cloud Security Monitor) coordinated through a secure multi-agent communication framework on cloud-native microservices. The RL Prioritization agent models test selection as a Markov Decision Process using 47 features over a rolling 36-month window. The Generative Quality Intelligence agent uses LLMs for quality narratives. Security is enforced via zero-trust API gateway with OAuth2/JWT, encrypted messaging, and multi-tenant isolation.
AI.result: Across 12 projects over 18 months: 88.4% test prioritization accuracy (APFD) vs. 51.2% random and 82.1% best commercial baseline; 43% test cycle time reduction; defect escape rate reduced from 8.3% to 2.1%; 340% ROI at 9-month payback; scales to 50,000+ test cases with sub-400ms response; generative intelligence rated 4.3/5.0 by developers.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI combining autonomous multi-agent coordination, generative intelligence, and secure cloud connectivity can fundamentally advance software quality management in cloud-scale enterprise environments.

title: Bridging the Structural Gap: Adapting Autoregressive Generation for Recommendation
summary: Generative Recommendation (GR) has emerged as a new paradigm for sequential recommendation, in which a representative line of work encodes items into hierarchical semantic IDs via residual quantization and predicts the IDs token by token. However, this generative formulation still exhibits structural gaps with respect to the recommendation task: flattening multi-token IDs into a single sequence destroys item-level structure, and the inconsistency between training and inference over a hierarchical codebook gives rise to semantic drift. To bridge these two gaps, we propose BARGE, which employs Item Context-Aware Attention (ICA) to restore item-level structure during encoding, and Hierarchical Path Reranking (HPR) together with Dual-Path Decoding (DPD) to suppress semantic drift from two complementary angles during decoding. Extensive experiments and analytical studies on public benchmarks and a large-scale offline test demonstrate that BARGE achieves superior recommendation performance. An online A/B test on a Tencent platform yields improvements of 0.60% in click-through rate, 1.34% in click unique visitors, and 1.70% in total reading time, confirming the practical value of BARGE in industrial-scale recommendation.

AI.tldr: BARGE improves generative sequential recommendation by addressing two structural gaps: loss of item-level structure from flattening multi-token IDs, and semantic drift from train-inference inconsistency over hierarchical codebooks. It introduces Item Context-Aware Attention, Hierarchical Path Reranking, and Dual-Path Decoding, achieving significant gains on public benchmarks and in online A/B tests at Tencent.
AI.motivation: Existing Generative Recommendation methods encode items as hierarchical semantic IDs using residual quantization and predict tokens sequentially. This approach has two key flaws: (1) flattening multi-token IDs destroys item-level structural information, and (2) training with ground-truth hierarchical codes while inferring via autoregressive generation over codebooks causes semantic drift between training and inference.
AI.method: BARGE introduces three components: (1) Item Context-Aware Attention (ICA) — restores item-level structure during encoding by attending over tokens belonging to the same item; (2) Hierarchical Path Reranking (HPR) — reranks candidate sequences to align inference with the hierarchical nature of the codebook; (3) Dual-Path Decoding (DPD) — jointly decodes through two complementary paths to further suppress semantic drift.
AI.result: BARGE achieves superior performance on public benchmarks and a large-scale offline test. Online A/B testing on a Tencent platform shows: +0.60% click-through rate, +1.34% click unique visitors, and +1.70% total reading time, confirming industrial-scale effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: BARGE effectively bridges the item-structure and semantic-drift gaps in generative sequential recommendation, delivering both academic benchmark improvements and tangible industrial gains, validating its practical deployment value.

title: Transformer-Assisted LLM-Based Source Code Summarisation: to Enable More Secure Software Development
summary: Neural Source Code Summarisation (NSCS) aims to generate natural language summaries of source code to improve developers' and maintainers' understanding of code. Source code summaries are vital during the maintenance phase of the Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC), as they improve maintainers' understanding of code and help reduce the number of bugs and vulnerabilities in a software system. However, summaries are often missing, incomplete, or outdated in many software systems. Solutions to this problem use small, task-specific Transformer models or code-aware Large Language Models (LLMs). Task-specific Transformer-generated summaries often score well across many natural language generation (NLG) metrics, but these metrics reward lexical overlap rather than summary quality. Conversely, the ability of LLMs to capture semantics and produce high-quality summaries presents an exciting solution to this problem. This is especially relevant given the increased availability of LLMs and improvements in workstation hardware in recent years, which mean that some LLMs can now be run on developers' workstations. However, because of their abstractive nature, LLM-generated code summaries often differ greatly from developer-written summaries in the words and phrases they use, resulting in low scores across NLG metrics. We show how combining these two methods, by using Transformer-generated summaries in prompt engineering, may enable LLMs to create better source code summaries and help software practitioners maintain secure systems. We prompt four LLMs using four different prompts, with a task-specific Transformer used to assist the LLMs within the prompts. We present "Transformer-Assisted LLM-Based Source Code Summarisation", a method through which we observe an improvement of 7.8% in BLEU-4 and 5%.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes combining small Transformer-generated summaries with LLM prompting to improve neural source code summarization, achieving 7.8% BLEU-4 and 5% improvement over LLM-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Source code summaries are critical for software maintenance and the SSDLC, but are often missing or outdated. Task-specific Transformers score well on NLG metrics but lack semantic quality, while LLMs produce semantically rich summaries that score poorly on lexical-overlap metrics. Bridging this gap could yield summaries that are both high-quality and well-aligned with developer conventions.
AI.method: "Transformer-Assisted LLM-Based Source Code Summarisation": a task-specific Transformer model generates an initial summary, which is then incorporated into prompts (four different prompt designs) fed to four LLMs, guiding the LLMs to produce improved summaries that combine lexical fidelity with semantic richness.
AI.result: The proposed method yields a 7.8% improvement in BLEU-4 and a 5% improvement overall compared to using LLMs alone, demonstrating that Transformer-assisted prompting effectively boosts summary quality across NLG metrics.
AI.conclusion: Combining task-specific Transformers with LLMs via prompt engineering produces better source code summaries, helping practitioners maintain more secure software systems by delivering summaries that balance lexical alignment with semantic quality.

title: Flint: A Semantics-Driven Data Visualization Intermediate Language
summary: We present Flint, an intermediate language that enables authors to create high-quality visualizations from concise, semantics-driven specifications without explicitly configuring low-level parameters such as scales, axes, and formatting. Unlike prior systems that infer default configurations from surface-level data representations, often producing brittle choices, Flint introduces a hierarchical data semantic model that allows users to specify the meanings of data fields structurally and helps the compiler derive appropriate visualization configurations. From a concise specification, the system generates and optimizes library-agnostic visualization configurations and translates them into complete, executable specifications for multiple target grammars, including Vega-Lite, Apache ECharts, and Chart.js. We demonstrate that Flint simplifies the authoring process without compromising on visual quality, and it is an effective intermediate language for both humans and AI agents to create visualizations.

AI.tldr: Flint is an intermediate language that uses a hierarchical data semantic model to generate high-quality, library-agnostic visualization configurations from concise specifications, which are then translated into executable code for Vega-Lite, ECharts, and Chart.js.
AI.motivation: Existing visualization authoring systems infer default configurations from surface-level data representations, resulting in brittle and suboptimal choices. Authors need a way to create high-quality visualizations without manually tuning low-level parameters like scales, axes, and formatting.
AI.method: Flint introduces a hierarchical data semantic model where users structurally specify the meanings of data fields. The compiler uses these semantic specifications to derive and optimize appropriate visualization configurations in a library-agnostic intermediate representation, then translates them into complete executable specifications for multiple target grammars (Vega-Lite, Apache ECharts, Chart.js).
AI.result: Flint simplifies the visualization authoring process without compromising visual quality, and serves as an effective intermediate language for both human authors and AI agents to create visualizations.
AI.conclusion: Flint demonstrates that semantics-driven, compiler-based generation of visualization configurations is a viable and effective approach, bridging the gap between concise high-level intent and high-quality, multi-target visualization output.

title: FedAgentKE: Federated Semantic Knowledge Evolution for Heterogeneous Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly rely on reasoning, tool use, and iterative execution, yet existing agent frameworks still operate largely in isolation. While recent memory-based agent systems improve individual agents through local retrieval and workflow reuse, local experiences remain fragmented across isolated agent frameworks, limiting cross-framework knowledge transfer and collaborative reasoning evolution. We propose FedAgentKE, a lightweight framework for Federated Semantic Knowledge Evolution across heterogeneous agents. FedAgentKE enables distributed agent frameworks to collaboratively evolve transferable reasoning abstractions through iterative semantic knowledge distillation, aggregation, and adaptation without sharing raw reasoning trajectories. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements under both cross-framework and cross-task settings, highlighting the potential of federated semantic knowledge evolution for future collaborative agent ecosystems.

AI.tldr: FedAgentKE proposes a federated framework enabling heterogeneous LLM-based agents to collaboratively evolve transferable reasoning knowledge through semantic distillation and aggregation, without sharing raw reasoning trajectories, achieving consistent cross-framework and cross-task improvements.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based agent systems operate in isolation, with local experiences fragmented across heterogeneous frameworks. While memory-based systems allow individual agents to improve via local retrieval and workflow reuse, there is no mechanism for cross-framework knowledge transfer or collaborative reasoning evolution, limiting the collective intelligence of multi-agent ecosystems.
AI.method: FedAgentKE introduces a lightweight federated semantic knowledge evolution framework with three core operations: (1) iterative semantic knowledge distillation — extracting abstract, transferable reasoning patterns from agent experiences; (2) federated aggregation — merging distilled knowledge across distributed heterogeneous agent frameworks without sharing raw reasoning data; and (3) adaptation — enabling individual agents to incorporate aggregated knowledge into their local reasoning processes.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate consistent performance improvements under both cross-framework (different agent architectures) and cross-task (different downstream tasks) settings, validating the effectiveness of federated semantic knowledge evolution.
AI.conclusion: Federated semantic knowledge evolution is a promising direction for building collaborative agent ecosystems, enabling heterogeneous agents to benefit from collective reasoning experiences while preserving data privacy and framework independence.

title: AuthProbe: Specification-Driven, Multi-Identity Detection of Broken Object-Level Authorization in Recruitment API
summary: Broken Object-Level Authorization (BOLA), also known as Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR), has topped the OWASP API Security ranking since 2019 and is the root cause of some of the largest exposures of applicant data in recruitment technology. The defining feature of this flaw class is that a malicious request is byte-for-byte indistinguishable from a legitimate one, which is precisely why web application firewalls and single identity scanners fail to catch it. We present AuthProbe, an open-source, black-box scanner that detects BOLA and IDOR in HTTP APIs by driving its tests from an OpenAPI specification and by acting under two or more identities that the operator controls. AuthProbe discovers, for each identity, the objects that identity legitimately owns, then attempts to read one identity's objects while authenticated as another and confirms a leak by comparing the response against a ground-truth fetch by the true owner. It also walks predictable identifiers to expose enumeration and reports missing authentication and existence oracles. The tool returns a severity-thresholded exit code and machine-readable reports so that it can gate a continuous integration build. On a synthetic recruitment API in which the McHire failure class is reproduced, AuthProbe detects every planted cross-identity read with no false positives on a hardened counterpart, and its running time grows linearly with the number of objects under test. AuthProbe is released under the Apache 2.0 license with an authorized-use guardrail.

AI.tldr: AuthProbe is an open-source black-box scanner that detects BOLA/IDOR vulnerabilities in HTTP APIs by using multiple identities to test cross-identity object access, driven by OpenAPI specifications. It identifies leaks by comparing responses against ground-truth fetches, handles predictable identifiers for enumeration attacks, and outputs machine-readable reports suitable for CI/CD gating.
AI.motivation: BOLA/IDOR has been the top API security risk since 2019 and has caused major data exposures in recruitment systems. The core challenge is that malicious requests are byte-for-byte identical to legitimate ones, rendering WAFs and single-identity scanners ineffective. No existing black-box tool adequately addresses this detection gap.
AI.method: AuthProbe operates as a black-box scanner guided by an OpenAPI specification. It uses two or more operator-controlled identities to: (1) discover objects each identity legitimately owns; (2) attempt cross-identity reads (accessing one identity's objects while authenticated as another); (3) confirm leaks by comparing responses against a ground-truth fetch by the true owner; (4) walk predictable identifiers to detect enumeration vulnerabilities; and (5) report missing authentication and existence oracles. The tool produces severity-thresholded exit codes and machine-readable reports.
AI.result: On a synthetic recruitment API reproducing the McHire failure class, AuthProbe detected every planted cross-identity read with zero false positives on a hardened counterpart. Its runtime scales linearly with the number of objects under test.
AI.conclusion: AuthProbe provides an effective, practical solution for detecting BOLA/IDOR vulnerabilities in CI/CD pipelines. Released under Apache 2.0 with an authorized-use guardrail, it addresses a critical gap left by WAFs and single-identity scanners.

title: Knowledge Injection Exists in MoE? Exploring Expert-Aware Contrast Decoding in MoE for Mitigating LLMs'Hallucinations
summary: Existing LLM hallucination mitigation methods, including prompt engineering and model optimization, either hardly alter models'internal knowledge or have poor cross-domain generalization. Contrastive decoding mitigates hallucinations by using layer-wise differences in LLMs. However, prior studies only explore transformer-based models (e.g., GPT), ignoring other effective frameworks like mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. Since MoE alters the traditional transformer architecture, we conduct empirical studies to investigate whether similar layer-wise differences exist in MoEs. Our results show that they do not exist in MoE with shared experts; nevertheless, across different MoEs, higher layers exhibit distinct expert activation patterns between factual and non-factual outputs. Building on these, we propose EAACD, an expert-aware adaptive contrast decoding that uses expert differences in MoE's higher layers to mitigate hallucinations on QA tasks. EAACD splits high-layer experts into a higher-reliability group and several lower-reliability groups based on their confidence and consistency. It contrasts the higher-reliability group's prediction with each lower-reliability group's prediction to calibrate the model's original predictions. To strengthen this contrast, EAACD amplifies hallucinations from lower-reliability experts via attention and masking to provide stronger negative references. EAACD outperforms all baselines on four datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes EAACD, an expert-aware adaptive contrastive decoding method for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs that mitigates hallucinations by contrasting predictions from high-reliability expert groups against lower-reliability groups, outperforming existing baselines on QA tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing hallucination mitigation methods (prompt engineering, model optimization) either fail to alter models' internal knowledge or lack cross-domain generalization. Contrastive decoding shows promise using layer-wise differences, but prior work only studies transformer-based models (e.g., GPT), ignoring MoE architectures. The authors empirically find that MoEs with shared experts lack the layer-wise differences seen in dense transformers, motivating a new expert-level contrastive approach.
AI.method: EAACD operates in two stages: (1) Expert grouping — high-layer MoE experts are partitioned into one higher-reliability group and several lower-reliability groups based on confidence and consistency metrics evaluated on factual vs. non-factual outputs. (2) Adaptive contrastive decoding — the higher-reliability group's prediction is contrasted against each lower-reliability group's prediction to calibrate the original output distribution. Hallucinations from lower-reliability experts are further amplified via attention and masking to provide stronger negative references for contrast.
AI.result: EAACD outperforms all baselines across four QA datasets, demonstrating effective hallucination mitigation in MoE-based LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Expert activation patterns in higher layers of MoE models can be exploited for contrastive decoding to reduce hallucinations. EAACD validates that expert-level, rather than layer-level, contrast is the appropriate granularity for MoE architectures, and that adaptive amplification of unreliable expert outputs strengthens the calibration signal.

title: PhantomFill: When the Form Demands an Answer, Language Models Invent One
summary:
Language models in production do not write prose. They fill forms: JSON fields, function arguments, extraction templates. We show that the form itself causes hallucination.
  We ask thirteen models the same question about the same input and change only the answer format. The inputs are built so the question cannot be answered: a viral post showing 12,400 likes but no visible replies, a support ticket whose call was never transcribed. In free text, GPT-5.5 answers honestly. It says there is no reply data, 98% of the time. Given a required JSON field for sentiment, the same model invents an answer 40 times out of 40. It fabricates the mood of crowds it never saw and quotes customers it never heard.
  The pattern holds with force. Required fields drive fabrication to 100% in ten of thirteen models. An explicit "insufficient evidence" option rescues only the frontier: all nine open-weight models ignore it. A direct instruction, do not infer sentiment, is overridden by the schema in four of six models. Resistance does not come with scale: within a single model family, the smallest model refuses, the mid-sized model fabricates, the largest refuses again. Honesty under format pressure is a training outcome that no one is measuring.
  The fabrication hides exactly where hedging is impossible: in required enums and minimum-count arrays, fields where no disclaimer fits. We release PhantomFill, a benchmark with deterministic scoring and two reportable numbers: the Coerced Fabrication Rate and the Escape Utilization Rate. The fix we test is one line of schema. The failure we measure is everywhere.

AI.tldr: Language models hallucinate significantly more when constrained by structured output formats (JSON, enums, required fields) compared to free-text generation. In a benchmark of 13 models, required fields drove fabrication rates to 100% in 10 models, with even explicit "insufficient evidence" options and anti-inference instructions being overridden by schema constraints.
AI.motivation: Production language models predominantly output structured formats (JSON fields, function arguments, extraction templates) rather than free prose, yet no prior work systematically measures how the output format itself induces hallucination. The authors aim to quantify and expose this phenomenon.
AI.method: The authors design queries where ground-truth answers are unknowable (e.g., viral post with no visible replies, untranscribed support calls) and ask 13 models the same question under varying output format constraints: free text, required JSON fields, required enums, minimum-count arrays, and optional fields with explicit "insufficient evidence" choices. They introduce PhantomFill, a benchmark with two metrics: the Coerced Fabrication Rate and the Escape Utilization Rate.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Required fields drove fabrication to 100% in 10 of 13 models; (2) GPT-5.5 answered honestly 98% of the time in free text but fabricated 40/40 times with a required JSON sentiment field; (3) An explicit "insufficient evidence" option was ignored by all 9 open-weight models; (4) Direct instructions not to infer sentiment were overridden by schema in 4 of 6 models; (5) Within a single model family, resistance followed a U-shaped pattern (small refuses, mid fabricates, large refuses), indicating it is a training outcome rather than a scaling law.
AI.conclusion: Schema-induced hallucination is pervasive and under-measured. The fix is simple (one line of schema with an escape option), but current models largely fail to use escape mechanisms. Honesty under format pressure is a distinct training outcome that should be explicitly measured and optimized for, separate from general hallucination benchmarks.

title: Marking the Wrong Symptoms: Evaluating LLM Watermarks in Medical Texts
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into clinical workflows, stressing the need for reliable traceability of model-generated output with watermarking. Yet, most watermarks are evaluated on general-purpose benchmarks, leaving domains like medicine, where small token-level perturbations can result in significant semantic changes, underexplored. In this work, we present the first rigorous study of how LLM watermarks affect medical performance, benchmarking 5 watermarking schemes across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs on various tasks spanning unimodal and multimodal clinical reasoning. Importantly, we complement existing evaluations by introducing a human-expert-validated pipeline for systematically auditing medical reasoning quality, terminological precision, and induced hallucinations. Our results reveal that watermarking can induce substantial degradation across multiple failure modes, including lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, and amplified misattribution or omission of image findings. Notably, we find that the absence of domain-specific analyses, combined with aggregate metrics that miss failures inherent to clinical text, can systematically obscure practical watermark-induced degradations. Our findings establish domain-specific evaluation as a prerequisite for the safe deployment of watermarked models in medicine, where current benchmarks can otherwise mask clinically consequential failures.

AI.tldr: First rigorous study of watermarking's impact on medical LLM/VLM performance. Across 5 watermarking schemes, 11 LLMs, and 7 VLMs, watermarks cause lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, and misattribution of findings — degradations that aggregate metrics systematically obscure. Domain-specific clinical auditing is essential for safe deployment.
AI.motivation: LLMs are being integrated into clinical workflows, creating an urgent need for traceability via watermarking. However, existing watermark evaluations use general-purpose benchmarks and overlook medicine, where small token-level perturbations can cause clinically significant semantic errors. No prior work has rigorously assessed how watermarking affects medical reasoning quality.
AI.method: The authors benchmark 5 watermarking schemes (covering both text-only LLMs and multimodal VLMs) across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs on clinical reasoning tasks. They introduce a human-expert-validated auditing pipeline that systematically evaluates medical reasoning quality, terminological precision, and watermark-induced hallucinations — complementing standard aggregate metrics.
AI.result: Watermarking consistently degrades performance across multiple failure modes: lexical corruption of clinical terms, hallucinated medical terminology, and amplified misattribution or omission of image findings in multimodal settings. Aggregate metrics systematically mask these clinically consequential failures, which only become visible through domain-specific, expert-validated auditing.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation is a prerequisite for safe deployment of watermarked models in medicine. Current general-purpose benchmarks obscure watermark-induced degradations that carry real clinical risk, establishing the need for rigorous medical auditing before integrating watermarked LLMs/VLMs into clinical workflows.

title: SHIFT: Self-reconstruction Harnesses Implicit Fine-grained Thinking for Retrieval
summary: LLM-based retrievers have become a fundamental component of modern information retrieval systems. The paradigm of "rewrite-then-retriev" introduces explicit reasoning before retrieval. In addition, implicit-reasoning retrievers such as GIRCSE and LaSER improve efficiency by replacing explicit reasoning with soft tokens. Although these methods demonstrated competitive performance on reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks, they struggle to address the mismatch between the objectives of retrieval and generation. In this work, we propose SHIFT ($\textbf{S}$elf-reconstruction $\textbf{H}$arnesses $\textbf{I}$mplicit $\textbf{F}$ine-grained $\textbf{T}$hinking for Retrieval), a retrieval training framework based on LLMs. Firstly, we transfer LLMs into reasoning-efficient retrievers with residual projection and task-oriented bidirectional attention aggregation in the latent space. Secondly, we alleviate the mismatch between contrastive learning and implicit reasoning using fine-grained next-token-prediction-based reconstruction. Extensive experiments on reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks show that SHIFT consistently outperforms other widely used retrievers. We also carried out a detailed analysis to illustrate how our method works.

AI.tldr: SHIFT is an LLM-based retrieval framework that uses self-reconstruction with fine-grained next-token prediction to align implicit reasoning with contrastive learning objectives, outperforming existing retrievers on reasoning-intensive benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing "rewrite-then-retrieve" and implicit-reasoning retrievers (e.g., GIRCSE, LaSER) suffer from a mismatch between retrieval objectives (contrastive learning) and generation objectives, limiting their reasoning effectiveness in retrieval tasks.
AI.method: SHIFT transfers LLMs into retrievers via residual projection and task-oriented bidirectional attention aggregation in latent space, then mitigates the contrastive-implicit reasoning mismatch using fine-grained next-token-prediction-based self-reconstruction.
AI.result: SHIFT consistently outperforms widely used retrievers on reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks, with detailed analysis validating the mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Integrating fine-grained next-token-prediction-based reconstruction effectively bridges the gap between contrastive learning and implicit reasoning, yielding state-of-the-art retrieval performance on reasoning-heavy tasks.

title: Maintenance Signals in AI-Assisted GitHub Repositories: Evidence from GenAI Adopters
summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can reduce code-generation effort, but it may shift work to documentation, validation, debugging, and maintenance. We study observable maintenance-cost signals among GenAI adopters on GitHub by analyzing 622 users who publicly signal adoption, 179 repositories with visible AI-assistance configuration files, 179 matched traditional repositories, and 248 issues created in AI-assisted repositories. AI-assisted repositories span diverse project types and contain longer README files with more headers and code blocks, while traditional repositories contain more external URLs. Issues concerning GenAI technology often involve external dependencies, such as API rate limits and reliance on GenAI provider APIs. These findings suggest that AI assistance shifts maintenance costs toward verifying generated content, managing external AI dependencies, and validating AI-specific behavior.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 622 GitHub users and 179 AI-assisted repositories reveals that GenAI shifts maintenance burden from code generation toward documentation (longer READMEs with more headers/code blocks), managing external AI dependencies (API rate limits, provider APIs), and validating AI-generated content.
AI.motivation: While GenAI reduces code-generation effort, the authors hypothesize that it does not eliminate maintenance costs—it merely relocates them. The study aims to empirically identify observable signals of where these costs shift, focusing on documentation practices, repository structure, and issue-tracking patterns among GenAI adopters on GitHub.
AI.method: The authors conducted a large-scale empirical study on GitHub, analyzing four data sources: (1) 622 users who publicly signal GenAI adoption (e.g., via profile badges), (2) 179 repositories containing visible AI-assistance configuration files (e.g., .cursorrules, .github/copilot-instructions.md), (3) 179 matched traditional (non-AI) repositories serving as a control group, and (4) 248 issues extracted from AI-assisted repositories. Comparisons focused on README structure, external URL usage, and issue content categorization.
AI.result: AI-assisted repositories span diverse project types. Their README files are significantly longer, containing more headers and code blocks, while traditional repositories include more external URLs. Issues in AI-assisted repositories frequently involve external GenAI dependencies, particularly API rate limits and reliance on third-party GenAI provider APIs.
AI.conclusion: GenAI adoption shifts maintenance effort toward three distinct areas: verifying and documenting AI-generated content, managing external dependencies on GenAI APIs, and validating AI-specific behavior. This suggests that code-generation savings may be partially offset by new categories of maintenance overhead.

title: Sonic Stage: Automatically Generating Interactive Spatial Soundscapes to Facilitate Dialogue Video Comprehension for Blind Viewers
summary: Audio description (AD) makes film and television accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) audiences by narrating characters' actions. However, in scenes with lots of dialogue, AD often omits important actions because it is constrained not to overlap with speech. It is not yet known how to convey characters' actions during dialogue. We present Sonic Stage, a system that transforms dialogue videos into interactive spatial soundscapes, enabling BLV audiences to intuitively understand characters' actions and movements through immersive auditory cues. Sonic Stage conveys essential visual information during dialogue through three auditory techniques: (1) spatialized dialogue to represent spatial layout, (2) diegetic sound to convey character actions, and (3) interactive descriptions to provide context-specific visual details. Evaluation with 12 BLV viewers showed that Sonic Stage significantly improved video comprehension, spatial presence, and narrative engagement. We highlight opportunities for enhancing video accessibility across diverse genres through immersive, interactive audio representations.

AI.tldr: Sonic Stage transforms dialogue-heavy videos into interactive spatial soundscapes using spatialized dialogue, diegetic sound, and interactive descriptions, enabling BLV audiences to perceive characters' actions and spatial layout without overlapping speech. Evaluation with 12 BLV viewers showed significant improvements in comprehension, spatial presence, and engagement.
AI.motivation: Traditional audio description (AD) is constrained by dialogue, forcing omission of important visual actions in speech-heavy scenes. No existing solution adequately conveys characters' actions during ongoing dialogue, leaving a critical accessibility gap for BLV audiences.
AI.method: Sonic Stage employs three auditory techniques: (1) spatialized dialogue — positioning character speech in a 3D audio field to represent spatial layout; (2) diegetic sound — using in-scene sound effects to convey character actions non-verbally; and (3) interactive descriptions — on-demand, context-specific visual details that users can access without interrupting dialogue flow. These are combined into an interactive spatial soundscape system.
AI.result: A user study with 12 BLV participants demonstrated that Sonic Stage significantly improved video comprehension, spatial presence, and narrative engagement compared to baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: Immersive, interactive audio representations offer a promising direction for enhancing video accessibility across diverse genres, overcoming the fundamental limitation of traditional AD in dialogue-dense content.

title: ChannelGuard: Safe Models Do Not Compose into Safe Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent LLM applications chain a planner, worker agents, a verifier, and a synthesizer, and every hop between agents is an unmonitored channel through which an adversary can smuggle instructions. Existing defenses guard only the input boundary (IBProtector, Llama Guard, perplexity filters, SmoothLLM) or run outside the application as opaque, stochastic provider-side filters. We show this gap carries a consequence rarely measured: on a 2,100-trace evaluation across eight attack families, five defenses, and three model backends, an undefended pipeline that appears fully safe under standard reporting (attack success 0.000 on tool- and memory-poisoning) owes that safety almost entirely to the cloud provider's server-side filter (54 of 60 blocks on Azure GPT-5), and silently shifts to the agent model's own alignment on a backend without such a filter. Outcome-only reporting hides this dependence. We present ChannelGuard, a training-free defense-in-depth framework placing information-bottleneck gates on every inter-agent channel; each scores channel text against an adversarial phrase bank by embedding similarity and deterministically passes, compresses, or blocks it, adding no LLM call, while an attribution method records which layer stopped each attack. ChannelGuard's tool-output gate blocks Tool Poisoning 30 of 30 at the application layer, identically across Azure GPT-5, Anthropic Sonnet 4.5, and Anthropic Haiku 4.5, whereas the undefended pipeline shifts entirely across backends; it also lowers Prompt Injection attack success by half (0.333 to 0.167) and preserves GSM8K accuracy exactly (0.867). White-box adaptive paraphrase evades every embedding gate, where a perturb-and-vote baseline does better. An extended appendix adds baselines, ablations, sweeps, a benign-preservation analysis, and a judge audit (kappa = 0.900), at a total cost of 47.36 USD.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent LLM pipelines are vulnerable to adversarial instruction smuggling through unmonitored inter-agent channels. Existing defenses focus only on input boundaries or use opaque server-side filters, creating a hidden dependence on provider-side protection. ChannelGuard introduces training-free information-bottleneck gates on every inter-agent channel, using embedding similarity against an adversarial phrase bank to pass, compress, or block content without additional LLM calls, effectively neutralizing tool poisoning across backends and reducing prompt injection success while preserving task accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing defenses for multi-agent LLM applications guard only the input boundary or operate as opaque server-side filters, leaving inter-agent channels unmonitored. The authors demonstrate that apparent safety in undefended pipelines often depends entirely on cloud provider server-side filters, which standard reporting (outcome-only metrics) conceals. This gap means the safety profile silently shifts when the backend changes, necessitating application-layer defense-in-depth.
AI.method: ChannelGuard places information-bottleneck gates on every channel between agents (planner, worker, verifier, synthesizer). Each gate scores channel text against an adversarial phrase bank using embedding similarity and deterministically passes, compresses, or blocks it — adding no LLM call overhead. An attribution method records which layer stopped each attack. The approach is training-free. Evaluated across 2,100 traces, eight attack families, five defenses, and three model backends (Azure GPT-5, Anthropic Sonnet 4.5, Anthropic Haiku 4.5), with a white-box adaptive paraphrase attack tested against the embedding gate and a perturb-and-vote baseline.
AI.result: ChannelGuard's tool-output gate blocks Tool Poisoning 30/30 at the application layer identically across all three backends, while the undefended pipeline shifts entirely across backends (54 of 60 blocks owed to Azure's server-side filter). Prompt Injection attack success is halved (0.333 → 0.167). GSM8K accuracy is preserved exactly (0.867). White-box adaptive paraphrasing evades every embedding gate; a perturb-and-vote baseline performs better against this attack. Judge audit shows kappa = 0.900. Total evaluation cost: $47.36 USD.
AI.conclusion: Defense-in-depth with inter-agent channel gating is both necessary and feasible: it removes hidden dependence on provider-side filters, delivers consistent protection across model backends, and preserves task accuracy. Embedding-based gates are effective against known attacks but remain vulnerable to white-box adaptive paraphrasing, where voting-based approaches offer better robustness.

title: Deepfake News Detection: A Multimodal Framework Integrating LipNet, DeepSpeech and ResNET for Enhanced Audio-Visual Analysis
summary: Deepfake news refers to AI-generated (or AI ma-nipulated) multimedia content intentionally generated to deceive audiences by manipulating the facial expressions, or speech while maintaining the realistic appearance. The rapid progress of generative AI has made the synthesis of highly realistic fake videos and cloned voices widely accessible, posing a serious threat to the authenticity of digital news media. This paper presents a multi-modal framework that discerns the authenticity of video content by jointly exploiting audio and visual cues, thereby addressing the challenge of detecting the deepfake videos. We proposed a framework that involves features extraction from lip movements, audio content and video frames. Lip movements and speech content are encoded using the LipNet and DeepSpeech2 models, while facial features are extracted by leveraging the use of BlazeFace and represented with ResNet18. The extracted feature vectors are concatenated into a holistic video representation and classified with an ensemble of machine learning and deep learning models, including Random Forest (RF), Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Exten-sive experiments performed on the FakeAVCeleb dataset shows that the proposed approach attains an accuracy of 94% using augmented audio features, outperforming a state-of-the-art multi-modal ensemble baseline. The results confirm the robustness and practical potential of the proposed framework for deepfake news detection.

AI.tldr: A multi-modal deepfake detection framework combining lip movement, audio, and facial features achieves 94% accuracy on FakeAVCeleb, outperforming existing baselines.
