AI.motivation: Generative AI has made realistic deepfake videos widely accessible, threatening digital news authenticity. Existing detection methods may be insufficient, motivating a multi-modal approach that jointly exploits audio-visual cues for more robust detection.
AI.method: A three-stream framework: (1) Lip movements encoded via LipNet, (2) audio content processed through DeepSpeech2, and (3) facial features extracted using BlazeFace and represented with ResNet18. Feature vectors are concatenated into a holistic representation, then classified using an ensemble of Random Forest, MLP, and LSTM networks. Audio augmentation is additionally applied.
AI.result: 94% accuracy on the FakeAVCeleb dataset with augmented audio features, outperforming a state-of-the-art multi-modal ensemble baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-modal framework demonstrates robustness and practical potential for deepfake news detection, with audio augmentation further boosting performance.

title: Is MoE Routing a Huffman Code? Discovering the Frequency-Diversity Law in Chain-of-Thought
summary: Mixture-of-Experts architectures have revolutionized scaling, yet the underlying logic of their routing remains a black box. In this paper, we uncover a fundamental governing principle: MoE routing is not merely selection, but a manifestation of Huffman Coding. We introduce the Frequency-Diversity Law, revealing that state-of-the-art models, such as Phi-3.5-MoE and Gemma-4-27B-A4B, spontaneously act as information-theoretic engines. These models allocate sparse expert resources for common tokens while invoking high-diversity expert committees for rare, complex tasks found in chain-of-thought trajectories. However, we identify a critical redundancy trap in Qwen3.5-35B-A3B: when effective sparsity (k/E_eff) is sufficiently low, load-balancing inadvertently imposes functional redundancy, masking the underlying Huffman efficiency signal. To bridge this gap, we propose Subset Difference Pruning, a surgical strategy to eliminate functional duplicates. We demonstrate that pruning does not degrade reasoning; instead, it unleashes the model's latent Huffman efficiency, forcing the logic to collapse into streamlined, high-density paths. Our findings suggest that the next generation of MoEs should move beyond forced load-balancing toward Minimum Description Length (MDL) optimality, assigning shorter expert-routing codes to high-frequency information and longer, more diverse codes to low-frequency information, thereby transforming routing from a heuristic into a principled compression engine.

AI.tldr: MoE routing is shown to be a manifestation of Huffman coding, where models spontaneously allocate sparse experts to common tokens and diverse expert committees to rare ones. A redundancy trap from load-balancing is identified in Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, and Subset Difference Pruning is proposed to eliminate functional duplicates, unleashing latent Huffman efficiency without degrading reasoning.
AI.motivation: The routing mechanism in Mixture-of-Experts architectures remains poorly understood, operating as a black box. The authors aim to uncover the fundamental information-theoretic principles governing expert routing, moving beyond viewing it as mere token-expert selection.
AI.method: The paper introduces the Frequency-Diversity Law — an information-theoretic framework showing MoE routing embodies Huffman coding principles. The authors then propose Subset Difference Pruning, a surgical pruning strategy that identifies and removes functionally duplicated experts that arise when load-balancing constraints force redundancy at low effective sparsity (k/E_eff). This pruning exposes the model's latent Huffman efficiency.
AI.result: State-of-the-art models (Phi-3.5-MoE, Gemma-4-27B-A4B) spontaneously exhibit Huffman coding behavior: sparse expert allocation for frequent tokens, diverse expert committees for rare/complex tokens. A redundancy trap was discovered in Qwen3.5-35B-A3B where load-balancing imposes functional redundancy. Pruning eliminates these duplicates without degrading reasoning performance, instead collapsing routing into streamlined, high-density paths.
AI.conclusion: Future MoE designs should move beyond forced load-balancing toward Minimum Description Length (MDL) optimality — assigning short routing codes to high-frequency information and longer, diverse codes to low-frequency information — transforming routing from a heuristic into a principled compression engine.

title: The Active Ingredient in Muon's Grokking
summary: The Muon optimizer reaches the grokking threshold on modular arithmetic faster than AdamW. Prior work attributes this to "spectral-norm constraints plus orthogonalized momentum" but does not isolate which mechanism matters. To better understand Moun's behavior, we run multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps to decompose and stress-test the effect. First, an ablation shows the speedup comes from orthogonalization (the Newton-Schulz iteration): orthogonalize-only matches full Muon, whereas spectral-only is no faster than AdamW and is unreliable, and this verdict holds across learning rates. Second, a mechanistic analysis finds that orthogonalizing optimizers reach generalization at roughly 3x lower spectral norm and, controlling for how much the embedding actually moves, settle into a lower-norm solution rather than simply perturbing the embedding less. Third, reducing the Newton-Schulz iteration count from five to one accelerates reaching the threshold but makes the grokked solution fragile, prone to transient collapse, with fragility that grows with learning rate; a single iteration is fast and stable only at small learning rate, while the canonical five iterations are the learning-rate-robust choice. We also show spectral scaling can be dropped at no measured cost. A methodological thread runs throughout: under a stability-aware metric, "faster" claims about grokking optimizers can invert, so we report both first-crossing and sustained-grok times. To support reproducibility, we release our full training and analysis code at https://github.com/louiswang524/muon-grokking-frontier

AI.tldr: Muon optimizer's grokking speed advantage over AdamW comes from momentum orthogonalization (Newton-Schulz), not spectral normalization. Ablations show orthogonalize-only matches full Muon, while spectral-only is unreliable. Orthogonalized optimizers reach generalization at ~3x lower spectral norm. Reducing Newton-Schulz iterations from 5 to 1 accelerates initial grokking but causes fragile, collapse-prone solutions — 5 iterations is the learning-rate-robust choice. Spectral scaling can be dropped at no cost. The paper advocates reporting both first-crossing and sustained-grok times, as "faster" claims can invert under stability-aware metrics.
AI.motivation: Prior work attributes Muon's grokking advantage to "spectral-norm constraints plus orthogonalized momentum" but fails to isolate which mechanism actually drives the speedup. The paper aims to decompose and stress-test these two components to determine the true causal factor.
AI.method: Multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps on modular arithmetic grokking tasks. Ablation study comparing full Muon, orthogonalize-only, and spectral-only variants. Mechanistic analysis of spectral norm dynamics and embedding movement. Sensitivity analysis varying Newton-Schulz iteration counts (1–5) across learning rates. Introduction of stability-aware evaluation metrics (first-crossing vs. sustained-grok times).
AI.result: (1) Orthogonalization alone matches full Muon; spectral-only performs no better than AdamW and is unreliable. (2) Orthogonalized optimizers achieve generalization at ~3x lower spectral norm and settle into lower-norm solutions. (3) Reducing Newton-Schulz iterations from 5 to 1 speeds up initial threshold crossing but introduces fragile, transiently collapsing solutions, with fragility increasing with learning rate; 5 iterations are learning-rate-robust. (4) Spectral scaling can be removed at no measured cost. (5) "Faster" grokking claims can invert depending on whether one measures first-crossing or sustained-grok time.
AI.conclusion: Momentum orthogonalization, not spectral normalization, is the critical mechanism behind Muon's grokking speedup. Five Newton-Schulz iterations provide the best robustness across learning rates. Researchers should adopt stability-aware metrics (both first-crossing and sustained-grok times) to avoid misleading claims about optimizer speed. Code is released for reproducibility.

title: ClickGuard: Detecting and Spoiling Clickbait News with Informativeness Measures and Large Language Models
summary: This paper presents an AI-driven browser extension that identifies clickbait to help users avoid misleading Internet articles. Moving beyond traditional detection, the application employs a hybrid machine learning architecture that combines transformer-based embeddings with linguistically motivated features and a custom "baitness" score. After evaluating various natural language processing techniques -- from classic vectorizers to large language model (LLM) embeddings -- an XGBoost-based model was developed that achieves an F1-score of 91% on the open combined dataset. Most importantly, the tool can warn users before and after they access a clickbait article. After opening an article, the user receives a percentage score indicating the likelihood that it is clickbait. The prediction is explained based on the analyzed metrics, including those specifically developed within the proposed system. The browser extension also provides a clickbait spoiler -- a one- to two-sentence summary of the entire article. Demo video:https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJ1gkQV82C4}{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJ1gkQV82C4

AI.tldr: An AI-driven browser extension using hybrid ML (XGBoost + transformer embeddings + linguistic features) detects clickbait with 91% F1-score, warns users pre/post access, provides a "baitness" percentage with explanations, and generates a concise article spoiler.
AI.motivation: To help users avoid misleading clickbait articles on the Internet by moving beyond traditional detection to a practical, explainable, real-time browser tool.
AI.method: A hybrid machine learning architecture combining transformer-based embeddings, linguistically motivated features, and a custom "baitness" score. Various NLP techniques (classic vectorizers to LLM embeddings) were evaluated; the final model uses XGBoost trained on an open combined dataset. The system is deployed as a browser extension with pre- and post-access warnings, prediction explanations, and a clickbait spoiler (1–2 sentence summary).
AI.result: The XGBoost-based model achieved an F1-score of 91% on the open combined dataset. The browser extension successfully warns users before and after accessing clickbait, displays a percentage likelihood score, explains predictions via analyzed metrics, and generates article spoilers.
AI.conclusion: The proposed system effectively bridges clickbait detection research and practical user-facing application, offering real-time, explainable detection with summarization capabilities in a browser extension format.

title: Diffusion Language Model for Recommendation
summary: Large language model (LLM)-empowered recommender systems have emerged as a promising paradigm for generative recommendation, leveraging their strong semantic reasoning and generative capacity to model complex, diverse user preferences. However, most existing approaches rely on an autoregressive paradigm that is suboptimal for recommendation. The next-token objective emphasizes sequential order rather than the structural inter-item dependencies underlying user preferences. In addition, prefix-constrained generation restricts bidirectional context and commits to left-to-right decoding, causing early errors to accumulate without correction. Inspired by the success of diffusion language models, we propose \textbf{DLMRec}, a discrete diffusion language model tailored for recommendation that offers a compelling alternative to autoregressive generation. Specifically, DLMRec introduces three key components to bridge diffusion language modeling with recommendation. First, a collaborative-aware stochastic tokenizer encodes multi-hop collaborative signals into expressive discrete tokens compatible with diffusion modeling. Second, a curriculum-driven training strategy aligns the denoising process with preference recovery through progressive item- and token-level learning. Third, a stability-aware voting mechanism aggregates iterative predictions to improve generation consistency and robustness.

AI.tldr: DLMRec proposes a discrete diffusion language model for recommendation, replacing autoregressive generation with a diffusion-based paradigm that better captures structural inter-item dependencies. It introduces a collaborative-aware tokenizer, curriculum-driven training, and stability-aware voting to improve recommendation generation.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive LLM-based recommenders suffer from two key limitations: (1) the next-token objective prioritizes sequential order over structural inter-item dependencies that reflect true user preferences, and (2) left-to-right prefix-constrained decoding causes error accumulation without bidirectional correction. Diffusion language models offer a promising alternative by enabling non-autoregressive, iterative refinement.
AI.method: DLMRec comprises three components: (1) a collaborative-aware stochastic tokenizer that encodes multi-hop collaborative signals into discrete tokens for diffusion modeling; (2) a curriculum-driven training strategy that progressively aligns the denoising process with preference recovery at both item and token levels; and (3) a stability-aware voting mechanism that aggregates iterative predictions to enhance generation consistency and robustness.
AI.result: Not specified in the provided abstract.
AI.conclusion: Not explicitly stated in the provided abstract; the paper positions DLMRec as a compelling alternative to autoregressive generation for LLM-empowered recommendation.

title: Improving Communication of Changes in Model-Based Engineering with Model-Independent Change Descriptions
summary: In model-based engineering, inter-disciplinary teams collaborate through models, which change over time for purposes of system development, what makes the proper description of such changes crucial for engineers. However, any change made by the engineer of one discipline will be difficult to understand by the engineers of other disciplines. To overcome this limitation, model-independent change descriptions can be derived instead, which preserve semantics of the changes and do not require model-specific knowledge. The two opposing approaches here are to describe changes using either informal language or formal notions of change. While informal language lacks objectivity and standardisation, formal notions of change lack human interpretability, and thus offering no support for inter-disciplinary communication. In this paper, we propose functions to map formally specified changes, represented in the approach of delta modelling, to change descriptions in model-independent language. In an exhaustive mixed-methods evaluation, we bridge the gap between the theoretical and the practical representation of changes. We quantitatively assess technical feasibility, with an implementation framework, and technical applicability, along a case study; and we qualitatively assess plausibility, practical applicability, and extensibility, in a user study. Our work shows a promising starting point for automated, model-independent description of changes in model-based engineering projects.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a mapping from formally specified model changes (delta modelling) to human-readable, model-independent change descriptions, bridging the gap between formal rigour and interdisciplinary communication. A mixed-methods evaluation combining quantitative (implementation, case study) and qualitative (user study) assessments demonstrates the feasibility and promise of automated, model-independent change description.
AI.motivation: In model-based engineering, cross-disciplinary teams struggle to understand changes made by engineers from other disciplines. Model-independent change descriptions can help, but existing approaches fall short: informal language lacks objectivity and standardisation, while formal change notations lack human interpretability — thus neither supports effective inter-disciplinary communication.
AI.method: The authors propose functions to map formally specified changes (using delta modelling) to model-independent natural-language change descriptions. They conduct an exhaustive mixed-methods evaluation: quantitative assessment of technical feasibility via an implementation framework, technical applicability through a case study, and qualitative assessment of plausibility, practical applicability, and extensibility via a user study.
AI.result: The implementation framework and case study confirm technical feasibility and applicability. The user study demonstrates plausibility, practical applicability, and extensibility of the approach. Overall, the work provides a promising starting point for automated, model-independent description of changes in model-based engineering projects.
AI.conclusion: Automated mapping from formally specified model changes to model-independent, human-interpretable descriptions is technically feasible and practically beneficial for interdisciplinary communication in model-based engineering. The approach successfully bridges the gap between formal rigour and practical usability.

title: Exploring the Design Space of LLM-Based Programming Support in CS Education: A Scoping Review through the Lens of Assistance Governance
summary: As large language models (LLMs) become integrated into programming education, learner-facing systems increasingly differ in how that assistance is bounded, enacted, and controlled. These governance decisions are often described implicitly, making it difficult to compare systems in educationally meaningful ways. To address this gap, we conduct a scoping review and qualitative synthesis of 90 peer-reviewed LLM-based programming support systems in CS education. We analyze assistance governance through three dimensions, which we refer to collectively as PEA: Policy, capturing what forms of help are allowed or restricted; Enforcement, capturing how those boundaries are operationalized through interaction and system behavior; and Authority, capturing who can configure, adapt, or override them during use. Our findings show that systems often share similar pedagogical goals, but implement those goals through varied enforcement mechanisms. At the same time, authority remains highly centralized in system logic, with fewer systems giving learners or instructors runtime control. This work contributes PEA as a three-dimensional analytic lens, a governance codebook empirically refined within these dimensions, and a map of underexplored configurations in the current design space of LLM-based programming support. By making these explicit and comparable, PEA offers a vocabulary for analyzing existing systems and designing future tools that are pedagogically bounded, configurable, and accountable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PEA (Policy, Enforcement, Authority), a three-dimensional framework for analyzing how LLM-based programming support systems govern learner assistance. Through a scoping review of 90 systems, it reveals that while pedagogical goals are shared, enforcement mechanisms vary widely and authority remains largely centralized in system logic rather than distributed to learners or instructors.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly integrated into programming education, learner-facing systems differ in how assistance is bounded, enacted, and controlled. These governance decisions are typically described implicitly, making it difficult to compare systems in educationally meaningful ways. The paper addresses this gap by providing an explicit, comparable vocabulary for analyzing governance.
AI.method: The authors conducted a scoping review and qualitative synthesis of 90 peer-reviewed LLM-based programming support systems in CS education. They developed the PEA framework — three dimensions: Policy (what help is allowed/restricted), Enforcement (how boundaries are operationalized through interaction), and Authority (who configures/adapts/overrides boundaries) — and refined an associated governance codebook through empirical analysis of the reviewed systems.
AI.result: Systems often share similar pedagogical goals but implement them through varied enforcement mechanisms. Authority remains highly centralized in system logic, with relatively few systems granting learners or instructors runtime control. The analysis also identifies underexplored configurations in the design space.
AI.conclusion: PEA provides a three-dimensional analytic lens and governance codebook that makes assistance governance explicit and comparable. It offers a vocabulary for analyzing existing systems and designing future tools that are pedagogically bounded, configurable, and accountable.

title: Human-in-the-Loop Large Language Model Framework for Identification of Cutaneous Immune-Related Adverse Events
summary: This study evaluated a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent large language model (LLM)-driven, human-in-the-loop framework for detecting cutaneous immune-related adverse events (cirAEs) from clinical notes. Compared with unassisted manual review, the LLM-assisted workflow improved accuracy (F1 = 0.88 vs 0.77), inter-rater agreement measured by Cohen's kappa (kappa = 0.82 vs 0.50), and reduced average review time by approximately half. This framework pilots how LLMs can be applied to identify immune-related toxicities across organ systems and, more broadly, enable accurate, scalable, and transparent adverse event data extraction.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent LLM framework with human-in-the-loop review improved accuracy (F1: 0.88 vs 0.77), inter-rater agreement (κ: 0.82 vs 0.50), and halved review time for detecting cutaneous immune-related adverse events from clinical notes compared to manual review.
AI.motivation: Manual extraction of adverse events from clinical notes is time-consuming, inconsistent, and poorly scalable. The authors sought to determine whether an LLM-driven, retrieval-augmented, multi-agent framework with human oversight could improve the accuracy, reliability, and efficiency of identifying cutaneous immune-related adverse events (cirAEs), serving as a pilot for broader immune-related toxicity detection across organ systems.
AI.method: A retrieval-augmented, multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework was deployed in a human-in-the-loop workflow to detect cirAEs from clinical notes. Performance was compared against unassisted manual review on metrics of accuracy (F1 score), inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa), and average review time.
AI.result: The LLM-assisted workflow achieved: (1) improved F1 score (0.88 vs 0.77), (2) improved inter-rater agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.82 vs 0.50), and (3) approximately 50% reduction in average review time compared to unassisted manual review.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates that LLM-driven, human-in-the-loop systems can enable accurate, scalable, and transparent extraction of immune-related adverse events from clinical text. This pilot supports broader application to toxicity detection across organ systems and other adverse event data extraction tasks.

title: Geometric Configurations of Perturbed Jailbreak Prompts
comment: 21 pages, 9 figures, 7 tables, 2nd Workshop on Safe AI (SafeAI)
summary: Perturbation techniques that turn unsuccessful jailbreak prompts into successful ones are continuously evolving, constituting a major security threat to LLM safety. In this paper, we investigate the internal representations of such string-level perturbed jailbreak inputs in the small weight models of the Qwen-2.5-1.5B/-3B/-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-1B/-3B/-3.1-8B-Instruct families. We select two representation spaces: the last-layer-last-token embedding space and the top-50 next-token probability space. The former space separates prompts based on their spelling and format, while the latter space is effectively one-dimensional but appears more complex to cluster. Within our refusal-dominated answer set we find no behavioral hyperplane in either space. Only the next token "Sure" in the 1.5B Qwen model, and both tokens "," and "ĊĊ" in the 1$ Llama model, display a significant association with a compliant-labeled answer.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates hidden states of small Qwen and Llama models when processing perturbed jailbreak prompts. It examines two representation spaces (last-layer-last-token embeddings and top-50 next-token probabilities) and finds no behavioral hyperplane separating refusals from compliant answers, with only a few tokens showing significant association with compliance.
AI.motivation: Perturbation techniques that convert failed jailbreak prompts into successful ones are rapidly evolving and pose a serious security risk to LLM safety. The authors aim to understand the internal representations of these string-level perturbed inputs to determine whether there exist clear separability patterns between refusal and compliant responses in the model's hidden states.
AI.method: The authors analyze two representation spaces across small-weight Qwen-2.5-Instruct (1.5B, 3B, 7B) and Llama-3.2/3.1-Instruct (1B, 3B, 8B) families: (1) the last-layer-last-token embedding space, and (2) the top-50 next-token probability space. They examine whether a behavioral hyperplane exists that separates refusal-dominated answers from compliant ones, and conduct token-level association analysis.
AI.result: The last-layer-last-token embedding space separates prompts by spelling and format rather than by behavioral outcome. The top-50 next-token probability space is effectively one-dimensional but resists clear clustering. No behavioral hyperplane separating refusal from compliance was found in either space. Only the token "Sure" in Qwen-2.5-1.5B and tokens "," and "ĊĊ" in Llama-3.2-1B showed significant association with compliant-labeled answers.
AI.conclusion: String-level perturbations do not produce cleanly separable internal representations for jailbreak success vs. refusal in the studied model families. The absence of a behavioral hyperplane and the sparsity of compliance-associated tokens suggest that detecting jailbreak attempts via these representation spaces is non-trivial, highlighting the challenge of defending against evolving perturbation-based attacks.

title: Scaling Closed-Loop Feature Channel Configuration with LLMs
summary: Promising initial results in closed-loop large-language-model-based channel-configuration search demonstrated that neural-network widths can be optimized directly through executable code generation and accuracy feedback. However, those results were obtained from a relatively sparse set of valid evaluations, leaving open whether the observed optimization behavior transfers to a denser sampling regime and whether additional architectural regularities emerge when more generated networks are evaluated. To test this, the same search setting is scaled to 250 candidate networks per fine-tuning cycle. The analysis covers 2000 generated candidates from 8 complete cycles, yielding 462 verified CIFAR-100 evaluations after task and metadata filtering. Per-cycle mean accuracy exhibits a positive linear trend with slope 9.87e-4 (p=0.043), while the high-performing frontier improves more strongly: the best observed accuracy increases from 0.3144 to 0.3676, and both the top-5 and top-10 cycle-level means exhibit positive trends. The scaled run also reveals improved parameter efficiency. The best model reaches 0.3676 with 11.8M parameters, compared with an early high-performing model at 0.3144 with 166.5M parameters. Beyond accuracy, the larger sample exposes architectural regularities that were difficult to assess from sparse observations. Non-power-of-two channel widths occur in 41.8% of verified candidates, and the strongest models share structured channel-allocation patterns characterized by moderate early widths and expanded middle or later blocks. These findings indicate that the channel-search signal observed in the initial study transfers

AI.tldr: Scaling a closed-loop LLM-based neural network channel-configuration search to 250 candidates per cycle (2000 total, 462 verified) confirms that the optimization signal transfers to denser sampling. Mean accuracy trends positively, parameter efficiency improves, and architectural regularities emerge—notably non-power-of-two widths in 41.8% of candidates and structured channel-allocation patterns favoring moderate early widths with expanded middle/later blocks.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed LLM-based closed-loop channel-configuration search can optimize neural network widths, but the results were based on sparse evaluations. The authors seek to determine whether the observed optimization behavior persists under denser sampling and whether additional architectural regularities become visible when more candidate networks are evaluated.
AI.method: The same closed-loop LLM-based search setting is scaled to 250 candidate networks per fine-tuning cycle. Across 8 complete cycles, 2000 candidates are generated, yielding 462 verified CIFAR-100 evaluations after task and metadata filtering. Per-cycle mean accuracy, top-k means, best accuracy, and parameter efficiency are tracked, and architectural patterns (e.g., channel-width distributions, block-wise allocation) are analyzed.
AI.result: Per-cycle mean accuracy shows a positive linear trend (slope=9.87e-4, p=0.043). Best accuracy rises from 0.3144 to 0.3676; top-5 and top-10 cycle-level means also trend upward. Parameter efficiency improves: best model achieves 0.3676 with 11.8M parameters vs. an early high-performer at 0.3144 with 166.5M. Non-power-of-two widths appear in 41.8% of verified candidates. Strongest models share structured patterns: moderate early widths and expanded middle/later blocks.
AI.conclusion: The channel-search signal transfers to denser sampling. The scaled run confirms positive accuracy trends, improved parameter efficiency, and reveals previously obscure architectural regularities, supporting the viability of LLM-based neural architecture search for channel configuration.

title: Stochastic Sampling is Epistemically Shallow: The Dimensionality Gap Between Temperature Variation and Model Diversity in LLMs
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at EIML@ICML 2026
summary: When a language model gives different answers on repeated runs, does that variation reveal what it does not know? Self-consistency turns the variation into a per-question uncertainty estimate via majority voting. But does the same variation reveal cross-question structure -- related questions flipping together, the way a diverse ensemble does? We compare two regimes on the same questions: one model run $100$ times at $τ=1$ versus an ensemble of $24$ LLMs run once each at $τ=0$. A Marchenko--Pastur random-matrix test separates signal from sampling noise on both sides. Within any single model, at most one dimension rises above noise across five families and three benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K). Across the ensemble, four eigenvalues clear the noise edge, while a matched-difficulty Bernoulli null produces at most one in $500$ Monte Carlo draws. Self-consistency gives accurate per-question uncertainty but no detectable cross-question structure; only a diverse ensemble surfaces what a model does not know.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether variation in a language model's repeated outputs reveals shared structure across questions (like a diverse ensemble) or merely per-question uncertainty. Using Marchenko-Pastur random matrix theory, the authors find that repeated sampling from a single model yields at most one significant eigenvalue (no cross-question structure), whereas an ensemble of diverse LLMs yields four significant eigenvalues above the noise threshold. Conclusion: self-consistency provides accurate per-question uncertainty but fails to surface what the model systematically does not know across questions.
AI.motivation: Self-consistency (majority voting over repeated samples) is widely used to estimate per-question uncertainty in LLMs. However, it is unknown whether the variation across repeated runs also captures cross-question structure — i.e., whether certain questions flip together, revealing systematic knowledge gaps — in the way that a diverse ensemble of models does. The authors aim to test whether within-model stochasticity encodes the same kind of structured uncertainty as cross-model diversity.
AI.method: Two regimes are compared on identical question sets: (1) a single model run 100 times at temperature τ=1; (2) an ensemble of 24 different LLMs run once each at τ=0. For each regime, the authors construct a questions × runs (or models) binary correctness matrix, compute the empirical eigenvalue spectrum of the covariance matrix, and apply the Marchenko-Pastur test to separate signal eigenvalues from sampling noise. A matched-difficulty Bernoulli null is used as a baseline, with 500 Monte Carlo draws to assess significance. Experiments span five model families and three benchmarks: MMLU, HellaSwag, and GSM8K.
AI.result: Within any single model, at most one eigenvalue rises above the Marchenko-Pastur noise edge across all five families and three benchmarks — indicating no detectable cross-question structure. In contrast, the 24-model ensemble produces four eigenvalues that clear the noise edge, significantly more than the matched-difficulty Bernoulli null, which yields at most one in 500 Monte Carlo draws. This demonstrates that only a diverse ensemble surfaces systematic, structured knowledge gaps across questions.
AI.conclusion: Self-consistency yields reliable per-question uncertainty estimates but reveals virtually no cross-question structure. The stochastic variation within a single model is effectively one-dimensional (capturing overall difficulty), whereas a diverse ensemble captures multi-dimensional, systematic gaps in knowledge. To understand what a model does not know in a structured way, cross-model diversity is essential; within-model sampling alone is insufficient.

title: Search-on-Graph: Iterative Informed Navigation for Large Language Model Reasoning on Knowledge Graphs
comment: Accepted to KDD '26 (32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) augmented with knowledge graphs (KGs) offer a promising approach for knowledge-intensive reasoning. Central to this approach is the selection of appropriate reasoning paths in the KG. Yet, existing methods face a common limitation: reasoning path selection is often performed by separate modules using criteria that are only weakly connected to the reasoning requirements. This often results in selecting incorrect relations or premature pruning of relevant paths. We propose Search-on-Graph (SoG), a method that strengthens the connection between path selection and reasoning by having the LLM itself select which relations to follow, informed by both the available KG structure and the complete reasoning history. SoG follows an \textit{observe-think-navigate} paradigm: at each step, the LLM observes the relational connections available at the current entity, reasons about which path best advances toward answering the question, and navigates accordingly. This context-aware navigation fully exploits the LLM's reasoning capabilities rather than relying on independent selection modules with surrogate criteria. Experiments on six knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) benchmarks demonstrate that SoG outperforms state-of-the-art methods while requiring no task-specific fine-tuning and generalizing across different KG schemas.

AI.tldr: SoG (Search-on-Graph) lets the LLM itself select reasoning paths in a KG using an observe-think-navigate paradigm, outperforming SOTA on six KGQA benchmarks without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing KG-augmented LLM methods separate path selection from reasoning, using weakly connected criteria that cause incorrect relation selection and premature pruning of relevant paths. The authors aim to tightly couple path selection with the LLM's own reasoning process.
AI.method: SoG follows an observe-think-navigate paradigm. At each step, the LLM observes available relational connections at the current entity, reasons about which path best advances toward the answer, and navigates accordingly. This leverages the full reasoning history and KG structure for context-aware navigation, eliminating separate selection modules.
AI.result: SoG outperforms state-of-the-art methods on six KGQA benchmarks, generalizes across different KG schemas, and requires no task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Integrating path selection directly into the LLM's reasoning loop, rather than delegating it to external modules, yields superior knowledge-intensive reasoning performance. The approach is both effective and broadly generalizable.

title: Information is all you need: Requirements Engineering Quality Reframed
summary: To move beyond this vague appeal to context, this vision proposes a novel holistic theory of requirements engineering (RE) quality. This theory models how information particles, i.e., discrete pieces of domain knowledge, are transferred between roles and artifacts. Since the RE process is ultimately an information transfer, holistic RE quality depends on the properties of information flow, i.e., how effectively and efficiently information is transferred from sources (like stakeholders) to targets (like developers and testers), uniting both artifact- and process-based perspectives on RE quality. In an exemplary simulation of the theory we illustrate why a high-quality specification gets bypassed in an agile context, thereby demonstrating that a simulation can provide actionable insights into calibrating the RE process to optimize the information flow. Beyond organizational applications, we envision that the theory can serve as a coherent theoretical framework for understanding the success or failure of RE processes and artifacts.

AI.tldr: Proposes a holistic theory of RE quality modeling knowledge transfer as information particles flowing between roles and artifacts; a simulation demonstrates how even high-quality specifications can fail in agile contexts, offering actionable insights for process calibration.
AI.motivation: Current appeals to "context" in RE quality are vague and underspecified. There is a need for a unified, theoretically grounded framework that bridges artifact-based and process-based perspectives to explain why RE succeeds or fails.
AI.method: Develops a holistic theory modeling RE as an information transfer process using "information particles" — discrete units of domain knowledge moving between roles (stakeholders, developers, testers) and artifacts. An exemplary simulation is built to illustrate the theory's explanatory power, particularly in agile settings.
AI.result: The simulation demonstrates that a high-quality specification can be bypassed in agile contexts, revealing that artifact quality alone is insufficient. The theory shows how information flow properties determine holistic RE quality and can guide process calibration.
AI.conclusion: The proposed theory unifies artifact- and process-based quality perspectives into a coherent framework for diagnosing RE success or failure. Beyond organizational applications, it lays groundwork for a generalizable theoretical foundation in requirements engineering.

title: Reimagining the Augmented Reality Accessibility Ecosystem for Deaf Students: Service Provider Perspectives in Experiential Learning
summary: In experiential learning environments, Deaf and hard of hearing (DHH) students often experience ``split attention,'' dividing their focus among tasks, instructors, and access providers. Augmented reality (AR) has been proposed as a means to centralize communication access within the student's field of view; however, little is known about how such systems affect the instructors, interpreters, and captioners who support access in these settings. We present a formative, expert-based evaluation of ARRAE, an AR-mediated communication access ecosystem, examining the experiences of an instructor, an American Sign Language (ASL) interpreter, and a real-time captioner in a simulated laboratory environment. Comparing in-person, traditional remote, and AR-mediated access, our findings suggest that AR reconfigures accessibility labor and interactional practices by redistributing communication, attention, and awareness across participants. While AR-mediated access supported integrated, in-situ communication and enhanced contextual awareness, it also altered interactional feedback mechanisms, such as gaze coordination and pacing, that support shared understanding during instruction. These observations highlight trade-offs between access, control, and coordination, and suggest that AR-mediated systems may be most effective when considered as part of a broader, hybrid ecosystem rather than as standalone replacements for existing modalities. This work contributes initial insights into how AR reshapes communication access in experiential learning and informs the design of systems that support coordinated, multi-user interaction in hands-on educational contexts.

AI.tldr: An expert evaluation of ARRAE, an AR-mediated communication access ecosystem, reveals that while augmented reality centralizes communication for DHH students and enhances contextual awareness, it also reconfigures accessibility labor and alters critical interactional feedback mechanisms like gaze coordination and pacing—suggesting AR works best as part of a hybrid ecosystem rather than a standalone solution.
AI.motivation: DHH students in experiential learning environments suffer from split attention across tasks, instructors, and access providers. While AR has been proposed to centralize access within the student's field of view, little is known about how AR-mediated systems impact the instructors, ASL interpreters, and captioners who support accessibility.
AI.method: The authors conducted a formative, expert-based evaluation of ARRAE (an AR-mediated communication access ecosystem) in a simulated laboratory environment. They compared three modalities—in-person, traditional remote, and AR-mediated access—examining the experiences of one instructor, one ASL interpreter, and one real-time captioner.
AI.result: AR-mediated access reconfigured accessibility labor and interactional practices by redistributing communication, attention, and awareness. It supported integrated, in-situ communication and enhanced contextual awareness but altered interactional feedback mechanisms—namely gaze coordination and pacing—that are critical for shared understanding during instruction.
AI.conclusion: AR-mediated systems introduce trade-offs between access, control, and coordination. They are most effective when integrated into a broader hybrid ecosystem rather than deployed as standalone replacements for existing modalities. The work provides initial insights for designing coordinated, multi-user AR systems in hands-on educational contexts.

title: Workload-Aware Caching for Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent systems decompose complex tasks into directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of specialized agent executions, creating natural opportunities for caching intermediate results across queries. However, existing cache eviction policies treat all cached entries uniformly based on access history, ignoring structural and workload signals uniquely available in agentic execution environments. We present a workload-aware eviction policy that combines three signals, namely recomputation cost, DAG dependency count, and agent invocation frequency, into a unified scoring function that retains the most valuable entries under memory constraints. Evaluated across three multi-agent benchmarks spanning diverse reuse regimes, our policy reduces latency by up to 64.7% relative to the uncached baseline and achieves on average a 31.1% latency reduction over the next best finite-capacity baseline, while approaching the performance of an unbounded cache and maintaining accuracy on par with or exceeding all competing finite-capacity methods. We further show that workload-aware content caching is complementary to other agentic system optimization methods, including plan-level caching and parallel agent execution, with each technique targeting a distinct efficiency bottleneck in multi-agent pipelines.

AI.tldr: A workload-aware cache eviction policy for multi-agent systems that combines recomputation cost, DAG dependency count, and agent invocation frequency into a unified scoring function, achieving up to 64.7% latency reduction over uncached baselines and 31.1% average improvement over the next best finite-capacity method.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent systems naturally decompose tasks into DAGs of specialized agent executions, creating opportunities for intermediate result caching. However, existing cache eviction policies treat all entries uniformly based solely on access history, ignoring structural and workload-specific signals unique to agentic execution environments (e.g., recomputation cost, dependency structures, invocation patterns). This gap leaves significant performance gains unrealized.
AI.method: A workload-aware eviction policy that integrates three signals into a unified scoring function: (1) recomputation cost — the computational expense of regenerating a cached entry; (2) DAG dependency count — the number of downstream tasks depending on a cached intermediate result; and (3) agent invocation frequency — how often a particular agent is invoked across queries. Entries with higher composite scores are preferentially retained under memory constraints.
AI.result: Evaluated on three multi-agent benchmarks with diverse reuse regimes, the policy achieves up to 64.7% latency reduction versus an uncached baseline, a 31.1% average latency reduction over the next best finite-capacity baseline, near-parity with unbounded cache performance, and accuracy on par with or exceeding all competing finite-capacity methods. The approach is also shown to be complementary to plan-level caching and parallel agent execution.
AI.conclusion: Workload-aware content caching that leverages domain-specific signals from agentic execution DAGs significantly outperforms generic, history-only eviction policies. It addresses a distinct efficiency bottleneck orthogonal to other optimizations like plan caching and parallelism, making it a valuable and composable component in multi-agent system design.

title: Enhancing Attack Detection Capabilities in BACnet/IP Networks Using Machine-Learning Models
summary: Building Automation Systems (BAS) manage critical building functions using protocols such as BACnet/IP, yet defenders have limited tooling and few labeled datasets for detecting BACnet-specific attacks. This work addresses these gaps through three contributions. First, CISA's Zeek BACnet parser is modified to produce a unified per-packet log, simplifying feature engineering for machine-learning (ML) pipelines. Second, a simulated BACnet/IP testbed is developed using bacpypes3 to model a small commercial HVAC system with physics-based device behavior, schedule-aware controller logic, and per-packet attack labeling. Third, five unsupervised anomaly detection models are evaluated using baseline traffic and six BACnet attack types, including denial of service, reconnaissance, property tampering, and false data injection. Results show that One-Class SVM achieved the strongest overall performance, with an average F1 score of 0.864 across all attacks and F1 scores above 0.99 for high-volume denial-of-service and reconnaissance attacks. Detection is much stronger for high-volume attacks, such as DoS attacks and reconnaissance, than stealthier techniques such as tampering and false data injection, which scored around 77%.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the lack of tooling and labeled datasets for detecting BACnet/IP attacks in Building Automation Systems. It modifies CISA's Zeek BACnet parser for unified logging, builds a physics-based simulated HVAC testbed with attack labeling, and evaluates five unsupervised anomaly detection models against six attack types, finding One-Class SVM achieves the best overall performance (avg F1=0.864).
AI.motivation: Defenders lack adequate tooling and labeled datasets for detecting attacks targeting BACnet/IP, the dominant protocol in Building Automation Systems. Existing network monitoring tools do not produce logs optimized for machine learning pipelines, and there are no realistic, labeled testbeds for BACnet-specific intrusion detection research.
AI.method: Threefold: (1) Modification of CISA's Zeek BACnet parser to emit a unified per-packet log for streamlined feature extraction; (2) Development of a simulated BACnet/IP testbed using bacpypes3 that models a small commercial HVAC system with physics-based device behavior, schedule-aware controllers, and per-packet ground-truth attack labels; (3) Benchmarking of five unsupervised anomaly detection models — including One-Class SVM — across six attack types: denial of service, reconnaissance, property tampering, and false data injection.
AI.result: One-Class SVM achieved the best overall performance with an average F1 score of 0.864 across all six attack types. For high-volume attacks (DoS, reconnaissance), F1 scores exceeded 0.99. Performance dropped substantially for stealthier attacks — tampering and false data injection scored approximately 77% F1.
AI.conclusion: Unsupervised anomaly detection is viable for BACnet/IP intrusion detection, particularly for high-volume attacks. However, significant challenges remain for detecting stealthy manipulation attacks (tampering, false data injection). The modified Zeek parser and simulated testbed provide a foundation for future research and improved defensive tooling in BAS security.

title: More Is Not More: What Matters for Diversity in LLM Opinions?
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate diverse human opinions in open-ended tasks such as synthetic surveys, focus group modeling, and public opinion prediction. However, LLM outputs exhibit systematic opinion homogenization. Practitioners have explored various interventions to increase diversity, but the landscape remains fragmented: different methods are evaluated in isolation with incomparable metrics, and in practice they are typically deployed and upgraded simultaneously, making it difficult to attribute gains to specific components. To advance a more scientific understanding of LLM output diversity, we design a factorial experiment that separates two primary intervention dimensions: input conditioning (operationalized through persona depth) and interaction architecture. We evaluate all conditions on 100 real-user open-ended questions across 7 models, measuring diversity with multiple complementary metrics. Our findings challenge several common assumptions. First, more persona detail does not monotonically increase diversity. The initial step of persona conditioning already captures the majority of the gain, while further elaboration with demographic detail does not consistently improve and can reduce diversity on some models. Second, rather than seeking a single best interaction architecture, we find that different architectures explore largely non-overlapping opinion regions. Combining multiple architectures yields broader coverage than optimizing any one. Third, commonly attempted low-cost alternatives such as raising sampling temperature and adding diversity instructions produce negligible effects compared to structured interventions. Overall, our work demonstrates that diversity is not a product of scaling along any single dimension, but is highly sensitive to the structural form and combination of interventions.

AI.tldr: A factorial experiment disentangling two dimensions of LLM opinion diversity interventions — persona depth and interaction architecture — reveals that more persona detail does not monotonically increase diversity, different architectures explore non-overlapping opinion regions, and low-cost alternatives like temperature or diversity prompts are negligible. Diversity is sensitive to structural intervention combinations rather than scaling along any single axis.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed to simulate human opinions in synthetic surveys and public opinion prediction, but they exhibit systematic opinion homogenization. The existing intervention landscape is fragmented: methods are evaluated in isolation with incomparable metrics, and multiple interventions are deployed simultaneously, obscuring attribution. A rigorous, factorial decomposition of diversity drivers is needed.
AI.method: A factorial experiment crossing two primary intervention dimensions: (1) input conditioning via persona depth (no persona → minimal persona → demographic-rich persona) and (2) interaction architecture (multiple structural forms). Evaluated across 100 real-user open-ended questions on 7 LLMs using multiple complementary diversity metrics, with additional comparison against low-cost baselines (sampling temperature, diversity instructions).
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Persona depth shows diminishing returns — the initial persona step captures most diversity gains, while adding demographic detail can reduce diversity on some models. (2) Different interaction architectures explore largely non-overlapping opinion regions; combining architectures yields broader coverage than optimizing any single one. (3) Low-cost alternatives (temperature, diversity prompts) produce negligible effects relative to structured interventions.
AI.conclusion: LLM output diversity is not achieved by scaling along a single dimension. It is highly sensitive to the structural form and combination of interventions. The field should move beyond isolated method comparisons toward understanding how intervention components interact and compose.

title: Multimodal CoLRAG-TF: Triple-Filtered Retrieval for Complex PDFs
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over heterogeneous PDF collections remains challenging due to multimodal content, domain-specific terminology, and the need for multi-hop reasoning across dispersed evidence. We present Multimodal CoLRAG-TF, a four-axis fusion architecture that integrates dense text embeddings, BM25 keyword matching, knowledge-graph triple filtering, and image-based similarity for robust retrieval over complex documents. Our system constructs a multimodal index of 2,403 blocks extracted from 43 Japanese disaster lesson PDFs, supported by a hybrid OCR pipeline and LLM-based caption generation. To enhance compositional reasoning, we extract 11,414 OpenIE triples and index them with FAISS, enabling sub-second triple lookup and hierarchical propagation of relevance signals. A HippoRAG2-inspired coarse-to-fine retriever (volume $\to$ chapter $\to$ block) narrows the search space before final fusion scoring. Bayesian optimization over fusion weights reveals that the triple axis must dominate ($α_\text{triple} = 0.44$) to counteract lexical bias and sustain multi-hop retrieval quality. Evaluated on a 457-pair benchmark, Multimodal CoLRAG-TF achieves a Retrieval Recall of 0.9909 and a 71.6$\%$ improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over single-hop queries. An image-to-lesson pipeline using a vision LLM further demonstrates the applicability of the approach to visual inputs. These results show that triple-filtered multimodal fusion is essential for structured reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous PDFs and provides a general framework applicable beyond the disaster domain.

AI.tldr: Multimodal CoLRAG-TF is a four-axis fusion retrieval system (dense embeddings, BM25, knowledge graph triples, image similarity) built on Japanese disaster lesson PDFs. By weighting the triple axis most heavily (0.44), it achieves 0.99 retrieval recall and 71.6% improved multi-hop answer similarity, demonstrating that triple-filtered multimodal fusion is essential for structured reasoning over heterogeneous documents.
AI.motivation: RAG over heterogeneous PDF collections is challenging due to multimodal content, domain-specific terminology, and the need for multi-hop reasoning across dispersed evidence. Existing approaches struggle to balance lexical matching, semantic understanding, and structured relational reasoning simultaneously.
AI.method: Four-axis fusion architecture combining: (1) dense text embeddings, (2) BM25 keyword matching, (3) knowledge-graph triple filtering via 11,414 OpenIE triples indexed with FAISS for sub-second lookup, and (4) image-based similarity. A HippoRAG2-inspired coarse-to-fine retriever (volume → chapter → block) narrows the search space. A hybrid OCR pipeline with LLM-based caption generation processes the PDFs. Bayesian optimization determines fusion weights, with the triple axis dominating at α_triple = 0.44.
AI.result: Evaluated on a 457-pair benchmark, the system achieves Retrieval Recall of 0.9909 and a 71.6% improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over single-hop queries. An image-to-lesson pipeline using a vision LLM validates applicability to visual inputs.
AI.conclusion: Triple-filtered multimodal fusion is essential for structured reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous PDFs. The framework generalizes beyond the disaster domain, and the dominance of the triple axis (α=0.44) is critical to counteract lexical bias and sustain multi-hop retrieval quality.

title: JAXBench: Benchmarking Autonomous TPU Kernel Optimization
summary: Rigorous benchmarks have driven progress in autonomous GPU kernel performance optimization by establishing a shared target to hillclimb on, but no equivalent exists for TPUs. We present JAXBench, a TPU-native benchmark suite for AI-generated kernel optimization on Google Cloud TPUs. JAXBench comprises 50 JAX workloads that are both relevant and provide headroom for optimization. We extract 17 production ML operators from architectures in the public MaxText library such as Llama-3.1, DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, Mamba-2, and AlphaFold2, and translate 33 operators from KernelBench that are validated for correctness and set with new problem sizes that achieve high TPU v6e MXU utilization. Eight of the 17 production operators ship with hand-optimized Pallas kernels from the public Tokamax library and block-size tuned to establish an expert upper-bound baseline. We evaluate four feedback-driven methods on generating candidate Pallas kernels for JAXBench. Across the full suite with Gemini 3 Flash, we find that target-specific context matters more than model scale on a sparsely-documented DSL like Pallas. Conditioning on curated TPU documentation raises per-sample correctness from 5.8% to 37.3% and solves 48 of 50 benchmarks at a 1.28x geomean speedup. Search structure yields significant gains once correctness is achieved, with Autocomp's beam-search pipeline reaching a 1.36x geomean speedup over XLA. On the 8 hand-tuned kernels, Autocomp reaches 1.60x geomean over XLA, recovering most of the 2.08x Tokamax upper bound but trailing on the specialized paged and ragged attention operators. High-quality TPU kernel optimization remains a challenging task, and we release the JAXBench benchmark, evaluation harness, and baseline results to support open source contributions.

AI.tldr: JAXBench is a 50-workload TPU kernel optimization benchmark suite, with 17 production operators from MaxText and 33 from KernelBench. Using Gemini 3 Flash with curated TPU documentation, correctness rises from 5.8% to 37.3%, solving 48/50 benchmarks at 1.28x geomean speedup. Autocomp's beam-search achieves 1.36x over XLA and 1.60x on hand-tuned kernels, nearing the 2.08x Tokamax upper bound.
AI.motivation: Rigorous benchmarks have driven progress in autonomous GPU kernel optimization, but no equivalent benchmark exists for TPUs. This gap hinders systematic evaluation and progress in AI-generated TPU kernel optimization.
AI.method: The authors construct JAXBench with 50 JAX workloads: 17 production ML operators extracted from MaxText (Llama-3.1, DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, Mamba-2, AlphaFold2) and 33 operators adapted from KernelBench with new TPU-optimized problem sizes. Eight production operators include hand-optimized Pallas kernels from Tokamax as expert baselines. Four feedback-driven code generation methods are evaluated using Gemini 3 Flash, comparing the impact of target-specific context (curated TPU documentation), model scale, and search structure (Autocomp's beam-search pipeline).
AI.result: (1) Target-specific context is more impactful than model scale on sparsely-documented DSLs like Pallas; curated TPU documentation raises per-sample correctness from 5.8% to 37.3%, solving 48/50 benchmarks at 1.28x geomean speedup. (2) Autocomp's beam-search pipeline achieves 1.36x geomean speedup over XLA across the suite and 1.60x on the 8 hand-tuned kernels, recovering most of the 2.08x Tokamax upper bound but trailing on specialized paged and ragged attention operators.
AI.conclusion: High-quality TPU kernel optimization remains challenging. JAXBench provides a standardized evaluation framework to drive open-source progress. Key insights: curated documentation is critical for sparse DSLs, and search-based refinement significantly improves performance once baseline correctness is achieved.

title: Search-on-Graph-R1: Training Large Language Models to Search Knowledge Graphs with Reinforcement Learning
summary: Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) requires navigating from topic entities to an answer several relations away. Recent methods prompt a frontier LLM to explore the graph through a retrieval tool, but their reliance on frontier-scale inference makes them costly to deploy. We present Search-on-Graph-R1 (\sogrone{}), which internalizes this navigation into a compact 8B model through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning (RL). Our central idea is to scaffold a frontier teacher with each question's gold SPARQL query, so the teacher traverses a known answer-bearing path with a live \texttt{Search} tool rather than having to discover the path itself. Since every call executes against a live Freebase server, the resulting trajectories are grounded in the knowledge graph by construction. On WebQSP, CWQ, and GrailQA, \sogrone{} at 8B surpasses every frozen frontier-LLM system in our comparison and posts the strongest results on CWQ of any system we compare against. It does so using no auxiliary module at inference and no LLM judge during training. Isolating each training stage shows that SFT and RL contribute complementary gains, our approach transfers across model families, and RL learns to reach answers in fewer \texttt{Search} calls than its SFT initialization.

AI.tldr: Search-on-Graph-R1 (SoG-R1) trains a compact 8B model for KGQA by first using a frontier LLM teacher guided by gold SPARQL queries to generate grounded search trajectories on Freebase, then applying SFT and RL. The resulting model surpasses all frozen frontier-LLM systems on WebQSP, CWQ, and GrailQA, achieving state-of-the-art on CWQ with no auxiliary modules at inference.
AI.motivation: Existing KGQA methods rely on prompting frontier LLMs (e.g., GPT-4) with retrieval tools to navigate knowledge graphs, but this incurs high inference costs. The authors aim to distill this capability into a compact, deployable 8B model while maintaining or exceeding frontier performance.
AI.method: The approach has two stages: (1) A frontier teacher LLM is scaffolded with gold SPARQL queries so it traverses known answer-bearing paths using a live Search tool against Freebase, producing grounded trajectories. These trajectories serve as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data for a compact 8B model. (2) The fine-tuned model is further optimized via reinforcement learning (RL), which reduces the number of Search calls needed to reach answers. No LLM judge is used during training, and no auxiliary modules are needed at inference.
AI.result: SoG-R1 (8B) surpasses every frozen frontier-LLM system compared on WebQSP, CWQ, and GrailQA, achieving the strongest results on CWQ among all compared systems. Ablations show SFT and RL contribute complementary gains, the approach transfers across model families, and RL reduces the number of Search calls relative to the SFT-only model.
AI.conclusion: Internalizing graph-navigation capability into a compact model via SFT + RL on teacher-scaffolded trajectories is both effective and cost-efficient for KGQA. The method eliminates reliance on frontier LLMs at inference while achieving superior accuracy and search efficiency.

title: Teaching Business Process Modeling to Leverage Soft Skills of Computing Students
summary: Background and Context: Organizations have highly depended on software systems to realize their business processes and achieve strategic business goals and competitive advantage; hence, computing professionals who can understand these processes could more effectively build such systems. At the same time, while Artificial Intelligence (AI) has increased the productivity in developing these and other systems, professionals should be better prepared due to the competitiveness of the job market; thus, soft skills could be an important factor to ensure their position in this market. Objective: This paper aims to analyze and present the impact of teaching business process modeling to leverage key soft skills of future computing professionals. Method and Findings: Our method involved an industry-driven, project-based approach with 53 computing students who actively interacted with stakeholders and modeled the organization's business process. We systematically collected the students' feedback, including the soft skills practiced and demonstrating that professionalism, initiative, motivation, communication, and teamwork can be leveraged. Implications: The main implication of this work for the Computer Science Education research community is to provide evidence that teaching business process modeling subjects is particularly beneficial for future professionals, as it could contribute to preparing them regarding their soft skills for the era of AI-assisted software development.

AI.tldr: Teaching business process modeling to computing students through industry-driven projects effectively develops key soft skills—professionalism, initiative, motivation, communication, and teamwork—preparing them for the AI-augmented job market.
AI.motivation: Organizations rely on software to achieve business goals, requiring computing professionals who understand business processes. Simultaneously, AI is reshaping productivity in software development, heightening job market competition and making soft skills critical for career resilience.
AI.method: An industry-driven, project-based pedagogical approach involving 53 computing students who engaged directly with organizational stakeholders to model real business processes. Feedback was systematically collected to identify which soft skills were practiced.
AI.result: The intervention demonstrated that business process modeling instruction can leverage key soft skills: professionalism, initiative, motivation, communication, and teamwork.
AI.conclusion: Teaching business process modeling is particularly beneficial for future computing professionals, providing evidence that such instruction contributes to soft skill development essential for the era of AI-assisted software development.

title: CRAFT: Exploring Wearable Creative AI on Smart Glasses for Fiction Writing in Real-World Contexts
comment: Conditionally accepted (pending minor revisions) for publication in Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies (PACM IMWUT), Vol. 10, No. 3, Article 81, September 2026
summary: Creative writing increasingly integrates AI assistance, yet current tools miss in-situ moments when writers draw inspiration from real-world experiences. We envision Context-aware Reality-Fiction Transformation (CRAFT), an approach for AI glasses that translates daily experiences into fiction narratives. We explored its desirability, feasibility, and potential viability through three studies. Interviews with nine writers yielded desires and three design goals: 1) augmenting in-situ perception to bridge reality-fiction gaps, 2) promoting authenticity grounded in real-world experiences while maintaining fictionalization, and 3) preserving creative agency, enjoyment, and life-art boundaries. Co-design workshops with 16 writers and researchers operationalized these goals into concrete interaction mechanisms using a technology probe. We then conducted supported field trials with eight writers across 24 sessions using a refined probe, revealing writer-perceived benefits (e.g., enriched fictional ideas from serendipitous encounters), emergent practices (e.g., micro-creation), and design considerations for future sustained use. We contribute design explorations for the CRAFT approach, offering design implications and empirical insights on ubiquitous human-AI creative collaboration in everyday life.

AI.tldr: CRAFT envisions AI glasses that transform everyday experiences into fiction narratives. Through interviews, co-design workshops, and field trials with writers, the authors derive design goals, interaction mechanisms, and empirical insights for context-aware, ubiquitous human-AI creative collaboration that preserves authenticity, agency, and life-art boundaries.
AI.motivation: Current AI-assisted creative writing tools fail to capture in-situ moments where writers draw inspiration from real-world experiences. There is a gap between the spontaneous, context-rich nature of real-world inspiration and the capabilities of existing AI writing aids, which operate outside the lived context of the writer.
AI.method: A three-phase study design: (1) Semi-structured interviews with 9 writers to elicit desires and derive design goals; (2) Co-design workshops with 16 writers and researchers using a technology probe to operationalize goals into interaction mechanisms; (3) Supported field trials with 8 writers across 24 sessions using a refined probe to evaluate perceived benefits, emergent practices, and design considerations.
AI.result: Three design goals emerged: augmenting in-situ perception, promoting authenticity with fictionalization, and preserving agency/enjoyment/boundaries. Field trials revealed benefits such as enriched fictional ideas from serendipitous encounters and emergent practices like micro-creation, along with design considerations for sustained use.
AI.conclusion: CRAFT represents a promising design space for ubiquitous human-AI creative collaboration. The paper contributes design explorations and empirical insights that advance understanding of how AI glasses can contextually transform daily life into fiction while respecting writer agency and authenticity.

title: MKEvolve: A Modular Multi-Agent Framework for Kernel Code Generation
summary: Despite rapid progress in LLM-based code generation, writing correct and performant kernels for hardware accelerators remains a key bottleneck in scaling modern ML workloads. We present MKEvolve (Modular Kernel Evolve), a framework that iteratively co-evolves a modular decomposition of complex PyTorch modules and the LLM-generated kernel for each submodule, refining the decomposition by splitting and fusing across iterations while independently improving each subkernel via LLM-driven beam search. The resulting kernels are programmatic compositions of independently verified subkernels, making them configurable (subkernel implementations are swappable), interpretable (errors and speedups are traceable to specific subkernels), and readily adaptable to related model architectures. Experiments with Triton on KernelBench L2 and L3, spanning multi-operator sequences and full model architectures, show that MKEvolve improves both correctness and speedup over end-to-end direct synthesis baselines while reducing LLM token usage by up to 35%.

AI.tldr: MKEvolve is a framework that iteratively co-evolves modular decomposition of complex PyTorch modules alongside LLM-generated kernels for each submodule. It refines decompositions via splitting/fusing and improves subkernels through beam search, producing configurable, interpretable, and adaptable kernel compositions. On KernelBench L2/L3 with Triton, it improves correctness and speedup over end-to-end baselines while cutting LLM token usage by up to 35%.
AI.motivation: Despite advances in LLM-based code generation, writing correct and performant kernels for hardware accelerators remains a critical bottleneck in scaling modern ML workloads. End-to-end synthesis struggles with complex multi-operator sequences and full model architectures.
AI.method: MKEvolve employs iterative co-evolution: it decomposes complex PyTorch modules into submodules, generates kernels for each via LLM-driven beam search, then refines the decomposition by splitting and fusing submodules across iterations. Each subkernel is independently verified, and the final kernel is a programmatic composition of swappable, independently verified subkernels.
AI.result: Experiments on KernelBench L2 (multi-operator sequences) and L3 (full model architectures) using Triton show MKEvolve improves both correctness and speedup over end-to-end direct synthesis baselines, while reducing LLM token consumption by up to 35%.
AI.conclusion: Modular decomposition co-evolved with per-submodule kernel generation yields more correct, faster, and more token-efficient kernel synthesis than monolithic end-to-end approaches. The resulting kernels are also more configurable, interpretable, and adaptable to related architectures.

title: Buzz to Boom: Detecting Message Progression Vulnerabilities in Electron Applications via Segmented Directed Fuzzing
summary: Electron is a popular framework for building cross-platform desktop applications using web technologies. Such applications consist of multiple processes with different privilege levels that communicate via message passing. When inter-process messages carry attacker-controlled inputs, they can propagate across processes and reach privileged APIs, e.g., command execution. Such a message propagation behavior is characterized as Message Progression Vulnerabilities (MPVs). The exploitation of MPVs is challenging because it often requires multiple steps, e.g., first arbitrary code execution in one process via message passing, and then command injection in another process using another message crafted in the first process. To our knowledge, existing works on Electron security only study unsafe configurations and malicious Document Object Model (DOM) content, i.e., they cannot detect or exploit these vulnerabilities that need to be triggered by complex cross-process exploits via message passing. We present Proton, a segmented directed fuzzing framework for detecting MPVs. Our key insight is to decompose end-to-end fuzzing into per-process segments along message-passing boundaries, where the goals of fuzzing each segment are either: (i) reaching a sink in the current process or (ii) propagating the payload to the next process, to enable the exploration of another process. In the second case, the messages seed the corpus of the next segment. Finally, Proton synthesizes crash inputs from each process to validate end-to-end exploits. We evaluate Proton against 589 real-world Electron applications, resulting in 23 zero-day MPVs. Among them, 22 lead to OS command execution, including projects with over 50k GitHub stars. We responsibly disclosed all findings. To date, we have received 13 acknowledgments, 11 fixes, and 11 CVEs, including a bug bounty from Vercel.

AI.tldr: Proton is a segmented directed fuzzing framework that detects Message Progression Vulnerabilities (MPVs) in Electron applications by decomposing cross-process fuzzing into per-process segments. It found 23 zero-day MPVs in 589 real-world apps, 22 leading to OS command execution, resulting in 11 CVEs.
AI.motivation: Existing Electron security research only examines unsafe configurations and malicious DOM content, failing to detect or exploit vulnerabilities requiring complex cross-process exploits via message passing. MPVs are particularly challenging because they involve multi-step exploitation across processes with different privilege levels.
AI.method: Proton uses segmented directed fuzzing that decomposes end-to-end fuzzing along message-passing boundaries. Each per-process segment is fuzzed with one of two goals: (1) reaching a sink in the current process, or (2) propagating the payload to the next process, where the output messages seed the next segment's corpus. Finally, crash inputs from each process are synthesized to validate end-to-end exploits.
AI.result: Evaluated against 589 real-world Electron applications, Proton discovered 23 zero-day MPVs. Of these, 22 enable OS command execution, including in projects with over 50k GitHub stars. The findings led to 13 acknowledgments, 11 fixes, 11 CVEs, and a bug bounty from Vercel.
AI.conclusion: Proton demonstrates that segmented directed fuzzing is an effective approach for uncovering complex, multi-step MPVs in Electron applications, filling a critical gap left by prior work that only addressed single-process vulnerabilities or configuration issues.

title: LLM-INSTRUCT at UZH Shared Task 2026: Constraint-Aware Retrieval and Selective Debate for Paragraph-Level Argument Mining
comment: Accepted to the 13th Workshop on Argument Mining (ArgMining 2026) at ACL 2026
summary: We present LLM-INSTRUCT, the winning system for the UZH Shared Task at ArgMining 2026 on paragraph-level argument mining in UN and UNESCO resolutions. The task requires paragraph-type classification, prediction of a subset of 141 official tags, and directed relation prediction under a strict JSON schema setting using only open-weight models up to 8B parameters. We frame the task as constrained structured prediction. The system first narrows the candidate tag space with metadata-aware dense retrieval, then applies constrained decoding with per-dimension caps, escalates only uncertain cases to a three-agent debate branch, and finally validates the output schema. On the official leaderboard, LLM-INSTRUCT ranked 1st overall, with 1st in F1 and 5th in LLM-as-a-Judge. During development, our configuration search further improved Task 1b Micro-F1 from 35.83% to 40.08% while keeping the internal Task 2 score at 4.421. The main lesson is simple: reducing the decision space before generation improves both accuracy and submission robustness. Our code and supporting scripts are publicly available at: https://github.com/LLM-Instruct-at-UZH-Shared-Task-2026/Method

AI.tldr: LLM-INSTRUCT won the ArgMining 2026 shared task on paragraph-level argument mining in UN/UNESCO resolutions by framing it as constrained structured prediction.
