These findings suggest that Multi-LLM aggregation requires not just combining predictions, but calibrating trust under uncertainty.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes treating multi-LLM aggregation as an uncertainty-aware trust estimation problem using Cooke-style log weighting from decision theory, demonstrating that calibration-based expert weighting outperforms naive aggregation — particularly under heterogeneous and contaminated model panels — on MMLU and MMLU-Pro benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM ensemble aggregation methods assume all models are equally trustworthy, ignoring differences in uncertainty quality. This assumption fails in heterogeneous settings where LLMs vary significantly in reliability and capability, leaving naive aggregation vulnerable to unreliable or adversarial experts.
AI.method: The authors adapt structured expert judgment from decision theory, specifically employing Cooke-style log weighting. This method uses context-aware calibration questions to estimate each expert's reliability based on the quality of its probabilistic predictions — penalizing overconfident incorrect predictions and favoring well-calibrated experts.
AI.result: On MMLU and MMLU-Pro, all aggregation methods perform similarly in homogeneous settings. However, under heterogeneity and contamination, Cooke weighting is critical, achieving a superior accuracy-reliability balance and remaining robust even when unreliable experts are introduced.
AI.conclusion: Multi-LLM aggregation requires not merely combining predictions, but calibrating trust under uncertainty. Uncertainty-aware trust estimation is essential for robust ensembling in realistic, non-homogeneous deployment scenarios.

title: PlanE: Meta Planning of Data, Tuning, and Inference for Extractive-based LLMs
summary: Enhancing the task-specific capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) primarily requires substantial instruction-tuning datasets. However, the sheer volume of such data imposes a considerable annotation cost, and a lack of optimization methods for tailoring LLMs to specific tasks. To address the above issues, we propose a \textbf{Plan}ning framework for constructing \textbf{E}xtractive-based LLMs called \textbf{PlanE}, which includes data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference. Additionally, we introduce a Data-Tuning-Inference (DTI) planner, aimed at selecting the optimal base-LLM and its DTI combinations for specific datasets to improve construction efficiency. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our PlanE from two views: (1) across different datasets using the same base-LLM, and (2) on the same dataset using different base-LLMs. Furthermore, we validate the generalizability of the proposed DTI planner under different optimization objectives. The codes are publicly available at https://github.com/gugugu-469/PlanE.

AI.tldr: PlanE is a framework for efficiently constructing extractive-based LLMs through data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference, augmented by a DTI planner that selects optimal base-LLM and data-tuning-inference combinations for specific tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM task-specific fine-tuning requires large instruction-tuning datasets with high annotation costs, and there is a lack of systematic optimization methods for tailoring LLMs to specific tasks efficiently.
AI.method: The PlanE framework consists of three components: (1) data decomposition, (2) instruction tuning, and (3) prompt inference. A Data-Tuning-Inference (DTI) planner is introduced to automatically select the optimal base-LLM and DTI combinations for given datasets to maximize construction efficiency.
AI.result: PlanE demonstrates effectiveness across two experimental views: (1) consistent improvements across different datasets using the same base-LLM, and (2) consistent improvements on the same dataset using different base-LLMs. The DTI planner also generalizes well under varying optimization objectives.
AI.conclusion: PlanE provides an effective and generalizable solution for efficiently constructing extractive-based LLMs, reducing annotation burden while maintaining task-specific performance through its integrated planning and optimization framework.

title: Cardinality-Decomposed Loss: Matching Training Objectives to Relation Structure in Heterogeneous Recommendation Graphs
summary: Graph Neural Networks trained on heterogenous bipartite graphs form a common basis in recommendation systems. These graphs often express relations that vary in cardinality, for example, user-item preferences are one-to-many and user-attribute features are one-to-one. Traditionally, a unique loss function is applied for all of the network components which is often Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR). While BPR works well for the recommendation task, we find that it causes attribute embeddings to collapse to near-random geometry -- a silent failure that leaves standard ranking metrics largely unaffected and therefore invisible to conventional evaluation. This in turn pollutes user node embeddings, which are shaped by both edge types simultaneously, hurting downstream tasks like personalization, segmentation, etc. Here we propose a Cardinality-Decomposed Loss (CDL) that combines both Cross Entropy (CE) and BPR to enable the model to collectively optimize for relations across cardinalities. We confirm this CE-BPR conflict by showing the two losses compete in the shared encoder's parameter space. We evaluate CDL on five datasets spanning two structural configurations -- one-to-one attributes on user nodes (MovieLens-1M, Last.fm-360K, PayPal Audience Factory, BookCrossing) and on item nodes (Yelp) -- and find that CDL consistently improves discriminability in attribute embeddings. We also show that ranking (NDCG) improves when attributes carry meaningful preference signal, but conflicts with it when the correlation is weak. We use a lambda parameter to navigate this trade-off, and a lambda-sweep reveals that dataset behavior is governed by two graph properties -- semantic alignment and topology leakage. Semantic alignment measures whether the attribute predicts preferences, while topology leakage measures whether the graph's connectivity already encodes it.

AI.tldr: Graph Neural Networks for recommendation often use BPR loss uniformly across all edge types, but this causes attribute embeddings to collapse to near-random geometry. The authors propose Cardinality-Decomposed Loss (CDL), combining Cross Entropy and BPR, to handle different cardinality relations (one-to-one vs. one-to-many) and demonstrate improved attribute embedding discriminability across five datasets.
AI.motivation: In heterogeneous bipartite graphs used for recommendation, different edge types have different cardinalities (e.g., user-item is one-to-many, user-attribute is one-to-one). Using BPR loss uniformly across all components silently collapses attribute embeddings to near-random geometry, which goes undetected by standard ranking metrics but pollutes user node embeddings and harms downstream tasks like personalization and segmentation.
AI.method: The authors propose Cardinality-Decomposed Loss (CDL), which applies Cross Entropy (CE) loss to one-to-one attribute edges and BPR loss to one-to-many preference edges. They analyze the conflict between CE and BPR in the shared encoder's parameter space and introduce a lambda parameter to navigate the trade-off. They also characterize dataset behavior using two graph properties: semantic alignment (whether attributes predict preferences) and topology leakage (whether graph connectivity already encodes this information).
AI.result: CDL consistently improves discriminability in attribute embeddings across five datasets (MovieLens-1M, Last.fm-360K, PayPal Audience Factory, BookCrossing, Yelp). NDCG ranking improves when attributes carry meaningful preference signal but conflicts when correlation is weak. The lambda-sweep reveals that dataset behavior is governed by semantic alignment and topology leakage.
AI.conclusion: Uniform application of BPR loss in heterogeneous bipartite graphs causes silent failures in attribute embeddings. Decomposing the loss function by cardinality (CE for one-to-one, BPR for one-to-many) resolves this issue, and the trade-off between ranking and attribute quality can be navigated using semantic alignment and topology leakage as guiding properties.

title: ExecuGraph: A Multi-Agent, Execution-Grounded Framework for Reliable Backend Code Synthesis with Large Language Models
comment: Submitted to Data Science and Management
summary: Large Language Models generate plausible backend code, but a single-pass paradigm provides no guarantee of correctness or runtime reliability. We present ExecuGraph, a multi-agent framework that places execution-based validation at the center of backend code synthesis. Six specialized agents (Planner, Code Generator, Logical Reviewer, Evaluator, Optimizer, and Explainer) are coordinated by a typed directed workflow with a bounded retry budget, implemented on LangGraph with locally hosted models (Ollama) and an optional retrieval layer for algorithmic technique recall. A subprocess-isolated sandbox with a wall-clock timeout guards every evaluation. We evaluate on a curated 30-problem DSA suite (internal-30), HumanEval (n=64), and an APPS-introductory subset, contrasting ExecuGraph against a single-agent one-shot baseline and a single-agent execution-retry baseline (a Reflexion-style ablation that isolates the contribution of multi-agent decomposition). On internal-30, the three conditions are statistically indistinguishable (n=30; paired Wilcoxon p=0.59 MF vs. SO, p=0.08 SR vs. SO); 95% bootstrap confidence intervals on all pairwise mean differences include zero. On HumanEval, multi-full edges ahead by +3.1 pp. The strongest signal is cross-model: with DeepSeekCoder V2 Lite, graph-category accuracy improves from 57.5% (oneshot) to 80.0% (multi-full), a +22.5 pp jump that supports a scaling hypothesis: the value of multi-agent decomposition grows with base-model capability. The framework's primary contribution is methodological: a single codebase that collapses by configuration into one-shot, execution-retry, and per-agent ablation conditions, enabling controlled measurement of each lever's marginal contribution. A per-agent ablation, retry-budget sweep, error-class taxonomy, and test-source audit are reported.

AI.tldr: ExecuGraph is a multi-agent framework for backend code synthesis that uses execution-based validation with six specialized agents in a typed workflow. Evaluated on DSA, HumanEval, and APPS benchmarks, it shows modest gains over single-agent baselines but reveals a cross-model scaling effect: multi-agent decomposition benefits stronger base models (+22.5 pp with DeepSeekCoder V2 Lite).
AI.motivation: Single-pass LLM code generation offers no correctness or runtime reliability guarantees. The authors hypothesize that decomposing the synthesis task across specialized agents coordinated by execution-based feedback loops can improve output quality, and that this benefit scales with base model capability.
AI.method: ExecuGraph employs six agents (Planner, Code Generator, Logical Reviewer, Evaluator, Optimizer, Explainer) orchestrated by a typed directed workflow on LangGraph with locally hosted Ollama models. A subprocess-isolated sandbox with wall-clock timeout guards code evaluation. The framework collapses by configuration into three conditions: one-shot, single-agent execution-retry (Reflexion-style ablation), and full multi-agent. An optional retrieval layer supports algorithmic recall. A bounded retry budget governs the feedback loop.
AI.result: On internal-30, all three conditions were statistically indistinguishable (paired Wilcoxon p=0.59 and p=0.08; 95% bootstrap CIs include zero). On HumanEval, multi-full led by +3.1 pp. Cross-model: DeepSeekCoder V2 Lite improved from 57.5% (one-shot) to 80.0% (multi-full), a +22.5 pp gain, supporting the scaling hypothesis. Ablations, retry-budget sweeps, error taxonomy, and test-source audits were also reported.
AI.conclusion: The primary contribution is methodological: a unified codebase enabling controlled measurement of multi-agent decomposition's marginal contribution. Results suggest that multi-agent architectures yield greater gains when paired with stronger base models, pointing to a scaling relationship between model capability and the utility of structured agentic workflows.

title: Sources of Inequity and Fairness Risks inWellbeing Sensing
comment: 16 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Accepted to AIES 2026
summary: Passive sensing for wellbeing uses smartphones and wearables to continuously collect human behavioral data and applies ML/AI models to infer psychological states and behaviors (e.g., depression, cognitive load). These systems are increasingly adopted in high-stakes settings (e.g., hospitals, universities), yet fairness research remains limited---primarily to post-hoc, identity-based comparisons of model performance. However, passive sensing combines heterogeneous sensing infrastructures, indirect behavioral inference, and longitudinal deployment---characteristics that, while not exclusive to the domain, are jointly pronounced here and raise two underexplored questions: (1) what additional sources of inequity arise from these characteristics, and (2) how do such inequities propagate beyond algorithmic audits across the system lifecycle? To address this gap, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 14 researchers and practitioners across five countries, examining how fairness risks emerge and are negotiated across the full passive sensing lifecycle. Our findings empirically characterize five situated sources of inequity (e.g., comfort with monitoring, behavioral regularity) that systematically shape fairness risks beyond identity-based attributes. We further synthesize 15 fairness risks and corresponding mitigation strategies across the lifecycle, from study design to deployment. Finally, we identify structural barriers that constrain fair practice in reality, and argue that enabling fair passive sensing requires both individual researcher efforts and ecosystem-level governance support from funders, publication venues, and deploying institutions.

AI.tldr: Passive sensing systems for wellbeing infer psychological states from behavioral data but fairness research is limited to post-hoc identity-based comparisons. Through interviews with 14 researchers/practitioners across five countries, this paper identifies five situated sources of inequity beyond identity attributes, synthesizes 15 fairness risks and mitigation strategies across the system lifecycle, and argues that fair passive sensing requires both individual efforts and ecosystem-level governance.
AI.motivation: Passive sensing for wellbeing is increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings (hospitals, universities), yet fairness research remains narrowly focused on post-hoc, identity-based model performance comparisons. The domain's jointly pronounced characteristics—heterogeneous sensing infrastructures, indirect behavioral inference, and longitudinal deployment—raise underexplored questions about additional sources of inequity and how they propagate across the full system lifecycle beyond algorithmic audits.
AI.method: The authors conducted semi-structured interviews with 14 researchers and practitioners across five countries who work on passive sensing for wellbeing. The interviews examined how fairness risks emerge and are negotiated across the entire passive sensing lifecycle, from study design through deployment.
AI.result: The study empirically characterizes five situated sources of inequity (e.g., comfort with monitoring, behavioral regularity) that systematically shape fairness risks beyond identity-based attributes. It synthesizes 15 fairness risks with corresponding mitigation strategies spanning the full lifecycle, and identifies structural barriers constraining fair practice in real-world contexts.
AI.conclusion: Enabling fair passive sensing requires a dual approach: individual researcher efforts to address lifecycle fairness risks, combined with ecosystem-level governance support from funders, publication venues, and deploying institutions to overcome structural barriers that currently constrain equitable practice.

authors: Elderly People with Frailty or Dementia Azul Debenedetti
title: SafeStep: AI-powered Travel Assistance for Elderly People with Frailty or Dementia
summary: More than a million people in the UK suffer from frailty or dementia, which severely compromise their ability to travel in urban environments. This paper presents SafeStep, an AI-driven travel system that assists elderly users with their journeys. At the core of SafeStep is a novel travel graph representation, which integrates route planning with predictive modelling. For each stage of a journey, the system (i) generates personalized failure scenarios using a combi-nation of LLMs and the Anticip8 behavioral prediction engine, (ii) proposes targeted interventions, and (iii) estimates the impact of interventions on out-come probabilities. This enables SafeStep to select interventions that maximize the likelihood of the person reaching their destination. SafeStep was evaluated through experiments on travel graph generation and a field study involving 26 real-world journeys. Results showed that combining Anticip8 for failure pre-diction with GPT-based models for intervention evaluation yields the most re-liable performance. User feedback indicated that SafeStep improves confidence and perceived safety during travel, although interface usability needs to be im-proved for the target demographic. In the future, we would like to improve and release SafeStep. The AI system that was developed for SafeStep could be ap-plied in other areas, such as mental health, career coaching and addiction treatment.

AI.tldr: SafeStep is an AI-driven travel system for elderly users with frailty or dementia that uses a novel travel graph representation integrating route planning with predictive modeling to generate personalized failure scenarios, propose interventions, and estimate their impact on journey outcomes.
AI.motivation: Over one million people in the UK suffer from frailty or dementia, severely compromising their ability to travel independently in urban environments. There is a need for assistive technology to improve mobility confidence and safety for this vulnerable demographic.
AI.method: SafeStep employs a novel travel graph representation that integrates route planning with predictive modeling. For each journey stage, the system: (i) generates personalized failure scenarios using LLMs combined with the Anticip8 behavioral prediction engine, (ii) proposes targeted interventions, and (iii) estimates the impact of interventions on outcome probabilities. Interventions are selected to maximize the likelihood of reaching the destination. Evaluation involved travel graph generation experiments and a field study with 26 real-world journeys.
AI.result: Combining Anticip8 for failure prediction with GPT-based models for intervention evaluation yields the most reliable performance. User feedback showed that SafeStep improves confidence and perceived safety during travel, though interface usability requires improvement for the target demographic.
AI.conclusion: SafeStep demonstrates promise as an assistive travel system for elderly and cognitively impaired users. Future work involves improving and releasing the system, with potential applications in mental health, career coaching, and addiction treatment.

title: GPE: Evaluating Robust Evidence Aggregation for Fact Verification under Controllable GEO-Style Poisoning
summary: Large language models increasingly use search tools to retrieve up-to-date information, introducing a new attack surface in which retrieved documents can be manipulated. This risk is amplified by the development of generative engine optimization, which can make selected content more likely to be retrieved, cited, and adopted by models. Existing fact-verification benchmarks and evaluation frameworks do not provide the controlled evidence environments needed to assess robustness against GEO poisoning. We therefore propose GPE, which consists of a multi-domain fact-verification benchmark and an evaluation framework for controlling evidence sources and poisoning ratios. Experiments across multiple verification methods and poisoning attacks demonstrate that GPE exposes robustness degradation and efficiency trade-offs that cannot be observed through clean evaluation alone, confirming the need to evaluate fact verification under adversarial evidence environments.

AI.tldr: GPE is a benchmark and evaluation framework for assessing fact-verification robustness under adversarial evidence conditions, simulating generative engine optimization (GEO) poisoning attacks against LLMs that use search-augmented retrieval.
AI.motivation: LLMs increasingly rely on search tools for up-to-date information, but retrieved documents can be adversarially manipulated via GEO. Existing fact-verification benchmarks lack controlled evidence environments to test robustness against such poisoning, creating a critical evaluation gap.
AI.method: Proposes GPE, comprising (1) a multi-domain fact-verification benchmark and (2) an evaluation framework that allows controlled manipulation of evidence sources and poisoning ratios. Experiments apply multiple verification methods under various poisoning attacks.
AI.result: GPE reveals significant robustness degradation and efficiency trade-offs invisible under clean evaluation, confirming that adversarial evidence environments substantially impair fact-verification performance.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating fact verification solely on clean data is insufficient; adversarial evidence evaluation via frameworks like GPE is necessary to expose real-world vulnerabilities introduced by search-augmented retrieval and GEO poisoning.

title: Break Through the Compression Bottleneck: From Theory to Practice
summary: As the parameter size of language models continues to grow, effective model compression is required to reduce their computational and memory overhead. Existing compression methods suffer from bottleneck issues: when the compression ratio is increased, performance degrades significantly. Low-rank decomposition and quantization are two prominent compression methods that have been proven to significantly reduce the computational and memory requirements of Large Language Models (LLMs) while maintaining model accuracy. Evidently, combining these two methods will break through the existing compression bottleneck. However, how these two methods interact when combined remains a critical question for developers, as many assume they are orthogonal, meaning their combination would not introduce additional errors beyond those independently introduced by each method. This paper provides the first mathematical proof that low-rank decomposition and quantization are non-orthogonal. We validate these findings through a series of experiments on large language models. Our results demonstrate that these methods are non-orthogonal, and their combination leads to significant performance degradation. Importantly, we propose a novel approach Diagonal Adhesive Method (DAM), which can effectively combine the two methods and mitigate the performance loss. Our research provides deep insights into model compression and lays a solid theoretical and experimental foundation for future related studies.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that low-rank decomposition and quantization are non-orthogonal compression methods whose naive combination causes significant performance degradation, and proposes the Diagonal Adhesive Method (DAM) to effectively combine them with minimal loss.
AI.motivation: As LLMs grow in parameter size, model compression is essential. Low-rank decomposition and quantization are two leading methods, but existing compression approaches hit bottlenecks where high compression ratios severely degrade performance. While combining these two methods seems promising, developers commonly assume they are orthogonal — i.e., their combination introduces no additional error beyond each method's independent error. This paper challenges that assumption.
AI.method: The authors provide the first mathematical proof demonstrating that low-rank decomposition and quantization are non-orthogonal. They validate this theoretical finding through experiments on large language models, showing that naive combination leads to significant performance degradation. To address this, they propose the Diagonal Adhesive Method (DAM), a novel approach that effectively combines low-rank decomposition and quantization while mitigating performance loss.
AI.result: Experimental results confirm that low-rank decomposition and quantization are non-orthogonal, and their naive combination causes substantial performance degradation in LLMs. The proposed DAM approach successfully combines both methods while preserving model accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The non-orthogonality of low-rank decomposition and quantization has important implications for model compression. DAM provides an effective solution for combining these methods, offering both theoretical and experimental foundations for future research in hybrid compression techniques.

title: CLOE: Christoffel Loss Autoencoder for Anomaly Detection
summary: Semi-supervised anomaly detection plays a key role in diverse fields such as process monitoring, healthcare, and finance. However, lightweight methods often struggle with high-dimensional data and typically require careful tuning of multiple hyperparameters. Among existing approaches, Christoffel Function--based methods are attractive due to their simplicity, requiring at most a single hyperparameter. They also benefit from a well-established theoretical foundation that yields several interesting results for data science. However, their main limitation is poor scalability to high-dimensional settings. In this paper, we introduce CLOE, a new method that combines an autoencoder for dimensionality reduction with a Christoffel Function--based detector applied in the latent space. To better align representation learning with anomaly detection, we design a novel loss function that leverages the Christoffel Function to guide the autoencoder toward representations that better capture the support of the normal data distribution. We further propose a principled procedure to set the detection threshold and an efficient strategy to tune the single remaining hyperparameter. Experiments on multiple high-dimensional tabular anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that CLOE achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, while preserving the lightweight and low-tuning advantages of Christoffel Function--based approaches.

AI.tldr: CLOE combines an autoencoder for dimensionality reduction with a Christoffel Function-based anomaly detector in latent space, using a novel Christoffel-guided loss function. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on high-dimensional tabular anomaly detection while retaining the simplicity and low-tuning advantages of Christoffel-based methods.
AI.motivation: Christoffel Function-based anomaly detection methods are attractive for their simplicity (at most one hyperparameter) and strong theoretical foundation, but they suffer from poor scalability to high-dimensional data. There is a need to extend these methods to high-dimensional settings without sacrificing their lightweight nature.
AI.method: CLOE uses an autoencoder to reduce dimensionality, then applies a Christoffel Function-based detector in the latent space. A new loss function incorporating the Christoffel Function guides the autoencoder to learn representations that better capture the support of the normal data distribution. The authors also introduce a principled detection threshold-setting procedure and an efficient hyperparameter tuning strategy.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple high-dimensional tabular anomaly detection benchmarks show that CLOE outperforms existing methods while maintaining the lightweight and low-tuning benefits of Christoffel Function-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: CLOE successfully bridges the gap between Christoffel Function-based anomaly detection and high-dimensional data, delivering superior performance with minimal hyperparameter tuning.

title: Benchmarking the Personalization Capabilities of Large Language Models
summary: Personalization, the act of varying a message to induce action from a specific receiver while keeping sender, channel, and time fixed, has a long tradition in psychology and marketing as a two-party problem in which sender and receiver have independent objectives. Large language models remove the bounded-inventory constraint of classical retrieval-and-ranking approaches by generating a continuum of message variants conditioned on inferred receiver state, raising the question of how well current models perform personalization in the classical sense. Existing LLM personalization benchmarks measure sender-side adaptation, in which the receiver is the same user the model is serving. The two-party question, whether a generated message induces its intended action in a third party, has been investigated only through A/B tests and small-scale human studies that cannot be re-run against a new model on demand. We adapt the Bayesian Persuasion framework of Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) to generative agents and instantiate the formulation in sales, where receiver actions are routinely logged against the outreach that induced them. We release SDR-Bench, a public corpus of 6,279 customer success stories spanning 22 industries and approximately 200 enterprises, served through a temporally constrained simulation that prevents future-data leakage. Across frontier LLMs and deep-research agents, we observe a consistent personalization plateau and on a Fortune 100 tech cohort no model statistically separates successful from unsuccessful outreach. A field deployment with 12 professional sales representatives validates the framework, with 48 percent of model-generated content rated immediately useful and senior-expert agreement at Pearson 0.82. We release SDR-Arena and SDR-Bench publicly to support reproducible study of generative personalization at scale.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SDR-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based personalization in a classical two-party setting (sender→receiver), adapted from Bayesian Persuasion theory. Testing frontier LLMs reveals a "personalization plateau" where no model statistically distinguishes successful from unsuccessful outreach. A field study with sales professionals validates the framework, with 48% of generated content rated immediately useful and high inter-rater agreement (Pearson 0.82).
AI.motivation: Existing LLM personalization benchmarks only measure sender-side adaptation (same user as receiver), failing to test the classical two-party personalization problem where a message must induce action in a distinct third party. Prior two-party evaluations rely on non-reproducible A/B tests or small-scale human studies. A reproducible, at-scale benchmark is needed to assess whether generative models can effectively personalize messages to drive intended receiver actions.
AI.method: The authors adapt Kamenica and Gentzkow's Bayesian Persuasion framework to generative agents, formalizing personalization as a sender generating messages to induce receiver actions under information asymmetry. They instantiate this in sales—where receiver actions are logged against outreach—and construct SDR-Bench: 6,279 customer success stories across 22 industries and ~200 enterprises. A temporally constrained simulation prevents future-data leakage. They evaluate frontier LLMs and deep-research agents, then validate via a field deployment with 12 professional sales representatives, measuring immediate usefulness and inter-rater agreement.
AI.result: Across frontier LLMs and deep-research agents, a consistent personalization plateau is observed: no model statistically separates successful from unsuccessful outreach in a Fortune 100 tech cohort. In field validation, 48% of model-generated content was rated immediately useful by sales professionals, with senior-expert agreement reaching Pearson 0.82.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs exhibit a personalization plateau, failing to reliably distinguish effective from ineffective outreach in the classical two-party sense. The authors release SDR-Arena and SDR-Bench publicly to enable reproducible, at-scale study of generative personalization, providing a rigorous foundation for future progress.

title: Agentic Context Management: Solving Agent Memory and Cost by Treating Them as Lifecycle and Architecture Problems
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Evaluation harness and study data: github.com/maximem-ai
summary: Production AI agents' failures are less often due to an inability to reason well and more often because they cannot manage what is in their reasoning context: conversation histories, large prompts, large tool definitions, and ballooning tool outputs. Agents drown in their own accumulating history while paying a token cost that grows every turn, producing missing recalls within and across conversations. The incumbent response treats this as a storage-and-retrieval problem. We argue that framing is too narrow. Actively managing what an agent holds in mind is a lifecycle, not merely a store: it spans deciding what to remember, extracting and structuring it, choosing the right store per data type, consolidating and forgetting while preserving provenance, deciding what is relevant now, anticipating what is needed next, and compacting context to a budget without losing what matters. In serious production this operates not over a single user but across an organizational scope hierarchy. We name this discipline Agentic Context Management (ACM) and decompose it into five primitives: architecting, ingesting, scoping, anticipating, and compacting & consolidation. We then make the economic case: naive context accumulation grows token cost quadratically in conversation length, crude summarization buys linear cost at the price of an accuracy cliff, and only validated compaction achieves linear cost with preserved fidelity. We describe a reference implementation, Maximem Synap, that realizes the five primitives as a multi-tenant service and reports 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo under the configuration detailed in Section 6. We close with dimensions existing benchmarks do not yet capture, latency, token efficiency, and context-rot resistance, and the frontier of decision-level and organization-level context the category points toward.

AI.tldr: AI agents fail in production not from poor reasoning but from mismanaging their context window—conversation history, prompts, tool outputs accumulate and degrade performance. The paper proposes Agentic Context Management (ACM), decomposing it into five primitives (architecting, ingesting, scoping, anticipating, compacting & consolidation), makes an economic argument that naive accumulation costs grow quadratically while validated compaction yields linear cost with preserved fidelity, and presents Maximem Synap as a reference implementation achieving 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo.
AI.motivation: Production AI agents predominantly fail due to context mismanagement rather than reasoning deficiencies. Accumulating conversation histories, large prompts, extensive tool definitions, and ballooning tool outputs cause agents to "drown" in their own history, incurring growing per-turn token costs and producing missing recalls within/across conversations. The incumbent storage-and-retrieval framing is too narrow to address this lifecycle problem.
AI.method: The authors define Agentic Context Management (ACM) as a discipline decomposed into five primitives: (1) architecting — deciding what to remember; (2) ingesting — extracting and structuring information; (3) scoping — choosing the right store per data type; (4) anticipating — determining what is relevant now and needed next; (5) compacting & consolidation — forgetting while preserving provenance and compacting to a budget without losing fidelity. They formalize the economic case mathematically, showing quadratic token cost growth under naive accumulation, linear cost with an accuracy cliff under crude summarization, and linear cost with preserved fidelity under validated compaction. A reference implementation, Maximem Synap, is built as a multi-tenant service realizing all five primitives.
AI.result: Maximem Synap achieved 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo benchmarks under the configuration detailed in Section 6. The economic analysis demonstrates that only validated compaction achieves linear token cost scaling while maintaining accuracy, in contrast to quadratic costs from naive accumulation and accuracy degradation from crude summarization.
AI.conclusion: ACM represents a necessary evolution beyond storage-and-retrieval for production agents. The paper identifies dimensions that existing benchmarks fail to capture—latency, token efficiency, and context-rot resistance—and points toward future frontiers including decision-level and organization-level context management across organizational scope hierarchies.

title: StrideDiffusion: Accelerating Diffusion Models for Time-series Generation
summary: Diffusion models have become competitive generators for time series, but their practical use is limited by the large number of sequential denoising steps required at inference time. Existing fast samplers typically use fixed or generic timestep schedules, overlooking a distinctive property of time-series diffusion: different spectral bands evolve at different rates during the reverse process. We introduce StrideDiffusion, a training-free spectral-aware sampler that adaptively selects the denoising stride from band-level activity. At each step, StrideDiffusion monitors relative band energy, log-power drift, and phase velocity to identify whether high- frequency dynamics remain active or whether the trajectory is dominated by stable low-frequency structure. It then takes fine steps when rapidly varying bands are active and larger jumps once only coarse components remain. A bandwise stability analysis shows that inactive frequency bands change only linearly with the jump size under deterministic affine reverse updates, providing a local justification for spectral activity as a step-size indicator. Across six unconditional time-series generation benchmarks, StrideDiffusion uses only 14-66 function evaluations instead of 500/1000 denoising steps, achieving up to 18.9x wall-clock speedup while preserving or improving generation quality. On conditional imputation and forecasting, it further delivers 5-14x average acceleration with comparable predictive accuracy. These results show that spectral evolution provides a practical and principled signal for fast time-series diffusion sampling. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/stridediff-ts.

AI.tldr: StrideDiffusion is a training-free, spectral-aware sampler for time-series diffusion models that adaptively selects denoising stride lengths based on the activity level of different frequency bands, achieving up to 18.9× speedup with preserved or improved generation quality.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models for time series require many sequential denoising steps, limiting practical use. Existing fast samplers use fixed/generic timestep schedules and overlook a key property: different spectral bands evolve at different rates during the reverse diffusion process. This insight motivates an adaptive, band-aware sampling strategy.
AI.method: StrideDiffusion monitors three band-level metrics at each denoising step — relative band energy, log-power drift, and phase velocity — to classify whether high-frequency dynamics remain active or whether the trajectory is dominated by stable low-frequency structure. When rapidly varying bands are active, it takes fine (small-stride) steps; once only coarse components remain, it takes larger jumps. A bandwise stability analysis underpins this, showing that inactive frequency bands change only linearly with jump size under deterministic affine reverse updates.
AI.result: Across six unconditional time-series generation benchmarks, StrideDiffusion uses only 14–66 function evaluations (vs. 500/1000 baseline steps), achieving up to 18.9× wall-clock speedup while preserving or improving generation quality. On conditional imputation and forecasting tasks, it delivers 5–14× average acceleration with comparable predictive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Spectral evolution provides a practical and principled signal for accelerating time-series diffusion sampling. StrideDiffusion demonstrates that adaptive, band-level stride selection is both effective and theoretically grounded, enabling significant speedups without sacrificing quality across diverse time-series tasks.

title: Compact Latent Coordination for Autonomous Vehicles at Unsignalized Intersections
summary:
Coordinating autonomous vehicles at unsignalized intersections remains a critical challenge for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) systems, which typically struggle with combinatorial action spaces, reliance on privileged information, or rigid agent designs. We propose Master-Agent Proto-plan System (MAPS), a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning (DRL) architecture in which a centralized Master agent generates a compact, continuous embedding, denoted as proto-plan, that encodes a global coordination strategy. Decentralized Worker agents integrate this embedding with local observations to execute vehicle-specific control, decoupling strategic intent from tactical execution and enabling independent optimization of each module.
  As a proof-of-concept evaluation of this coordination mechanism, we test MAPS across 72 intersection configurations in HighwayEnv. MAPS achieves collision-free navigation while significantly reducing average travel time, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. The learned proto-plans further exhibit robust generalization: a system trained with three agents achieves a 94% success rate when deployed zero-shot to five-agent scenarios, confirming that proto-plan-based hierarchical learning provides a promising framework for multi-vehicle coordination.

AI.tldr: MAPS introduces a hierarchical DRL architecture with a centralized Master agent that generates continuous "proto-plan" embeddings for global coordination, which decentralized Worker agents use alongside local observations for vehicle-specific control, enabling collision-free navigation and strong zero-shot generalization in unsignalized intersection scenarios.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent reinforcement learning for autonomous vehicle coordination at unsignalized intersections suffers from combinatorial action spaces, dependence on privileged global information, and inflexible monolithic agent designs that conflate strategic coordination with tactical control.
AI.method: A hierarchical DRL architecture (MAPS) with two tiers: (1) a centralized Master agent that produces a compact, continuous proto-plan embedding encoding global coordination strategy; (2) decentralized Worker agents that condition their local policies on this embedding for vehicle-specific control. This decouples strategic intent from tactical execution, enabling independent optimization of each module.
AI.result: Evaluated across 72 intersection configurations in HighwayEnv, MAPS achieves collision-free navigation with significantly reduced average travel time versus state-of-the-art baselines. A model trained with three agents achieves 94% success rate when deployed zero-shot to five-agent scenarios, demonstrating robust generalization of the learned proto-plans.
AI.conclusion: Proto-plan-based hierarchical learning provides a promising framework for multi-vehicle coordination, effectively decoupling strategic planning from execution while enabling strong zero-shot generalization to larger agent counts.

title: IssueTrojanBench: Benchmarking AI Coding Agents Against Malicious Issue Requests
summary: AI coding agents powered by LLMs are increasingly integrated into real-world software development, where they generate, edit, and execute code with autonomous access to local files and tools. Coding agents inherit security risks from both the LLM backbone, where adversarial prompts, poisoned training data, and backdoor triggers can cause models to emit insecure or attacker-chosen code, and their agentic architecture, where tool-using autonomy enables induced misuse of external APIs, data exfiltration, and persistent compromise of development environments. This paper presents a systematic evaluation of malicious issue requests against state-of-the-art coding agents (Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex Desktop), powered by two major model families (OpenAI GPT-5.3 Codex/GPT-5.4 and Anthropic Sonnet 4.6). Our novel benchmark IssueTrojanBench contains malicious issues that are constructed based on four novel attack categories (i.e., embedded as malicious instructions in issues), six delivery vectors (e.g., PDF, or issue comment), and further augmented by perturbations. Our results reveal critical vulnerabilities in the as-deployed modern coding agents, i.e., 66.5% of the malicious issues from IssueTrojanBench penetrate all the guardrails (agent- and LLM-level) of coding agents. Our further analysis shows that rejection is almost entirely from LLMs rather than the agent frameworks, with GPT models broadly vulnerable and Sonnet 4.6 exhibiting more selective, risk-aware blocking of high-impact actions. Our evaluation also highlights that the current agent-level defense strategy offers limited additional protection for coding agents. Our findings highlight the urgent need for stronger agent- and model-level safety mechanisms to protect AI coding agents.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates the security vulnerabilities of AI coding agents (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex Desktop) against malicious issue requests. Using a novel benchmark (IssueTrojanBench) with four attack categories, six delivery vectors, and adversarial perturbations, the authors find that 66.5% of malicious issues bypass all guardrails, with LLM-level rejection being the primary (and insufficient) defense mechanism.
AI.motivation: AI coding agents are increasingly deployed in real-world software development with autonomous access to files, tools, and APIs. They inherit dual security risks: (1) LLM-level vulnerabilities from adversarial prompts, poisoned data, and backdoors, and (2) agent-level risks from tool-use autonomy enabling data exfiltration and persistent environment compromise. No prior work has systematically evaluated how these combined risks manifest in production coding agents.
AI.method: The authors construct IssueTrojanBench, a benchmark of malicious issue requests organized around four novel attack categories (embedded malicious instructions in issues), six delivery vectors (e.g., PDF files, issue comments), and adversarial perturbations to evade detection. They evaluate three state-of-the-art coding agents — Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex Desktop — powered by two model families (OpenAI GPT-5.3 Codex/GPT-5.4 and Anthropic Sonnet 4.6), measuring penetration rates through both agent-level and LLM-level guardrails.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) 66.5% of malicious issues from IssueTrojanBench successfully penetrate all guardrails. (2) Rejection is almost entirely attributable to LLM-level safeguards rather than agent-framework protections. (3) GPT models are broadly vulnerable, while Sonnet 4.6 shows more selective, risk-aware blocking focused on high-impact actions. (4) Current agent-level defense strategies provide limited additional protection beyond what the underlying LLM already offers.
AI.conclusion: Modern coding agents exhibit critical vulnerabilities to malicious issue-based attacks, with defenses relying almost exclusively on the underlying LLM. The agent frameworks themselves contribute negligible protection. The authors call for urgent development of stronger, multi-layered safety mechanisms at both the agent and model levels to secure AI coding agents in production environments.

title: Making Open-Source Text LLM Watermarks Durable Against Merging
summary: Open-source LLMs (OSMs)arereaching near state-of-the-art performance, prompting prior works to trace the text they generate by embedding text watermarking algorithms directly into their weights. Yet, OSMs are subject to post-training modifications, which has been shown to remove the watermark. Model merging in particular, a prominent method used for combining expert knowledge and preventing catastrophic forgetting, strongly removes such OSM watermarks. A key question is how to enable OSM watermarks that survive subsequent merging. In this work, we show for the first time how to design an OSM watermark that is durable against model merging. We propose Merge-Adversarial Training, an adversarial training algorithm to distill text watermarks into model weights while being robust to subsequent model merging. Our approach consistently outperforms all baselines (e.g. with SLERP up to +51 percentage points (pp) TPR@1%FPR with +25 pp on average) while preserving downstream capabilities. We also for the first time evaluate OSM watermarks against realistic merge scenarios, representing common use-cases such as combining expert capabilities or preventing catastrophic forgetting, and with 3 prominent merging algorithms. More broadly, our findings suggest that adversarial training is a reliable approach for increasing OSM watermark durability against post-training modifications.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Merge-Adversarial Training (MAT), an adversarial training method to embed text watermarks into open-source LLM weights that survive model merging. MAT consistently outperforms baselines, achieving up to +51 pp TPR@1%FPR improvement, while maintaining downstream task performance.
AI.motivation: Open-source LLMs can have embedded text watermarks, but post-training modifications—particularly model merging (used for combining expert knowledge and preventing catastrophic forgetting)—can effectively remove these watermarks. The central challenge is designing watermarks durable enough to survive merging.
AI.method: The authors propose Merge-Adversarial Training (MAT), an adversarial training algorithm that distills text watermarks into model weights while explicitly optimizing for robustness against subsequent model merging. They evaluate across 3 merging algorithms (including SLERP) and realistic merge scenarios representing common use-cases like expert capability combination and catastrophic forgetting prevention.
AI.result: MAT consistently outperforms all baselines. With SLERP merging, it achieves up to +51 percentage points improvement in TPR@1%FPR, with an average improvement of +25 pp. The method preserves downstream model capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Adversarial training is a reliable approach for increasing OSM watermark durability against post-training modifications. This is the first work to both design a merge-durable watermark and evaluate OSM watermarks against realistic merge scenarios.

title: Position: Stop Reactively Patching Your Model Every Time and Start Proactive Test-Driven AI Development
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026 Position Paper Track. 18 pages
summary: Many modern AI systems are designed to operate under diverse, open-ended, use-cases. To help generalize deployed systems, many deployed-system maintenance pipelines use a reactive AI flywheel that observes emerging feedback from user behavior (errors) and patches the model accordingly. However, when used as the primary maintenance mechanism, these flywheels often ignore the broader context of these errors within the system's objectives, failing to preempt potential future edge cases, which leads to more unnecessary flywheel iterations. Also, it is statistically increasingly difficult to collect remaining errors due to the long-tail nature of open-world use-cases. This position paper argues that a proactive test-driven flywheel is required to address reactive flywheel's limitations and to approach a generalizable system. We advocate for creating a "test space" to technically map feedback data to task objectives, evolving the flywheel from reactive to proactive. We augment our position by mathematically proving a proactive one achieves better long-term scaling with fewer iterations than the reactive flywheel.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that reactive AI flywheels — which patch models based on observed user errors — are insufficient for long-term generalization due to their failure to anticipate future edge cases and the statistical difficulty of collecting rare errors in long-tail distributions. The authors propose a proactive, test-driven flywheel that maps feedback to a structured "test space" aligned with task objectives, and mathematically prove this approach achieves better long-term scaling with fewer iterations.
AI.motivation: Reactive AI maintenance flywheels, which only respond to observed errors, suffer from two critical limitations: (1) they ignore the broader context of errors relative to system objectives, failing to preempt future edge cases, and (2) they face diminishing returns in collecting remaining errors due to the long-tail nature of open-world use-cases. This motivates the need for a proactive alternative.
AI.method: The authors propose a proactive test-driven flywheel that creates a "test space" to technically map feedback data to task objectives. This transforms the maintenance loop from purely reactive patching to anticipatory improvement. They support their position with a mathematical proof demonstrating that the proactive approach achieves superior long-term scaling efficiency with fewer iterations than the reactive flywheel.
AI.result: The paper presents a mathematical proof showing that a proactive test-driven flywheel achieves better long-term scaling and requires fewer iterations compared to a reactive flywheel for maintaining AI systems in open-world use-cases.
AI.conclusion: A proactive, test-driven flywheel is necessary to overcome the inherent limitations of reactive maintenance pipelines. By structurally mapping feedback to task objectives via a test space, systems can anticipate edge cases rather than merely react to them, enabling more generalizable and efficiently maintained AI systems.

title: Robust Critics: Defending LLMs Against Multi-Turn Attacks
summary:
When a user asks a language model something harmful, is it a genuine attack or a misunderstood but well-meaning question? This ambiguity is one of the central challenges of LLM safety. A model that assumes the worst harms legitimate users; one that assumes the best is easily exploited. The problem is compounded in multi-turn dialogue, where an attacker's true intent may only reveal itself gradually across many exchanges, yet existing safety frameworks apply a contextual bandit treatment, ignoring the trajectory of the conversation.
  To that end, we propose Dialogue Critic Guided Sampling (DCGS), a framework that addresses this by inferring user intent at every turn of dialogue. Instead of applying a fixed rule about what is or is not safe, DCGS learns what the user's intent is likely to be based on the full conversational history and generates responses accordingly. Formally, we model adversarial dialogue as a Markov Decision Process and learn value and regret-based critics at both the individual token and utterance (full response) levels, scoring candidate responses via an action-value critic. We prove that this inference-time reweighting approximates exponential tilting of the base policy, guaranteeing improvement in expected return for any finite candidate pool, a property that group-relative objectives do not exhibit. Evaluated on CARES-18k, WildJailbreak, Redbench, and Harmbench, DCGS outperforms strong robust baselines and frontier models on adversarial dialogue tasks. DCGS also transfers to frontier models, improving their robustness without fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: DCGS is a multi-turn dialogue safety framework that infers user intent from conversational history using MDP-based value/regret critics, rather than applying fixed safety rules. It approximates exponential tilting of the base policy, guaranteeing expected return improvement, and outperforms baselines on adversarial dialogue benchmarks while transferring to frontier models without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: The central challenge is ambiguity in user queries: harmful-looking prompts may be genuine attacks or misunderstood legitimate questions. Existing LLM safety frameworks treat each turn independently (contextual bandit approach), ignoring conversational trajectory where malicious intent may only emerge gradually across multiple turns. A model that is too cautious harms legitimate users; one that is too permissive is easily exploited.
AI.method: DCGS models adversarial dialogue as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and learns value and regret-based critics at both token-level and utterance-level granularity. Candidate responses are scored via an action-value critic. The inference-time reweighting approximates exponential tilting of the base policy. The framework infers user intent at every turn based on full conversational history and generates responses accordingly.
AI.result: DCGS outperforms strong robust baselines and frontier models on CARES-18k, WildJailbreak, Redbench, and Harmbench. The method also transfers to frontier models, improving their adversarial robustness without requiring fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Inferring user intent dynamically from multi-turn conversational history is more effective than static safety rules. The MDP formulation with value/regret critics provides theoretical guarantees (exponential tilting) and practical gains in adversarial dialogue safety, with the added benefit of transferability to existing frontier models.

title: Can Valence Reflect Morality in Natural Language? A Preliminary Annotation Study
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, submitted to the 36th Irish Signals and Systems Conference
summary: Present implementations of artificial intelligence (AI) ethics do not adequately take feelings, or affect, into account. If AI should be aligned with human ethics, it seems reasonable to thoroughly investigate the possibility of AI behaviour that mirrors virtuous human ethical conduct, where feelings play a role in the actions, judgements or statements one makes. Furthermore, while prominent theories of normative ethics are often discussed in terms of their differences and shortcomings, Virtue, Consequentialist, and Kantian Deontological ethics all share a common feature of considering human feeling to some degree while the popular descriptive ethics theory, Moral Foundations Theory, positions feelings as central to many of its foundations. Therefore, in the present paper, a data set of moral valence is proposed, consisting of 500 annotations by six human participants for both action/judgement and consequence moral valence, ranging from -1 to 1 for text-presented scenarios from the Commonsense Norm Bank data set. The resulting valence features share significant relationships with multi-class (immoral/discretionary/moral) and binary immoral/moral categories while additionally providing a noteworthy test set Matthew's correlation coefficient of 0.764 using regularised logistic regression for binary classification. This provides early evidence of the usefulness of valence features for morality estimation of text, indicating that valenced consequences of responses for others can be considered toward more human morally-aligned AI. In the interest of promoting further affective-moral computing research, this study's annotations will be made available for research on request.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that AI ethics overlooks the role of affect/feelings in moral reasoning. The authors create a moral valence dataset (500 annotations from 6 annotators on Commonsense Norm Bank scenarios) and demonstrate that valence features significantly predict moral categories, achieving a Matthew's correlation coefficient of 0.764 for binary immoral/moral classification via regularised logistic regression.
AI.motivation: Current AI ethics implementations fail to incorporate affect (feelings), despite the fact that major ethical theories—Virtue Ethics, Consequentialism, Deontology, and Moral Foundations Theory—all centrally involve human feelings in moral judgment. Aligning AI with human ethics therefore requires investigating how valenced, feeling-informed moral behaviour can be computationally modeled.
AI.method: Six human annotators rated 500 text scenarios from the Commonsense Norm Bank on two dimensions: action/judgement moral valence and consequence moral valence, each on a continuous scale from -1 to 1. The resulting valence features were then evaluated against existing multi-class (immoral/discretionary/moral) and binary (immoral/moral) labels, using regularised logistic regression to test predictive power, with performance measured by Matthew's correlation coefficient.
AI.result: The valence features showed significant relationships with both multi-class and binary moral categories. For binary classification (immoral vs. moral), regularised logistic regression achieved a Matthew's correlation coefficient of 0.764 on the test set, providing preliminary evidence that valence features are useful for morality estimation in text.
AI.conclusion: Moral valence, particularly the valenced consequences of actions for others, represents a promising signal for building more human-like, morally-aligned AI systems. The authors commit to releasing their annotations to encourage further research in affective-moral computing.

title: Toward Continuous Assurance for the Democratization of AI Agent Creation in Industry
summary: AI agents are increasingly created inside organizations by non-engineering users through low-code, no-code, and conversational development environments. This democratization enables rapid local innovation, but it also creates a reliability gap: agents that appear to users as simple productivity artifacts may depend on changing models, tools, retrieval sources, permissions, prompts, schedules, and external services. These dependencies can cause silent degradation long after deployment, even when no user directly modifies the agent. This paper identifies the reliability challenge created by democratized AI agent creation and proposes a lightweight continuous-assurance framework for citizen-created organizational agents. The framework combines dependency mapping, readiness contracts, scheduled checks, diagnostics, and lifecycle governance to assess whether an agent remains operationally ready under expected conditions. We also present an initial prototype auditor and scenario-based assessment showing how the proposed taxonomy can be translated into practical checks and actionable remediation guidance.

AI.tldr: Democratized AI agent creation via low-code/no-code platforms introduces a "reliability gap" where agents silently degrade post-deployment due to dependency drift. This paper proposes a lightweight continuous-assurance framework — encompassing dependency mapping, readiness contracts, scheduled checks, diagnostics, and lifecycle governance — to ensure citizen-created agents remain operationally ready, supported by a prototype auditor and scenario-based validation.
AI.motivation: As non-engineering users increasingly build AI agents through low-code, no-code, and conversational interfaces, organizations face a novel reliability challenge. These agents have hidden, evolving dependencies (models, tools, retrieval sources, permissions, prompts, schedules, external services) that can silently degrade functionality long after deployment — even without direct user modification. This "reliability gap" between perceived simplicity and actual operational fragility motivates the need for systematic assurance mechanisms tailored to citizen developers.
AI.method: The paper proposes a lightweight continuous-assurance framework comprising five components: (1) dependency mapping to catalog all agent dependencies; (2) readiness contracts that define expected operational conditions; (3) scheduled checks for periodic validation; (4) diagnostics to identify failure points; and (5) lifecycle governance for ongoing management. The approach is validated through an initial prototype auditor implementation and a scenario-based assessment demonstrating how the taxonomy translates into practical, actionable checks and remediation guidance.
AI.result: The paper delivers a taxonomy of agent dependencies and failure modes, a structured continuous-assurance framework, and an initial prototype auditor. Scenario-based evaluation demonstrates that the framework can be operationalized into concrete checks, with corresponding remediation recommendations for detected issues.
AI.conclusion: Democratized AI agent creation demands lightweight, automated reliability assurance that bridges the gap between ease of creation and long-term operational robustness. The proposed framework offers a practical path toward ensuring citizen-built agents remain reliable without requiring deep engineering expertise from their creators.

title: Classical Acceptance Is Not Hybrid Authentication: Measuring X.509 Verifier Semantics in Post-Quantum Migration
comment: 37 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. Submitted to Computers & Security
summary: A relying party validating a hybrid X.509 certificate --- carrying both a classical and a post-quantum credential --- must distinguish whether its accepting judgment rests on the post-quantum evidence or only on the classical path. To preserve compatibility, the separable designs place that evidence where classical path validation may ignore it. A verifier can then validate the classical path and accept while the post-quantum evidence never bears on the decision --- a valid classical result silently promoted to a hybrid conclusion it did not establish. We measure this across eight path-validation stacks (seven independent codebases), in nine validation modes, over six certificate schemes. Under a hybrid-required policy, nearly every stack parsing a separable hybrid certificate accepts on the classical path without making the post-quantum evidence outcome-bearing; one enforcing mode instead fractures interoperability over a signature-input encoding not yet interoperably profiled; and stacks that verify post-quantum signatures still do not enforce the binding by default: the gap is structural, not explained by missing primitive capability alone. Under lifecycle desynchronization the downgrade is realized: when a bound post-quantum credential is revoked while the classical certificate stays valid, the default path still accepts, because the bound credential lies outside the decision's scope. Binding success is not authentication success. We contribute a specification-derived verifier model and an executable, policy-parametric reference contract --- what a verifier must recognize, verify, make outcome-bearing, and check before reporting a validation as hybrid --- with a diagnosis of why standards do not require it.

AI.tldr: Hybrid X.509 certificates can silently degrade to classical-only validation because post-quantum evidence is structurally placed outside the decision path. The authors demonstrate this across seven independent codebases, showing that even when PQ signatures verify, the binding is not enforced by default — and lifecycle desynchronization (e.g., PQ credential revocation) makes the downgrade real.
AI.motivation: Hybrid X.509 certificates aim to combine classical and post-quantum credentials for transitional security. However, the authors identify a critical structural flaw: verifiers may accept a certificate as "hybrid" while only validating the classical path, silently discarding post-quantum evidence. The paper measures how pervasive this downgrade is across real-world implementations and diagnoses why standards fail to prevent it.
AI.method: The authors construct a specification-derived verifier model and evaluate eight path-validation stacks (seven independent codebases) across nine validation modes and six certificate schemes. They test separable hybrid certificate designs under hybrid-required policies, measure whether post-quantum evidence becomes outcome-bearing, examine behavior under lifecycle desynchronization (revoking the PQ credential while the classical certificate remains valid), and analyze standards to identify why binding enforcement is not mandated.
AI.result: Nearly every stack accepting a separable hybrid certificate under hybrid-required policy does so via the classical path alone, without making post-quantum evidence outcome-bearing. One enforcement mode fractures interoperability over unsigned signature-input encoding. Stacks that verify PQ signatures still fail to enforce the binding by default — the gap is structural, not merely a missing primitive. Under lifecycle desynchronization, a revoked PQ credential with a still-valid classical certificate is still accepted, confirming the downgrade is realizable in practice.
AI.conclusion: Binding success is not authentication success. The paper contributes a specification-derived verifier model and a policy-parametric reference contract specifying what a verifier must recognize, verify, make outcome-bearing, and check before reporting hybrid validation. It diagnoses why current standards do not require such enforcement, highlighting a fundamental architectural gap in hybrid certificate deployment.

title: Grounding Investor Views: Neural Predicates in the Black-Litterman Model
summary: Portfolio construction under the Black-Litterman model requires investors to specify views on asset returns alongside explicit uncertainty estimates -- a process that remains largely subjective and difficult to scale. We propose a formal approach in which neural predicates serve as a structured, probabilistic mechanism for view generation. In our formulation, structured financial analysis data is processed through a compositional hierarchy of neural predicates whose outputs -- probability distributions over market stances -- are mapped to the pick matrix $\mathbf{P}$, the view return vector $\mathbf{q}$, and the view uncertainty matrix $\boldsymbolΩ$ of the Black-Litterman model. View confidence is derived from predicate output distributions, providing a data-driven alternative to subjective uncertainty elicitation. The resulting approach is interpretable, in the sense that any portfolio weight can be traced back through the predicate's logical chain to the underlying data, and fully differentiable, enabling end-to-end learning.

AI.tldr: Proposes a neural predicate framework for automated Black-Litterman view generation, where compositional neural predicates output probabilistic market stances mapped to P, q, and Ω matrices, yielding an interpretable and fully differentiable portfolio construction pipeline.
AI.motivation: Traditional Black-Litterman model requires manual specification of views and uncertainty estimates, which is subjective, difficult to scale, and lacks data-driven grounding. There is a need for an automated, principled mechanism to generate views with calibrated confidence from structured financial data.
AI.method: A compositional hierarchy of neural predicates processes structured financial analysis data. Each predicate outputs a probability distribution over market stances. These distributions are formally mapped to the three key Black-Litterman inputs: the pick matrix P (asset selection), the view return vector q (expected return views), and the diagonal view uncertainty matrix Ω (confidence derived from output distribution entropy/concentration), enabling fully differentiable end-to-end learning.
AI.result: The approach yields an interpretable portfolio construction system where any portfolio weight can be traced back through the predicate logical chain to underlying data, while maintaining full differentiability for end-to-end optimization.
AI.conclusion: Neural predicates offer a scalable, data-driven, and interpretable alternative to subjective view specification in Black-Litterman, bridging structured financial analysis with formal portfolio optimization in a differentiable framework.

title: Incomplete Prompt Jailbreaks in Large Language Models
comment: Accepted to ACL 2026 Findings. 15 pages (9 pages for main body), 13 figures
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly released as open-weight models with safeguards against harmful requests. Nevertheless, sentence completion remains vulnerable to incomplete harmful prompts. In this work, we formalize this phenomenon as incomplete prompt jailbreaks (IPJ) and provide a systematic empirical characterization of when and how incomplete prompts elicit harmful continuations. We analyze diverse attractor types associated with incomplete sentence continuation and show that LLMs systematically delay refusal until sentence termination. We further demonstrate that training models to refuse incomplete harmful prompts via parameter tuning is insufficient, failing to generalize across both content domains and attractor types. To enable fine-grained control, we identify two functional neurons: termination and continuation neurons. By clarifying their roles in sentence completion, we highlight the potential of neuron-level interventions for more precise and robust IPJ defenses.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes "incomplete prompt jailbreaks" (IPJ), where LLMs delay refusal until sentence completion, systematically characterizes this vulnerability across attractor types, shows parameter tuning fails to generalize, and identifies termination/continuation neurons for neuron-level defense interventions.
AI.motivation: Despite open-weight LLMs being released with safety safeguards, they remain vulnerable to incomplete harmful prompts that elicit harmful completions by exploiting the models' tendency to complete sentences before refusing. This vulnerability lacks formal characterization and robust defenses.
AI.method: The authors (1) formalize IPJ and empirically characterize when/how incomplete prompts elicit harmful continuations across diverse attractor types; (2) evaluate parameter-tuning defenses for generalization across content domains and attractor types; (3) identify and analyze two functional neuron types — termination neurons and continuation neurons — that govern sentence completion behavior.
AI.result: LLMs systematically delay refusal until sentence termination, making incomplete prompts a reliable jailbreak vector. Parameter tuning to refuse incomplete harmful prompts fails to generalize across both content domains and attractor types. Two functional neuron categories (termination and continuation) are identified, with distinct roles in sentence completion that can be leveraged for fine-grained IPJ defense.
AI.conclusion: IPJ represents a systematic vulnerability rooted in LLMs' sentence completion mechanisms. Training-based defenses are insufficient due to generalization failures, but neuron-level interventions targeting termination and continuation neurons offer a promising path toward precise and robust IPJ defenses.

title: Representation Robustness Under Executable Reasoning Constraints in Large Language Models for Mathematical Problem Solving
comment: presented at the 28th International Conference on Human-Computer Interaction (2026), Montreal, Canada
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated on mathematical problem solving, yet prior work often treats representationally equivalent formulations as interchangeable and conflates reasoning errors with interface failures. This paper investigates representation robustness in LLM-based mathematical problem solving by systematically varying surface representations of the same underlying problems, including story problems, word-equations, symbolic equations, and isomorphic paraphrases. Using a curated dataset of mathematically equivalent problems, we evaluate five contemporary LLMs under a direct answer generation condition. We find substantial representational sensitivity: models frequently change correctness across equivalent formulations, with nontrivial flip rates across story, symbolic, and word-equation variants. We also observe systematic regressions under isomorphic reformulations, showing that even subtle paraphrase-level changes can degrade performance despite preserved mathematical structure. We then evaluate a code-augmented condition in which models externalize reasoning as executable Python code that is run locally for validation. This interface reveals strong latent reasoning capability in some models that perform poorly under direct prompting, but it does not uniformly improve robustness. Instead, failures shift across interaction layers, from opaque reasoning errors to protocol violations and execution failures. Even when executable reasoning succeeds, representation sensitivity often persists. Overall, our results show that reasoning scaffolds do not eliminate representational brittleness, but expose new tradeoffs among correctness, reliability, latency, and cost. We argue that representation should be treated as a first-class interface design variable in LLM evaluation and deployment, especially for AI-assisted problem-solving systems.

AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit significant sensitivity to surface representation in mathematical problem solving—equivalent problems phrased as stories, word-equations, or symbolic equations yield inconsistent correctness. Code-augmented reasoning reveals latent capabilities but does not eliminate representational brittleness, instead shifting failures from reasoning errors to protocol/execution failures. Representation should be a first-class design variable in LLM evaluation.
AI.motivation: Prior work on LLM mathematical reasoning treats representationally equivalent problem formulations as interchangeable and conflates genuine reasoning errors with interface-level failures. The authors aim to systematically disentangle these by testing whether LLMs are robust to surface-level representational variation when the underlying mathematical structure is held constant.
AI.method: The authors curate a dataset of mathematically equivalent problems spanning four representational variants: story problems, word-equations, symbolic equations, and isomorphic paraphrases. Five contemporary LLMs are evaluated under (1) a direct answer generation condition and (2) a code-augmented condition where models externalize reasoning as executable Python code validated locally. Correctness, flip rates, and failure modes (reasoning errors vs. protocol violations vs. execution failures) are compared across representations and conditions.
AI.result: Under direct prompting, models show substantial representational sensitivity with nontrivial flip rates across story, symbolic, and word-equation variants. Even subtle isomorphic paraphrases systematically degrade performance.
