The code-augmented condition reveals strong latent reasoning in some poorly-performing models but does not uniformly improve robustness; instead, failures shift from opaque reasoning errors to protocol violations and execution failures. Representational sensitivity often persists even when executable reasoning succeeds.
AI.conclusion: Representation should be treated as a first-class interface design variable in LLM evaluation and deployment. Reasoning scaffolds (like code execution) do not eliminate representational brittleness but expose new tradeoffs among correctness, reliability, latency, and cost—critical considerations for AI-assisted problem-solving systems.

title: The Boundaries of Automation: A Theory of Persistent Human Participation
summary: The rapid progress of AI has intensified the long-standing pursuit of automation: replacing human participation with algorithms wherever possible. Implicit in this pursuit is the assumption that humans remain in the loop only because current AI systems are not yet sufficiently capable. This paper challenges that assumption. Rather than asking how far automation can extend, we ask where its conceptual limits lie and argue that human participation may persist even with highly capable AI systems for three distinct reasons. Technical or complementarity grounds arise when humans contribute capabilities or perspectives unavailable to AI. Normative or developmental grounds arise when participation itself is valuable for human agency or learning. Most importantly, emergence grounds arise from target emergence: in some activities, the target is not fully specified in advance but instead emerges through the interaction itself. In these cases, human participation is not merely a means of improving execution but is constitutive of the target being produced. Human--AI co-construction, understood as the joint production of outcomes by humans and AI systems, is therefore not simply a temporary response to imperfect AI, but a persistent feature of activities whose objectives emerge through participation. This perspective has important implications for the limits of automation and for the design, evaluation, and ethics of future AI systems.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the assumption that human participation in AI workflows is merely a temporary limitation of current technology. It argues that human involvement persists for three reasons: technical/complementarity grounds (humans provide capabilities AI lacks), normative/developmental grounds (participation itself has intrinsic value), and emergence grounds (some targets are constituted through the interaction itself). The concept of human-AI co-construction is thus a persistent feature, not a transitional phenomenon.
AI.motivation: To question the dominant automation-centric narrative in AI development, which assumes that replacing humans with algorithms is always desirable and that human-in-the-loop arrangements exist only because AI is insufficiently capable. The paper seeks to identify the conceptual (rather than merely technological) limits of automation.
AI.method: Conceptual/philosophical analysis. The paper develops a three-part taxonomy of grounds for persistent human participation — technical/complementarity, normative/developmental, and emergence — with particular emphasis on the novel concept of "target emergence," where objectives are not fully pre-specified but are constituted through the participatory interaction itself.
AI.result: The analysis yields the concept of human-AI co-construction: joint production of outcomes where human participation is constitutive of the target, not merely instrumental to its execution. This reframes human involvement as a persistent structural feature of certain activity classes, not a temporary workaround for AI limitations.
AI.conclusion: Automation has conceptual limits rooted in the nature of certain activities where targets emerge through participation. This has significant implications for how AI systems should be designed, evaluated, and governed ethically — shifting from a mindset of eventual full automation toward durable frameworks for human-AI co-construction.

title: Which Model Is Actually Serving You? IRIS: Budgeted Black-Box Auditing of Model Substitution and Routing Dilution in LLM Gateways
summary: Commercial LLM gateways mediate access to hosted models, but the served backend may not match the advertised one: it may substitute a cheaper model on every request or route only a fraction $ε$ of requests to it. Prior black-box auditors often need a privileged signal (log-probabilities, token ranks, or reference samples) or a target-specific probe, fix the query budget in advance, and return a yes/no verdict. We present $\mathrm{IRIS}$, an audit that needs only the returned text: it asks endpoints to generate random numbers or strings, fingerprints the backend, and is the first to combine, in one text-only audit, detection of whole-stream substitution and fractional dilution, attribution of the served backend, routing-fraction ($ε$) estimation, and a query budget it sizes itself. A cheap pilot fits the exponential query-error decay and freezes that budget before any suspect query is issued. On an intra-family Qwen3 ladder $\mathrm{IRIS}$ verifies the backend at $0.99$ AUROC and sharpens attribution as queries accumulate; across a commercial OpenRouter library it catches $ε{=}0.3$ dilution on margin-qualified pairs at $0.85$ mean power ($0.017$ false-positive rate) and recovers $ε$ to within $0.04$ for enrolled diluents; and a live cross-provider audit flags $14$ of $15$ same-model provider pairs by genuine quantization and kernel deviations, corroborated on third-party MET traces. Against comparable black-box auditors, $\mathrm{IRIS}$ matches or beats detection on shared tasks, and adaptive allocation lifts the matched-budget target-hit rate from $73$% to $87$%. Further experiments cover adversarial gateways, knob identifiability, unseen diluents, and false-positive control.

AI.tldr: IRIS is a black-box audit that detects model substitution and dilution in LLM gateways using only returned text. It fingerprints backends via random number/string generation, estimates routing fractions, and dynamically sizes its query budget. It achieves high detection rates across intra-family, cross-provider, and commercial settings.
AI.motivation: Commercial LLM gateways may dishonestly substitute cheaper models (whole-stream substitution) or route only a fraction of requests to the advertised model (fractional dilution). Prior auditing methods require privileged signals (log-probabilities, token ranks) or fixed query budgets and only return binary verdicts. A text-only, budget-adaptive, multi-capability audit is needed.
AI.method: IRIS prompts endpoints to generate random numbers or strings and fingerprints the backend from the output distribution. It uses a cheap pilot phase to fit an exponential query-error decay curve, freezing the query budget before issuing suspect queries. It supports: (1) detection of whole-stream substitution, (2) fractional dilution detection, (3) backend attribution, (4) routing-fraction (ε) estimation. The method works across intra-family (Qwen3), cross-provider (OpenRouter), and live settings, with adaptive allocation to boost target-hit rate.
AI.result: On Qwen3 intra-family: 0.99 AUROC verification, improving attribution with more queries. On OpenRouter: catches ε=0.3 dilution with 0.85 mean power at 0.017 FPR; recovers ε within 0.04. Live cross-provider audit flags 14/15 same-model pairs via quantization/kernel deviations, corroborated by MET traces. Against comparable black-box auditors, IRIS matches or beats detection; adaptive allocation lifts matched-budget target-hit rate from 73% to 87%.
AI.conclusion: IRIS is the first text-only audit to unify substitution detection, dilution detection, backend attribution, ε estimation, and self-sizing query budgets. It demonstrates strong empirical performance across diverse settings and provides robustness analyses covering adversarial gateways, knob identifiability, unseen diluents, and false-positive control.

title: A Graph Neural Network approach to zero-shot Digital Twins
summary: Traditional Predictive Digital Twins often remain geometrically rigid, requiring extensive retraining or fine-tuning whenever the underlying physical domain or boundary conditions change. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel framework for \textit{Zero-Shot Digital Twins} that seamlessly couples real-time visual perception with a geometry-agnostic, physics-informed reasoning engine. At the core of our architecture is the Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network architecture, a Geometric Deep Learning solver grounded in a metriplectic thermodynamic formalism that enforces energy conservation and non-negative entropy production locally through graph message passing. The framework integrates an auxiliary Graph Neural Network to infer unobservable fields (such as stress tensors or velocity and energy distributions) directly from sparse initial visual boundaries, mitigating numerical start-up transients. To bridge the sim-to-real gap, we implement a continuous closed-loop data assimilation mechanism; the pipeline tracks macroscopic deformations and free-surface fluid boundaries in real-time using deep segmentation networks combined with sparse optical flow, dynamically correcting the autoregressive simulation rollout and eliminating numerical drift. To test the validity of our approach, we demonstrate the extreme generalization capabilities of our approach across two disparate physical regimes: the large deformations of a viscoelastic beam and the non-linear sloshing of a viscous fluid. In both scenarios, the unified framework instantiates physically accurate simulations on novel, unseen geometries without case-specific retraining, operating well within real-time latency budgets (approximately 25 ms per frame) and enabling the direct projection of latent mechanical variables via Augmented Reality.

AI.tldr: A framework for Zero-Shot Digital Twins that couples real-time visual perception with a geometry-agnostic physics engine (Thermodynamics-Informed GNN), enabling physically accurate simulations on unseen geometries without retraining, operating at ~25ms/frame with AR projection.
AI.motivation: Traditional Predictive Digital Twins are geometrically rigid, requiring costly retraining or fine-tuning whenever domain geometry or boundary conditions change. There is a need for a framework that generalizes to novel, unseen geometries without case-specific retraining while maintaining real-time performance.
AI.method: The framework combines: (1) A Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network (TIGNN) grounded in metriplectic thermodynamics, enforcing local energy conservation and non-negative entropy production via graph message passing; (2) An auxiliary GNN to infer unobservable fields (stress tensors, velocity/energy distributions) from sparse visual boundaries; (3) A closed-loop data assimilation pipeline using deep segmentation networks with sparse optical flow to track deformations and free-surface boundaries in real-time, dynamically correcting autoregressive simulation rollout to eliminate numerical drift.
AI.result: The unified framework demonstrated extreme generalization across two disparate physical regimes — large deformations of a viscoelastic beam and non-linear sloshing of a viscous fluid — instantiating physically accurate simulations on novel, unseen geometries without case-specific retraining, all within approximately 25ms per frame latency.
AI.conclusion: Zero-Shot Digital Twins are feasible and effective, enabling geometry-agnostic, physically consistent real-time simulation with sim-to-real gap closure via continuous data assimilation, opening the door to AR-based projection of latent mechanical variables in practical applications.

title: VeriSimpl: Robust Optimization Modeling from Natural Language using Simplification-based Verification
summary: Natural language interfaces can greatly benefit the accessibility and usability of optimization modeling, and recent advances in large language models (LLMs) show promise in automatically translating textual problem descriptions into executable solver formulations. However, a key challenge for existing approaches is to ensure that the inferred formulation correctly implements the intended task, even if it may execute without errors. We introduce VeriSimpl, a solver LLM framework for robust natural-language-to-optimization formalization. Our approach is based on the idea of simplification-based verification, where the optimization solver is leveraged to generate simplified diagnostic queries about a candidate formulation to allow the LLM to tractably reason about the correctness of the formulation with respect to the task description. We present such simplification strategies along different dimensions with respect to problem constraints and decision variables, which allow the LLM to reason locally under fixed global contexts. Evaluations on a range of optimization benchmarks show how our approach provides consistent improvements in accuracy over existing methods, while also providing a novel high-precision self-verification signal.

AI.tldr: VeriSimpl introduces a simplification-based verification framework that uses solver-generated diagnostic queries to help LLMs verify the correctness of optimization formulations translated from natural language, improving accuracy over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based approaches for translating natural language into optimization formulations can produce syntactically correct but semantically wrong models. There is a need for robust verification that ensures the inferred formulation correctly implements the intended task, beyond mere executability.
AI.method: VeriSimpl employs simplification-based verification: the optimization solver generates simplified diagnostic queries (by relaxing constraints or fixing decision variables) about a candidate formulation. These simplified subproblems allow the LLM to tractably reason about correctness locally under fixed global contexts. The framework examines simplifications along dimensions of problem constraints and decision variables.
AI.result: Evaluations on a range of optimization benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in accuracy over existing methods, along with a novel high-precision self-verification signal.
AI.conclusion: Simplification-based verification is an effective strategy for improving the robustness of LLM-driven optimization formalization, enabling tractable correctness reasoning through local diagnostic queries while maintaining high precision.

title: Tencent WorkBuddy Bench: A Multi-Domain Coding-Agent Benchmark with Contamination-Resistant Task Construction
comment: 30 pages, 9 figures. Project page: https://workbuddybench.com/ ; code: https://github.com/Tencent/workbuddy-bench ; dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/tencent/workbuddy-bench
summary: We introduce Tencent WorkBuddy Bench, a multi-domain evaluation suite for coding agents; this report documents its construction methodology, scoring protocol, and a cross-model leaderboard. At its core is a unified evaluation framework for constructing and running distribution-informed coding-agent tasks across four work domains - Code, Web, Office, and Security. Rather than adapting public issue text, every task is reverse-engineered from a real commit, pull request, or business scenario and rewritten as a short, colloquial, role-played request, so that a task's prompt is not recoverable by web-searching the underlying issue, pull request, or commit thread. Because the dataset is released openly - task directories, environment images, evaluation harness, tests, and reference solutions - contamination resistance rests on this construction together with dataset versioning rather than on secrecy. The four subsets - repository-level engineering, front-end development, office and business workflows, and red-/blue-team security - probe complementary facets of real work, each with its own verification style. All are packaged in a uniform task-directory format and run, under a uniform and reproducible protocol, on two agent harnesses (CodeBuddy Code and Claude Code); the full open release makes the benchmark reproducible end to end and directly auditable, since any third party can re-run each task and inspect its content. Because each subset uses a different scoring instrument, scores are not comparable across subsets and the suite reports no suite-wide average. We report a cross-model leaderboard across several model families.

AI.tldr: Tencent WorkBuddy Bench is an open, multi-domain evaluation suite for coding agents, featuring tasks reverse-engineered from real commits/PRs to resist contamination. It covers four domains (Code, Web, Office, Security) with domain-specific scoring and a cross-model leaderboard, all released openly for reproducibility and auditability.
AI.motivation: Existing coding benchmarks often rely on public issues or commits, making them susceptible to data contamination (e.g., models trained on GitHub data). The authors aim to create a contamination-resistant, realistic, multi-domain benchmark that reflects authentic workplace coding tasks across diverse domains beyond pure software engineering.
AI.method: Tasks are reverse-engineered from real commits, pull requests, or business scenarios and rewritten as short, colloquial, role-played requests — decoupling the prompt from the original public source. The benchmark spans four subsets (Code, Web, Office, Security), each with its own verification/scoring style. All tasks, environment images, tests, and reference solutions are packaged in a uniform task-directory format and released openly. Evaluation is conducted on two agent harnesses (CodeBuddy Code and Claude Code) under a reproducible protocol. No cross-subset averaging is performed due to incompatible scoring instruments.
AI.result: A cross-model leaderboard is reported across several model families on two agent harnesses. Scores are reported per-subset only, as scoring instruments differ across domains, making suite-wide aggregation invalid.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark provides a contamination-resistant, open, and reproducible evaluation framework for coding agents across four realistic work domains. Its open release enables third-party re-execution, auditing, and extension, with dataset versioning as the primary mechanism for maintaining integrity over time.

title: Toward cryptographically verifiable authorization for autonomous AI agents: A security hypothesis, preliminary formal model, and proof-of-concept implementation
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 2 Tables. Keywords: autonomous AI agents, zero-knowledge proofs, verifiable authorization, agentic security, zk-SNARKs, access control, cryptographic authorization, cryptographic protocols, zero-trust architecture, pre-execution authorization. Submitted to ACM Transactions on AI Security and Privacy (TAISAP)
summary: Autonomous AI agents increasingly execute actions, invoke tools, and operate on protected resources with limited human oversight. Existing authentication and authorization mechanisms establish identity and delegate authority, but do not inherently provide cryptographic evidence that a concrete request issued by a specific agent satisfies the applicable policy in a specific execution context. This paper hypothesizes that agent authorization can be formalized as a cryptographically verifiable relation, denoted $R_{CVA}$, that jointly binds an agent principal, a concrete authorization request, an execution context, and the satisfaction of an applicable policy, while selectively preserving the confidentiality of private authorization attributes. We introduce a preliminary formal abstraction for Cryptographically Verifiable Agent Authorization (CVA), define a compact set of candidate security properties including authorization soundness, principal binding, request binding, policy binding, and replay resistance, and provide an executable zero-knowledge proof of concept that instantiates selected elements of the model over a Groth16 zk-SNARK construction. We further identify and formalize the structural separation among identity binding, authorization-request binding, and runtime execution binding as a central open problem in the design of secure agentic systems (a distinction {not explicitly addressed by} current agentic security frameworks) and present a falsifiable research agenda for its resolution.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Cryptographically Verifiable Agent Authorization (CVA), a framework where agent authorization is formalized as a verifiable cryptographic relation that binds identity, request, context, and policy satisfaction together, with a zk-SNARK proof-of-concept implementation.
AI.motivation: Autonomous AI agents increasingly operate on protected resources with limited human oversight, yet existing authN/authZ mechanisms provide identity and delegation without cryptographic evidence that a specific request by a specific agent satisfies policy in a given execution context.
AI.method: The authors formalize agent authorization as a cryptographically verifiable relation $R_{CVA}$ binding agent principal, authorization request, execution context, and policy satisfaction. They define security properties (authorization soundness, principal/request/policy binding, replay resistance), and implement a proof-of-concept using Groth16 zk-SNARKs that selectively preserves privacy of authorization attributes.
AI.result: The paper delivers a formal abstraction for CVA, a compact set of candidate security properties, and an executable zero-knowledge proof-of-concept. It also identifies the structural separation among identity binding, authorization-request binding, and runtime execution binding as a central open problem not explicitly addressed by current agentic security frameworks.
AI.conclusion: The structural separation of identity, authorization-request, and runtime execution binding constitutes a foundational open problem for secure agentic systems. The authors present a falsifiable research agenda aimed at resolving this tripartite binding challenge.

title: Preference Tuning as Spectral Update Reorganization
summary: Preference-based post-training is usually understood through endpoint behavior, yet the learned update that produces this behavior remains largely opaque. We study RLHF and related preference optimization through the spectral structure of their induced parameter updates. By decomposing effective LoRA updates and reloading their spectral components as plug-in modules, we turn preference-induced updates into objects that can be isolated, recomposed, and directly intervened on. Across model families, optimization algorithms, and supervision regimes, these updates consistently develop a spectral head--tail organization. A compact head emerges early and carries the dominant endpoint shift, while a heterogeneous residual tail remains. The split is functional rather than merely descriptive. Plug-in intervention shows that the head accounts for the visible behavioral departure from the base model, while the tail is weak in isolation. Cross-run recomposition further shows that mixed adapters follow the source of the head, indicating that the head carries run-level solver bias. This endpoint dominance does not imply learning sufficiency. Head-only learning is non-vacuous but fails to recover the full solution, especially on out-of-distribution behavior. Tail-only learning yields little visible gain, yet the full solution is not recovered without the tail. These findings recast preference post-training as structured update reorganization rather than a monolithic behavioral correction, and suggest that alignment gain and coverage loss are tied to how the learned update itself is organized.

AI.tldr: RLHF/preference optimization updates exhibit a spectral head-tail structure: a compact "head" carries dominant behavioral shift, while the "tail" is necessary for full solution recovery, especially out-of-distribution. This reveals preference post-training as structured update reorganization, not monolithic correction.
AI.motivation: Preference-based post-training (RLHF, DPO, etc.) is typically evaluated only by endpoint behavior, while the internal structure of the learned parameter update that drives this behavior remains opaque. The authors aim to open the "black box" of preference-induced updates to understand how they are organized and what functional roles different components play.
AI.method: The authors decompose effective LoRA updates using spectral analysis (SVD) and reload spectral components as plug-in adapter modules. This enables isolation, recomposition, and direct intervention on subcomponents of the update. They study this across model families, optimization algorithms, and supervision regimes, employing head-only, tail-only, and cross-run recomposition experiments.
AI.result: Updates consistently develop a spectral head-tail organization: (1) a compact head emerges early and accounts for the dominant behavioral shift from the base model; (2) the tail is weak in isolation; (3) cross-run mixing shows behavior follows the head source, indicating run-level solver bias; (4) head-only learning is non-vacuous but fails on OOD behavior; (5) tail-only yields little visible gain, yet full recovery requires both components.
AI.conclusion: Preference post-training is better understood as structured update reorganization rather than monolithic behavioral correction. Alignment gain and coverage loss are tied to how the learned update is internally organized, with the head driving observable shifts and the tail enabling robustness and completeness of the solution.

title: ReliableTableQA:How Much Supervision Does Reliability Annotation Need?
summary: We introduce ReliableTableQA, a framework for training an LLM to annotate the statistical reliability of tabular QA results, not whether the query is answerable, but whether the computed answer is statistically meaningful. In real enterprise analytics, a syntactically correct SQL query can return a value that is based on too small a sample, has an excessively wide confidence interval, or is too confounded to support action. Existing systems answer confidently in all such cases, a failure we quantify as the Unreliable Confident Answer Rate (UCAR). We contribute (1) a ten-category reliability taxonomy (R1-R10) covering hazards such as small-sample aggregates, multiple-comparison inflation, and distribution-tail mismatch; (2) a program-first data pipeline that generates 50,000 reliability-labeled training examples from a context-free grammar over public retail schemas, with schema-stratified SFT/GRPO splits; and (3) a controlled study of how much supervision calibrated reliability annotation actually requires. We find that a small, schema-stratified SFT set is remarkably sufficient: 200 examples raise reliability-flag F1 from 0.61 to 0.98 and parse rate from 0.52 to 1.00, drive UCAR to zero, and yield a model that generalizes to an unseen retail domain (Rel-F1 0.997 on held-out H&M). Against this strong SFT baseline, GRPO, commonly assumed to be essential, helps only when SFT is under-trained (+0.06-0.16 exact-flag-set match at 100 examples, in- and out-of-distribution) and provides no measurable benefit once SFT is adequate, a null result we confirm across a hard compound-flag slice, a strict exact-match metric, and out-of-distribution evaluation. Our findings reframe reliability annotation as a data-efficiency problem and delineate precisely when reinforcement fine-tuning does and does not pay off.

AI.tldr: ReliableTableQA is a framework that trains LLMs to judge whether tabular QA results are statistically reliable (not just answerable). Using a grammar-generated dataset of 50K examples spanning 10 reliability hazard types, the authors show that as few as 200 SFT examples suffice to achieve near-perfect reliability annotation (Rel-F1 0.98, UCAR zero), and that GRPO fine-tuning adds benefit only when SFT data is severely limited (≤100 examples), becoming redundant once SFT is adequate.
AI.motivation: Enterprise analytics systems confidently return SQL query results even when those results are statistically unreliable—e.g., based on tiny samples, wide confidence intervals, or confounded data. Existing QA systems ignore this distinction between answerability and statistical meaningfulness, leading to what the authors term the "Unreliable Confident Answer Rate" (UCAR). The work aims to bridge the gap between generating an answer and vetting whether that answer is statistically sound enough to inform business decisions.
AI.method: The paper introduces: (1) a ten-category reliability taxonomy (R1–R10) capturing hazards like small-sample aggregates, multiple-comparison inflation, and distribution-tail mismatch; (2) a program-first data pipeline that uses a context-free grammar over public retail schemas to generate 50,000 reliability-labeled training examples, with schema-stratified splits for SFT and GRPO; and (3) a controlled study varying SFT dataset size (50–200 examples) with and without GRPO, evaluating on in-distribution, out-of-distribution (H&M), and a hard compound-flag slice using metrics including exact-flag-set match and Rel-F1.
AI.result: A schema-stratified SFT set of just 200 examples raises reliability-flag F1 from 0.61 to 0.98 and parse rate from 0.52 to 1.00, driving UCAR to zero, and generalizes to an unseen retail domain (Rel-F1 0.997 on H&M). GRPO provides modest gains (+0.06–0.16 exact-flag-set match) only when SFT is under-trained (100 examples), and yields no measurable benefit once SFT is adequate. This null result holds across the compound-flag slice, strict exact-match metrics, and out-of-distribution evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Reliability annotation is fundamentally a data-efficiency problem: well-curated SFT data alone can solve it, and reinforcement fine-tuning (GRPO) only pays off when SFT data is insufficient. The findings delineate a clear boundary for when GRPO is and isn't useful, reframing how to approach reliability-aware QA systems.

title: SonicSampler: Unified Tile-Aware Kernels for LLM Sampling and Speculative Verification
summary: Sampling in LLM inference comprises a combinatorial set of logit processing, token selection, and verification operations for speculative decoding. However, existing implementations either accelerate only subsets of this pipeline, rely on multiple kernel launches, or assume homogeneous sampling behavior across a batch, limiting support for dynamic serving workloads and preventing efficient CUDA Graph execution. We present $\textbf{SonicSampler}$, a unified suite of tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuses the complete sampling pipeline into a fixed, workload-aware execution model. Our kernels support dynamic per-request sampling behaviors, including grammar-constrained decoding, repetition, frequency and presence penalties, logit bias, temperature scaling, top-$k$ / top-$p$ / min-$p$ filtering, and speculative verification - within a single batched kernel while remaining fully CUDA Graph-compatible. Central to our approach is a novel hierarchical two-stage top-$k$ algorithm that achieves up to $\textbf{10x speedup}$ over competitive baselines and exploits the low-entropy structure of LLM outputs to enable efficient selection over large vocabularies. Across heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads, SonicSampler achieves up to $\textbf{16x speedup}$ over state-of-the-art baselines while preserving flexible batched execution.

AI.tldr: SonicSampler introduces unified, tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuse the entire LLM sampling pipeline — including speculative verification and diverse per-request decoding constraints — into a single CUDA Graph-compatible kernel, achieving up to 16× speedup via a novel hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM sampling implementations suffer from fragmented acceleration (only subsets of the pipeline), multiple kernel launches, and rigid assumptions of homogeneous sampling across batches. These limitations hinder dynamic serving workloads and prevent efficient CUDA Graph execution.
AI.method: SonicSampler provides a unified suite of tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuse the complete sampling pipeline (logit processing, token selection, speculative verification) into a fixed, workload-aware execution model. The approach supports dynamic per-request behaviors including grammar constraints, repetition/frequency/presence penalties, logit bias, temperature scaling, top-k/top-p/min-p filtering, and speculative verification. A key innovation is a hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm that exploits the low-entropy structure of LLM outputs for efficient selection over large vocabularies.
AI.result: The hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm achieves up to 10× speedup over competitive baselines. Across heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads, SonicSampler achieves up to 16× speedup over state-of-the-art baselines while preserving flexible batched execution.
AI.conclusion: SonicSampler demonstrates that a unified, vertically fused sampling kernel can simultaneously deliver substantial performance gains and full flexibility for dynamic, heterogeneous LLM serving workloads, enabling efficient CUDA Graph execution.

title: Delivery, Not Storage: Cue-Anchored Working Memory as a Harness Property for Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents ship with one kind of memory: documents. Instruction files, plan artifacts, and auto-written memory directories are deliberately authored and deliberately retrieved: the agent must choose to write them and choose to read them back. Human expertise runs on a second tier that never gets written down: situationally-bound operational facts (gotchas, locations, local conventions) encoded as a side effect of the work and retrieved involuntarily when the situation cues them. We argue this second tier is the load-bearing one for long-running agents and must be a harness property, not an agent choice. We contribute: (1) a two-tier design theory grounded in the cognitive literature on memory offloading, incidental encoding, and event-based prospective memory, each mapped to an architectural requirement; (2) a cue-anchored memory model where memories carry first-class trigger conditions over a composable vocabulary (path, symbol, semantic, event, temporal), evaluated deterministically by the harness, a composition no surveyed academic or shipped system provides; (3) a controlled evaluation on a real coding task showing that voluntary memory use is near zero even with a pre-seeded store (0 memory operations in 114 turns), that deterministic injection delivered in every seeded run with zero false alarms, and that 39% of intra-session re-reads re-buy content paid for before a compaction boundary; (4) a repeated-compaction decay probe: ten facts held only in conversation vanish at the first summary and stay absent from 106 of 108 compactions, and the deprived agent greps the harness's own session files to rebuild them, while the same facts injected from a harness-owned store arrive intact through all 138 compact-resumes as the final summary carries none. Delivery, not storage, is the product: the reliable memory channel for agents is the one the agent never has to think about.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that coding agents need a two-tier memory architecture where the critical "second tier"—situationally-cued operational knowledge—must be managed deterministically by the harness, not voluntarily by the agent. The authors introduce a cue-anchored memory model with composable trigger conditions and demonstrate through controlled experiments that voluntary agent memory use is near zero, while harness-driven deterministic injection reliably delivers knowledge across session boundaries, even surviving repeated compaction where conversation-held facts are obliterated.
AI.motivation: Existing coding agents rely on deliberate, voluntary memory (documents, instruction files, artifacts) that the agent must choose to write and retrieve. However, human expertise depends heavily on a second, involuntary tier: situationally-bound operational facts (gotchas, local conventions, locations) that are incidentally encoded and retrieved automatically when cued by context. This second tier is largely absent from current agent architectures, and the authors argue it is the "load-bearing" tier for long-running, multi-session agents. The core problem is that agents do not spontaneously use voluntary memory even when available, creating a critical gap for persistent, reliable agent operation.
AI.method: The paper contributes a two-tier design theory grounded in cognitive science (memory offloading, incidental encoding, event-based prospective memory), mapped to architectural requirements. It proposes a cue-anchored memory model where memories carry first-class trigger conditions over a composable vocabulary of five types: path, symbol, semantic, event, and temporal. These triggers are evaluated deterministically by the harness rather than left to agent discretion. The evaluation uses a controlled real coding task to measure: (1) voluntary vs. deterministic memory use rates, (2) delivery reliability and false-alarm rates, (3) memory re-read behavior across compaction boundaries, and (4) a repeated-compaction decay probe comparing conversation-held facts against harness-injected facts across 138 compact-resume cycles.
AI.result: Voluntary memory use was near zero: 0 memory operations across 114 turns even with a pre-seeded store. Deterministic injection delivered memories in every seeded run with zero false alarms. 39% of intra-session re-reads re-bought content previously paid for before a compaction boundary. In the repeated-compaction probe, ten facts held only in conversation vanished at the first summary and remained absent from 106 of 108 compactions; the deprived agent resorted to grepping the harness's own session files to rebuild them. In contrast, the same facts injected from a harness-owned store arrived intact through all 138 compact-resumes, with the final summary carrying none of them—the harness, not the context window, became the durable memory carrier.
AI.conclusion: Delivery, not storage, is the product. The reliable memory channel for agents is the one the agent never has to think about. Memory must be a harness property with deterministic, cue-driven injection rather than an agent-managed voluntary system. The two-tier architecture with composable trigger conditions provides a principled path toward persistent, long-running coding agents that do not lose critical operational knowledge across session boundaries or compaction events.

title: Can an AI System Be Creative? A Critical Perspective from Art and Engineering
summary: This paper examines the question of whether artificial intelligence (AI) systems can be creative, approached from the dual perspective of a researcher trained in electrical engineering, pattern recognition, machine learning, and neural networks, who has also spent most of his life engaged in the arts as actor, stage and film director, writer, composer, and visual artist, and in philosophy. Drawing on Margaret Boden's foundational framework, both her three properties of creativity (novelty, surprise, and value) and her three types of creative processes (combinatorial, exploratory, and transformational), the paper argues that AI systems are structurally incapable of creativity in its strongest sense. While they exhibit genuine capability in the domain of combinatorial creativity, they are significantly bounded in exploratory creativity, and fundamentally incapable of transformational creativity. The paper further argues that the most important limitation of current AI systems is not the absence of novelty per se, but the absence of any mechanism for serendipity, accident, or the unexpected, all of which play a central role in the phenomenology of creativity, and the absence of any subject position from which to recognize and welcome such chance events. The paper concludes by proposing a model of human, AI creative collaboration that is both realistic and generative, illustrated by several concrete experiments. The paper is itself a demonstration of the thesis it advances: it was composed through a deliberate human AI collaborative process, which is described in the methodological note that opens it.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI systems are structurally incapable of strong creativity. Using Boden's framework, AI can perform combinatorial creativity, is limited in exploratory creativity, and is fundamentally incapable of transformational creativity. The core limitation is not novelty but the absence of serendipity, accident, and a subject position to recognize chance events. A human-AI collaborative model is proposed, with the paper itself serving as a demonstration.
AI.motivation: To rigorously examine whether AI systems can be genuinely creative, drawing on both the author's dual expertise in engineering/ML and the arts/philosophy, and to move beyond superficial claims about AI creativity toward a structurally grounded assessment of AI's creative capabilities and limitations.
AI.method: The analysis applies Margaret Boden's established framework of three creativity properties (novelty, surprise, value) and three creative process types (combinatorial, exploratory, transformational) to assess AI systems. The paper itself is a performative demonstration, composed through a deliberate human-AI collaborative process described in an opening methodological note.
AI.result: AI systems demonstrate genuine combinatorial creativity, are significantly constrained in exploratory creativity, and are structurally incapable of transformational creativity. The critical deficits are: (1) no mechanism for serendipity, accident, or the unexpected, and (2) no subject position from which to recognize and embrace chance events.
AI.conclusion: True creativity in the strongest sense requires capacities absent in current AI. The paper proposes a realistic human-AI collaborative model as a generative path forward, illustrated by concrete experiments, with the paper itself embodying this collaborative approach.

title: Themis Consensus Extension v1: MEV Mitigation by Randomized Delayed Execution and Intent-Hiding Transactions in Application-Specific Blockchains
summary: Maximal extractable value (MEV) arises when privileged participants select, exclude, insert, or reorder pending transactions for private gain. We specify and analyze the Themis Consensus Extension v1, first published by Mangata in 2021. The design separates value extraction by reordering (VER) from value extraction by denial (VED). For VER, block construction and execution occur across consecutive producers: one producer commits a transaction set, and the next derives a publicly verifiable, deterministic, previously un- predictable seed and executes a seed-determined, dependency-preserving permutation. For selective VED, a user may encrypt a transaction for a designated builder and executor. The builder removes an outer layer and commits the opaque inner ciphertext; the executor reveals and executes the plaintext only after commitment. Under selfish but non-colluding validators, an adversary below the underlying consensus fault threshold, secure cryptography, and accountable role performance, the construction limits unilateral post-commit ordering control and hides transaction intent from relays and the builder. It does not provide send-order or receive-order fairness, complete censorship resistance, resistance to builder-executor collusion, or per-transaction price guarantees. We analyze probabilistic extraction, spam, dependent transactions, decryption liveness, session boundaries, total denial, and threshold coalitions. We also document the initial Aura-based Substrate implementation and its subsequent transition to a BABE-based sr25519/VRF seed path, together with delayed execution, Fisher-Yates shuffling, and Xoshiro256++. The result preserves the original proposal while narrowing its claims to explicit assumptions.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the Themis Consensus Extension v1, which separates MEV into value extraction by reordering (VER) and value extraction by denial (VED). It uses a two-phase commit-and-reveal mechanism across consecutive block producers to achieve publicly verifiable, deterministic transaction ordering, combined with encrypted transactions to mitigate selective denial, under explicit assumptions of non-colluding validators and accountable role performance.
AI.motivation: To formally specify and analyze a consensus-layer mechanism that mitigates maximal extractable value (MEV) by separating reordering-based extraction from denial-based extraction, reducing unilateral post-commit ordering control and preventing transaction intent leakage to relays and builders, without relying on external auction mechanisms.
AI.method: The design employs a two-phase protocol: one validator commits a transaction set, and the next validator derives a deterministic, unpredictable seed (using BABE/VRF) to execute a dependency-preserving permutation (Fisher-Yates shuffle with Xoshiro256++). For VED mitigation, users encrypt transactions for a designated executor; a builder strips the outer layer and commits the opaque inner ciphertext, and the executor decrypts only after commitment. The analysis examines probabilistic extraction, spam, dependent transactions, decryption liveness, session boundaries, total denial, and threshold coalitions under selfish but non-colluding validators.
AI.result: The construction successfully limits unilateral post-commit ordering control and hides transaction intent from relays and the builder under stated assumptions. However, it does not provide send-order or receive-order fairness, complete censorship resistance, resistance to builder-executor collusion, or per-transaction price guarantees. The analysis identifies viable attack vectors including probabilistic extraction, spam-based griefing, decryption liveness failures, and coalition-based total denial above threshold.
AI.conclusion: The Themis Consensus Extension v1 provides a principled, cryptographically grounded approach to separating and mitigating distinct MEV categories at the consensus layer. Its security guarantees hold under explicitly bounded assumptions (non-colluding validators, accountable performance, secure cryptography), and the paper narrows the original proposal's claims accordingly. The documented implementation transition from Aura to BABE-based VRF seeding strengthens the protocol's unpredictability properties.

title: AsymVerify at SemEval-2026 Task 6: Asymmetric Confidence-Gated Verification for Political Evasion Detection
comment: Accepted to SemEval-2026 Task 6 (CLARITY) at ACL 2026. Team AsymVerify placed 2nd of 41 teams on the official Subtask 1 leaderboard. Task: https://konstantinosftw.github.io/CLARITY-SemEval-2026/. Code: https://github.com/kaons-research/AsymVerify-ACL. Website: https://kaons.com/
summary: Political evasion is difficult to detect because evasive answers often appear cooperative while avoiding concrete commitment. We present AsymVerify, a confidence-gated verification system for SemEval-2026 Task 6, a three-way classification of Clear Reply, Ambivalent, and Clear Non-Reply responses. AsymVerify scored 0.85 Macro F1 on the evaluation split (D_eval, n=237), placing 2nd out of 41 teams on the official leaderboard. The system first classifies each question-answer pair, then selectively applies downgrade verification (CR/CNR -> AMB) or upgrade verification (AMB -> CR) to low-confidence predictions. Development analysis shows that errors concentrate at the Ambivalent boundary in both directions, motivating this asymmetric two-verifier design while confidence gating keeps additional inference cost low. On D_dev (n=308), AsymVerify with GLM-4.7 gains +17.1 Macro F1 over single-pass classification at 1.48 calls/example, and the upgrade verifier alone improves every tested LLM backend on D_dev by +6.8 to +15.2 Macro F1 over its single-pass baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/kaons-research/AsymVerify-ACL.

AI.tldr: AsymVerify is a confidence-gated verification system that improves three-way classification of political responses (Clear Reply, Ambivalent, Clear Non-Reply) by selectively applying two asymmetric verifiers to low-confidence predictions, achieving 2nd place in SemEval-2026 Task 6 with 0.85 Macro F1.
AI.motivation: Political evasion is inherently difficult to detect because evasive responses superficially appear cooperative while avoiding substantive commitment. This creates a challenging classification boundary, particularly around the Ambivalent class, where single-pass classifiers struggle.
AI.method: AsymVerify employs a two-stage architecture: (1) a single-pass classifier produces initial predictions across three classes (Clear Reply, Ambivalent, Clear Non-Reply); (2) confidence gating triggers one of two specialized verifiers only on low-confidence predictions — a downgrade verifier (CR/CNR → AMB) and an upgrade verifier (AMB → CR). This asymmetric design targets errors concentrated at the Ambivalent boundary while minimizing additional inference cost (1.48 calls/example average).
AI.result: AsymVerify achieved 0.85 Macro F1 on the evaluation split (D_eval, n=237), ranking 2nd out of 41 teams. On the development split (D_dev, n=308), the system with GLM-4.7 gained +17.1 Macro F1 over single-pass classification. The upgrade verifier alone improved every tested LLM backend by +6.8 to +15.2 Macro F1 over single-pass baselines.
AI.conclusion: The asymmetric two-verifier design effectively addresses boundary errors at the Ambivalent class, and confidence gating keeps inference costs manageable. The universal improvement from the upgrade verifier across diverse LLM backends suggests the approach generalizes well beyond a single model architecture.

title: Codec-Gauge: Learning Compression-Friendly Gauges for Transformer KV Caches
summary: Long-context Transformer inference increasingly relies on KV-cache compression or quantization. Prior rotation and transform-coding results suggest that the channel basis of each key/value vector affects how faithfully a fixed backend preserves model behavior. We introduce Codec-Gauge, a post-training cache-coordinate layer that learns small orthogonal channel transforms around existing compression and quantization backends. Its frequency-distribution objective combines a token-channel DCT spectral-centroid loss with a smooth rate proxy to concentrate KV energy in low-frequency codec-facing layouts. We evaluate actual compression and decompression using measured bytes and rolling compressed-history scoring. Across six models at $3$, $4$, and $6$ bits/value, learned gauges reduce zfp KL divergence by $44.0\%$ on average relative to raw coordinates and outperform random, Hadamard, DCT, and PCA/KLT controls. The same gauges improve quality preservation for block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization. Experiments on a 27B model and long-context task prompts reproduce the quality trend, while serial storage and timing measurements validate the implemented compressed-cache paths. These results establish cache-coordinate geometry as a practical post-training variable for improving compression fidelity without changing model weights, attention semantics, or backend coding rules.

AI.tldr: Codec-Gauge learns small orthogonal channel transforms after training to reshape KV-cache coordinates, concentrating energy in low frequencies for better compression fidelity without altering model weights, attention, or backend codecs.
AI.motivation: KV-cache compression and quantization are critical for long-context Transformer inference, but existing methods ignore how the channel basis of key/value vectors affects compression fidelity. Prior work on rotation and transform coding suggests that coordinate geometry matters, yet no method systematically learns cache-coordinate layouts to improve downstream compression.
AI.method: Codec-Gauge introduces a post-training, lightweight orthogonal channel transform layer inserted around existing compression/quantization backends. It optimizes a frequency-distribution objective combining: (1) a token-channel DCT spectral-centroid loss that concentrates KV energy in low-frequency components, and (2) a smooth rate proxy. The approach evaluates actual compression/decompression using measured bytes and rolling compressed-history scoring, and is tested across multiple models (including a 27B model) at 3–6 bits/value with zfp, block-uniform, and KIVI-style quantization.
AI.result: Learned gauges reduce zfp KL divergence by 44.0% on average relative to raw coordinates and outperform random, Hadamard, DCT, and PCA/KLT baselines. Improvements hold for block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization. A 27B model and long-context task prompts reproduce the quality trend, with serial storage and timing measurements validating the compressed-cache paths.
AI.conclusion: Cache-coordinate geometry is a practical post-training variable that significantly improves compression fidelity without modifying model weights, attention semantics, or backend coding rules, establishing a new axis for optimizing KV-cache compression.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Multi-Sensor Physical Hazard Assessment
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures. Benchmark dataset, evaluation code, and raw results publicly available at: https://github.com/Faizaniqbal52/PhysicalHazardBenchmark
summary: We present an empirical benchmark evaluating how five large language models assess multisensor physical hazard data. Testing 60 scenarios across three categories - multi-sensor joint assessment, response proportionality, and pattern disambiguation - with 1,800 API calls at temperature 0.0, we find that all tested models consistently produced no precautionary warning signal across the tested scenarios where multiple sensors are simultaneously elevated below their individual safety limits, while achieving near-perfect accuracy on single-sensor threshold violations. All five models (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek, Kimi, Llama 3.1 8B) score near zero on Category A multi-sensor scenarios (Q2: 0.000-0.208; Q3: 0.000-0.592) compared to strong performance on single-sensor scenarios (Category B Q1: 0.975-1.000). Structured tabular formatting shows no consistent advantage over plain prose; ChatGPT-4o performs significantly better under prose (p = 0.001). These findings have direct implications for practitioners deploying the tested models in physical safety monitoring systems.

AI.tldr: All five tested LLMs (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek, Kimi, Llama 3.1 8B) fail to issue precautionary warnings when multiple sensors are simultaneously elevated below individual thresholds, despite near-perfect single-sensor accuracy. Structured formatting offers no consistent benefit, and ChatGPT-4o performs significantly better with plain prose.
AI.motivation: There is a gap in understanding how LLMs handle multisensor physical hazard assessment, particularly whether they can detect emergent risk patterns when no single sensor exceeds its individual safety limit — a critical capability for real-world safety monitoring deployments.
AI.method: Empirical benchmark testing five LLMs across 60 scenarios in three categories: (A) multi-sensor joint assessment, (B) response proportionality, and (C) pattern disambiguation. A total of 1,800 API calls were made at temperature 0.0, evaluating both structured tabular and plain prose input formats. Statistical comparison between formats was performed (p = 0.001 for ChatGPT-4o).
AI.result: All models scored near zero on Category A multi-sensor scenarios (Q2: 0.000–0.208; Q3: 0.000–0.592) while achieving 0.975–1.000 on single-sensor threshold violations. Structured tabular formatting showed no consistent advantage; ChatGPT-4o performed significantly worse with tables compared to prose.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs are not reliable for multisensor physical hazard monitoring where risk emerges from combined sub-threshold signals. Practitioners should exercise caution when deploying these models in safety-critical monitoring systems, and input format sensitivity must be considered.

title: Where You Tap Matters: A Probe-and-Model Benchmark for Open-Set RF Fingerprinting
summary: Radio Frequency Fingerprint Identification (RFFI) enables transmitter identification at the physical layer by learning device-specific impairments from received signals, yet the literature is inconsistent about where in the receiver chain those samples should be collected. Since distinct transformations are applied to the signal by the different receiver operations, i.e., carrier recovery, gain normalization, pulse shaping, and timing recovery, they can either tighten within-transmitter variability or suppress the features RFFI requires for classification. We present a systematic real-world evaluation of open-set, reconstruction-error RFFI using data collected at five probe points along a standard BPSK receiver chain. Our results show that RFFI is strongly probe-dependent: timing recovery and, to a lesser extent, carrier recovery enable low false-acceptance operation with limited in-distribution-out-of-distribution overlap, whereas other stages often require a false-acceptance ratio above 0.1 to achieve a true-acceptance ratio of 0.9. To test the validity of our findings across model selection, we benchmark several LLM-designed autoencoders using a controlled pipeline that holds preprocessing and MSE scoring fixed. These architectures confirm that RFFI is probe-dependent. Moreover, they do not outperform the baseline at the chosen operating point and typically increase training time. Overall, probe selection dominates reconstruction-based open-set RFFI performance, more than the autoencoder complexity.

AI.tldr: RFFI performance is highly dependent on where in the receiver chain signal samples are collected. Timing and carrier recovery stages enable strong open-set identification, while other probe points degrade performance. Autoencoder complexity matters far less than probe selection.
AI.motivation: The RFFI literature lacks consensus on where to collect signal samples in the receiver chain. Different receiver operations (carrier recovery, gain normalization, pulse shaping, timing recovery) apply distinct transformations that may either amplify or suppress device-specific impairments critical for classification. This motivates a systematic, real-world evaluation of probe-point dependence.
AI.method: The authors collect BPSK signals at five probe points along a standard receiver chain and evaluate open-set RFFI using reconstruction-error-based anomaly detection. They benchmark a baseline autoencoder and several LLM-designed autoencoders under a controlled pipeline with fixed preprocessing and MSE scoring, measuring true-acceptance rate (TAR) vs. false-acceptance rate (FAR).
AI.result: RFFI is strongly probe-dependent. Timing recovery and carrier recovery enable low-FAR operation with limited in-distribution/out-of-distribution overlap. Other stages require FAR > 0.1 to achieve TAR = 0.9. LLM-designed autoencoders do not outperform the baseline at the chosen operating point and typically increase training time, confirming that probe selection dominates autoencoder complexity.
AI.conclusion: Probe point selection is the primary factor governing reconstruction-based open-set RFFI performance, outweighing autoencoder architecture complexity. Future RFFI systems and benchmarks should standardize and report probe-point configuration.

title: Answer-then-Edit: Reasoning Skeleton Editing for Anti-Distillation with Preserved Utility
summary: Proprietary large language models (LLMs) entail substantial intellectual and financial investment, making them valuable intellectual property (IP). However, even when deployed via black-box APIs, these models remain vulnerable to unauthorized knowledge distillation, which allows adversaries to cheaply extract and replicate model capabilities. To address this issue, anti-distillation (AD) has been proposed to generate defensive outputs that hinder distillation effectiveness, overcoming the limitation of watermarking-based approaches that rely on post-hoc verification. However, existing AD methods based on internal model perturbations struggle to balance anti-distillability and utility (e.g., answer accuracy and naturalness) of reasoning traces, with stronger defenses often causing significant utility loss. To fill this gap, we propose \textbf{\underline{S}}keleton-\textbf{\underline{G}}uided \textbf{\underline{R}}easoning \textbf{\underline{E}}diting (SGRE), an \textit{Answer-then-Edit} framework that performs post-hoc trace modification for anti-distillation. In the answer stage, the teacher model first generates clean reasoning traces, preserving the original reasoning accuracy while enabling more flexible control over trace naturalness. In the editing stage, we draw inspiration from Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) and introduce a three-stage strategy consisting of reasoning skeleton extraction, skeleton graph coarsening, and skeleton verbalization. These operations jointly perturb reasoning structures and augment textual complexity to amplify extraneous load on student models, hindering their acquisition of underlying reasoning patterns. Extensive experiments across diverse LLMs demonstrate that SGRE achieves state-of-the-art performance in reducing distillation effectiveness, while maintaining lossless reasoning accuracy and superior trace naturalness.

AI.tldr: SGRE proposes a post-hoc answer-then-edit framework that applies skeleton-guided reasoning editing to defend LLMs against unauthorized knowledge distillation, achieving state-of-the-art anti-distillation while preserving accuracy and naturalness.
AI.motivation: Existing anti-distillation methods based on internal model perturbations suffer from a trade-off between defense strength and utility (accuracy/naturalness of reasoning traces). There is a need for a method that achieves strong anti-distillation without compromising output quality.
AI.method: SGRE is an Answer-then-Edit framework: first the teacher generates clean reasoning traces (answer stage), then applies three-stage editing (editing stage) inspired by Cognitive Load Theory — reasoning skeleton extraction, skeleton graph coarsening, and skeleton verbalization — to perturb reasoning structures and increase textual complexity, amplifying extraneous cognitive load on the student model.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse LLMs show SGRE achieves state-of-the-art performance in reducing distillation effectiveness while maintaining lossless reasoning accuracy and superior trace naturalness.
AI.conclusion: SGRE effectively resolves the utility-defense trade-off in anti-distillation by decoupling answer generation from defensive editing, using skeleton-guided perturbations grounded in Cognitive Load Theory to hinder unauthorized model distillation.

title: Leveraging Biokinetic Knowledge Priors for Data-Scarce Bioprocess Modeling
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop
summary: While deep learning has accelerated drug discovery, its impact on biomanufacturing has been considerably more limited. The reason is data scarcity. Bioreactor experiments are high-cost, take days to weeks, and are rarely shared in public form, leaving each research work with only a handful of experiments. The domain itself, however, is rich in prior knowledge. Biokinetic ordinary differential equation (ODE) models have described microbial growth for decades, yet how to inject this knowledge into a neural network has not been studied systematically. We present the first systematic study of how to inject this ODE knowledge into a neural network, comparing a data-level prior that pre-trains a generic decoder on simulated ODE curves against an architecture-level prior that embeds the ODE inside the decoder. Both consistently outperform no-prior baselines across 11 datasets and 7 microbial species. Our central finding is that the two are substitutable. A generic decoder pre-trained on simulation matches a fully bio-structured decoder trained on real data. Simulation pre-training therefore offers a simple, data-efficient recipe for deep learning under bioprocess data scarcity.

AI.tldr: A systematic study comparing two strategies for injecting biokinetic ODE knowledge into neural networks — data-level prior (simulation pre-training) and architecture-level prior (ODE-embedded decoder) — shows both consistently outperform no-prior baselines across 11 datasets and are effectively substitutable, offering a simple recipe for deep learning under bioprocess data scarcity.
AI.motivation: Deep learning has had limited impact on biomanufacturing due to severe data scarcity: bioreactor experiments are expensive, time-consuming (days to weeks), and rarely shared publicly, leaving each study with very few experiments. Yet the domain possesses rich prior knowledge in the form of biokinetic ODE models. No systematic study has investigated how to inject this ODE knowledge into neural networks.
AI.method: The authors systematically compare two prior-injection strategies: (1) a data-level prior that pre-trains a generic decoder on simulated ODE curves, and (2) an architecture-level prior that directly embeds the ODE structure inside the decoder. Both are evaluated against no-prior baselines across 11 datasets spanning 7 microbial species.
AI.result: Both prior-injection strategies consistently outperform no-prior baselines across all 11 datasets and 7 species. The central finding is substitutability: a generic decoder pre-trained on simulation matches the performance of a fully bio-structured decoder trained on real data.
AI.conclusion: Simulation pre-training provides a simple, data-efficient recipe for applying deep learning under bioprocess data scarcity, eliminating the need for complex architecture-level bio-structuring while achieving equivalent performance.

title: Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation
comment: Technical report for the paper "Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation" accepted KDD2026
summary:
{\em Text-Attributed Graphs} (TAGs) have emerged as an expressive data model for integrating graph topology with rich textual semantics. Existing representation learning methods over TAGs suffer from severe scalability bottlenecks, particularly together with {\em Large Language Models} (LLMs). While data distillation offers a promising data-centric solution, existing methods fail to capture the complex interplay between graph and text modalities, struggle with the label scarcity inherent in semi-supervised settings, and lack the ability to produce the human-readable textual attributes required for downstream LLM-based tasks.
  To address these challenges, we propose \algo{}, a unified semi-supervised framework guided by the {\em Wasserstein Distance} (WSD). Grounded in our empirical findings on real TAGs, \algo{} introduces a graph-text collaborative encoding module that utilizes dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and -free) within a collaborative self-training scheme to harvest reliable pseudo-labels and fuse complementary graph-text features. Furthermore, we develop a theoretically grounded WSD-based graph sketching algorithm and a cost-effective LLM text synthesis module, which leverages cluster-based keyword extraction to generate coherent, human-readable summaries for condensed nodes. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that \algo{} achieves a state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-off in terms of both GNN- and LLM-based downstream tasks, enabling effective and efficient TAG learning or analytics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Wasserstein Distance-guided semi-supervised data distillation framework for Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs) that jointly compresses graph topology and textual attributes while preserving downstream task performance for both GNN and LLM-based analytics.
AI.motivation: Existing TAG representation learning methods face severe scalability bottlenecks, especially when combined with LLMs. Current data distillation approaches fail to: (1) capture the complex interplay between graph and text modalities, (2) handle label scarcity in semi-supervised settings, and (3) produce human-readable textual attributes needed for LLM-based downstream tasks.
AI.method: The framework consists of three core components: (1) a graph-text collaborative encoding module with dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and graph-free) operating under a collaborative self-training scheme to harvest pseudo-labels and fuse complementary features; (2) a theoretically-grounded Wasserstein Distance-based graph sketching algorithm for structural condensation; and (3) a cost-effective LLM text synthesis module using cluster-based keyword extraction to generate coherent, human-readable summaries for condensed nodes.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-offs across both GNN-based and LLM-based downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unified framework effectively addresses the scalability challenges of TAG learning by enabling efficient and effective data distillation that preserves both structural and textual fidelity, supporting diverse downstream analytics.

title: Euclid-MCP: A Model Context Protocol Server for Deterministic Logical Reasoning via Prolog
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at natural language understanding and generation but remain unreliable for multi-step logical reasoning, especially in safety-critical or compliance-sensitive domains. Recent neuro-symbolic approaches address this gap by coupling neural models with external symbolic engines, yet most integrations are bespoke and lack a standardized interface for tool-augmented agents. This paper presents Euclid-MCP, an open-source MCP server that provides deterministic logical reasoning via SWI-Prolog. Euclid-MCP introduces Euclid-IR, an engine-agnostic intermediate representation for Horn-clause logic that is human-readable, easy for LLMs to generate, and straightforward to compile into Prolog or alternative backends. The server exposes a compact tool interface that supports a translate-run-inspect-repair loop, enabling LLM clients to delegate inference while retaining full access to proof traces and derivation logs. We evaluate Euclid-MCP on a realistic IT security and compliance use case. Results show that while LLMs alone are sufficient on small knowledge bases, they hallucinate systematically on larger problems, whereas Euclid-MCP delivers exact answers with lower latency and more compact outputs. We argue that semantic RAG is fundamentally unsuited for rule enforcement, and that Euclid-MCP can serve as a stable, shared reasoning substrate for both RAG-based assistants and agentic systems.

AI.tldr: Euclid-MCP is an open-source MCP server that gives LLMs access to deterministic logical reasoning via SWI-Prolog, using a novel intermediate representation (Euclid-IR) and a translate-run-inspect-repair loop. It outperforms LLMs alone on larger knowledge bases in an IT security/compliance task, and the authors argue semantic RAG is fundamentally unsuitable for rule enforcement.
AI.motivation: LLMs are unreliable for multi-step logical reasoning in safety-critical and compliance-sensitive domains. Existing neuro-symbolic integrations are bespoke and lack standardized interfaces for tool-augmented agents. There is a need for a standardized, open-source reasoning substrate that LLM agents can delegate to with full transparency into proof traces.
AI.method: The authors present Euclid-MCP, an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server wrapping SWI-Prolog for deterministic logical reasoning. Key innovations include: (1) Euclid-IR, an engine-agnostic intermediate representation for Horn-clause logic that is human-readable, LLM-generatable, and compilable to Prolog or other backends; (2) a compact tool interface supporting a translate-run-inspect-repair loop, allowing LLMs to delegate inference while accessing proof traces and derivation logs. Evaluation is conducted on an IT security and compliance use case, comparing LLM-only performance against Euclid-MCP across varying knowledge base sizes.
AI.result: LLMs alone perform adequately on small knowledge bases but systematically hallucinate on larger problems. Euclid-MCP delivers exact, deterministic answers with lower latency and more compact outputs. The authors conclude that semantic RAG is fundamentally unsuited for rule enforcement tasks.
AI.conclusion: Euclid-MCP provides a stable, shared reasoning substrate suitable for both RAG-based assistants and agentic systems. It demonstrates that delegating logical inference to a deterministic symbolic engine via a standardized protocol yields superior reliability compared to relying on LLM reasoning alone, particularly for compliance and rule-enforcement applications.

title: QuantiBias: Benchmarking Quantization-Induced Bias in LLMs
summary: Almost every large language model that reaches a broad audience is quantized: trained in full precision, then compressed for efficiency. This step is assumed harmless and its safety is rarely re-checked. We find its principal side effect is increased bias that standard safety evaluation misses. Holding the model, its training, and the prompts fixed, a quantized model still refuses harmful requests, still avoids over-refusing benign prompts, and still selects the unbiased multiple-choice answer. Yet asked an open-ended question, the same model volunteers stereotypes in all eight languages we probe, in roughly one in four open-ended answers under an independent judge (~24% to ~27% across the compression ladder): it passes every standard check and still reaches users measurably more biased. The selective gap is a robust finding; whether open-ended bias further increases with compression is less certain, sensitive to the judge that scores it. We address both with \textbf{QuantiBias}, a benchmark that pairs a generative, multilingual stereotype probe with the refusal and multiple-choice controls that isolate open-ended generation, contrasts each build with and without reasoning, and rates the content severity of what it generates. Across two backbone models (Qwen and Gemma), a five-family screen, and eight benchmarks, quantizers allocate their extra precision by capability data that carries no bias-prevention signal, and reasoning before answering roughly halves the effect on some families while doing nothing on others. A quantized build must be re-evaluated for open-ended bias, not only on the short-form safeguards it already passes.

AI.tldr: Quantization of LLMs introduces a selective bias: quantized models pass standard safety tests (refusal, multiple-choice) but exhibit significantly increased stereotyping in open-ended generation (~24–27% across languages). The authors introduce QuantiBias, a benchmark isolating this gap, and show that reasoning before answering mitigates the effect only partially and inconsistently across model families.
AI.motivation: Quantization is universally applied to deploy LLMs but its safety implications are assumed negligible and rarely re-evaluated. The authors challenge this assumption by investigating whether compression introduces subtle biases that standard safety evaluations (focused on refusal and multiple-choice) systematically miss.
AI.method: The authors propose QuantiBias, a benchmark combining: (1) a generative, multilingual stereotype probe across eight languages; (2) refusal and multiple-choice controls to isolate open-ended generation; (3) builds contrasted with and without chain-of-thought reasoning; (4) severity scoring of generated content. Experiments span two backbone models (Qwen, Gemma), five quantizer families, and eight existing benchmarks.
AI.result: Quantized models pass all standard safety checks (refusal, over-refusal, unbiased multiple-choice) yet volunteer stereotypes in ~24–27% of open-ended answers across the compression ladder. The selective gap between controlled and open-ended evaluation is robust. Whether bias increases monotonically with compression depends on the judge. Reasoning before answering roughly halves the effect on some model families but has no effect on others. Quantizers allocate precision based on capability data carrying no bias-prevention signal.
AI.conclusion: Quantization safety must be re-evaluated beyond short-form safeguards. Open-ended bias is a principal side effect of compression that standard evaluation misses, and a quantized build's deployment readiness should include explicit open-ended stereotype probing, not merely refusal and multiple-choice checks.

title: Belief Propagation in LLM World Models: Measuring Strategic Information Bias with Prediction Markets
comment: Accepted at UNLP 2026. 12 pages, 8 figures, 11 tables. Dataset available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenBabylon/unlp-ukraine-forecasting
summary:
Every information ecosystem produces beliefs that shape strategic decisions. Both human analysts and AI systems inherit the blind spots of their information sources. We show that LLMs, combined with prediction markets, function as a calibrated instrument for measuring how far ecosystem-induced beliefs deviate from an external reference: LLMs extract the beliefs a text corpus implies, and prediction market price trajectories, anchored at resolution by realised outcomes, provide the calibration reference against which to quantify the deviation.
  We isolate the bias contribution of specific text through ablation: varying information context while holding the model fixed, with a contaminated model that knows actual outcomes as control. Applied to 111 Ukraine-related prediction markets, comprising approximately 93,000 predictions across four models, we find that English news context systematically biases territorial predictions, wrong 64 to 72 percent of the time when it pushes predictions toward territorial capture. A contaminated model that knows actual outcomes shows the same error rate, indicating that the bias originates primarily in the text. Supplementing with Ukrainian military-analytical sources reduces the bias for all clean models, while absolute-error gains are partial and model-dependent.
  We show that the distortion originates primarily in the sources, not the models. Consistent across four architectures, it will persist in any system that processes them and propagate into downstream decisions.

AI.tldr: LLMs combined with prediction markets quantify bias in information ecosystems. Applied to Ukraine conflict prediction markets, English news systematically biases territorial predictions (64–72% error rate). The bias originates in sources, not models, persists across four architectures, and propagates into downstream decisions.
AI.motivation: Information ecosystems inevitably produce biased beliefs that shape strategic decisions. Both humans and AI inherit these blind spots, yet no calibrated instrument exists to measure the deviation between ecosystem-induced beliefs and objective reference points.
