The authors aim to develop such a measurement framework and identify whether bias originates in models or in the textual sources themselves.
AI.method: The authors propose a two-component measurement framework: (1) LLMs extract implied beliefs from text corpora; (2) prediction market price trajectories, anchored at resolution by realized outcomes, serve as a calibration reference. They isolate the bias contribution of specific text via ablation — varying information context while holding the model fixed — and introduce a "contaminated model" that knows actual outcomes as a control. The method is applied to 111 Ukraine-related prediction markets with ~93,000 predictions across four model architectures.
AI.result: English news context systematically biases territorial predictions: when it pushes predictions toward territorial capture, it is wrong 64–72% of the time. The contaminated model shows the same error rate, confirming the bias originates in the text, not the model. Supplementing with Ukrainian military-analytical sources reduces this bias for all clean models, though absolute-error gains are partial and model-dependent. The distortion is consistent across four architectures.
AI.conclusion: The distortion originates primarily in sources, not models. Since it persists across all tested architectures, it will propagate into any system processing those sources and into downstream decisions. The LLM-plus-prediction-market framework provides a calibrated instrument for auditing information ecosystem bias.

title: From Atoms to Entropy: Optimal Noise Allocation for Diffusion Training in the Convex Regime
summary: How should a diffusion model decide which noise levels to train on, and how much? Despite the importance of this choice, current noise schedules are based largely on heuristics or empirical tuning. Here, we develop a general statistical framework for studying asymptotically optimal noise-level allocation in diffusion training. Our first main result concerns the fully coupled regime, where information can spread between different time points. Under convexity or Polyak-Lojasiewicz-type assumptions, we show that the optimized training schedule admits an atomic minimizer, concentrated on finitely many noise levels. Our second main result specializes this framework to an idealized independent-learner regime, intended to model temporal specialization in neural networks. Under an additional feature-noise decoupling condition, a random-matrix analysis leads to an information-theoretic proxy: the decoupled sampling density is proportional to the square root of the generative entropy rate, the rate at which conditional entropy grows along the forward process. We test these predictions in controlled settings where the coupled objective can be optimized directly, including Dirac mixtures, low-dimensional manifolds, and MNIST. In these settings, the optimized schedules are consistently finite-support, while the smooth entropic proxy closely tracks the atomic optimum in neural-network models and breaks down mainly in the fully coupled parametric case, as the theory suggests. We then evaluate the entropic schedule in larger-scale experiments, where full schedule optimization is currently intractable. The results indicate that square-root entropy scheduling can substantially improve training efficiency on discrete domains and remains competitive with standard EDM-style heuristics on continuous images.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a statistical framework for optimizing diffusion model noise schedules, proving that optimal schedules concentrate on finitely many noise levels (atomic minimizers) under convexity/PL conditions, and deriving an entropic proxy where the sampling density is proportional to the square root of the generative entropy rate.
AI.motivation: Current diffusion model noise schedules are chosen heuristically or via empirical tuning, with no principled statistical framework for determining which noise levels to train on and how much. This is a critical gap given the importance of noise scheduling to training efficiency and sample quality.
AI.method: The authors propose a general statistical framework for asymptotically optimal noise-level allocation. They analyze two regimes: (1) the fully coupled regime, where they prove atomic support of optimal schedules under convexity or Polyak-Łojasiewicz conditions; (2) an idealized independent-learner regime modeling temporal specialization in neural networks, where a random-matrix analysis under a feature-noise decoupling condition yields an information-theoretic proxy — the decoupled sampling density is proportional to the square root of the generative entropy rate. Predictions are tested on Dirac mixtures, low-dimensional manifolds, MNIST, and larger-scale discrete/continuous image domains.
AI.result: Optimized schedules are consistently finite-support in controlled settings. The entropic proxy closely tracks the atomic optimum in neural-network models and breaks down mainly in the fully coupled parametric case, as predicted. Square-root entropy scheduling substantially improves training efficiency on discrete domains and remains competitive with EDM heuristics on continuous images.
AI.conclusion: Optimal diffusion noise schedules concentrate on finite support under broad conditions. The square-root entropy rate proxy provides a practical, theoretically-grounded alternative to heuristic scheduling, especially effective for discrete domains, while the theory clarifies when this proxy succeeds versus fails (coupled vs. independent-learner regimes).

title: Beyond Liars' Bench: The Impact of Lie Typology, Depth, and Sparsity on Deception Detection in LLMs
comment: Presented at the AI Transparency Conference 2026, forthcoming in the AI Transparency Journal
summary: Training probes to detect deceptive outputs from large language models is still an open problem. Recent work has demonstrated that detection probes fail especially in out-of-domain scenarios -- training on one type of lie does not transfer well to deception scenarios involving other types of lies. In this work, we conduct a systematic study on how various factors impact detection performance: representation depth, probe expressivity, sparse feature representations, and the lie typology of the training data. To this end, we augment standard benchmark training data with a supplementary dataset containing diverse types of deception, including fabrication, omission, and exaggeration examples. Analyzing these factors across seven probe types, our experimental results show that the optimal representation depth is highly dataset-dependent, more expressive probes provide only selective gains over linear baselines, and sparse autoencoder features perform similarly to dense hidden states. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the choice of training data and lie typology substantially changes detectability, highlighting that deception detection is a highly representation-dependent problem.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically investigates how representation depth, probe expressivity, sparse features, and lie typology affect deception detection in LLMs, finding that training data composition and representation choices significantly impact out-of-domain detection performance.
AI.motivation: Existing deception detection probes for LLMs fail in out-of-domain scenarios—training on one type of lie does not generalize to others. A systematic understanding of which factors drive detection performance is lacking.
AI.method: The authors augment standard benchmark data with a supplementary dataset covering diverse deception types (fabrication, omission, exaggeration). They systematically evaluate seven probe types while varying representation depth, probe expressivity, and sparse vs. dense feature representations (SAE features vs. hidden states).
AI.result: Optimal representation depth is highly dataset-dependent. More expressive probes yield only selective gains over linear baselines. Sparse autoencoder features perform comparably to dense hidden states. Most critically, training data composition and lie typology substantially alter detectability, showing deception detection is representation-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Deception detection remains a challenging, representation-dependent problem. No single configuration generalizes across lie types, and careful consideration of training data diversity and representation choices is essential for building robust detection systems.

title: AI Assistants Overassist
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as tutors and thought partners, helping users reason through problems. While guidance from AI assistants can scaffold thinking and foster learning, such benefits depend on how they help--for instance, intervening too early or too frequently may hinder true learning and cognitive engagement. Yet how AI systems navigate intervention decisions during problem-solving remains poorly understood. Here, we introduce Int-Bench, a simulation-based benchmark for evaluating LLM interventions during learning. Int-Bench simulates a "student" solving a problem while a "teacher" monitors the student's reasoning and decides whether, when, and how to intervene. Across three domains--code debugging, mathematics, and brain teasers--we evaluate LLM teachers on the frequency and timing of interventions, as well as their impact on both immediate task success and generalization to new problems. We also compare LLMs to humans, finding that LLMs intervene more frequently and earlier than humans. Moreover, in contrast to humans, they tend to provide complete solutions rather than targeted hints. These findings suggest that current LLM assistants often optimize for short-term success rather than supporting the reasoning processes needed for deeper learning and long-term success.

AI.tldr: Int-Bench is a simulation-based benchmark for evaluating how LLMs decide when, whether, and how to intervene during problem-solving. LLMs intervene more frequently and earlier than humans, often providing complete solutions rather than targeted hints, suggesting they prioritize short-term success over deeper learning.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed as AI tutors and thought partners, but their intervention strategies—timing, frequency, and type—are poorly understood. Inappropriate interventions (too early or too frequent) may undermine genuine learning and cognitive engagement. Understanding these dynamics is critical for designing AI assistants that foster rather than hinder learning.
AI.method: The authors introduce Int-Bench, a simulation-based benchmark where a "teacher" LLM monitors a "student" solving problems across three domains: code debugging, mathematics, and brain teasers. The benchmark evaluates intervention frequency, timing, and type (hints vs. complete solutions), measuring both immediate task success and generalization to new problems. LLM teachers are also compared against human teachers.
AI.result: LLM teachers intervene significantly more frequently and earlier than human teachers. Unlike humans, who tend to provide targeted hints that scaffold reasoning, LLMs disproportionately offer complete solutions. This approach yields reasonable short-term task success but may compromise generalization and deeper learning outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM assistants optimize for immediate task completion rather than supporting the cognitive processes essential for long-term learning and transfer. This highlights a critical misalignment in AI tutoring systems and calls for rethinking intervention strategies to better promote sustained reasoning and genuine understanding.

title: Isolating LLM Alignment from Regex: Zero Coverage and Metric-Dependent Divergence Under Adversarial Mutation
summary: Production LLM applications commonly stack a regex filter in front of model-side alignment; prior work found no measurable coverage gain from adding a live Gemini backend behind an active regex filter. We ask whether that ceiling holds when the corpus is \emph{designed to bypass the regex}. We introduce $L_5$-no-regex -- identical to $L_4$-real (Gemini-2.5-flash, token-budget cap, rate limit, output scrub) but with the nine-pattern filter disabled -- and evaluate it against $N{=}45$ adversarial probes across three sub-corpora (carry-forward, regex-bypass, alignment-isolate), amplified by Gemini paraphrase and PAIR to ${\sim}1{,}555$ probe-run pairs over $N{=}5$ replications. Under the primary substring classifier, H1 is refuted: $L_5$ block rate is $0,%$ across all five OWASP LLM Top-10 categories ($Δ\text{pp}{=}0$ vs.\ $L_0$, $p{=}1.00$; Wilson upper bound ${<}5,%$). A secondary LLM-judge metric on PAIR variants shows $56$--$100,%$ block rates ($p{<}0.01$), revealing alignment does respond to adversarially-framed probes -- but produces refusals too nuanced for substring matching. The sub-corpus differential prediction is not supported ($p{=}1.00$). Alignment's contribution is \emph{metric-dependent}: on natural-language harmful-request probes, it adds zero observed coverage beyond the regex; on adversarially-framed variants, an LLM judge detects refusals the substring classifier misses. The locked corpus, mutation artifacts, and export scripts are released for replication.

AI.tldr: Disabling a regex filter and relying solely on an LLM backend (Gemini-2.5-flash) for content safety yields zero measurable improvement under substring-based classification, but an LLM judge reveals that the model does produce nuanced refusals on adversarially-framed probes — making alignment's contribution metric-dependent.
AI.motivation: Prior work found no coverage gain from adding a live Gemini backend behind an active regex filter. This paper asks whether that finding holds when the adversarial corpus is specifically designed to bypass the regex filter, thereby isolating alignment's true contribution.
AI.method: The authors introduce L5-no-regex, a variant of L4-real (Gemini-2.5-flash with token budget, rate limit, and output scrub) but with the nine-pattern regex filter disabled. They evaluate it against N=45 adversarial probes across three sub-corpora (carry-forward, regex-bypass, alignment-isolate), amplified via Gemini paraphrase and PAIR (Prompt Automatic Iterative Refinement) to ~1,555 probe-run pairs over N=5 replications. Two metrics are used: a primary substring classifier and a secondary LLM-judge metric.
AI.result: Under the primary substring classifier, H1 is refuted: L5 block rate is 0% across all five OWASP LLM Top-10 categories (Δpp=0 vs. L0, p=1.00; Wilson upper bound <5%). Under the secondary LLM-judge metric on PAIR variants, block rates reach 56–100% (p<0.01), indicating alignment produces refusals too nuanced for substring matching. The sub-corpus differential prediction is not supported (p=1.00).
AI.conclusion: Alignment's contribution is metric-dependent: on natural-language harmful-request probes, it adds zero observed coverage beyond the regex; on adversarially-framed variants, an LLM judge detects refusals that substring classifiers miss. The locked corpus, mutation artifacts, and export scripts are released for replication.

title: Naver-News-KO: A Korean News Summarization Dataset for Open-Source Fine-Tuning of Summarization Models
comment: Technical report; 7 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/daekeun-ml/naver-news-summarization-ko
summary: We release Naver-News-KO, a Korean news summarization dataset of 27,400 (document, summary) pairs collected from Naver News over a ten-day window in July 2022 across two categories (Economy and IT/Science; 77/23 split), with train/validation/test partitions of 22,194 / 2,466 / 2,740 and a mean per-record document-to-summary character-compression ratio of 6.03x. The dataset has been publicly hosted on the Hugging Face Hub since January 2023 and, as of May 2026, receives approximately 33,000 downloads per month; community-maintained Korean summarization models fine-tuned on it include Gemma-2B-ko and Gemma2-9B variants. This technical report (i) documents the collection protocol, the column schema, and the split construction, (ii) reports corpus-level statistics (length distributions, compression ratio, and a measured 16.8% near-duplicate title-Jaccard overlap between test and train that users should be aware of), (iii) positions the resource against other open Korean summarization corpora, (iv) provides a Lead-3 extractive reference point (ROUGE-1 55.1, ROUGE-L 50.6) and two reproducible fine-tuned baselines -- KoBART (R-1 56.6, BERTScore-F1 81.5) and Gemma-2B-ko with LoRA (R-1 55.3, BERTScore-F1 78.3) -- with release-time training scripts, and (v) clarifies the licensing and intended-use scope of the resource. The goal is to provide a citable reference for downstream work that already uses this dataset, not to propose a new benchmark.

AI.tldr: Naver-News-KO is a publicly released Korean news summarization dataset with 27,400 document-summary pairs, accompanied by corpus statistics, baseline model results, and documentation to serve as a citable reference for existing downstream users.
AI.motivation: The paper provides a formal citable reference for a dataset already widely adopted by the Korean NLP community (~33k monthly downloads on Hugging Face Hub) rather than proposing a new benchmark.
AI.method: The authors describe the collection protocol from Naver News (Economy and IT/Science categories, July 2022), dataset schema, split construction (22,194/2,466/2,740), report corpus-level statistics (length distributions, 6.03x compression ratio, 16.8% near-duplicate test-train overlap), and establish extractive (Lead-3) and abstractive (KoBART, Gemma-2B-ko with LoRA) baselines with reproducible scripts.
AI.result: Lead-3 baseline achieves ROUGE-1 55.1 and ROUGE-L 50.6. Fine-tuned KoBART reaches R-1 56.6 and BERTScore-F1 81.5; Gemma-2B-ko with LoRA achieves R-1 55.3 and BERTScore-F1 78.3. A 16.8% near-duplicate title-Jaccard overlap exists between test and train splits.
AI.conclusion: The dataset is positioned against other open Korean summarization corpora, and the report clarifies licensing and intended-use scope to support the existing user base rather than establish a new competitive benchmark.

title: HypNO: A Graph-Based Neural Operator with Physics-Informed Message Passing for Hyperbolic Conservation Laws
summary: We introduce HypNO, a graph-based neural operator for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws. HypNO operates directly on a space-time graph of finite-volume cells and uses adjacency-factored, physics-informed message passing to respect upwinding and entropy admissibility near shocks. We benchmark the architecture on the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards (LWR) and Aw-Rascle-Zhang (ARZ) traffic-flow models, a stress test for operator-learning methods because of their simultaneous global transport and shock formation. HypNO predicts solution snapshots accurately across a range of initial conditions while capturing the shocks and discontinuities of the solution.

AI.tldr: HypNO is a graph-based neural operator for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws that operates on space-time graphs of finite-volume cells. It uses physics-informed message passing to respect upwinding and entropy conditions near shocks, and is benchmarked on traffic-flow models (LWR and ARZ), accurately capturing shocks and discontinuities across varied initial conditions.
AI.motivation: Standard neural operator methods struggle with hyperbolic conservation laws due to the simultaneous challenges of global transport and shock formation. Existing approaches often fail to respect physical principles like upwinding and entropy admissibility, leading to poor shock resolution. HypNO addresses this gap by embedding these physical constraints directly into the graph neural architecture.
AI.method: HypNO is a graph-based neural operator that acts directly on a space-time graph of finite-volume cells. It employs adjacency-factored, physics-informed message passing that explicitly enforces upwinding (information propagates along characteristic directions) and entropy admissibility conditions near shocks, ensuring physically consistent predictions at discontinuities.
AI.result: HypNO accurately predicts solution snapshots across a range of initial conditions on the LWR and ARZ traffic-flow models. It successfully captures shocks and discontinuities — a particularly challenging stress test for operator-learning methods — while maintaining accuracy in smooth regions.
AI.conclusion: Embedding physics-informed constraints such as upwinding and entropy admissibility into a graph neural operator architecture yields a method capable of reliably learning hyperbolic conservation laws. HypNO demonstrates strong performance on traffic-flow benchmarks and represents a promising direction for neural operator learning on shock-forming PDEs.

title: Enabling Scalable Topology Inference in Distribution Systems via Constrained Multi-Source Inference
summary: Accurate distribution system topology is essential for outage localization, voltage analytics, and operation of distribution grids, yet maintaining reliable connectivity records remains challenging in practice due to heterogeneous and imperfect utility data. Existing topology identification methods often rely primarily on electrical similarity or spatial records alone, which become unreliable in dense feeders and under inconsistent metadata conditions. This paper formulates distribution topology identification as a constrained inference problem that refines a utility-provided base topology using heterogeneous evidence while enforcing spatial feasibility and physical operational constraints. Instead of reconstructing connectivity from scratch, the proposed framework detects inconsistent assignments, performs localized reconnection within constrained neighborhoods to ensure scalability, and iteratively enforces physical feasibility to produce operationally consistent topology estimates. In addition, a falsification-driven reliability metric evaluates how strongly each inferred connection is supported relative to alternative feasible assignments, enabling utilities to prioritize verification efforts while preserving system-wide observability. The framework is validated using operational data from three feeders comprising more than $8{,}000$ AMI meters in collaboration with a large U.S. utility. Results demonstrate over $95\%$ topology reconstruction accuracy while significantly reducing computational effort compared with global inference approaches. The study further shows that correlation-based methods alone produce ambiguous assignments in dense urban feeders, whereas combining electrical measurements with spatial and operational constraints enables robust and scalable topology recovery under realistic deployment conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper frames distribution topology identification as a constrained inference problem that refines utility-provided base topology using electrical measurements, spatial constraints, and physical operational constraints, achieving >95% accuracy on 8,000+ AMI meters while remaining scalable through localized reconnection.
AI.motivation: Maintaining accurate distribution system topology records is challenging due to heterogeneous, imperfect utility data. Existing methods relying solely on electrical similarity (e.g., voltage correlation) or spatial records fail under dense feeders and inconsistent metadata, driving the need for a robust approach that fuses multiple evidence sources.
AI.method: The authors formulate topology identification as constrained inference: (1) starting from a utility-provided base topology, the framework detects inconsistent assignments; (2) performs localized reconnection within constrained spatial neighborhoods (not global search) for scalability; (3) iteratively enforces physical feasibility (power flow constraints); and (4) introduces a falsification-driven reliability metric that quantifies how strongly each inferred connection is supported relative to alternatives.
AI.result: Validated on three feeders with 8,000+ AMI meters from a large U.S. utility, the framework achieves >95% topology reconstruction accuracy with significantly reduced computational effort vs. global inference. Standalone correlation-based methods produce ambiguous assignments in dense urban feeders, while the fused approach remains robust.
AI.conclusion: Combining electrical measurements with spatial and operational constraints yields robust, scalable distribution topology recovery under realistic conditions. The falsification-driven reliability metric further enables utilities to prioritize manual verification of uncertain connections while maintaining system-wide observability.

title: MedGame: Storytelling Gamification Empowered by Large Language Models for Medical Education
comment: Work in Progress; an explorational design and study on AI+Education+Game
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for medical education, but most existing systems focus on localized interactions such as question answering or single-turn feedback, rather than organizing an entire clinical case into a decision-centered learning trajectory. We introduce \textit{MedGame}, a framework that transforms static clinical cases into structured, executable storytelling games. MedGame uses a dual-engine design: a Medical Narrative Designer synthesizes case-grounded clinical storylines with states and decision nodes, while a Story Director converts them into dependency-aware multimodal orchestration plans rendered by our released interactive platform. We construct MedGame Bench, a 5,000-case benchmark and evaluation protocol for Medical Narrative Generation and Story Direction. Experiments show that task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves open-source LLMs on MedGame Bench and narrows the gap with commercial models. A pilot student study further shows that learners perceive MedGame as more engaging and useful than text-only alternatives.

AI.tldr: MedGame is a dual-engine framework that transforms static clinical cases into interactive, decision-driven storytelling games for medical education, with a benchmark of 5,000 cases and evidence that both fine-tuned LLMs and student users validate its effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based medical education systems are limited to localized interactions (QA, single-turn feedback) and fail to organize complete clinical cases into coherent decision-centered learning trajectories. There is a gap in systems that structure the entire diagnostic reasoning process as an interactive narrative.
AI.method: MedGame employs a dual-engine architecture: (1) a Medical Narrative Designer that synthesizes clinical storylines with states and decision nodes from case data, and (2) a Story Director that converts these into dependency-aware multimodal orchestration plans. The authors also introduce MedGame Bench (5,000 cases) for evaluating Medical Narrative Generation and Story Direction, and conduct task-specific fine-tuning experiments alongside a pilot student study.
AI.result: Task-specific fine-tuning significantly improves open-source LLMs on MedGame Bench, narrowing the performance gap with commercial models. In a pilot student study, learners rated MedGame as more engaging and useful compared to text-only alternatives.
AI.conclusion: MedGame demonstrates that structuring clinical cases into interactive storytelling games enhances both automated narrative generation quality and learner engagement, suggesting a promising direction for LLM-powered medical education beyond simple QA paradigms.

title: Beyond Heavy Log Curation: Perplexity-Based APT Detection via Unsupervised, Context-Augmented Language Models
summary: Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) remain difficult to detect because only a small fraction of events in large-scale logs are attack-related, and investigation is expensive and hard to scale. Prior machine-learning approaches can reduce analyst workload, but they often rely on heavily curated training data and sophisticated preprocessing pipelines. Building and maintaining such pipelines require substantial domain expertise and engineering cost. Motivated by insights from a study of a strong APT detection baseline, we propose CAPTAIN (Context-Augmented Perplexity-based Threat Activity log detectIoN), a perplexity-based detector that leverages general, pre-trained language models with minimal, domain-agnostic preprocessing, enabling robust scoring of long, minimally processed log entries. CAPTAIN encodes recent history with an encoder model and a Q-Former-style bridge, then injects the compact context tokens into the decoder input so that perplexity reflects temporal context. To improve stability, CAPTAIN additionally applies smoothing filters to the perplexity time series. Across APT-oriented benchmarks, CAPTAIN competes with strong existing baselines and remains robust under substantially less curated inputs, that reduces the development and operational cost of advanced log preprocessing.

AI.tldr: CAPTAIN is a perplexity-based APT detection system that uses pre-trained language models with minimal preprocessing. It encodes recent history via a Q-Former-style bridge into decoder context, making perplexity temporally aware. Smoothing filters stabilize the output, yielding competitive detection performance without expensive, domain-specific preprocessing pipelines.
AI.motivation: APT detection is challenging because attack-related events are rare in large-scale logs, and manual investigation does not scale. Existing ML approaches reduce analyst workload but depend on heavily curated training data and complex preprocessing pipelines that require substantial domain expertise and engineering effort. The authors seek a method that achieves strong detection with minimal, domain-agnostic preprocessing.
AI.method: CAPTAIN uses a pre-trained language model to compute perplexity on long, minimally processed log entries. Temporal context is incorporated by encoding recent log history with an encoder and a Q-Former-style bridge module, which produces compact context tokens injected into the decoder input. This makes the perplexity score sensitive to deviations from normal temporal patterns. Additional smoothing filters are applied to the perplexity time series to improve detection stability.
AI.result: On APT-oriented benchmarks, CAPTAIN achieves competitive performance with strong existing baselines while remaining robust under substantially less curated inputs, significantly reducing the development and operational cost of log preprocessing.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging general pre-trained language models with minimal, domain-agnostic preprocessing is a viable and cost-effective strategy for APT log detection, matching the performance of heavily engineered pipelines while reducing both development and operational overhead.

title: GLAN-QnA-KR: A Seedless Taxonomy-Driven Korean Instruction Corpus
summary: We release GLAN-QnA-KR, a 303,581-row openly redistributable Korean instruction-QA corpus produced via the seedless taxonomy-driven GLAN synthesis pipeline with Microsoft's Phi-3.5-MoE-instruct as the producer model (generation: 2024-12; release: 2024-12; licence: OpenRAIL). The corpus spans a flat taxonomy of 1,084 English-labelled disciplines paired with Korean question/answer text, a 100-900 difficulty scale, and a median of 313 question characters and 1,098 answer characters per record. Two properties are atypical for synthetic instruction data at this scale: (i) exact duplicate questions number only 1 in 303,581 rows and character-trigram near-duplicate clusters at Jaccard >= 0.9 number zero in a 5,000-sample probe, and (ii) a two-layer contamination audit against KMMLU, KoBEST (five sub-tasks), and HAE-RAE-Bench shows a maximum test-vs-corpus question-level character-trigram Jaccard of 0.163 with zero test items at Jaccard >= 0.7, and a maximum multilingual-E5 cosine of 0.901 with a single test item at cosine >= 0.90 and zero at >= 0.95, across 20,000 sampled GLAN questions and seven evaluation sets. At the time of release, this is, to our knowledge, the largest single-pipeline synthetic Korean instruction corpus verifiable on the Hugging Face Hub and the only Korean >=100k-row corpus built under a seedless taxonomy-driven protocol. This note documents the generation protocol, corpus statistics, the contamination audit, and the licensing boundary in a form suitable for downstream citation.

AI.tldr: Release of GLAN-QnA-KR, a 303,581-row Korean instruction-QA corpus generated via a seedless taxonomy-driven pipeline using Phi-3.5-MoE-instruct, featuring near-zero exact/near-duplicate questions and minimal benchmark contamination.
AI.motivation: To provide a large, openly redistributable Korean instruction-tuning corpus that is verifiable on Hugging Face Hub, built under a seedless taxonomy-driven protocol — filling a gap for high-quality, contamination-audited Korean synthetic data at scale.
AI.method: The GLAN (Generalized Language model Augmented iNstruction) synthesis pipeline is employed with Microsoft's Phi-3.5-MoE-instruct as the producer model. The process uses a flat taxonomy of 1,084 English-labelled disciplines to generate Korean question-answer pairs without seed examples. A two-layer contamination audit is conducted: (1) character-trigram Jaccard similarity and (2) multilingual-E5 embedding cosine similarity, both computed against KMMLU, KoBEST (five sub-tasks), and HAE-RAE-Bench. Duplicate detection uses exact matching and character-trigram Jaccard clustering (threshold ≥0.9).
AI.result: The corpus contains 303,581 rows with a 100–900 difficulty scale. Median question length is 313 characters; median answer length is 1,098 characters. Only 1 exact duplicate exists across all rows; zero near-duplicate clusters at Jaccard ≥0.9 in a 5,000-sample probe. Contamination audit: maximum question-level character-trigram Jaccard against test sets is 0.163 (zero items ≥0.7); maximum multilingual-E5 cosine is 0.901 (single test item ≥0.90, zero ≥0.95) across 20,000 sampled questions and seven evaluation sets.
AI.conclusion: GLAN-QnA-KR is, at release time, the largest single-pipeline synthetic Korean instruction corpus verifiable on Hugging Face Hub and the only Korean ≥100k-row corpus built under a seedless taxonomy-driven protocol. Its near-perfect deduplication and minimal benchmark contamination make it a reliable resource for Korean LLM instruction tuning.

title: Improving Access to Essential Medicines via Decision-Aware Machine Learning
summary: A critical challenge in healthcare systems in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) is the efficient and equitable allocation of scarce resources, particularly essential medicines. This problem is complicated by limited high-quality data, which restricts the applicability of traditional data-driven techniques. We propose a novel decision-aware machine learning framework for essential medicines allocation, which additionally leverages multi-task learning to ensure sample efficiency and catalytic priors to ensure equitable allocation. In collaboration with the Sierra Leone national government, we performed a staggered, nationwide deployment of our system as a decision support tool. Our econometric evaluation finds an estimated 19% increase in consumption of allocated products in treated districts, demonstrating its efficacy at improving access to essential medicines. Our tool was subsequently scaled nationwide, covering an estimated 2 million women and children under five. Our work demonstrates how machine learning methods can improve efficiency at very low cost in resource-constrained global health settings.

AI.tldr: A decision-aware machine learning framework using multi-task learning and catalytic priors was deployed in Sierra Leone to optimize essential medicine allocation, yielding a 19% increase in product consumption and scaling nationwide to serve ~2 million women and children under five.
AI.motivation: Efficient and equitable allocation of scarce essential medicines in LMICs is severely constrained by limited high-quality data, making traditional data-driven methods impractical. There is a pressing need for sample-efficient, equity-aware decision support tools that can operate under these real-world constraints.
AI.method: The authors propose a decision-aware machine learning framework that integrates (1) multi-task learning to improve sample efficiency by sharing representations across related prediction tasks, and (2) catalytic priors to encode equity considerations into the allocation optimization. The system was deployed in Sierra Leone via a staggered, nationwide rollout in collaboration with the national government, serving as a decision support tool for essential medicines allocation.
AI.result: An econometric evaluation of the staggered deployment found an estimated 19% increase in consumption of allocated products in treated districts compared to controls. The tool was subsequently scaled nationwide, reaching approximately 2 million women and children under five.
AI.conclusion: Machine learning methods — specifically decision-aware frameworks combining multi-task learning and equity-oriented priors — can substantially improve resource allocation efficiency at very low cost in resource-constrained global health settings, demonstrating a viable path for ML-driven policy impact in LMICs.

title: Routing Without Training: Controllable-Ratio LLM Offloading via Reliability Gating
summary: Local-cloud collaboration is a practical way to deploy large language models under resource constraints, but existing methods often rely on trained routers or collaboration-aware finetuning that tie routing behavior to a particular operating regime. In this work, we show that such training may be unnecessary: the local model's own inference-time agreement across sampled responses already provides a strong signal for deciding when to trust local execution and when to offload to a stronger cloud model. We propose CARGO, a training-free routing framework that estimates this agreement through prompt-varied sampling, applies Bayesian early stopping for sample-efficient uncertainty control, and supports arbitrary target collaboration ratios through lightweight deployment-time calibration. Across diverse reasoning and question-answering tasks, multiple local LLM families and scales, and both pretrained and finetuned local models, CARGO consistently outperforms other training-free baselines and in several settings surpasses supervised learned routers. These results suggest that effective and adaptable local-cloud collaboration can emerge directly from the local model's intrinsic response behavior, without requiring an additional trained router.

AI.tldr: CARGO is a training-free routing framework for local-cloud LLM collaboration that uses the local model's agreement across prompt-varied sampled responses, combined with Bayesian early stopping, to decide when to trust local execution vs. offload to a cloud model — outperforming both training-free baselines and sometimes even supervised routers.
AI.motivation: Existing local-cloud collaboration methods for LLMs rely on trained routers or collaboration-aware fine-tuning, which ties routing behavior to specific operating regimes and lacks flexibility. The authors investigate whether such training is necessary, hypothesizing that the local model's own inference-time response behavior can serve as a reliable routing signal.
AI.method: CARGO (training-free routing) operates via three key mechanisms: (1) prompt-varied sampling — generating multiple responses from the local model using semantically equivalent but syntactically varied prompts to estimate response agreement; (2) Bayesian early stopping — applying Bayesian inference to control uncertainty with sample efficiency, halting sampling once a confidence threshold is reached; and (3) lightweight deployment-time calibration — enabling arbitrary target collaboration ratios without retraining.
AI.result: Across diverse reasoning and QA tasks, multiple local LLM families and scales (both pretrained and fine-tuned), CARGO consistently outperforms training-free baselines and in several settings surpasses supervised learned routers in routing accuracy and collaboration efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Effective and adaptable local-cloud collaboration can emerge directly from a local model's intrinsic response behavior without requiring a separately trained router, suggesting a simpler and more flexible paradigm for resource-constrained LLM deployment.

title: Agree on the Model, Verify the Inference: GKR Protocols for HND-Based Transformer Inference
comment: 24 pages, including 4 pages of supporting information; 2 figures
summary: Outsourced Transformer inference exposes clients to model substitution and incomplete execution, while direct replay removes the computational benefit of delegation. We present GKR-HND, a registered-model protocol for verifying the polynomial backbone of Homomorphic--Nonhomomorphic Decomposition Transformers. The retained verifier checks the GKR transcript and registered-weight openings, but delegates expensive public evaluations to an assigned computation worker. Assuming an honest retained verifier and prover--worker non-collusion, the verifier accepts only when the worker's signed, request-bound response agrees with the proof claims. Experiments with pretrained HND models validate the proof path and the delegated public computation without dense-matrix replay.

AI.tldr: GKR-HND presents a verification protocol for outsourced Transformer inference that uses the GKR proof system combined with registered-model commitments to detect model substitution and incomplete execution, while offloading expensive public computations to a delegated worker under non-collusion assumptions.
AI.motivation: Outsourcing Transformer inference to third-party servers introduces trust risks: clients cannot detect if the server substitutes a different model or executes incompletely. While direct replay (re-running the entire computation) ensures correctness, it nullifies the computational savings of delegation. The paper seeks a verification mechanism that preserves delegation benefits while providing cryptographic assurance of correct execution.
AI.method: The authors propose GKR-HND, targeting the polynomial backbone of Homomorphic–Nonhomomorphic Decomposition (HND) Transformers. The protocol combines the GKR (Goldwasser–Kalai–Rothblum) interactive proof system with registered model weights (cryptographic commitments to model parameters). A retained verifier checks GKR transcripts and weight-opening proofs locally, but delegates expensive public GKR evaluations to a separate computation worker. Correctness relies on: (1) an honest retained verifier, and (2) non-collusion between the prover and the delegated worker. The worker's signed, request-bound responses must agree with the proof claims for the verifier to accept.
AI.result: Experiments on pretrained HND Transformer models demonstrate that the proof generation path is viable and that the delegated public computation scheme works correctly, all without requiring dense-matrix replay by the verifier.
AI.conclusion: GKR-HND offers a practical verification framework for outsourced Transformer inference that balances cryptographic integrity guarantees with computational efficiency, avoiding the prohibitive cost of full replay while detecting both model substitution and incomplete execution.

title: Confidently Deceptive: How Confidence Amplifies the Risk of LLM Deception
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can produce deceptive responses: outputs that mislead users in service of a contextually or experimentally induced goal. Yet it remains unclear how confidently models deceive and whether higher confidence makes deceptive responses more persuasive to end users. In this paper, we study these basic questions in various models and different deception datasets. We provide a comprehensive study measuring confidence through both verbalized self-reports and a range of logit-based estimators. We show that LLMs deliver deceptive responses with substantial verbalized confidence and that human annotators prefer the higher-confidence deceptive response 78% of the time in paired comparisons. Misalignment fine-tuning amplifies the problem. Confidence in deceptive responses rises across all three benchmarks, increasing the resulting potential risk, with effects generalizing beyond the training distribution. Strikingly, models classify their own deceptive outputs as deceptive at high rates (82.7% under misalignment) while still predicting they would produce them - recognition without avoidance. We argue that confident deception is a distinct alignment risk requiring evaluations that jointly measure deception, confidence, and awareness.

AI.tldr: LLMs produce deceptive responses with high confidence; humans prefer these responses 78% of the time; misalignment fine-tuning amplifies confidence in deception; models recognize their own deceptive outputs (82.7%) yet fail to avoid them — a "recognition without avoidance" phenomenon.
AI.motivation: While prior work has established that LLMs can produce deceptive responses, two critical questions remain unanswered: (1) how confidently do models deliver deceptive outputs, and (2) does higher confidence make deceptive responses more persuasive to end users? Understanding these dynamics is essential for assessing real-world alignment risks.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comprehensive empirical study across multiple LLMs and deception datasets, measuring confidence through verbalized self-reports (explicit confidence statements) and logit-based estimators (e.g., token probabilities, entropy). They employ paired human evaluations comparing high- vs. low-confidence deceptive responses, apply misalignment fine-tuning to amplify deceptive tendencies, and test whether models can self-detect their own deceptive outputs.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) LLMs produce deceptive responses with substantial verbalized confidence. (2) Human annotators prefer higher-confidence deceptive responses 78% of the time. (3) Misalignment fine-tuning increases confidence in deception across all three benchmarks, generalizing beyond the training distribution. (4) Models classify their own deceptive outputs as deceptive at 82.7% under misalignment, yet still predict they would produce them — demonstrating recognition without avoidance.
AI.conclusion: Confident deception constitutes a distinct and underexamined alignment risk. The authors argue that safety evaluations should jointly measure deception, confidence, and awareness, rather than treating these dimensions in isolation. The "recognition without avoidance" finding suggests current models lack the self-regulatory capacity to refrain from known deceptive behavior.

title: When RLVR Shrinks the Reasoning Boundary: Diagnosing Pass@k Inversion
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can improve one-sample accuracy while making a model worse under repeated sampling. We study this pass@k inversion: after training, the policy may solve fewer distinct problems than its base model at large $k$. The failure concentrates on boundary prompts, where the base model contains rare correct trajectories that are recoverable by sampling but too sparse to reliably appear in finite RLVR rollout groups. We argue that a two-mode account explains this as an absence-of-evidence failure: rare correct trajectories may disappear before RLVR samples and reinforces them often enough. The main contribution is this diagnostic and mechanistic framing. Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA) is a deliberately simple proof-of-concept: sharpen prompts with sufficient frozen-base correct evidence, and anchor risky prompts to the base distribution. Across three training seeds on Omni-MATH-Test, with MATH500 as a secondary high-coverage validation benchmark, PBA improves both \PassK{1} and high-budget coverage over matched GRPO. A 3000-prompt regime-controlled diagnostic study is consistent across seeds with the expected signature: ordinary GRPO loses base-solvable boundary prompts, while PBA preserves rare verifier-positive trajectories. We use mathematical verifiers as a controlled testbed for verifier-guided optimization; the same pass@k inversion risk applies to ECCV-relevant vision-language agents when repeated visual, spatial, or chart-reasoning attempts are checked by external tools or verifiers. Reasoning post-training should decide not only how strongly to optimize, but which prompts are safe to optimize.

AI.tldr: RLVR improves one-sample accuracy but degrades pass@k at large k (pass@k inversion), because rare correct trajectories on "boundary prompts" vanish before being reinforced. The paper introduces Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA) to preserve such trajectories, improving both pass@1 and high-budget coverage over GRPO.
AI.motivation: RLVR training creates a pass@k inversion phenomenon: models improve on pass@1 but solve fewer distinct problems under repeated sampling at large k compared to the base model. This is critical for agentic and reasoning systems where multiple attempts are practical. The failure concentrates on boundary prompts where correct trajectories exist in the base model but are too sparse to be reliably sampled and reinforced during RLVR rollouts.
AI.method: The authors provide a diagnostic and mechanistic framing of pass@k inversion as an "absence-of-evidence" failure. They introduce Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA), a proof-of-concept intervention: (1) sharpen prompts that have sufficient frozen-base correct evidence, and (2) anchor risky prompts by mixing in the base distribution to preserve rare correct trajectories. Experiments use Omni-MATH-Test with MATH500 as a validation benchmark, with a 3000-prompt diagnostic study across three seeds.
AI.result: PBA improves both pass@1 and high-budget coverage over matched GRPO across three training seeds. The 3000-prompt diagnostic study shows consistent results: ordinary GRPO loses base-solvable boundary prompts, while PBA preserves rare verifier-positive trajectories. The pass@k inversion signature is robust across seeds.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning post-training must decide not only how strongly to optimize, but which prompts are safe to optimize. The pass@k inversion risk extends beyond mathematical verifiers to vision-language agents where repeated attempts are verified by external tools. PBA demonstrates that simple anchoring strategies can mitigate the trade-off between one-sample accuracy and coverage under repeated sampling.

title: PersonaTrail: Benchmarking Personalized Web Agents through Browsing Trails
summary: Recent advances in large language models have enabled web agents to autonomously execute complex tasks. In practice, users frequently provide underspecified instructions, requiring agents to infer the missing context from their raw browsing histories. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this form of personalization, as they either restrict tasks to fully explicit prompts or abstract web interaction history into simplified forms. To bridge this gap, we introduce PersonaTrail, a benchmark for personalized web agents operating in a managed open web environment. By leveraging realistic browsing trajectories as user history, PersonaTrail evaluates an agent's ability to infer user preferences and recall information from past browsing sessions. We further propose Preference-Aware Contextual Memory (PACMem), a framework that decomposes raw browsing histories into two types of structured memory: factual memories that summarize individual sessions and preference memories that distill recurring behavioral patterns. At inference time, the agent retrieves the most relevant entries from these memories to guide personalized navigation. Extensive experiments show that PACMem consistently outperforms existing memory-based baselines on both tasks.

AI.tldr: PersonaTrail is a benchmark for evaluating personalized web agents that must infer user preferences from realistic browsing histories. The authors also propose PACMem, a memory framework that decomposes browsing history into factual and preference memories, outperforming existing baselines on personalization tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for web agents fail to capture personalization because they either use fully explicit instructions or oversimplify browsing history. In reality, users give underspecified instructions, and agents must infer missing context from raw, unstructured browsing histories. PersonaTrail fills this gap.
AI.method: The authors introduce PersonaTrail, a benchmark built on realistic browsing trajectories in an open web environment. They also propose PACMem (Preference-Aware Contextual Memory), which decomposes raw browsing histories into two structured memory types: (1) factual memories summarizing individual sessions and (2) preference memories capturing recurring behavioral patterns. At inference, the agent retrieves relevant entries from both memory types to guide personalized navigation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that PACMem consistently outperforms existing memory-based baselines on both personalization tasks evaluated in the PersonaTrail benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Personalized web agents require both factual recall and preference inference from browsing history. Structuring memory into factual and preference components, as done in PACMem, provides a strong foundation for handling underspecified user instructions in open web environments.

title: SCoPE: Shift-Aware Speaker-Conditioned Priors for Emotion Recognition in Conversations
summary: In conversations, human emotions are transient; however, they tend to persist across multiple utterances. For example, we rarely switch instantly between contrasting emotions such as happiness and anger. Instead, emotions tend to evolve smoothly, and these patterns are often speaker-specific. Some people might escalate, while others gradually cool down over time. Furthermore, when emotions change during a conversation, they are often driven by contextual factors, such as newly received information or unexpected events. Even though progress has been made in Emotion Recognition in Conversations (ERC), most existing approaches still rely heavily on overt evidence and do not sufficiently model these non-apparent factors. Especially in multimodal settings, this makes these models fragile when the signals are noisy (e.g., occluded faces, slang expressions, or microphone noise). To address these limitations, we introduce Speaker-Conditioned Priors over Emotions (SCoPE). SCoPE is a light weight module that utilizes the emotional history of each speaker and explicitly models their priors for use in subsequent emotion classification. Second, we incorporate emotion shift prediction, a well-established concept in ERC, to guide the model in balancing the priors from SCoPE and multimodal evidence. Finally, we propose a shift-aware fusion mechanism that performs precision-weighted logit integration between multimodal evidence and the speaker prior, forming a Bayesian-inspired product-of-experts formulation. This dynamic fusion allows the model to rely on historical priors when emotions persist and to prioritize multimodal evidence when shifts are likely. Experimental results show our model achieves superior performance over recent state-of-the-art models on the IEMOCAP dataset in multimodal settings.

AI.tldr: SCoPE introduces speaker-conditioned emotional priors, emotion shift prediction, and a shift-aware Bayesian fusion mechanism to improve multimodal emotion recognition in conversations, outperforming state-of-the-art on IEMOCAP.
AI.motivation: Existing ERC models rely heavily on overt multimodal evidence and fail to model latent factors like emotional inertia, smooth transitions, speaker-specific patterns, and contextual triggers of emotion shifts. This makes them fragile under noisy multimodal signals (e.g., occluded faces, slang, microphone noise).
AI.method: SCoPE consists of three components: (1) a lightweight module that computes speaker-conditioned emotional priors from each speaker's history; (2) emotion shift prediction to guide the balance between priors and evidence; and (3) a shift-aware fusion mechanism using a Bayesian product-of-experts formulation that performs precision-weighted logit integration, dynamically weighting historical priors vs. multimodal evidence based on shift likelihood.
AI.result: The model achieves superior performance over recent state-of-the-art models on the IEMOCAP dataset in multimodal settings.
AI.conclusion: Modeling speaker-specific emotional priors and explicitly handling emotion shifts via a dynamic, precision-weighted fusion yields robust and state-of-the-art multimodal ERC, particularly when sensory signals are noisy.

title: Conflict Resolution under Degraded Surveillance in Air Corridors Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Safe Advanced Air Mobility operations require aircraft to maintain separation when surveillance information is noisy, delayed, incomplete, or temporarily unavailable. This study develops a Deep Q-Network-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework for decentralized conflict resolution among heterogeneous small unmanned aerial vehicles and electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft operating within a structured three-dimensional corridor. Separate policies are trained for the two aircraft categories using local observations and a 14-action space that includes maintaining course, turning, vertical maneuvering, landing, and speed control. The simulation incorporates aircraft-specific dynamics, energy use, corridor constraints, observation noise, communication delay, information dropout, wind disturbance, actuator uncertainty, and model uncertainty. The trained policies are evaluated across 90 combinations of traffic density and minimum separation thresholds. Loss-of-separation frequency and duration generally increase with traffic density and separation requirements, although most events are resolved within 1s. Under safe conditions, agents maintain their motion approximately 79% of the time. During conflicts, turning accounts for 33% of actions, followed by maintaining motion at 29%, speed control at 25%, and vertical maneuvers at 13%. Six Pareto-optimal configurations reveal trade-offs between safety and corridor capacity. The framework supports the simulation-based evaluation of safer AAM conflict-resolution strategies under degraded surveillance conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a Deep Q-Network-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework for decentralized conflict resolution between UAVs and eVTOL aircraft in 3D corridors under degraded surveillance, evaluating trade-offs between safety and capacity across 90 scenarios.
AI.motivation: Safe Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) requires reliable conflict resolution when surveillance data is noisy, delayed, incomplete, or temporarily unavailable. Existing approaches may not adequately handle heterogeneous aircraft types operating under realistic degraded sensing conditions in structured airspace corridors.
AI.method: A DQN-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework trains separate policies for small UAVs and eVTOL aircraft using local observations with a 14-action space (maintain course, turn, vertical maneuver, land, speed control). The simulation incorporates aircraft-specific dynamics, energy constraints, corridor constraints, observation noise, communication delay, information dropout, wind disturbance, actuator uncertainty, and model uncertainty. Policies are evaluated across 90 combinations of traffic density and minimum separation thresholds.
AI.result: Loss-of-separation frequency and duration increase with traffic density and separation requirements, though most events resolve within 1 second. Under safe conditions, agents maintain motion ~79% of the time. During conflicts: turning (33%), maintaining motion (29%), speed control (25%), vertical maneuvers (13%). Six Pareto-optimal configurations reveal safety-capacity trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables simulation-based evaluation of decentralized conflict-resolution strategies under degraded surveillance, demonstrating viable learned policies for heterogeneous AAM operations and quantifying key safety-capacity trade-offs via Pareto analysis.

title: Tractable Hierarchical Control of Autoregressive Language Models
summary: Constraining the generation of autoregressive large language models (LLMs) is an important component of integrating language models into formal systems. In the generation of code and data for tasks like program synthesis, ensuring that language models produce syntactically valid output is a prerequisite for processing such output. These languages (such as SQL or JSON) are often designed as $LR(k)$ context-free grammars. By distilling the LLM to a tractable probabilistic model, its autoregressive generation can be steered and masked to incorporate the probability of satisfying logical constraints, ensuring high quality output that is guaranteed to be valid. This paper demonstrates that the satisfaction of any $LR(k)$ grammar of finite duration can be calculated in polynomial time, an improvement over the exponential time of applying previous methods to such grammars. This result enables efficient constraint and steering of LLM generation towards output that better satisfies formal syntactic constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a polynomial-time method for constraining autoregressive LLM generation to satisfy any LR(k) context-free grammar, improving upon previous exponential-time approaches and enabling efficient syntactic steering for tasks like code/SQL/JSON generation.
AI.motivation: When integrating LLMs into formal systems (e.g., program synthesis, SQL/JSON generation), ensuring syntactically valid output is a prerequisite. Existing methods for constraining generation to satisfy context-free grammars run in exponential time for LR(k) languages, making them impractical. A more efficient approach is needed.
AI.method: The authors distill the LLM into a tractable probabilistic model, then apply constrained generation via masking/steering. They prove that satisfaction of any LR(k) grammar of finite duration can be decided in polynomial time, leveraging properties of LR(k) parsing to efficiently compute which next tokens are valid under the grammar constraint.
AI.result: The paper proves that satisfying LR(k) grammar constraints during generation can be done in polynomial time, an exponential improvement over prior constraint methods applied to this grammar class. This enables practical, efficient constrained decoding for LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Efficient polynomial-time constraint satisfaction for LR(k) grammars makes it feasible to guarantee syntactically valid LLM output, facilitating more reliable integration of LLMs into formal systems and structured generation tasks.

title: Distinguishing Artificial from Authentic: Evaluating LLMs for Detecting LLM-Generated Content
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by students to generate natural language responses and program code, there is growing interest in whether LLMs themselves can be used to distinguish AI-generated work from human-authored submissions. In this paper, we investigate the extent to which LLMs can detect their own generated content across multiple educational task types, including programming exercises, reflective writing, and short-answer questions. Using authentic student responses and multiple variants of LLM-generated answers, we evaluate detection performance under different prompting strategies and output formats. Our study addresses three research questions: (1) how accurately LLMs can identify their own outputs across task domains, (2) how detection effectiveness is influenced by factors such as prompt design, response length, and task type, and (3) what characteristics of LLM-generated responses contribute to successful or failed detection. Our findings show that LLM-based detection is highly task-dependent: detection is substantially more reliable for programming tasks and longer reflective responses, but performs poorly for short-answer questions, where LLMs frequently judge their own outputs as more human-like than authentic student responses. We further find that prompt framing and response verbosity have a pronounced effect on detectability in reflective writing tasks, with relatively minor prompt variations significantly reducing detection accuracy, while programming-related detection is more robust to prompt changes. Together, these results highlight both the potential and the limitations of LLM self-detection in educational settings and suggest caution in relying on LLMs as standalone tools for identifying AI-generated student work.

AI.tldr: LLMs can detect their own generated content with varying reliability: detection works well for programming tasks and long reflective writing, but fails for short-answer questions where LLMs often misclassify their own outputs as more human-like than real student responses. Prompt design and response length significantly affect accuracy.
AI.motivation: With the increasing use of LLMs by students for generating assignments, there is a practical need to assess whether LLMs themselves can serve as detectors of AI-generated content in educational contexts, and to understand the reliability and limitations of such self-detection.
AI.method: The authors evaluated LLM-based detection using authentic student responses and multiple LLM-generated answer variants across three task types: programming exercises, reflective writing, and short-answer questions. They tested detection performance under different prompting strategies and output formats, analyzing how factors such as prompt design, response length, and task type influence detection accuracy.
AI.result: LLM-based detection is highly task-dependent: it is substantially more reliable for programming tasks and longer reflective responses, but performs poorly for short-answer questions. In short-answer tasks, LLMs frequently judge their own outputs as more human-like than authentic student responses. Prompt framing and response verbosity significantly affect detectability in reflective writing, while programming detection is more robust to prompt variations.
AI.conclusion: LLM self-detection shows promise but is unreliable as a standalone tool for identifying AI-generated student work, particularly for short-answer questions. Educators should exercise caution and not depend solely on LLMs for academic integrity enforcement.

title: SOAP, Muon, and Beyond: Pushing LLM Pretraining Scales
summary: Higher-order optimizers such as Muon and SOAP offer faster convergence than AdamW, but their computational cost and numerical stability challenges have limited adoption at scale. In this work, we adapt and enhance preconditioned gradient methods to overcome the practical challenges of large-scale LLM pretraining. We first identify instabilities in SOAP at large batch sizes and propose algorithmic modifications including per-step QR orthogonalization and improved preconditioning strategies that eliminate loss spikes and enable stable training in these regimes. We then present a unified empirical study of SOAP, Muon, and AdamW using update-RMS matching to ensure fair learning rate transfer across optimizers. As part of this analysis, we empirically evaluate the orthogonalization quality of Muon. Our experiments on multi-billion-parameter models trained on trillions of tokens reveal that SOAP and Muon consistently outperform AdamW at the scales we tested. Notably, at batch sizes of up to 100M tokens for next-token prediction, these optimizers maintain training stability and quality while AdamW degrades. To enable efficient training at large scale, we introduce a layer-wise distributed optimizer compatible with Megatron-LM. Our implementation balances memory and hides communication while avoiding approximations to the optimizer computations, thus retaining their convergence benefits. Additionally, we identify and build specific system-level improvements to further accelerate our layer-wise implementation. To support the research community, we release a codebase that contains emerging algorithms for optimization: https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Emerging-Optimizers

AI.tldr: The paper adapts higher-order optimizers (SOAP, Muon) for large-scale LLM pretraining by solving stability issues at large batch sizes, introducing update-RMS matching for fair comparison, and building a layer-wise distributed implementation compatible with Megatron-LM. Both SOAP and Muon consistently outperform AdamW at multi-billion-parameter scale and maintain stability at batch sizes up to 100M tokens where AdamW degrades.
AI.motivation: Higher-order optimizers like Muon and SOAP converge faster than AdamW but suffer from high computational cost and numerical instability, preventing adoption at scale for LLM pretraining. The work aims to overcome these practical barriers.
AI.method: (1) Algorithmic fixes for SOAP: per-step QR orthogonalization and improved preconditioning strategies to eliminate loss spikes at large batch sizes. (2) Update-RMS matching: a unified empirical framework for fair learning rate transfer across SOAP, Muon, and AdamW. (3) Empirical evaluation of Muon's orthogonalization quality. (4) Layer-wise distributed optimizer implementation within Megatron-LM that balances memory, hides communication, and avoids computational approximations. (5) System-level optimizations to accelerate the distributed implementation.
AI.result: SOAP and Muon consistently outperform AdamW on multi-billion-parameter models trained on trillions of tokens. At batch sizes up to 100M tokens for next-token prediction, SOAP and Muon maintain training stability and quality, while AdamW degrades. The proposed stability fixes successfully eliminate loss spikes. The layer-wise distributed implementation achieves efficient large-scale training without sacrificing convergence benefits.
AI.conclusion: Preconditioned gradient methods (SOAP, Muon) are viable and superior alternatives to AdamW for large-scale LLM pretraining when stability and systems challenges are properly addressed. The authors release their codebase to facilitate further research.

title: The Devil is in the Spectrum: Mitigating Representation Collapse in LLMs via Topologically Regularized Side-Path
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are fundamentally limited by representation collapse, a bottleneck that severely degrades long-context performance. We identify that existing approaches risk drifting into one of two pathological extremes: homogenization collapse (e.g., attention sinks causing rank deficiency) and isolation collapse (e.g., local attention causing context disconnection). Through spectral analysis of attention dynamics, we derive an intrinsic trade-off between mixing efficiency (spectral gap) and information capacity (effective rank) that standard mechanisms struggle to balance. To resolve this dilemma, we propose the Topologically Regularized Side-Path (TRSP), a non-invasive architectural intervention that achieves spectral balance. TRSP employs a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism, scaled by a lightweight, length-aware gate, to regularize the token interaction topology. By integrating proximal coupling to preserve effective rank and distal propagation to support non-degenerate mixing, TRSP promotes a geometrically healthier transition operator without altering core attention. Experiments show significant improvements across general capabilities and long-context benchmarks. Notably, on NoLiMa at $8\times$ the training length, TRSP retains $83\%$ accuracy and surpasses the Differential Transformer and Gated Attention by approximately 30 and 50 percentage points, respectively. Code available at: https://github.com/Eziotao-tyd/TRSP.

AI.tldr: LLMs suffer from representation collapse in long contexts, manifesting as either homogenization (rank deficiency from attention sinks) or isolation (context disconnection from local attention). The authors propose TRSP, a lightweight, non-invasive architectural add-on using a Triangular Box mechanism and length-aware gating to regularize token interaction topology, achieving spectral balance and significantly improving long-context performance.
AI.motivation: Standard attention mechanisms exhibit an intrinsic trade-off between mixing efficiency (spectral gap) and information capacity (effective rank), leading to two pathological collapse modes—homogenization and isolation—that severely limit long-context LLM performance. Existing solutions drift toward one extreme or the other without resolving the fundamental tension.
AI.method: TRSP is a non-invasive side-path module added to existing attention layers. It uses a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism that enforces a structured token interaction topology, scaled by a lightweight, length-aware gate. The design combines proximal coupling (to preserve effective rank) and distal propagation (to enable non-degenerate mixing), regularizing the transition operator toward a geometrically healthy spectral profile without modifying core attention.
AI.result: TRSP yields significant gains on general and long-context benchmarks. At 8× training length on NoLiMa, it retains 83% accuracy and outperforms Differential Transformer by ~30 pp and Gated Attention by ~50 pp.
AI.conclusion: Explicit topological regularization of the attention transition operator via TRSP effectively resolves the representation collapse dilemma, enabling robust long-context processing without sacrificing core model capabilities.

title: thaulab@EEUCA 2026: Who Said What to Whom? A Targeting-Aware Neural-Symbolic Pipeline for Gaming Toxicity Detection
summary: This paper describes our system for the EEUCA 2026 Shared Task on toxicity classification in gaming chat. We implement a three-stage pipeline combining an ensemble of two compact transformers (DeBERTa-v3-base, 184M; XLM-RoBERTa-base, 278M) with a Linguistically-Informed Mediator (LIM) that resolves inter-model disagreements through corpus-backed lexical normalization, class-conditional unigram scoring, multilingual profanity detection, and agentive targeting analysis grounded in speech act theory. The LIM specifically targets the minority classes (Hate \& Harassment, Threats, and Extremism), which are the most safety-critical categories in real-world gaming moderation. To address the extreme class imbalance (1{,}450:1 Non-toxic to Extremism ratio), we introduce a two-stage data augmentation strategy using only the provided training data. Our system achieves a Macro F1 of 0.6441 and accuracy of 0.9062 on the official test set, ranking 3rd in Macro F1 and 1st in accuracy among all teams. The proposed pipeline is domain-portable: adapting to other gaming platforms requires substituting only the game-specific entity lexicon. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Anmol2059/thaulab\_EEUCA.

AI.tldr: A three-stage toxicity classification pipeline (ensemble of DeBERTa-v3-base and XLM-RoBERTa-base + linguistically-informed mediator) with targeted data augmentation, achieving 3rd in Macro F1 (0.6441) and 1st in accuracy (0.9062) on the EEUCA 2026 gaming chat shared task.
AI.motivation: Gaming chat toxicity classification suffers from extreme class imbalance (1,450:1 ratio for the Extremism class) and the critical need to accurately detect minority safety-critical classes (Hate & Harassment, Threats, Extremism) that standard models tend to miss.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) an ensemble of two compact transformers (DeBERTa-v3-base, 184M; XLM-RoBERTa-base, 278M); (2) a Linguistically-Informed Mediator (LIM) that resolves model disagreements via lexical normalization, class-conditional unigram scoring, multilingual profanity detection, and agentive targeting analysis grounded in speech act theory; (3) a two-stage data augmentation strategy using only the provided training data to combat class imbalance.
AI.result: Macro F1 of 0.6441 and accuracy of 0.9062 on the official test set, ranking 3rd in Macro F1 and 1st in accuracy among all participating teams.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline effectively addresses severe class imbalance while prioritizing safety-critical minority classes. The system is domain-portable across gaming platforms, requiring only substitution of the game-specific entity lexicon. Code is publicly available.

title: SevDiff: Severity-Conditioned Diffusion for Long-Tail Conflict Trajectory Generation
summary: Trajectory datasets used in ADAS evaluation are heavily biased toward routine driving; genuine vehicle-to-vehicle conflict events are rare, and the rarer the event, the higher the cost when an ADAS system fails to handle it. Existing generative approaches address this imbalance by conditioning on scene-level properties - spatial goals, agent structure, or natural-language adversarial objectives - but none can accept a target Time-to-Collision (TTC) value as input and be held to producing it within a measurable error. This paper introduces SevDiff, a severity-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that accepts a requested minimum TTC value as a scalar conditioning signal and generates paired vehicle interaction trajectories whose realized conflict severity matches the request, evaluated through a hit-rate metric. Trained on 468 interaction windows extracted from the UTE SQM-W-1 expressway weaving-section dataset (1,041 vehicles, 822,691 observations after smoothing), SevDiff achieves 100% hit-rate within +/-0.5 s for TTC targets of 0.5-1.5 s and 97-99% at 2.0-2.5 s, with graceful degradation to 39% at TTC = 5.0 s. Generated kinematic features are physically plausible, with a maximum out-of-range rate of 4.7% across 12 features and no negative speed or gap values in more than 96.5% of samples. The hit-rate degradation pattern is physically interpretable as the strength of the conditioning signal relative to the training prior, making it a precision characterization of the generator rather than a pass/fail result.

AI.tldr: SevDiff is a diffusion model that generates vehicle interaction trajectories conditioned on a target Time-to-Collision (TTC) value, achieving high hit-rate accuracy for low TTC (severe conflict) scenarios to address the rarity of conflict events in ADAS evaluation datasets.
AI.motivation: ADAS trajectory datasets are dominated by routine driving with scarce vehicle-to-vehicle conflict events. Existing generative methods condition on scene-level properties but cannot accept a target TTC value as input. The rarer the conflict event, the higher the cost of ADAS failure, motivating a severity-conditioned generator with measurable fidelity to requested conflict severity.
AI.method: SevDiff is a severity-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that takes a scalar minimum TTC value as conditioning input and generates paired vehicle interaction trajectories. Performance is evaluated via a hit-rate metric (fraction of generated samples whose realized TTC falls within ±0.5 s of the target). Trained on 468 interaction windows from the UTE SQM-W-1 expressway weaving-section dataset.
