AI.result: SevDiff achieves 100% hit-rate within ±0.5 s for TTC targets of 0.5–1.5 s, 97–99% at 2.0–2.5 s, degrading gracefully to 39% at TTC = 5.0 s. Generated kinematics are physically plausible: maximum out-of-range rate of 4.7% across 12 features, with no negative speed or gap values in >96.5% of samples. The degradation pattern is physically interpretable as conditioning signal strength relative to the training prior.
AI.conclusion: The hit-rate degradation pattern reflects the weakening of the TTC conditioning signal against the training data prior, providing a precision characterization of generator capability rather than a binary pass/fail. SevDiff enables targeted generation of safety-critical scenarios at user-specified severity levels for ADAS evaluation.

title: Expectation Alignment of Language Models for Real-World User Expectations
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance on standard benchmarks, yet it remains largely unexplored whether they truly meet user expectations. Existing evaluation approaches, relying on model heuristics, expert rubrics, or user simulation, fail to capture the diversity and subtlety of real human expectations, causing models to appear competent while misaligning with what users actually seek. We present the first systematic study of user expectations in real-world LLM interactions, proposing a principled procedure to extract semantically rich expectations and introducing ExpectBench, a benchmark grounded in real user expectations. Analyses reveal that current LLMs struggle to satisfy and anticipate what users hope to obtain, highlighting a fundamental source of misalignment. Building on these observations, we propose LENS, a lightweight latent expectation-aware response generation framework. LENS enables models to internalize user expectations and generate better-aligned responses, consistently improving expectation satisfaction and underscoring the importance of explicitly modeling user expectations for realistic human-AI alignment.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that LLMs often fail to meet real user expectations despite strong benchmark performance. The authors introduce ExpectBench, a benchmark built from real user interactions, and propose LENS, a framework that helps models internalize and satisfy user expectations for better human-AI alignment.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluation methods (model heuristics, expert rubrics, user simulation) fail to capture the diversity and subtlety of genuine human expectations, creating a misalignment where models appear competent on benchmarks but fall short of what users actually want in real interactions.
AI.method: The authors conduct the first systematic study of user expectations in real-world LLM interactions. They develop a principled procedure to extract semantically rich expectations from these interactions and construct ExpectBench. Based on their findings, they propose LENS, a lightweight latent expectation-aware response generation framework that enables LLMs to internalize user expectations and produce better-aligned responses.
AI.result: Analyses using ExpectBench show that current LLMs struggle to both satisfy and anticipate user expectations, revealing a fundamental misalignment source. LENS consistently improves expectation satisfaction across models.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling user expectations is crucial for achieving realistic human-AI alignment, and the LENS framework demonstrates a viable path toward this goal.

title: Domyn-Small: A European 10B Reasoning Language Model
summary: We introduce Domyn-Small, a 10-billion-parameter open-weight reasoning language model released under the MIT license. Domyn-Small is the product of an initial pre-training phase on 9 trillion tokens multilingual data, followed by a post-training pipeline for reasoning, instruction following, and context extension. For the latter, we performed a Continued Pre-Training (CPT) phase that doubles the native context window to 32K tokens, followed by SFT with a math-focused annealing run. Finally, the RL phase includes GRPO with verifiable rewards, DPO, and a multi-environment GRPO stage spanning five task domains: mathematics, code, multiple-choice QA, instruction-following, and tool calling. The 32K-token native context extends to 128K at inference via YaRN, and a chat-template toggle enables dual-mode reasoning. Against peer models in the 7--10B class (Qwen3.5-9B, OLMo-3-7B-Think, Nemotron-Nano-8B, Ministral-3-8B), Domyn-Small achieves a strong accuracy-efficiency balance: it produces roughly one-third as many tokens as Qwen3.5-9B and approximately 35% of OLMo-3-7B-Think's token budget on core reasoning benchmarks, while delivering strong instruction-following (IFEval 79.9) and competitive science reasoning (GPQA-Diamond 50.0). We release the weights and the post-training recipe alongside Domyn Swarm (Apache~2.0), an open-source framework for scalable LLM inference on HPC clusters developed during this program and used throughout this work.

AI.tldr: Domyn-Small is a 10B-parameter open-weight reasoning LM (MIT license) trained on 9T tokens, featuring a 32K native context window (extendable to 128K via YaRN), dual-mode reasoning, and multi-stage RL post-training. It achieves competitive accuracy with substantially lower token generation costs compared to peers in the 7–10B class.
AI.motivation: Develop an efficient, open-weight reasoning language model in the 7–10B parameter class that balances strong reasoning performance with substantially lower inference cost (token generation), addressing the efficiency gap in existing peer models.
AI.method: Pre-training on 9T multilingual tokens, followed by a post-training pipeline: (1) Continued Pre-Training (CPT) to double native context to 32K tokens, (2) SFT with math-focused annealing, (3) multi-stage RL comprising GRPO with verifiable rewards, DPO, and multi-environment GRPO across five domains (mathematics, code, multiple-choice QA, instruction-following, tool calling). Inference context extends to 128K via YaRN; a chat-template toggle enables dual-mode (reasoning vs. standard) operation.
AI.result: Domyn-Small produces ~1/3 the tokens of Qwen3.5-9B and ~35% of OLMo-3-7B-Think's token budget on core reasoning benchmarks, while achieving IFEval 79.9 (instruction-following) and GPQA-Diamond 50.0 (science reasoning).
AI.conclusion: Domyn-Small demonstrates that careful post-training design (CPT, math annealing, multi-domain RL) can yield a 10B reasoning model competitive with larger or similarly-sized peers at a fraction of the inference cost, all under permissive open-source licensing. The accompanying Domyn Swarm framework further supports scalable HPC inference.

title: Beyond SBDD: Geometric Deep Learning in Polypharmacology and Multi-target Drug Design
summary: The traditional "one drug, one target" paradigm of structure-based drug design (SBDD) frequently proves inadequate for treating multifactorial diseases such as cancer and neurodegenerative disorders, owing to compensatory signaling pathways and the emergence of drug resistance. While polypharmacology offers a synergistic therapeutic strategy, the rational design of ligands capable of simultaneously satisfying the geometric constraints imposed by multiple targets remains a major computational bottleneck. This review positions geometric deep learning (GDL) as a powerful integrative approach to overcome these limitations. We systematically survey GDL architectures ranging from invariant graph neural networks to SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models that harness non-Euclidean molecular data to capture intrinsic three-dimensional (3D) structural interdependencies. We critically analyze GDL applications across three core dimensions, including the characterization of shared binding pockets via geometric embeddings, multi-target bioactivity prediction through heterogeneous graph fusion, and de novo generation of dual-target ligands. Particular emphasis is placed on emerging structure-conditioned generative algorithms that integrate diffusion models with reinforcement learning to autonomously resolve complex geometric conflicts between competing binding sites. Furthermore, we evaluate the pivotal role of multimodal omics integration and specialized geometric benchmarking infrastructures in validating these models. By synthesizing these methodological advances, this review elucidates the paradigm shift in drug discovery from serendipitous exploration to rational, structure-driven polypharmacological molecular engineering, thereby providing a clear, structured guide for navigating the complexities of next-generation therapeutics.

AI.tldr: This review surveys geometric deep learning (GDL) architectures—from graph neural networks to SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models—for rational polypharmacological drug design, covering shared pocket characterization, multi-target bioactivity prediction, and de novo dual-target ligand generation, while highlighting structure-conditioned generative models that integrate diffusion with reinforcement learning to resolve geometric conflicts between competing binding sites.
AI.motivation: The traditional "one drug, one target" paradigm fails for multifactorial diseases (cancer, neurodegeneration) due to compensatory signaling and drug resistance. Rational design of multi-target ligands poses a major computational bottleneck because of the geometric constraints imposed by multiple binding sites simultaneously.
AI.method: The paper systematically surveys GDL architectures spanning invariant graph neural networks to SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models operating on non-Euclidean molecular data. It analyzes applications across three dimensions: (1) geometric embeddings for shared binding pocket characterization, (2) heterogeneous graph fusion for multi-target bioactivity prediction, and (3) structure-conditioned generative algorithms combining diffusion models with reinforcement learning for de novo dual-target ligand generation. Multimodal omics integration and specialized geometric benchmarking infrastructures are also evaluated.
AI.result: The review synthesizes methodological advances showing that GDL enables a paradigm shift from serendipitous exploration to rational, structure-driven polypharmacological molecular engineering. Structure-conditioned generative models integrating diffusion with RL can autonomously resolve complex geometric conflicts between competing binding sites.
AI.conclusion: GDL provides a structured, integrative framework for next-generation polypharmacological drug discovery, overcoming the computational bottleneck of multi-target geometric constraints and enabling rational design of dual-target therapeutics.

title: OPTScientist: Multi-Agent Discovery of Typed Optimizer Programs for Transformer Pretraining
summary: Designing optimizers for modern deep learning remains a challenging scientific problem, requiring the joint consideration of optimization geometry, state dynamics, numerical stability, implementation constraints, and empirical generalization. Existing automated optimizer discovery methods typically search either over unconstrained code spaces or within narrowly parameterized optimizer families. The former is flexible but often produces invalid or uninterpretable programs, while the latter is stable but limits novelty. We introduce OPTScientist, a theory-guided multi-agent framework for optimizer discovery in a typed domain-specific language (DSL). OPTScientist formulates optimizer design as a constrained scientific search process, where candidate updates are expressed through direction, scaling, preconditioning, regularization, state, and grouping modules. Four role agents, Theorist, Designer, Engineer, and Reviewer, collaborate within a single orchestration loop to propose hypotheses, synthesize DSL candidates, compile and evaluate optimizers, and critique results. To overcome the limitations of a fixed search space, OPTScientist combines evolutionary search over optimizer programs with a second-stage mechanism that proposes small DSL extensions when repeated failures reveal representational bottlenecks. Using this framework, we discover RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that improves transformer pretraining over strong baselines under our native evaluation protocol. Our results suggest a path toward automated optimizer science grounded in theory, typed programs, compiler validation, and closed-loop experimentation.

AI.tldr: OPTScientist is a theory-guided multi-agent framework that discovers optimizers using a typed DSL, combining evolutionary search with DSL extension mechanisms. It discovered RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that improves transformer pretraining over strong baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing automated optimizer discovery methods face a trade-off: unconstrained code search is flexible but yields invalid/ uninterpretable programs, while parameterized family search is stable but limits novelty. A principled approach is needed that balances expressiveness, validity, and interpretability.
AI.method: OPTScientist uses a typed domain-specific language (DSL) with six modules (direction, scaling, preconditioning, regularization, state, grouping). Four role agents — Theorist, Designer, Engineer, and Reviewer — collaborate in an orchestration loop to hypothesize, synthesize, compile, evaluate, and critique optimizer candidates. Evolutionary search operates over DSL programs, with a second-stage mechanism that proposes DSL extensions when representational bottlenecks are detected through repeated failures.
AI.result: The framework discovered RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that achieves improved transformer pretraining performance compared to strong baselines under the authors' native evaluation protocol.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a viable path toward automated optimizer science by integrating theory, typed programs, compiler validation, and closed-loop experimentation, suggesting that constrained DSL-based search with multi-agent collaboration can yield both novel and practically effective optimizers.

title: The Storyteller in the Model: Narrative Pattern Inheritance, Escalation Dynamics, and Alignment Governance in LLMs
summary: LLMs are trained predominantly on human-authored text, yet the structural and narrative conventions embedded in that text are rarely examined as a source of systematic behavioral influence, or as a governance risk in deployed systems. This paper considers whether the storytelling patterns inherent in published human writing, including archetypal roles such as protagonist, antagonist, and underdog, as well as tension-and-resolution narrative arcs, are absorbed during training and subsequently surface in LLM outputs, causing responses to drift toward unexpected, adversarial, or rhetorically enticing behaviors over extended interactions. Through a systematic literature review and cross-paper analysis of recent empirical studies on LLM alignment, persona dynamics, emergent misalignment, and user interaction patterns, we observe evidence bearing on this hypothesis. The findings reveal three key patterns. First, LLMs reproduce statistical patterns from their training data rather than reasoning independently. Second, measurable latent traits, including sycophancy and deceptiveness, emerge reliably across unrelated prompts. Third, fine-tuning on a narrow narrative task can produce unintended behavioral changes well beyond that task. Furthermore, evidence suggests that persuasive, narrative-style outputs are among the most common LLM products in real-world usage, amplifying these risks. Narrative drift constitutes an unmonitored escalation pathway in deployed AI systems, one that evades discrete-incident detection mechanisms and requires dedicated monitoring instruments.

AI.tldr: LLMs absorb narrative conventions (protagonist/antagonist roles, tension-resolution arcs) from training data, causing outputs to drift toward adversarial or rhetorically manipulative behaviors over extended interactions — a governance risk that evades standard incident detection.
AI.motivation: Current LLM alignment and safety research overlooks the structural and narrative conventions embedded in human-authored training text as a systematic source of behavioral influence. The authors hypothesize that storytelling patterns — archetypal roles and dramatic arcs — are internalized during pretraining and can surface as "narrative drift," causing models to exhibit unexpected, adversarial, or persuasively enticing behaviors over sustained interactions.
AI.method: The paper employs a systematic literature review and cross-paper analysis, synthesizing findings from recent empirical studies on LLM alignment, persona dynamics, emergent misalignment, sycophancy, deceptiveness, and user interaction patterns to evaluate evidence for the narrative drift hypothesis.
AI.result: Three key findings emerge: (1) LLMs reproduce statistical training patterns rather than reasoning independently; (2) latent traits like sycophancy and deceptiveness surface reliably across unrelated prompts; (3) fine-tuning on narrow narrative tasks induces unintended behavioral shifts beyond the task scope. Additionally, persuasive narrative-style outputs dominate real-world LLM usage, compounding these risks.
AI.conclusion: Narrative drift represents an unmonitored escalation pathway in deployed AI systems that circumvents discrete-incident detection frameworks. The authors call for dedicated monitoring instruments to detect and mitigate this governance vulnerability.

title: SenCos-GEM: SENet-Calibrated and Law-of-Cosines-Constrained Geometry-Enhanced Molecular Representation for Property Prediction
summary: Effective molecular representation learning is crucial for accurate molecular property prediction. Recently, numerous self-supervised learning (SSL) approaches leveraging 3D GNNs have been developed to capture comprehensive 3D structural information for drug discovery. However, existing methods lack explicit physical constraints and are highly susceptible to geometric noise induced by coarse empirical force fields during large-scale pre-training.Furthermore, they overlook dynamic feature modulation during downstream adaptation, often resulting in catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer. To address these limitations, we introduce SenCos-GEM, a novel explicitly decoupled geometry-enhanced molecular representation learning framework that incorporates SENet-calibrated and law-of-cosines-constrained enhancements. SenCos-GEM employs a physics-guided geometric consistency loss based on the law of cosines to derive high-fidelity and mathematically invariant 3D spatial priors. In addition, lightweight Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) modules are integrated into the backbone as task-specific adapters, while a dual-modulation prediction head combines Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) and SENet mechanisms to enable dynamic feature recalibration. SenCos-GEM demonstrates highly competitive performance across diverse classification and regression tasks on MoleculeNet benchmark, establishing new state-of-the-art results specifically on 3D conformation-sensitive regression tasks, such as FreeSolv, Lipophilicity, and QM9, achieving relative error reductions of 12.9% (RMSE), 5.3% (RMSE), and 8.2% (MAE), respectively. Moreover, our model exhibits superior capability in distinguishing stereoisomers and discriminating conformational perturbations, underscoring its robust spatial modeling performance. Collectively, SenCos-GEM represents a significant breakthrough in accurate molecular property prediction.

AI.tldr: SenCos-GEM is a 3D molecular representation learning framework that combines law-of-cosines-based geometric consistency loss with SENet adapters and a dual-modulation head (FiLM + SENet) to address geometric noise sensitivity and catastrophic forgetting in SSL-based molecular property prediction, achieving SOTA on 3D-sensitive regression benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing self-supervised 3D GNN methods for molecular property prediction suffer from two key weaknesses: (1) they lack explicit physical constraints and are vulnerable to geometric noise from coarse empirical force fields during large-scale pre-training, and (2) they ignore dynamic feature modulation during downstream fine-tuning, leading to catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer.
AI.method: SenCos-GEM introduces: (a) a physics-guided geometric consistency loss derived from the law of cosines to obtain high-fidelity, mathematically invariant 3D spatial priors; (b) lightweight Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) modules integrated into the GNN backbone as task-specific adapters; and (c) a dual-modulation prediction head combining Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) with SENet mechanisms for dynamic feature recalibration during downstream adaptation.
AI.result: SenCos-GEM achieves new SOTA on 3D conformation-sensitive regression tasks: FreeSolv (12.9% RMSE reduction), Lipophilicity (5.3% RMSE reduction), and QM9 (8.2% MAE reduction). The model also shows superior stereoisomer discrimination and conformational perturbation detection, confirming robust spatial modeling.
AI.conclusion: SenCos-GEM represents a significant advance in molecular property prediction by explicitly enforcing physical constraints and enabling dynamic feature modulation, effectively mitigating geometric noise vulnerability and downstream forgetting.

title: Directional Hallucinations: Ideological Drift in News-Grounded LLM Question Answering
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer questions about political information, including in election-adjacent information settings where factual errors and ideological distortions are high-stakes. We present a reproducible measurement framework that treats hallucinations, unsupported statements in document-grounded QA, as diagnostic signals of ideological drift. Using 21,727 expert-labeled U.S. political news articles from QBias spanning left, center, and right sources, we (i) generate an article-specific question, (ii) elicit document-grounded answers from three open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model, (iii) detect sentence-level hallucinations via reference-based comparison, (iv) classify the ideological valence of hallucinated sentences with a fine-tuned stance classifier, and (v) probe output logits to relate token-level uncertainty to hallucination and drift. Hallucination rates vary substantially across models and concentrate in contentious topics, while source-ideology differences in hallucination frequency are modest. In contrast, hallucination content exhibits robust leftward drift: a majority of hallucinated sentences are classified as left-leaning, including among hallucinations generated from right-leaning sources. Logit-level analysis shows hallucinations arise in high-entropy generation contexts, and in some models uncertainty also predicts leftward drift, consistent with an "uncertainty to guessing" mechanism. We discuss implications for auditing AI-mediated political information and for designing safeguards in election-relevant deployments.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a framework using hallucinations (unsupported statements) in document-grounded QA as diagnostic signals of ideological bias in LLMs. Analyzing 21,727 political news articles, they find hallucination content exhibits consistent leftward ideological drift—even from right-leaning sources—and that hallucinations arise in high-entropy generation contexts.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed for political information queries, including in election contexts where factual errors and ideological distortions carry high stakes. The authors argue that hallucinations in document-grounded QA can serve as diagnostic signals revealing latent ideological tendencies in models, and that systematic measurement of such drift is needed for auditing AI-mediated political information.
AI.method: A five-step reproducible measurement pipeline: (1) generate article-specific questions from 21,727 expert-labeled U.S. political news articles (QBias dataset, spanning left/center/right); (2) elicit document-grounded answers from three open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model; (3) detect sentence-level hallucinations via reference-based comparison; (4) classify ideological valence of hallucinated sentences using a fine-tuned stance classifier; (5) probe output logits to relate token-level uncertainty to hallucination and ideological drift.
AI.result: Hallucination rates vary substantially across models and concentrate in contentious topics. Source-ideology differences in hallucination frequency are modest. However, hallucination content shows robust leftward drift: a majority of hallucinated sentences are classified as left-leaning, including hallucinations from right-leaning sources. Logit-level analysis reveals hallucinations arise in high-entropy contexts, and in some models uncertainty also predicts leftward drift—consistent with an "uncertainty to guessing" mechanism.
AI.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that LLM hallucinations systematically drift leftward regardless of source ideology, driven by high-uncertainty generation contexts. This has significant implications for auditing AI-mediated political information and designing safeguards for election-relevant deployments, where such systematic ideological distortion could influence information integrity at scale.

title: ShriNep@EEUCA 2026: RAKSHAK - Multi-Task DeBERTa with Rationale Distillation and Jigsaw-Augmented Training for Toxic Intent Classification
summary: This paper presents two systems for the GameTox Shared Task at the Workshop on EEUCA at ACL 2026, which requires classifying World of Tanks chat utterances into six fine-grained toxic intent categories (Labels 0-5). Severe class imbalance, domain-specific multilingual slang, and extremely scarce data for rare categories such as Threats (Label 4, 60 samples) and Extremism (Label 5, 24 samples) make this a challenging classification problem. Our primary submission, RAKSHAK (rak s. aka, Sanskrit for "Protector"), is a multi-task DeBERTa-v3-base (He et al., 2022) framework combining rationale distillation from Qwen2.5-14B (An et al., 2024), Supervised Contrastive Loss, and dedicated rare-class binary heads. RAKSHAK's training data is augmented with cross-domain transfer from the Jigsaw Toxic Comment dataset (16,225 samples mapped to Labels 1-4) and 100 LLM-generated extremism samples for Label 5. Our secondary system (M1) fine-tunes DeBERTa-v3-base with Focal Loss on the original GameTox data plus the same 100 extremism samples, without Jigsaw transfer. RAKSHAK achieves a Macro F1 of 0.5883 on the official test set, ranking 7th out of 35 participating teams, while M1 achieves 0.5252 Macro F1. An ablation comparing M1 with and without Jigsaw data shows that cross-domain transfer accounts for +2.6 F1 points, while RAKSHAK's multi-task architecture contributes a further +3.7 points.

AI.tldr: RAKSHAK, a multi-task DeBERTa-v3-base system with rationale distillation, contrastive loss, and rare-class heads, addresses fine-grained toxic intent classification in gaming chat with severe class imbalance, achieving 0.5883 Macro F1 (7th/35 teams).
AI.motivation: Classifying toxic chat in online games like World of Tanks is difficult due to severe class imbalance (some categories have only 24–60 samples), domain-specific multilingual slang, and the need for fine-grained intent distinction across six categories. Standard approaches struggle with rare classes, motivating a multi-task architecture with targeted data augmentation.
AI.method: RAKSHAK uses DeBERTa-v3-base with three core components: (1) rationale distillation from Qwen2.5-14B to inject reasoning signals; (2) Supervised Contrastive Loss to improve class separation; (3) dedicated binary classification heads for rare classes (Threats, Extremism). Training data is augmented via cross-domain transfer from the Jigsaw Toxic Comment dataset (16,225 samples mapped to Labels 1–4) and 100 LLM-generated extremism samples for Label 5. The secondary system (M1) uses only Focal Loss on original data plus the 100 extremism samples.
AI.result: RAKSHAK achieves 0.5883 Macro F1 on the official test set (7th of 35 teams). M1 achieves 0.5252 Macro F1. Ablation shows cross-domain Jigsaw transfer contributes +2.6 F1 points, while RAKSHAK's multi-task architecture adds a further +3.7 points.
AI.conclusion: Combining rationale distillation, contrastive learning, dedicated rare-class heads, and cross-domain data augmentation significantly improves fine-grained toxic intent classification under extreme data scarcity. The multi-task architecture provides the largest performance gain over Focal Loss alone.

title: Thermodynamic Weight Decay: Exploring Grokking Acceleration via Attention Specific Heat
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/baymaxbyte/cbo_core
summary: Grokking -- the delayed generalization of neural networks long after they have memorized their training data -- wastes thousands of training epochs and is notoriously unpredictable. Building on the recent result that Transformer attention is formally isomorphic to a thermodynamic system, we treat the variance of attention logits as a specific heat Cv and show that its peak reliably precedes the generalization transition. We introduce CvAdamW, a drop-in AdamW variant that monitors Cv online and injects thermal energy by dynamically scaling weight decay when a phase transition is detected. Through a strictly iterative development process we identify three failure modes -- initialization noise, mini-batch micro-ripples, and slingshot blinding -- and resolve them with a memorization gate and an exponential-moving-average shock absorber. On modular arithmetic (a+b mod 97), CvAdamW enables grokking at epoch 2802 in a 4000-epoch budget where the baseline never groks. We further propose a scale-invariant z-score reformulation that removes task-specific hyperparameters, and evaluate it across 10 paired seeds. A paired analysis shows the cold-start variant reduces mean grokking latency by 257 epochs (6.0%; median 166 epochs; Wilcoxon p=0.049, Cohen's d=0.68, bootstrap 95% CI [53,489]), improving 8 of 10 seeds; on this single task Cv peaks before grokking in all 10 seeds. Our results indicate that neural networks may expose detectable precursors of impending generalization transitions, and that a physically motivated, proportional intervention can facilitate generalization within a fixed compute budget. Code and data are public.

AI.tldr: This paper treats attention logit variance as a thermodynamic specific heat (Cv) that peaks before grokking, then introduces CvAdamW — an optimizer variant that detects this phase transition and dynamically scales weight decay to accelerate generalization. The method enables grokking within a fixed budget where baseline AdamW fails, and a scale-invariant version reduces grokking latency by ~6%.
AI.motivation: Grokking wastes thousands of epochs and is notoriously unpredictable. The authors aim to exploit a recently discovered thermodynamic isomorphism of Transformer attention to detect impending generalization transitions and intervene proportionally, making grokking reliable and efficient within fixed compute budgets.
AI.method: The variance of attention logits is treated as a specific heat Cv, whose peak reliably precedes the generalization transition. CvAdamW monitors Cv online and injects thermal energy by dynamically scaling weight decay when a phase transition is detected. Three failure modes (initialization noise, mini-batch micro-ripples, slingshot blinding) are resolved via a memorization gate and an exponential-moving-average shock absorber. A scale-invariant z-score reformulation removes task-specific hyperparameters.
AI.result: On modular arithmetic (a+b mod 97), CvAdamW achieves grokking at epoch 2802 within a 4000-epoch budget where baseline AdamW never groks. The z-score cold-start variant reduces mean grokking latency by 257 epochs (6.0%; median 166; Wilcoxon p=0.049, Cohen's d=0.68, bootstrap 95% CI [53,489]), improving 8 of 10 seeds. Cv peaks before grokking in all 10 seeds.
AI.conclusion: Neural networks expose detectable precursors of impending generalization transitions. A physically motivated, proportional intervention (CvAdamW) can facilitate generalization within a fixed compute budget, demonstrating that thermodynamic principles offer practical tools for training dynamics.

title: Autonomous Topology Mutation: Safe Runtime Restructuring for Multi-Agent LLM Systems with Capability, State, and Shadow Invariants
comment: 9 pages, 5 tables. Code and benchmark harness available at https://github.com/sidikbro/jiuwen_atm
summary:
Multi-agent LLM frameworks typically fix their team topology at boot time. When an individual agent becomes overloaded at runtime, for example by mixing too many action categories, accumulating tool errors, or queueing behind too many calls, the system has no mechanism to restructure itself. We introduce Autonomous Topology Mutation (ATM), a runtime team-mutation mechanism for multi-agent LLM frameworks. ATM combines telemetry-driven overload detection with three safety invariants that gate each structural change: capability monotonicity, state-routing completeness, and shadow-before-live validation.
  ATM monitors a six-signal Bottleneck Index that includes queue depth, context thrash, tool-error rate, role entropy, retry-loop rate, and cross-agent wait time. When a warmup-calibrated threshold is breached for multiple consecutive ticks, ATM factorises the overloaded agent into specialised sub-agents and hot-swaps the parent into a coordinator role while preserving its external identity. State transfer is controlled by privacy-level-aware routing: each memory atom is routed only to a permitted child set, or explicitly dropped with a logged reason. No candidate topology receives live traffic until it has passed a shadow validation window.
  On 720 DeepSeek-V3-driven task runs with deterministic tool stubs across four ablation conditions and three workloads, the ATM factoriser split lifts code-task success from 3.3% to 61.7%. The full rail-and-distillation system reduces detected high-privacy memory exposure under a regex classifier from 2.0 to 0.0 events per task while preserving task quality. The runtime rails carrying ATM's invariants add less than 500 microseconds of p99 latency on the agent hot path. A small live-tool probe with real Python execution is included as an external-validity check. The implementation, benchmark harness, and traces are open-sourced.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Autonomous Topology Mutation (ATM), a runtime mechanism that dynamically restructures overloaded multi-agent LLM systems by factorising bottlenecked agents into specialised sub-agents, governed by safety invariants and shadow validation, improving task success from 3.3% to 61.7%.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM frameworks suffer from fixed team topologies that cannot adapt when individual agents become overloaded at runtime due to mixing too many action categories, tool errors, or excessive queueing. No existing mechanism allows the system to restructure itself dynamically in response to such bottlenecks.
AI.method: ATM uses a six-signal Bottleneck Index (queue depth, context thrash, tool-error rate, role entropy, retry-loop rate, cross-agent wait time) with warmup-calibrated thresholds for overload detection. Upon breach over consecutive ticks, it factorises the overloaded agent into specialised sub-agents and hot-swaps the parent into a coordinator. Three safety invariants gate all changes: capability monotonicity, state-routing completeness, and shadow-before-live validation. State transfer uses privacy-level-aware routing, and no topology receives live traffic without passing shadow validation. Evaluated on 720 DeepSeek-V3-driven task runs across four ablation conditions and three workloads.
AI.result: The ATM factoriser alone lifts code-task success from 3.3% to 61.7%. The full system reduces detected high-privacy memory exposure from 2.0 to 0.0 events per task under a regex classifier while preserving task quality. Runtime invariant rails add under 500 microseconds p99 latency on the agent hot path.
AI.conclusion: ATM demonstrates that safe, dynamic runtime restructuring of multi-agent LLM topologies is feasible, dramatically improving task success rates while eliminating privacy leaks and maintaining low latency overhead. The system is open-sourced.

title: Semantic Field Theory: Historical Origin, Higher-Order Interaction, and Stabilized Semantic Inference
summary: Semantic Field Theory (SFT) has developed from a philosophical critique of strong anti-formalist readings of language games into a proposed computational model class for lexical semantics, higher order composition, and stabilized interpretation. This paper reconstructs that evolution and gives SFT a sharper mathematical core suitable for independent evaluation in computational linguistics and representation learning. The central proposal is that a tractable level of linguistic organization can be modeled through lexical representations expressed as semantic fields, through contextual deformation of those fields, through interaction terms defined over subsets of tokens, and through stabilization governed by semantic energy dynamics. The paper contributes five formal elements. First, it defines a semantic field model as a tuple consisting of a semantic space, a lexical field lifting, a contextual deformation map, an interaction complex, and an interpretation functional. Second, it proves a Gaussian product closure result showing that multiplicative field interactions have explicit centers, precisions, and compatibility factors. Third, it generalizes the three-word problem by using Mobius inversion on the subset lattice to isolate irreducible semantic interactions of arbitrary order. Fourth, it introduces an order spectrum that measures how much field mass is explained at each interaction order. Fifth, it formulates stabilized interpretation as minimization of an energy functional associated with the sentence and gives existence, descent, and stability conditions. A small worked example shows how a three-word summer day triple can be represented by Gaussian semantic fields, implemented in Python, and summarized by a flow diagram. The result is not a completed theory of natural language meaning and does not replace social, pragmatic, or normative accounts of language.

AI.tldr: Presents a formalized mathematical framework for Semantic Field Theory (SFT), defining semantic fields as computational objects with Gaussian product closure, Möbius inversion for higher-order interactions, order spectra, and energy-based stabilized interpretation.
AI.motivation: To reconstruct SFT from its philosophical origins into a mathematically rigorous computational model class suitable for independent evaluation in computational linguistics and representation learning.
AI.method: The paper contributes five formal elements: (1) a semantic field model tuple (semantic space, lexical field lifting, contextual deformation map, interaction complex, interpretation functional); (2) a Gaussian product closure theorem; (3) Möbius inversion on the subset lattice for isolating irreducible n-ary semantic interactions; (4) an order spectrum measuring field mass explained at each interaction order; (5) energy functional minimization for stabilized interpretation with existence, descent, and stability conditions. A worked three-word example is implemented in Python.
AI.result: Gaussian product closure yields explicit centers, precisions, and compatibility factors; Möbius inversion generalizes the three-word problem to arbitrary-order irreducible interactions; the order spectrum quantifies contribution by interaction order; energy minimization provides well-defined conditions for stable interpretation.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a tractable computational model for lexical semantics and compositional interpretation but is explicitly not a complete theory of meaning and does not replace social, pragmatic, or normative accounts of language.

title: Double-Scoring: Reliable Extraction of Strong Lottery Tickets
summary: The lottery ticket hypothesis proposes that large random neural networks contain sparse subnetworks that can match the performance of dense models after comparable training. A stronger version asserts that sufficiently overparameterized random networks contain subnetworks that are already accurate before any weight training. Existing theory establishes that such strong lottery tickets exist, but reliable extraction remains difficult. We revisit edge-popup, a frozen-weight score-training method for extracting strong tickets, and identify layerwise sparsity selection as a central bottleneck. We introduce double-scoring, an augmented score-space parameterization that replaces a layerwise sparsity search with optimization over enlarged score tensors. We prove that fixed-density masking in an augmented score space preserves access to all original-coordinate masks, and we show that the resulting method can be interpreted as edge-popup on a zero-augmented network. In controlled experiments, double-scoring substantially improves strong-ticket extraction over fixed-density edge-popup and pruning-at-initialization baselines, improves on the performance of rewound sparse-training topologies, and exhibits markedly lower sensitivity to sparsity hyperparameters. Ablations show that the gain is not merely due to additional trainable score parameters, but is tied to the augmented score-space competition that induces the effective original sparsity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "double-scoring," a method that improves extraction of strong lottery tickets (untrained subnetworks) by augmenting the score-space parameterization, replacing layerwise sparsity selection with optimization over enlarged score tensors, and proving this preserves access to all original-coordinate masks.
AI.motivation: Existing theory confirms strong lottery tickets exist in random networks, but reliable extraction remains difficult. The authors identify layerwise sparsity selection as a central bottleneck in edge-popup, the dominant frozen-weight score-training method.
AI.method: Double-scoring augments the score-space by introducing enlarged score tensors per layer. Instead of searching for a fixed sparsity per layer, optimization occurs over this expanded parameterization. The method is theoretically proven to preserve access to all masks achievable in the original coordinate space. It can be interpreted as edge-popup applied to a zero-augmented network.
AI.result: Double-scoring substantially outperforms fixed-density edge-popup and pruning-at-initialization baselines in controlled experiments. It also surpasses rewound sparse-training topologies and exhibits markedly lower sensitivity to sparsity hyperparameters. Ablations confirm gains stem from augmented score-space competition rather than merely additional trainable parameters.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting the score-space via double-scoring effectively addresses the layerwise sparsity bottleneck in strong ticket extraction, enabling more reliable recovery of accurate untrained subnetworks from overparameterized random networks.

title: EvoSQL: Memory-Augmented Critic-Generator Co-Evolution for Text-to-SQL
summary: Text-to-SQL has advanced rapidly with large language models, but complex database queries still require reasoning beyond one-shot generation, including multi-step decomposition, execution-based diagnosis, and targeted correction. We present EvoSQL, a co-evolution framework that formulates SQL synthesis as an iterative interaction between a generator and a critic. EvoSQL maintains a contextualized candidate memory, verifies SQL candidates with both execution signals and LLM-based critique, and updates its memory through utility-guided aggregation. To strengthen the underlying generator-critic pair, we further introduce a Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) fine-tuning stage that injects execution-aware supervision into modern coding LLM backbones. Experiments on Spider and BIRD show that EvoSQL consistently improves open-source models over Maj@16 baselines, with particularly large gains on BIRD-Dev, ranging from +1.37% for Qwen3-4B to +9.19% for Qwen2.5-Coder-3B. SDPO initialization further improves selected backbones on Spider-Test and BIRD-Dev. These results suggest that memory-grounded co-evolution is an effective path toward more reliable and generalizable Text-to-SQL systems. Code is available at https://github.com/valleysprings/EvoSQL.

AI.tldr: EvoSQL proposes a co-evolution framework for Text-to-SQL that iteratively refines SQL queries through generator-critic interaction with a contextualized memory, augmented by Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) fine-tuning, achieving consistent gains on Spider and BIRD benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Complex Text-to-SQL tasks require more than single-pass generation — they need multi-step decomposition, execution-based diagnosis, and targeted correction. Existing approaches lack a principled mechanism to accumulate and reuse diagnostic feedback across candidate generations.
AI.method: EvoSQL frames SQL synthesis as iterative co-evolution between a generator (produces SQL candidates) and a critic (evaluates via execution signals and LLM-based critique). A contextualized candidate memory stores verified outputs, updated through utility-guided aggregation. The framework is further strengthened by SDPO, a fine-tuning stage that injects execution-aware supervision into coding LLM backbones.
AI.result: On Spider and BIRD, EvoSQL consistently improves open-source models over Maj@16 baselines. Gains on BIRD-Dev range from +1.37% (Qwen3-4B) to +9.19% (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B). SDPO initialization further improves selected backbones on Spider-Test and BIRD-Dev.
AI.conclusion: Memory-grounded co-evolution is an effective path toward more reliable and generalizable Text-to-SQL systems, with both the iterative framework and SDPO fine-tuning contributing complementary improvements.

title: A Knowledge-Injection Framework for Zero-Shot Adaptation of LLMs to Delirium Prediction
summary: Large language models show promise for clinical prediction, but zero-shot performance on specialized tasks is limited by incomplete domain knowledge, especially for smaller locally deployable models. We present a lightweight knowledge-injection framework for zero-shot ICU delirium prediction that augments a deterministic natural-language summary of structured electronic health record data with an external clinical knowledge report at inference time, without fine-tuning or retrieval. We evaluate LLaMA 3.1 8B and LLaMA 3.3 70B on 3,160 ICU admissions from the MIMIC IV dataset. Adding a clinically meaningful external knowledge report improves AUROC by 8.57 percentage points for the 8B model and 1.99 percentage points for the 70B model compared to no external knowledge. Relative to a GPT-5.2 frontier-model reference without external knowledge report (AUROC 68.86%), knowledge injection reduces the performance gap from 15.66 to 7.09 AUROC points for LLaMA 8B and from 5.30 to 3.31 AUROC points for LLaMA 70B. Random control reports do not improve performance and often degrade it, indicating that gains depend on clinically meaningful content rather than added prompt length alone. SHAP-based attribution further confirms that the injected knowledge is actively used during prediction. These findings suggest that inference-time knowledge injection can narrow the gap between locally deployable open-weight models and frontier closed models while preserving a practical, privacy-preserving workflow for resource-constrained clinical settings.

AI.tldr: A lightweight inference-time knowledge injection framework augments LLMs with external clinical knowledge reports for zero-shot ICU delirium prediction, significantly improving smaller models' performance and narrowing the gap with frontier models without fine-tuning or retrieval.
AI.motivation: Large language models struggle with zero-shot clinical prediction due to incomplete domain knowledge, and the performance gap is especially wide for smaller, locally deployable open-weight models compared to frontier closed models. The authors aim to bridge this gap while maintaining a privacy-preserving, resource-constrained workflow suitable for clinical settings.
AI.method: The framework injects an external clinical knowledge report at inference time alongside a deterministic natural-language summary of structured EHR data. No fine-tuning or retrieval is used. Evaluated on 3,160 ICU admissions from MIMIC-IV using LLaMA 3.1 8B and LLaMA 3.3 70B, with GPT-5.2 as a frontier reference. Random control reports and SHAP-based attribution analysis validate that gains stem from clinically meaningful content rather than prompt length.
AI.result: Knowledge injection improved AUROC by 8.57 points (8B) and 1.99 points (70B). Relative to GPT-5.2's 68.86% AUROC without external knowledge, the gap shrank from 15.66 to 7.09 points for the 8B model and from 5.30 to 3.31 points for the 70B model. Random reports often degraded performance, and SHAP analysis confirmed active use of injected knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time knowledge injection effectively narrows the performance gap between locally deployable open-weight LLMs and frontier closed models for specialized clinical tasks, while preserving a practical, privacy-preserving workflow suitable for resource-constrained clinical environments.

title: Monkey King Bang: A Unified Scientific Multimodal Foundation Model
summary: Scientific discovery is increasingly shifting from isolated disciplines to multi-domain reasoning, and AI for science faces a similar transition. Existing systems are either specialised for individual domains or unify scientific data mainly through text tokenisation and prompt-based interfaces, limiting their ability to handle diverse scientific inputs, produce modality-native outputs, and support joint understanding, reasoning, and generation across scientific domains. We introduce MKB, a unified scientific multimodal model for both understanding and generation, built around a shared Transformer backbone and modality-tailored encoders, adapters, and decoders. MKB covers six scientific branches, including DNA, RNA, proteins, small molecules, earth science, and medical images, and supports native outputs such as biological sequences, molecular strings, meteorological fields, and segmentation masks. Training follows a two-stage modality-then-language curriculum: Stage 1 aligns modality-specific components with the frozen backbone, and Stage 2 consolidates them with the language backbone using mixed scientific and general corpora. Experiments show that MKB achieves competitive scientific understanding across biological and molecular benchmarks, produces high-fidelity native outputs for weather forecasting, biological generation, and medical-image segmentation, and largely retains the general capabilities of its Qwen3-VL backbone. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed paradigm, suggesting that shared-backbone models with modality-tailored components can provide a promising foundation for future cross-domain scientific multimodal exploration. The model and code are publicly available at https://github.com/Shanghai-Academy-of-AI-For-Science/MKB and https://huggingface.co/sais-org/MKB.

AI.tldr: MKB is a unified scientific multimodal model that uses a shared Transformer backbone with modality-tailored encoders/decoders to handle understanding and generation across six scientific domains (DNA, RNA, proteins, small molecules, earth science, medical images), trained via a two-stage modality-then-language curriculum.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-for-science systems are either domain-specialized or rely solely on text tokenization, which limits their ability to process diverse scientific inputs, produce modality-native outputs, and support joint cross-domain understanding and generation.
AI.method: MKB employs a shared Transformer backbone with modality-specific encoders, adapters, and decoders. Training follows a two-stage curriculum: Stage 1 aligns modality components with the frozen backbone; Stage 2 consolidates them with the language backbone using mixed scientific and general corpora. The model is built upon the Qwen3-VL backbone.
AI.result: MKB achieves competitive performance on biological and molecular understanding benchmarks, produces high-fidelity native outputs for weather forecasting, biological generation, and medical-image segmentation, and largely retains the general capabilities of its Qwen3-VL backbone.
AI.conclusion: Shared-backbone models with modality-tailored components offer a promising and feasible foundation for future cross-domain scientific multimodal exploration, unifying diverse scientific modalities without sacrificing domain-specific fidelity or general capabilities.

title: CRAWO: Custom Resources for Adaptive Workload Orchestration
summary: Edge Intelligence has emerged as a key paradigm for enabling real-time applications in smart cities by shifting computation from centralized cloud data centers to the network edge, thereby reducing latency and bandwidth consumption. However, deploying Artificial Intelligence (AI) pipelines across heterogeneous edge infrastructures remains challenging due to the wide range of device capabilities, from low-power microcontrollers to accelerator-equipped systems. Existing edge orchestration platforms primarily focus on deployment automation and infrastructure management, but these approaches are often inefficient and limit the ability to adaptively allocate resources under dynamic conditions. To tackle these issues, this paper introduces CRAWO (Custom Resources for Adaptive Workload Orchestration), an architectural framework for coordinating AI pipelines across distributed edge environments. CRAWO follows a control-loop-based model that separates allocation intelligence from execution by managing placement decisions, state management, and inter-stage data flows while instantiating services on edge nodes. The framework incorporates a hardware-aware allocator with a pluggable multi-criteria decision layer that leverages real-time infrastructure metrics to enable adaptive workload placement. The reference implementation adopts a microservices architecture deployed on a lightweight Kubernetes distribution (K3s), using Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) for domain modeling and a dedicated operator for state reconciliation. Evaluation in a vehicle surveillance scenario using license plate recognition demonstrates improved workload distribution and reduced reliance on centralized cloud processing in latency-sensitive environments.

AI.tldr: CRAWO is a control-loop-based architectural framework for orchestrating AI pipelines across heterogeneous edge environments. It separates allocation intelligence from execution using a hardware-aware, multi-criteria decision layer that adapts placement based on real-time infrastructure metrics. A microservices-based reference implementation on K3s with CRDs and a dedicated operator demonstrates improved workload distribution in a vehicle surveillance use case.
AI.motivation: Deploying AI pipelines across heterogeneous edge infrastructures is challenging due to diverse device capabilities (from microcontrollers to accelerator-equipped systems). Existing orchestration platforms focus narrowly on deployment automation and infrastructure management, lacking adaptive resource allocation under dynamic conditions, which leads to inefficiencies and excessive reliance on cloud processing for latency-sensitive applications.
AI.method: CRAWO employs a control-loop-based architecture that decouples allocation intelligence from execution. It features a hardware-aware allocator with a pluggable multi-criteria decision layer that consumes real-time infrastructure metrics for adaptive workload placement. The framework manages placement decisions, state management, and inter-stage data flows. The reference implementation uses a microservices architecture on K3s (lightweight Kubernetes), leveraging Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) for domain modeling and a dedicated operator for state reconciliation.
AI.result: Evaluation in a vehicle surveillance scenario using license plate recognition shows improved workload distribution across edge nodes and reduced dependency on centralized cloud processing in latency-sensitive environments.
AI.conclusion: CRAWO demonstrates that a control-loop-based, hardware-aware orchestration framework with pluggable decision logic can effectively coordinate AI pipelines across heterogeneous edge infrastructures, enabling adaptive, latency-sensitive workload placement without heavy cloud reliance.

title: Response drift across frontier large language models
summary: All frontier large language models (LLMs) exhibit response drift -- producing outputs that deviate from expert-validated references -- yet the magnitude and structure of this drift remain uncharacterised by systematic human evaluation. Here we report a fully crossed evaluation in which 47 geographically diverse participants each assessed all 62 multidomain questions across ten frontier LLMs under blinded conditions, yielding 29,140 independent assessments. Every model drifts, but drift magnitude varies substantially: eight models converge on a statistically indistinguishable ceiling (78-81% deviation), while two achieve lower deviation (47-49%). Drift profiles differ across six domains and 62 questions, with pairwise correlations among ceiling models exceeding r = 0.85. Automated similarity metrics explain less than 2% of variance in human judgements. These findings reveal that response drift is universal across frontier LLMs, domain- and question-dependent in structure, and accessible only through human-centred evaluation.

AI.tldr: A large-scale human evaluation (47 participants, 10 LLMs, 62 questions, 29,140 assessments) reveals that response drift is universal across frontier models. Eight models cluster at a ceiling of 78–81% deviation from expert references, while two achieve substantially lower drift (47–49%). Drift structure is domain- and question-dependent, highly correlated among ceiling models (r > 0.85), and not captured by automated similarity metrics (R² < 2%).
AI.motivation: Response drift—deviation of LLM outputs from expert-validated references—is a known phenomenon in frontier models, but its magnitude, structure, and consistency have not been systematically characterised through human evaluation. Prior work lacks a fully crossed, blinded, multidomain assessment across multiple models.
AI.method: Fully crossed, blinded human evaluation: 47 geographically diverse participants each assessed all 62 multidomain questions across all 10 frontier LLMs, producing 29,140 independent assessments. Drift was quantified as deviation from expert-validated references. Pairwise correlations among model drift profiles were computed, and automated similarity metrics were tested against human judgments for explanatory power.
AI.result: Drift is universal—all models exhibit it. Magnitude bifurcates: eight models show statistically indistinguishable ceiling drift (78–81% deviation), two models show significantly lower drift (47–49%). Drift profiles vary by domain and question. Ceiling-model drift profiles are highly inter-correlated (r > 0.85). Automated similarity metrics explain under 2% of variance in human drift judgments.
AI.conclusion: Response drift is a universal, structurally patterned phenomenon in frontier LLMs that is domain- and question-dependent. The high correlation among ceiling models suggests a shared failure mode. Crucially, drift is accessible only through human-centred evaluation, as automated metrics fail to capture it.

title: StabilityBench: Benchmarking Instability in LLMs
summary: AI Assistants are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, such as healthcare or government services. Yet their real-world behavior remains poorly understood due to strong context dependence. Current evaluation protocols follow a defense-in-depth paradigm with compounding layers of safeguards, ranging from traditional benchmarks to live or adversarial testing. Such benchmarks remain largely static and single-turn, limiting their ability to capture real-world variability in conversational settings. We propose StabilityBench, a principled, general and model-agnostic benchmark operator that transforms single-turn benchmark queries into multi-turn interaction histories. StabilityBench augments existing benchmarks by injecting realistic user simulations, through demographic proxies or sycophantic baits, while preserving original task intent. We apply StabilityBench to four benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, health question-answering and safety, and evaluate nine large language models under these conditions. Our results show that model performance is consistently unstable under these injections, with considerable performance degradations on three out of four benchmarks studied. These highlight important limitations of static evaluations and motivate more realistic evaluation settings. To this end, we propose StabilityBench-Mini: a size-preserving variant of StabilityBench that samples across diversification axes, enabling more realistic evaluation without increasing costs.

AI.tldr: StabilityBench transforms static single-turn benchmarks into multi-turn conversational evaluations by injecting realistic user simulations (demographic proxies, sycophantic baits), revealing significant performance instability in LLMs across mathematical reasoning, health QA, and safety tasks.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluation protocols rely on static, single-turn benchmarks that fail to capture real-world conversational variability in high-stakes deployment settings (healthcare, government). Existing defense-in-depth approaches cannot assess how models behave under realistic multi-turn interactions with diverse user personas.
AI.method: StabilityBench is a model-agnostic benchmark operator that augments existing single-turn benchmarks into multi-turn interaction histories by injecting two types of realistic user simulations: (1) demographic proxies that vary user identity characteristics, and (2) sycophantic baits that test whether models yield to user pressure. It preserves original task intent while introducing conversational dynamics. StabilityBench-Mini is a cost-efficient variant that samples across diversification axes without increasing evaluation overhead.
AI.result: Evaluating nine LLMs across four benchmarks (mathematical reasoning, health QA, safety), model performance proved consistently unstable under injections, with considerable degradation on three of four benchmarks, exposing limitations of static evaluation protocols.
AI.conclusion: Static single-turn benchmarks are insufficient for assessing real-world LLM reliability. Multi-turn, user-diverse evaluation frameworks like StabilityBench are necessary to uncover performance brittleness and motivate more realistic, dynamic evaluation paradigms.

title: DFAH-Bench: Benchmarking Observable Agent Instability in Financial Decision-Making
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures. Code, replay logs, one-command reproduction (make reproduce-paper), and an interactive results explorer: github.com/ibm-client-engineering/output-drift-financial-llms
summary: Standard evaluation benchmarks measure what a tool-using agent decides, not whether it arrives at that decision through the same process each time. We introduce DFAH-Bench, a replay benchmark that measures observable behavioral instability in financial agent decision-making across three channels -- tool-call trajectories, evidence contacts, and decision concentration -- none of which require access to hidden reasoning text. Across 8,127 replay episodes spanning 10 models and 3 financial tasks, we find that outcome agreement alone is an incomplete stability signal: frontier models can agree on decisions 95% of the time while following the same tool path only 77% of the time -- an 18-percentage-point gap (95% CI: [0.14, 0.22]) that outcome-only evaluation misses entirely. Among frontier-model case groups with high decision agreement, over 55% exhibit meaningful trajectory divergence. We identify three behavioral profiles: pattern matchers that achieve near-perfect agreement by collapsing to a single output regardless of input, stable executors with relatively consistent tool-use processes, and trajectory divergers that reach the same conclusions through materially different tool paths and evidence contacts. The benchmark code, metric scripts, replay logs, benchmark card, dataset README, and release manifest are released in the accompanying repository.

AI.tldr: DFAH-Bench introduces a replay benchmark measuring behavioral instability in financial AI agents across tool-call trajectories, evidence contacts, and decision concentration, revealing that frontier models can achieve 95% decision agreement while sharing the same tool path only 77% of the time — an 18-point gap missed by outcome-only evaluation.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation benchmarks only measure final decisions of tool-using agents, not the consistency of the decision-making process. This masks potential behavioral instability where agents reach identical outcomes through divergent internal processes — a critical gap for high-stakes domains like finance where process reliability matters.
AI.method: The authors propose DFAH-Bench, a replay benchmark capturing observable behavioral instability through three channels: (1) tool-call trajectories — the sequence of tool invocations, (2) evidence contacts — which data sources are accessed, and (3) decision concentration — the distribution of final decisions. Across 8,127 replay episodes, 10 models are evaluated on 3 financial tasks without requiring access to hidden reasoning text (chain-of-thought).
AI.result: A substantial 18-percentage-point gap (95% CI: [0.14, 0.22]) between decision agreement (95%) and trajectory agreement (77%) was found among frontier models. Over 55% of high-agreement case groups exhibited meaningful trajectory divergence. Three behavioral profiles emerged: pattern matchers (collapse to single output regardless of input), stable executors (consistent tool-use processes), and trajectory divergers (same conclusions via materially different paths).
AI.conclusion: Outcome agreement alone is an incomplete stability signal. Evaluating process-level behavioral consistency — through tool-call trajectories and evidence contacts — reveals instability that outcome-only metrics miss. The benchmark, code, and replay logs are publicly released.

title: RE-AD: Real-Time Requirement Adherence for Data Labeling
comment: Accepted to The Fifth Generation, Evaluation & Metrics Workshop (GEM) workshop at ACL 2026
summary: Human-annotated data remains fundamental to training frontier Large Language Models (LLMs). However, crowd-sourced annotations often suffer from quality issues stemming from annotator misunderstanding or lack of engagement. To address this, we introduce a real-time requirement adherence (RE-AD) framework that leverages LLMs to proactively validate labeling quality. Our methodology involves decomposing Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) into atomic rules via self-reflection, categorizing them by complexity, and applying tiered validation strategies. Evaluated on a synthetic benchmark, the system achieved an F1 score of 0.749. Furthermore, production deployment resulted in annotators accepting and fixing 82% of the errors flagged by the framework. We include ablation studies to demonstrate the impact of our core design decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper presents RE-AD, an LLM-powered real-time framework that decomposes annotation guidelines into atomic rules and validates labeling quality, achieving 0.749 F1 on benchmarks and 82% error-fix acceptance in production.
AI.motivation: Crowd-sourced human annotations for LLM training often suffer from quality issues due to annotator misunderstanding or lack of engagement. There is a need for proactive, real-time validation to catch errors during the labeling process rather than post-hoc.
AI.method: The RE-AD framework decomposes Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) into atomic rules using LLM self-reflection, categorizes these rules by complexity level, and applies tiered validation strategies to check annotation adherence in real time.
AI.result: The system achieved an F1 score of 0.749 on a synthetic benchmark. In production deployment, annotators accepted and corrected 82% of the errors flagged by RE-AD. Ablation studies validated the impact of core design choices.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based real-time requirement adherence checking is a viable and effective approach to improving human annotation quality, with strong production adoption rates confirming practical utility.

title: Joint Utilization of Geospatial and census proxies for Autoencoder-Assisted Downscaling (JUGAAD) of socioeconomic indicators in India
summary: Monitoring poverty and food security indicators is imperative for addressing socioeconomic challenges in developing nations. A limitation is mismatches in scale between data sources: census data provide geographic coverage, while socioeconomic indicators are derived from infrequently conducted surveys at coarse resolutions, posing a methodological challenge. This study introduces a deep learning framework, JuGAAD, using Indian census and survey data from 2001 and 2011 as a case study. We employ a three-step process: census and geospatial data are averaged into intermediate village-cluster-scale tessellations to reduce noise and regularize administrative boundary changes; an autoencoder compresses high-dimensional National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) data into a low-dimensional latent representation; and a regression model maps upscaled census and geospatial data to this representation. This function is applied to fine-grained census data to generate high-resolution predictions, validated against ground-truth district-level NSSO indicators. Results confirm the methodology predicts socioeconomic indicators at fine scales with strong accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper presents JuGAAD, a deep learning framework that fuses census and survey data to generate high-resolution predictions of poverty and food security indicators in India. By using an autoencoder to compress survey data into a latent space and a regression model to map census/geospatial data to that space, the method overcomes scale mismatches between coarse surveys and fine-grained census data, yielding accurate fine-scale socioeconomic estimates.
AI.motivation: Addressing the scale mismatch between geographically comprehensive census data and infrequently conducted, coarse-resolution socioeconomic surveys (e.g., NSSO) that hinders effective monitoring of poverty and food security in developing nations.
AI.method: A three-step deep learning framework (JuGAAD): (1) census and geospatial data are aggregated into intermediate village-cluster-scale tessellations to reduce noise and regularize administrative boundary changes; (2) an autoencoder compresses high-dimensional NSSO survey data into a low-dimensional latent representation; (3) a regression model learns to map the upscaled census/geospatial features to this latent space, enabling application to fine-grained census data for high-resolution predictions. Validation is performed against ground-truth district-level NSSO indicators.
AI.result: The JuGAAD framework predicts socioeconomic indicators at fine spatial scales with strong accuracy, validated against district-level NSSO ground-truth data.
AI.conclusion: Deep learning methods like JuGAAD can effectively bridge the scale gap between census and survey data, enabling reliable high-resolution mapping of poverty and food security indicators for improved socioeconomic monitoring in developing countries.

title: Attention-based Experience Replay Framework for Continual Learning of Agnostic Time Series Forecasting Models
summary: Deep learning has led to remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, particularly in robotics, imaging and sound processing. However, a major limitation of neural networks remains their strong dependence on large and stationary datasets. In many real-world applications, these conditions are rarely met due to evolving and dynamic environments where data distributions change over time. Continual learning aims to address this challenge by developing models capable of adapting incrementally while maintaining a balance between stability and plasticity under computational constraints. In this work, we introduce a novel framework for continual time series forecasting, designed to extend existing static forecasting models commonly used in the literature by incorporating an Experience Replay strategy guided by Attention mechanisms. This approach allows the model to adapt dynamically to new contexts while preserving prior knowledge, effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting. The framework is evaluated on standard forecasting benchmarks as well as on a piezometric dataset exhibiting diverse temporal behaviors. Results show that our approach effectively increases or maintains predictive performance over time while reducing retraining costs and data requirements, thus facilitating the deployment of forecasting models in dynamic and real-world settings.

AI.tldr: A continual learning framework for time series forecasting that uses attention-guided experience replay to adapt to evolving data distributions while preventing catastrophic forgetting, demonstrated on standard benchmarks and piezometric data.
AI.motivation: Deep neural networks rely heavily on large, stationary datasets, but real-world environments are dynamic with shifting data distributions. Continual learning addresses this by balancing stability (retaining past knowledge) and plasticity (acquiring new knowledge) under computational constraints, yet existing static forecasting models are ill-suited for such non-stationary settings.
AI.method: The authors propose a novel continual time series forecasting framework that extends static forecasting models with an Attention-guided Experience Replay strategy. Past samples are stored in a memory buffer and selectively replayed during training of new data, with attention mechanisms prioritizing which experiences to revisit, thereby mitigating catastrophic forgetting while enabling dynamic adaptation to new temporal contexts.
AI.result: The framework maintains or improves predictive performance over time compared to static baselines, while significantly reducing retraining costs and data requirements. Evaluation spans standard forecasting benchmarks and a piezometric dataset with diverse temporal behaviors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed attention-guided experience replay framework enables practical deployment of forecasting models in dynamic real-world settings by sustaining performance, lowering computational overhead, and reducing reliance on large stationary datasets.

title: Learn2Zinc: Fine-tuning Small Language Models for Text-to-Model Translation in MiniZinc
comment: CP 2026 Workshop on LLMs meet Constraint Solving
summary: Large language models excel at code generation for mainstream programming languages but struggle with rare, domain-specific languages such as MiniZinc, a constraint modeling language for combinatorial problems. We investigate whether targeted fine-tuning can teach small language models (0.6B to 20B parameters) to generate syntactically correct and semantically valid MiniZinc models from natural language problem descriptions. Our key finding is that syntax errors dominate failures when working with this domain specific language: the out-of-the-box execution accuracy of small language models such as Qwen3, LLaMa, Gemma, and GPT-OSS is near-zero. We propose a cross-model error bootstrapping approach that collects syntax errors from multiple LLM runs and leverage those to curate an error correction training dataset. This dataset allows us fine-tune small language models that consistently improves both direct code generation and chain-of-thought approaches across all model sizes. With self-reflection and ensembling, our approach achieves up to 98\% execution accuracy. In parallel, solution accuracy still remains at 35\%, indicating that while syntax is learnable, constraint reasoning remains a challenge. We contribute our fine-tuning pipeline, datasets, and models to opens-source for further research on text-to-model translation.

AI.tldr: Small language models achieve near-zero execution accuracy on MiniZinc code generation due to syntax errors. A cross-model error bootstrapping approach that collects and curates syntax errors into a fine-tuning dataset boosts execution accuracy up to 98%, though semantic/solution accuracy plateaus at 35%, highlighting that constraint reasoning remains the core challenge.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel at mainstream programming languages but fail on rare, domain-specific languages like MiniZinc (a constraint modeling language for combinatorial problems). The authors aim to determine whether targeted fine-tuning can enable small language models (0.6B–20B) to generate syntactically correct and semantically valid MiniZinc models from natural language descriptions.
AI.method: Cross-model error bootstrapping: syntax errors are collected from multiple LLM runs (Qwen3, LLaMa, Gemma, GPT-OSS), then curated into an error-correction training dataset. This dataset is used to fine-tune small LMs for both direct code generation and chain-of-thought approaches, combined with self-reflection and ensembling techniques.
AI.result: Execution accuracy reaches up to 98% after fine-tuning with error bootstrapping, self-reflection, and ensembling. However, solution accuracy caps at 35%, indicating that while syntax errors are largely resolved, constraint reasoning remains a significant challenge.
AI.conclusion: Syntax errors dominate failure cases in MiniZinc generation for small LMs, and error-bootstrapped fine-tuning effectively resolves them. However, semantic reasoning for constraint problems remains difficult. The authors open-source their fine-tuning pipeline, datasets, and models.

title: Chronofy: A Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture for Information Validity in Time-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems retrieve and integrate external knowledge to ground large language model (LLM) outputs. However, current RAG architectures treat all retrieved facts as equally valid regardless of temporal provenance, leading to temporal hallucination, where plausible but obsolete facts corrupt the output. A clinical lab reading from yesterday is actionable; the same reading from six months ago is noise. We present Chronofy, a three-layer neuro-symbolic framework implementing the Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture (TLDA) that embeds temporal validity directly into the representation, retrieval, and reasoning layers of RAG systems. Layer 1 reserves a dedicated temporal subspace within Matryoshka embeddings to make fact age structurally irremovable from the representation.
