Layer 2 integrates learnable exponential decay functions into graph-based retrieval, where the decay coefficient $β_j$ is grounded in Bayesian decision theory as an approximation of twice the latent process mean-reversion rate. Layer 3 applies Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness functions to evaluate the temporal validity of retrieved knowledge, not LLM output confidence, and enforces the possibilistic weakest-link principle to bound output confidence by the most decayed evidence in the reasoning chain. We evaluate Chronofy on temporal knowledge graph forecasting benchmarks, the TimE temporal QA benchmark, and a domain-specific sensitivity analysis, demonstrating that explicit temporal decay modeling improves retrieval precision, reduces temporal hallucination, and enables principled data re-acquisition triggers when temporal context is insufficient.

AI.tldr: Chronofy introduces a neuro-symbolic framework (TLDA) with three layers — temporal subspace embeddings, decay-grounded graph retrieval, and STL-based temporal validity enforcement — to combat temporal hallucination in RAG systems by treating fact age as a first-class structural property.
AI.motivation: Current RAG systems treat all retrieved facts as equally valid regardless of their temporal provenance, leading to temporal hallucination where plausible but obsolete facts corrupt LLM outputs. The core insight is that information utility decays with time: a recent clinical reading is actionable, while an old one is noise.
AI.method: Chronofy proposes the Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture (TLDA) with three layers: (1) a dedicated temporal subspace within Matryoshka embeddings that structurally encodes fact age; (2) learnable exponential decay functions integrated into graph-based retrieval, with decay coefficient β_j grounded in Bayesian decision theory as twice the latent process mean-reversion rate; (3) Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness functions that evaluate temporal validity of retrieved knowledge and enforce a possibilistic weakest-link principle to bound output confidence by the most decayed evidence.
AI.result: Chronofy demonstrates improved retrieval precision, reduced temporal hallucination, and principled data re-acquisition triggers on temporal knowledge graph forecasting benchmarks, the TimE temporal QA benchmark, and domain-specific sensitivity analysis.
AI.conclusion: Explicit temporal decay modeling via a neuro-symbolic architecture effectively addresses temporal hallucination in RAG systems, providing both theoretical grounding (Bayesian decision theory, STL, weakest-link principle) and practical mechanisms for time-aware retrieval and reasoning.

title: Dropping the Anchor: Statistical Context Summarization for Distributed Systems via Pulsar Attention
summary: Inference with large language models (LLMs) on long sequences is computationally expensive due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Distributed blockwise methods such as Star Attention reduce this cost by sharding context across hosts, but rely on prepending a static, content-blind copy of the first block to every host. We propose Pulsar Attention, which replaces the static anchor with two lightweight, content-aware components: a small attention-sink prefix that stabilizes softmax, and compact cross-block summaries built via a Max-IDF heuristic that selects chunks containing globally rare tokens. This reduces the Phase 1 per-GPU FLOPs by up to 3.3$\times$ over Star Attention while retaining an identical KV cache footprint. On RULER and BABILong with Llama-3.1-8B, Pulsar Attention outperforms both Star Attention and dense attention at sequence lengths up to 128K tokens, with absolute gains of up to 4.7% over the dense baseline.

AI.tldr: Pulsar Attention improves distributed long-sequence LLM inference by replacing Star Attention's static anchor block with content-aware components (attention-sink prefix + Max-IDF cross-block summaries), achieving up to 3.3× FLOP reduction while outperforming both Star and dense attention on benchmarks up to 128K tokens.
AI.motivation: Standard self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, making long-sequence LLM inference expensive. Distributed blockwise methods like Star Attention shard context across hosts but rely on a static, content-blind copy of the first block prepended to every host, which incurs redundant computation and ignores contextual relevance.
AI.method: Pulsar Attention introduces two lightweight, content-aware replacements for the static anchor: (1) a small attention-sink prefix that stabilizes the softmax distribution by providing a constant sink for excess attention mass, and (2) compact cross-block summaries constructed via a Max-IDF heuristic that selects chunks containing globally rare tokens — maximizing information density. These components reduce Phase 1 per-GPU FLOPs by up to 3.3× over Star Attention while maintaining an identical KV cache footprint.
AI.result: On RULER and BABILong benchmarks using Llama-3.1-8B, Pulsar Attention outperforms both Star Attention and dense attention at sequence lengths up to 128K tokens, with absolute accuracy gains of up to 4.7% over the dense baseline.
AI.conclusion: Content-aware anchor design (attention sinks + Max-IDF summaries) can substantially reduce the computational overhead of distributed blockwise attention without sacrificing — and even improving — long-context task performance.

title: CT-Merging: Consensus Directions and Task-Level Scaling for LoRA Adapter Merging
summary: LoRA adapters provide an efficient way to specialize a pretrained model for many downstream tasks, but deploying one adapter per task requires adapter storage and task selection at inference time. Model merging addresses this issue by combining independently trained adapters into one multi-task adapter. Recent SVD-based LoRA merging methods mainly focus on constructing shared or task specific directions, while the coefficients assigned to the final directions are often directly from the original task SVD. On a fixed merged basis, inherited coefficients preserve component order with high rank correlation, yet their magnitudes differ substantially from the coefficients induced by the task updates. To address this mismatch, we propose CT-Merging, a LoRA-aware merging algorithm that estimates consensus directions from average task subspace projectors and assigns task-level RMS coefficient scales in the final update. CT-Merging uses repeated support across task SVD subspaces to construct the common basis, while reducing reliance on rank wise SVD magnitudes after direction construction. On the DC-Merge CLIP adapter benchmark, CT-Merging achieves superior average normalized accuracy compared to state-of-the-art merging methods and further improves over DC-Merge by 2.56 points on ViT-B/32 and 1.51 points on ViT-L/14 KnoTS-trained checkpoints.

AI.tldr: CT-Merging introduces a LoRA-aware model merging algorithm that constructs consensus directions from average task subspace projectors and applies task-level RMS coefficient scaling, outperforming SOTA methods on CLIP adapter benchmarks by 2.56 points on ViT-B/32 and 1.51 points on ViT-L/14.
AI.motivation: Existing SVD-based LoRA merging methods inherit coefficients directly from original task SVDs, creating a mismatch: while the coefficient ordering is preserved (high rank correlation), their magnitudes deviate substantially from what the task updates actually induce on the merged basis. This degrades multi-task performance.
AI.method: CT-Merging estimates consensus directions via average task subspace projectors to form a common basis, then assigns task-level RMS coefficient scales to the final update. It leverages repeated support across task SVD subspaces for basis construction and decouples direction construction from rank-wise SVD magnitudes.
AI.result: On the DC-Merge CLIP adapter benchmark, CT-Merging achieves superior average normalized accuracy over SOTA merging methods, improving by 2.56 points on ViT-B/32 and 1.51 points on ViT-L/14 using KnoTS-trained checkpoints.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling direction construction from inherited SVD magnitudes and instead using task-level RMS scaling yields significant gains in multi-task adapter merging, establishing CT-Merging as a new state-of-the-art approach for LoRA merging.

title: CAMeR: Keyword-Gated Hybrid Activation for Adaptive Memory Retention in LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents operating over extended dialogues accumulate vast amounts of information, yet existing memory systems either retain everything indiscriminately or apply uniform forgetting heuristics that fail to distinguish relevant from irrelevant knowledge. We present CAMeR (Context-Activated Memory Reinforcement), a memory retention framework combining keyword-gated hybrid activation -- a joint symbolic (word-level Jaccard) and sub-symbolic (embedding cosine) gating mechanism -- with adaptive weight dynamics. CAMeR computes a hybrid similarity score for each memory-query pair; memories exceeding a threshold receive reinforcement while all memories undergo controlled decay. We introduce CAMeR-Bench, a 76-memory, 100-round benchmark spanning 8 topic clusters with graded activation frequency, designed to test adaptive retention where existing benchmarks (LoCoMO, LongMemEval) cannot. On CAMeR-Bench, CAMeR's keyword gate achieves a 1.6$\times$ larger retention gap between high-frequency and never-referenced memories compared to embedding-only gating (scissors gap: 0.039 vs. 0.024), while time-driven baselines (Oblivion, SuperLocalMemory) collapse to near-zero weights over 100 rounds. CAMeR's top-5 retrieval saves 83.2\% tokens versus full-context approaches (39k vs. 231k cumulative) while producing weight signals that improve retrieval precision. Through 8 ablation conditions we establish that the keyword gate -- not learnable decay -- is the primary performance driver at this scale. Our findings demonstrate that hybrid symbolic-neural gating provides a simple yet effective mechanism for adaptive memory retention in LLM agents.

AI.tldr: CAMeR introduces a hybrid symbolic-neural gating mechanism (keyword Jaccard + embedding cosine similarity) with adaptive weight dynamics for LLM agent memory retention, demonstrating on a new benchmark (CAMeR-Bench) that the keyword gate drives superior retention discrimination between relevant and irrelevant memories compared to embedding-only or time-decay baselines, while saving 83.2% tokens in retrieval.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent memory systems suffer from two failure modes: retaining everything indiscriminately (wasteful) or applying uniform forgetting heuristics (loss of relevant knowledge). Neither approach distinguishes relevant from irrelevant memories across extended dialogues. Current benchmarks (LoCoMO, LongMemEval) also fail to test adaptive, graded retention.
AI.method: CAMeR (Context-Activated Memory Reinforcement) uses a hybrid activation gate: a symbolic word-level Jaccard similarity gate combined with a sub-symbolic embedding cosine similarity gate. Memory-query pairs compute a hybrid similarity score; memories exceeding a threshold are reinforced while all memories undergo controlled decay via adaptive weight dynamics. The authors also introduce CAMeR-Bench, a 76-memory, 100-round benchmark across 8 topic clusters with graded activation frequency for testing adaptive retention. Eight ablation conditions isolate the contributions of components.
AI.result: On CAMeR-Bench, the keyword gate achieves a 1.6× larger retention gap (0.039) between high-frequency and never-referenced memories versus embedding-only gating (0.024). Time-driven baselines (Oblivion, SuperLocalMemory) collapse to near-zero weights over 100 rounds. CAMeR's top-5 retrieval saves 83.2% tokens versus full-context (39k vs. 231k cumulative). Ablations reveal the keyword gate, not learnable decay, is the primary performance driver.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid symbolic-neural gating provides a simple, effective mechanism for adaptive memory retention in LLM agents, with the keyword gate being the critical component. The approach offers strong practical benefits in token efficiency while maintaining retrieval precision.

title: AI-Driven Surrogate Models for Predicting Electrode-Scale Discharge Behavior in Lithium-Ion Batteries
summary: Physics-based simulations are essential for understanding the electrode-scale discharge behavior of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) but suffer from prohibitive computational costs. To address this, we introduce a novel deep learning surrogate pipeline based on the Swin3D Transformer to predict spatiotemporal discharge dynamics directly from volumetric data. Our approach integrates two key innovations: Gaussian Positional Encoding (GPE), which enhances spatial feature representation by adapting to the complex geometry of electrode microstructures, and a specialized Temporal Encoding module to capture non-linear timeseries evolution. Experimental validation on an Electrochemical Simulation (ES) dataset demonstrates that our pipeline significantly outperforms state-of-the-art point cloud baselines in prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed method reduces the computational overhead by orders of magnitude, providing a scalable and efficient framework for high-throughput battery design and optimization.

AI.tldr: A Swin3D Transformer-based deep learning surrogate with Gaussian Positional Encoding and Temporal Encoding is proposed to accelerate physics-based lithium-ion battery discharge simulations, achieving orders-of-magnitude speedup over traditional methods while outperforming point-cloud baselines in accuracy.
AI.motivation: Physics-based simulations of electrode-scale discharge in lithium-ion batteries are critical for understanding behavior but are computationally prohibitive, creating a need for efficient, accurate surrogate models.
AI.method: A deep learning surrogate pipeline using Swin3D Transformer that ingests volumetric electrode microstructure data. Two innovations are introduced: (1) Gaussian Positional Encoding (GPE) to better represent complex electrode geometries, and (2) a specialized Temporal Encoding module to capture non-linear time-series discharge evolution.
AI.result: The pipeline significantly outperforms state-of-the-art point cloud baselines in prediction accuracy on an Electrochemical Simulation (ES) dataset and reduces computational cost by orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method offers a scalable and efficient framework for high-throughput battery design and optimization, effectively replacing expensive physics-based simulations with a fast, accurate deep learning surrogate.

title: From Errors to Rules: Iterative Prompt Optimization for Text Classification
summary: Prompt optimization for text classification spans diverse approaches, from demonstration selection to exploration-based search to error-driven diagnosis, each with known but incompletely characterized strengths and limitations. We conduct a comprehensive empirical study across diverse classification benchmarks (2 to 150 classes) comparing these paradigms through both quantitative evaluation and qualitative analysis of optimization traces, revealing that each paradigm excels on structurally different task types and that no single method dominates. Guided by these insights, we propose Error-Guided Optimization (ERGO), an error-driven method that iterates over the full training set in non-overlapping batches, diagnoses classification failures, and generates targeted decision rules through a diagnose-prescribe-rewrite feedback loop. ERGO achieves the best accuracy on tasks where errors concentrate in specific confused label pairs (which we term boundary-learnable tasks): TREC: 90.0%, CLINC150: 94.4%, converges in 3-5 iterations, and produces interpretable decision rules. While ERGO does not achieve the highest overall average, it fills a complementary role: demonstration-based ICL wins on coverage-dependent tasks, exploration-based search wins on many-class intent, and ERGO wins where decision boundaries are learnable from error patterns. We provide a complementarity framework linking task characteristics to optimal paradigm selection, offering practical guidance for practitioners.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically compares three paradigms for prompt optimization in text classification (demonstration selection, exploration-based search, error-driven diagnosis), reveals that each excels on structurally different task types, and proposes ERGO—an error-driven method using a diagnose-prescribe-rewrite loop that achieves top accuracy on "boundary-learnable" tasks where errors cluster around confused label pairs.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt optimization approaches for text classification (demonstration-based ICL, exploration-based search, error-driven diagnosis) each have known but incompletely characterized strengths and limitations. No prior work has systematically compared them across diverse benchmarks to understand which paradigm suits which task structure, nor provided a unified framework linking task characteristics to optimal paradigm selection.
AI.method: First, a comprehensive empirical study comparing three paradigms across benchmarks spanning 2–150 classes, using both quantitative evaluation and qualitative analysis of optimization traces. Second, the proposal of ERGO (Error-Guided Optimization), an error-driven method that iterates over the full training set in non-overlapping batches, diagnoses classification failures, and generates targeted decision rules via a diagnose-prescribe-rewrite feedback loop. Finally, a complementarity framework linking task characteristics (coverage-dependence, many-class intent, boundary-learnability) to optimal paradigm selection.
AI.result: Each paradigm excels on structurally different task types; no single method dominates overall. ERGO achieves best accuracy on boundary-learnable tasks: TREC 90.0%, CLINC150 94.4%, converging in 3–5 iterations while producing interpretable decision rules. Demonstration-based ICL wins on coverage-dependent tasks; exploration-based search wins on many-class intent tasks. The complementarity framework provides actionable guidance for practitioners.
AI.conclusion: Prompt optimization paradigms are complementary rather than competitive. ERGO fills a specific niche—tasks where decision boundaries are learnable from error patterns—while other paradigms dominate elsewhere. The proposed complementarity framework enables practitioners to select the optimal paradigm based on task characteristics, and ERGO's interpretable decision rules offer additional practical value.

title: THOR: A Theta-Gamma Hierarchical Oscillatory Reasoning Framework for Multi-hop QA
summary: Multi-hop question answering requires retrieving and integrating evidence from multiple contexts. Despite the rapid progress of current research, multi-hop reasoning remains constrained by two persistent limitations: attention decay, where the model's focus on main question degrades as the reasoning chain grows, and error accumulation, where mistakes propagate across hops and compounds into final failure. Inspired by Theta-Gamma hierarchical oscillation which decouples global planning from local retrieval, enabling efficient attention transfer between hops and a verification and repair mechanism that interrupts the accumulation of errors in the wrong paths, we present THOR, a brain-inspired Theta-Gamma hierarchical oscillatory reasoning framework. Extensive comparative experiments and specific validation experiments on multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that THOR improves answer accuracy and robustness while mitigating limitations, showcasing its generalization across different backbones.

AI.tldr: THOR is a brain-inspired multi-hop reasoning framework that uses Theta-Gamma hierarchical oscillation principles to decouple global planning from local retrieval, addressing attention decay and error accumulation in multi-hop QA.
AI.motivation: Current multi-hop QA systems suffer from two key limitations: (1) attention decay — the model progressively loses focus on the original question as the reasoning chain lengthens, and (2) error accumulation — mistakes in early hops compound and propagate, leading to final answer failures. Biological brains address analogous problems via Theta-Gamma hierarchical oscillation, inspiring a computational solution.
AI.method: THOR adopts a hierarchical oscillatory reasoning framework mimicking Theta-Gamma neural oscillations. The Theta rhythm governs global planning and maintains focus on the overarching question across hops, while the Gamma rhythm handles local evidence retrieval per hop. Additionally, a verification-and-repair mechanism interrupts error propagation by detecting and correcting mistakes in erroneous reasoning paths.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multi-hop QA benchmarks show that THOR improves both answer accuracy and robustness compared to baselines. Specific validation experiments confirm the framework effectively mitigates attention decay and error accumulation, and demonstrates strong generalization across different backbone models.
AI.conclusion: THOR provides a biologically inspired, effective solution to core multi-hop reasoning challenges, offering improved performance and robustness while being backbone-agnostic.

title: Fisher Widths: Local Learning Geometry and Anisotropic Recovery
summary:
We study Gaussian-width complexity on statistical manifolds through a pair of functionals: the primal Fisher width $w_G(T) = w(G^{1/2}T)$, induced by the Fisher metric, and the inverse-Fisher width $w_{G^{-1}}(T) = w(G^{-1/2}T)$, induced by the inverse Fisher metric. The two widths play complementary statistical roles.
  On the learning side, the Fisher width measures the size of local parameter fluctuations in the geometry induced by the Fisher information. For Fisher-regular losses, we prove that the scale \(w_G(H_r)/\sqrt n\) is attained on sufficiently small Fisher balls.
  On the recovery side, the inverse-Fisher width captures the effect of anisotropic Gaussian measurements whose covariance is determined by the inverse Fisher information. For sparse recovery, the resulting geometry depends not only on sparsity but also on the position of the active coordinates in the Fisher spectrum. We obtain a two-sided estimate for the corresponding statistical dimension, together with support-sensitive recovery estimates and a natural ordering of supports with different curvature profiles.
  Finally, we establish a sharp relation between the primal and inverse-Fisher widths. On any common compact coordinate set $T$, they satisfy \[ w_G(T)w_{G^{-1}}(T)\geq w(T)^2. \] Thus, Fisher anisotropy may transfer complexity from one geometry to the other, but cannot reduce both widths relative to the Euclidean scale.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces two functionals — the Fisher width and inverse-Fisher width — to study Gaussian-width complexity on statistical manifolds. The Fisher width governs local parameter fluctuations in learning, while the inverse-Fisher width captures anisotropic measurement effects in sparse recovery. A key result is the inequality w_G(T)w_{G^{-1}}(T) ≥ w(T)², showing that Fisher anisotropy cannot simultaneously reduce both widths below the Euclidean scale.
AI.motivation: To understand how the Fisher information geometry affects Gaussian complexity measures in statistical problems, distinguishing between learning (where the Fisher metric governs local fluctuations) and recovery (where the inverse Fisher metric governs anisotropic measurements). The authors seek a unified framework that relates these dual geometric perspectives.
AI.method: The paper defines two width functionals: the primal Fisher width w_G(T) = w(G^{1/2}T) using the Fisher metric, and the inverse-Fisher width w_{G^{-1}}(T) = w(G^{-1/2}T) using the inverse Fisher metric. It proves asymptotic attainment of scaled Fisher width on small Fisher balls for Fisher-regular losses, derives two-sided estimates for the statistical dimension in sparse recovery with support-sensitive bounds, and establishes the product inequality relating both widths.
AI.result: For Fisher-regular losses, the scale w_G(H_r)/√n is attained on sufficiently small Fisher balls. For sparse recovery, two-sided statistical dimension estimates are obtained along with support-sensitive recovery guarantees and a natural ordering of supports by curvature. The sharp inequality w_G(T)w_{G^{-1}}(T) ≥ w(T)² is proven, showing Fisher anisotropy transfers complexity between geometries but cannot reduce both widths simultaneously below the Euclidean baseline.
AI.conclusion: Fisher information geometry introduces a fundamental trade-off between primal and inverse-Fisher widths, formalized by the product inequality. This duality provides a principled framework for analyzing both learning and recovery problems on statistical manifolds, with practical implications for support selection based on Fisher spectral positioning.

title: AISE-Bench: A Full-Cycle Curated Benchmark for Information Seeking on Academic Knowledge Graphs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) augmented with tools are emerging as autonomous agents capable of using Web engine, APIs, and code to solve complex, long-horizon tasks. Current tool-using benchmarks for information seeking on academic graphs rely on synthetic templates, simplified solution spaces, or narrow tasks such as paper-centric tasks, leaving key challenges underexplored - realistic user intent, complex multi-step API planning, rich parameter filling for APIs, grounded answers with references, and comprehensive evaluation of both the process and the outcome. We introduce AISE-Bench, a real-world, full-cycle annotated benchmark for information seeking on academic knowledge graphs. AISE-Bench release contains 1,133 QA pairs, including query taxonomies, full API execution trajectories, validated parameters, and source-grounded answers with reference links. To support high-quality annotation, we design a customized agent workflow to enable annotators to plan, execute, and revise complex API workflows efficiently. We develop a comprehensive evaluation protocol measuring answer quality, reference grounding, API-planning correctness, and execution success. Among the 14 evaluated methods, even the strongest model (PLAY2PROMPT with Gemini-3-Pro) achieves only moderate performance and often struggles with API planning and execution. AISE-Bench establishes a challenging new testbed for quantitatively evaluating and improving the stepwise correctness, grounded summarization, and traceable reasoning of multi-step API-using LLM agents. Our code and data are available at https://aise-bench.github.io/.

AI.tldr: AISE-Bench is a new benchmark of 1,133 QA pairs for evaluating LLM agents on realistic, multi-step academic knowledge graph information seeking, featuring full API execution trajectories, grounded answers, and a comprehensive evaluation protocol. Even the strongest tested model achieves only moderate performance.
AI.motivation: Existing tool-using benchmarks for academic graph information seeking rely on synthetic templates, simplified solution spaces, or narrow paper-centric tasks, failing to capture realistic user intent, complex multi-step API planning, rich parameter filling, grounded answers with references, and comprehensive process-and-outcome evaluation.
AI.method: The authors construct AISE-Bench with 1,133 QA pairs annotated via a custom agent workflow that enables annotators to plan, execute, and revise complex API workflows. The benchmark includes query taxonomies, full API execution trajectories, validated parameters, and source-grounded answers with reference links. A comprehensive evaluation protocol measures answer quality, reference grounding, API-planning correctness, and execution success across 14 methods.
AI.result: Among 14 evaluated methods, the strongest (PLAY2PROMPT with Gemini-3-Pro) achieves only moderate performance and frequently struggles with API planning and execution, demonstrating that the benchmark poses significant challenges for current LLM agents.
AI.conclusion: AISE-Bench establishes a challenging testbed for quantitatively evaluating and improving stepwise correctness, grounded summarization, and traceable reasoning of multi-step API-using LLM agents on academic knowledge graphs.

title: Instruct-FD: Can Your Full-Duplex Speech System Follow Turn-Taking Instructions?
summary: Current full-duplex (FD) spoken dialogue systems can produce fluid interactions, yet it remains unclear whether they can adapt their turn-taking behavior when explicitly instructed. This is critical for real-world deployment, where conversational policies vary across applications (e.g., proactive tutoring vs. passive counseling). We introduce Instruct-FD, an instruction-conditioned benchmark for evaluating controllable turn management in FD systems. To enable this, we develop a human-validated, scalable synthetic pipeline that generates instruction-conditioned conversations, along with a deployment-agnostic multi-turn evaluation protocol and an LLM-based judge. Benchmarking six state-of-the-art full-duplex systems reveals a substantial gap in instruction-following turn management: the best model achieves only 64.4% adherence. Performance is highly uneven across behaviors and scenarios, with proactive behaviors such as model backchanneling and interruption remaining particularly challenging. These findings establish instruction-following turn management as a crucial direction for building adaptable and deployable full-duplex dialogue systems.

AI.tldr: Instruct-FD is a benchmark for evaluating whether full-duplex spoken dialogue systems can follow explicit instructions to control turn-taking behavior. The best model achieves only 64.4% instruction adherence, with proactive behaviors like backchanneling and interruption proving especially difficult.
AI.motivation: Current FD systems enable fluid spoken interactions, but it is unknown whether they can adapt turn-taking policies when given explicit instructions. Real-world applications require different conversational styles (e.g., proactive tutoring vs. passive counseling), making controllable turn management essential for deployment.
AI.method: The authors introduce Instruct-FD, comprising: (1) a human-validated synthetic data pipeline generating instruction-conditioned conversations, (2) a deployment-agnostic multi-turn evaluation protocol, and (3) an LLM-based judge for assessing instruction adherence. Six state-of-the-art FD systems are benchmarked using this framework.
AI.result: The best-performing model reaches only 64.4% instruction-following adherence. Performance is highly uneven across behaviors and scenarios: proactive turn-taking behaviors such as model-initiated backchanneling and interruption remain particularly challenging for all systems tested.
AI.conclusion: Instruction-following turn management represents a critical and underexplored direction for building adaptable, deployable full-duplex dialogue systems. The substantial performance gap highlights the need for dedicated research in this area.

title: Exact ReLU realization of affine one-dimensional refinement iterates via residual memory and offset frames
summary:
We study vector-valued affine refinement operators of the form [
(Wγ)(t)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}} A_jγ(Mt-j)+B(t), ]
with finitely supported matrix mask and compactly supported continuous piecewise linear input and forcing data. Building on the homogeneous realization theorem for (B\equiv 0), we prove that, for (M\ge 3), every finite affine iterate (W^nγ) admits an exact fixed-width ReLU realization whose depth is (O(n)).
  The main new ingredient is a residual memory controller. It replaces the noninvertible residual dynamics by an injective skew-product and permits exact backward replay of the residual states required by a Horner-type evaluation of the affine forcing sum. Offset frames align the forcing atoms away from residual seams, allowing complementary loop readouts to recover their values exactly. The remaining branch-selection ambiguity occurs only where the accumulated affine state has already vanished.
  For (M\ge 3), the result applies to arbitrary compactly supported continuous piecewise linear forcing terms. For (M=2), the same construction applies to ordinary-frame seam-separated forcing. We also prove a stage-dependent extension for forcing terms in a fixed finite-dimensional continuous piecewise linear span and record the resulting linear-depth upgrade for open-curve, finite-state, and Hilbert- and Morton-type recursive constructions.

AI.tldr: For dilation factor M≥3, any finite affine iterate of a vector-valued refinement operator with compactly supported continuous piecewise linear data can be exactly represented by a fixed-width ReLU network of depth O(n). The key innovation is a residual memory controller that uses an injective skew-product to enable exact backward replay of residual states, overcoming noninvertibility of the homogeneous dynamics.
AI.motivation: To establish that affine refinement operators—which generalize classical subdivision schemes by including a forcing term—admit exact deep ReLU network realizations with linear depth scaling, thereby connecting multiscale refinement theory with neural network expressivity.
AI.method: The authors build on the homogeneous realization theorem (B≡0). The central technical novelty is a residual memory controller that replaces noninvertible residual dynamics with an injective skew-product, enabling exact backward replay of residual states via Horner-type evaluation of the affine forcing sum. Offset frames are used to separate forcing atoms from residual seams, and complementary loop readouts recover values exactly. Branch-selection ambiguity is confined to regions where the accumulated affine state has already vanished.
AI.result: For M≥3, every finite affine iterate admits an exact fixed-width ReLU realization of depth O(n), for arbitrary compactly supported continuous piecewise linear forcing. For M=2, the same holds for ordinary-frame seam-separated forcing. A stage-dependent extension covers forcing terms in a fixed finite-dimensional continuous piecewise linear span, yielding linear-depth upgrades for open-curve, finite-state, and Hilbert- and Morton-type recursive constructions.
AI.conclusion: Affine refinement operators possess a deep ReLU network representation with linear depth, with the residual memory controller being the critical mechanism for handling the forcing term. The results bridge subdivision theory and neural network architecture, with the M=2 case requiring additional seam-separation conditions.

title: FlowEdit: Information-Theoretic Control of LLM Reasoning Flows for Ill-posed Problems Involving Conflicts
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform strongly on well-specified reasoning tasks with a feasible answer. However, problems encountered in the open world can become ill-posed due to inconsistent conditions, conflicting statements, or mutually incompatible requirements, admitting no valid responses. We argue that reasoning of such ill-posed problems involving conflicts require novel LLM capabilities to make hidden conflicts explicit, maintain competing hypotheses via multiple reasoning branches, and generate alternative responses in a single pass, all of which are challenging due to the limitation of the next-token prediction mechanism in LLMs. To this end, we propose FlowEdit, a novel framework that leverages information-theoretic principles to quantify and regulate internal reasoning flows of LLMs, for generating a full set of alternative responses under valid hypotheses. FlowEdit can be viewed as enforcing a branch-aware reasoning process using two dual information-theoretic objectives on the model's internal reasoning representations: maximizing the information flow from each selected hypothesis to the branch outcome, while minimizing the overlap and conditional dependence across sibling branches, to provide a diverse, informative set of responses with broad coverage. We show that this is achieved through tractable variational bounds under boundary embeddings being ε-sufficient, optimizing the underlying conditional mutual information in LLM reasoning process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlowEdit outperforms leading proprietary models, improving exact-set-match accuracy by 68%, while boosting overall response informativeness by 24%. We further show that flow regulation surfaces in the token stream as a redistribution of next-token entropy that concentrates inside each branch, amplifies at flow boundaries, and scales with the number of flows the problem requires.

AI.tldr: FlowEdit is an information-theoretic framework that enables LLMs to handle ill-posed reasoning problems with conflicting conditions by enforcing branch-aware reasoning: maximizing information flow from each hypothesis to its branch outcome while minimizing overlap across sibling branches, achieving 68% improvement in exact-set-match accuracy over proprietary models.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel at well-specified reasoning tasks but struggle with ill-posed, open-world problems involving inconsistent conditions, conflicting statements, or mutually incompatible requirements that admit no single valid response. The next-token prediction mechanism inherently limits the ability to maintain competing hypotheses, reason across multiple branches, and generate alternative responses simultaneously.
AI.method: FlowEdit uses two dual information-theoretic objectives on internal reasoning representations: (1) maximizing mutual information between each selected hypothesis and its corresponding branch outcome, and (2) minimizing conditional mutual information across sibling branches to reduce overlap and dependence. These are optimized via tractable variational bounds under the assumption of ε-sufficient boundary embeddings, enabling flow regulation through the LLM's reasoning process.
AI.result: FlowEdit outperforms leading proprietary LLMs, improving exact-set-match accuracy by 68% and boosting overall response informativeness by 24%. Flow regulation manifests in the token stream as a redistribution of next-token entropy that concentrates within each branch, amplifies at flow boundaries, and scales with the number of flows required by the problem.
AI.conclusion: FlowEdit demonstrates that explicit information-theoretic regulation of internal reasoning flows can overcome fundamental limitations of next-token prediction in LLMs for ill-posed problems, enabling structured, diverse multi-hypothesis reasoning in a single pass.

title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Persona Simulation in Opinion Prediction with GPT-4.1
comment: ICDM 2025 Undergraduate and High School Symposium
summary: Persona simulation involves utilizing large language models (LLMs) to anticipate human choices or interactions based on specific characteristic information. To further understand current limitations and future directions, we tested persona simulation in opinion prediction with GPT-4.1 (knowledge cutoff by June 2024). Using personas from nine U.S. states provided by Columbia University's Personas dataset, GPT-4.1 accurately predicted 2024 election outcomes in eight out of the nine states, only failing in one of the swing states. We then focused on opinions related to medicine and healthcare. With the American Trends Panel Wave 123 dataset from Pew Research Center, GPT-4.1 was able to anticipate beliefs about childhood vaccines with an accuracy of up to 0.94. Furthermore, we applied GPT-4.1 to generate conversations among personas and observed that the simulated dialogues and opinions adhered well to personas' personalities and backgrounds, albeit lacking natural human-like flow. Persona simulation proves to be a promising application of artificial intelligence as long as biases are addressed. In the near future, it will be beneficial to apply it to opinion analysis and reaction prediction in diverse fields ranging from public health to lawmaking to economics.

AI.tldr: GPT-4.1 was tested on persona simulation for opinion prediction, achieving high accuracy in forecasting 2024 U.S. election outcomes (8/9 states) and beliefs about childhood vaccines (accuracy up to 0.94). Simulated dialogues aligned with persona traits but lacked natural conversational flow. The study concludes persona simulation is a promising AI application across public health, lawmaking, and economics, contingent on addressing biases.
AI.motivation: To assess the current capabilities and limitations of LLMs in persona simulation — using demographic/characteristic information to predict human choices and opinions — and to explore its potential for real-world opinion analysis and reaction prediction.
AI.method: The authors used GPT-4.1 to simulate personas from two datasets: (1) Columbia University's Personas dataset covering nine U.S. states, used to predict 2024 presidential election outcomes; (2) Pew Research Center's American Trends Panel Wave 123, used to predict opinions on childhood vaccines. They also generated simulated multi-persona conversations and qualitatively evaluated how well dialogues reflected persona traits and conversational naturalness.
AI.result: GPT-4.1 correctly predicted 2024 election results in 8 of 9 states, failing only in one swing state. For vaccine beliefs, it achieved up to 0.94 accuracy. Simulated conversations were well-aligned with assigned personas' personalities and backgrounds but lacked natural human-like flow.
AI.conclusion: Persona simulation via LLMs shows strong promise for opinion prediction and analysis across domains such as public health, lawmaking, and economics. Addressing underlying biases remains a critical prerequisite for responsible deployment.

title: Detecting Neural Network Failures through Spectral Analysis of Internal Activations
summary:
Neural network misclassifications exhibit characteristic spectral instability in internal activations that is invisible at the output layer. This phenomenon is identified and formalized as Spectral Drift -- the frequency-domain distance between consecutive layer activations -- with empirical validation showing that failures exhibit significantly higher drift than correct predictions (1.9% increase, p<0.001). This spectral signature emerges during internal processing but becomes masked in final outputs, explaining why confidence-based detection methods struggle.
  This work introduces Self-Detecting Neural Networks (SDNN), a framework that monitors spectral dynamics across network depth using Short-Time Fourier Transform, wavelet decomposition, and statistical moments to capture multi-scale spectral features. A lightweight detector network (5% parameter overhead) learns to identify failure-indicative patterns via curriculum learning on progressively challenging distributions: natural misclassifications, distribution shifts, and adversarial perturbations.
  Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate that SDNN achieves 79.0 +/- 25.3% AUROC across three seeds, substantially outperforming confidence-based baselines including MaxSoftmax (50.5%) and Energy Score (52.9%) by approximately 25-30 percentage points. Ablation studies reveal that wavelet decomposition and statistical features make consistent contributions, while STFT's role remains unclear. This work establishes spectral analysis of internal activations as a promising direction for neural network reliability, revealing diagnostic information inaccessible to output-based approaches.

AI.tldr: Neural network failures produce a characteristic "Spectral Drift" — increased frequency-domain distance between internal layer activations — that is masked at the output layer. The authors propose Self-Detecting Neural Networks (SDNN), which monitor multi-scale spectral dynamics via STFT, wavelet decomposition, and statistical moments, using a lightweight detector trained with curriculum learning to flag misclassifications. SDNN achieves ~79% AUROC on CIFAR-10, outperforming confidence-based baselines by 25-30 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Standard confidence-based failure detection methods (e.g., MaxSoftmax, Energy Score) operate on final outputs, where spectral signatures of misclassification are masked. The authors observe that internal activations exhibit measurable spectral instability during failures, motivating a method that monitors spectral dynamics across network depth to detect errors before the output layer obscures them.
AI.method: The method comprises: (1) formalizing Spectral Drift as the frequency-domain distance between consecutive layer activations; (2) extracting multi-scale spectral features using Short-Time Fourier Transform, wavelet decomposition, and statistical moments across network depth; (3) training a lightweight detector network (~5% parameter overhead) with curriculum learning, progressing from natural misclassifications through distribution shifts to adversarial perturbations.
AI.result: SDNN achieves 79.0 ± 25.3% AUROC on CIFAR-10 across three seeds, substantially exceeding MaxSoftmax (50.5%) and Energy Score (52.9%). Failures exhibit 1.9% higher Spectral Drift (p<0.001). Ablations show wavelet and statistical features contribute consistently, while STFT's role is ambiguous.
AI.conclusion: Spectral analysis of internal activations is a promising direction for neural network reliability, revealing diagnostic information inaccessible to output-based approaches. The SDNN framework demonstrates that monitoring spectral dynamics can substantially improve failure detection over confidence-based baselines.

title: Frontier Financial Judgement: Can agents tell what might move a stock?
summary: We introduce Frontier Financial Judgement, a challenging new benchmark developed in collaboration with professional equity analysts to assess agents' ability to replicate expert human judgements. Rapidly identifying new information, evaluating its implications and determining its valuation impact is one of the most time-consuming and challenging aspects of real-world equity coverage. This is becoming ever more difficult and important as AI rapidly increases the quantity of new information to process. The strongest agent we evaluate on Frontier Financial Judgement matches all expert labels in only 52.4% of cases. We also find significant divergence in estimated false-positive rates among frontier agents, ranging from ~1% for GPT-5.6 Sol to ~32% for Claude Sonnet 4.6. To construct the benchmark and make it representative of real-world settings, we combine human-designed and labelled synthetic articles with live news articles and historical documents, creating 656 items for assessment. The resulting task requires agents to distinguish genuinely new, valuation-relevant financial information from stale, immaterial or misleading news under realistic conditions. We find substantial trade-offs among agent accuracy, cost, false positives and reliability that continue to hinder the reliable deployment of news-flow filtering in practice.

AI.tldr: Frontier Financial Judgement is a benchmark developed with equity analysts to evaluate AI agents' ability to identify valuation-relevant financial news. The strongest agent matches expert labels in only 52.4% of cases, with false-positive rates varying widely (1%–32%). The benchmark uses 656 items combining synthetic and real articles. Significant trade-offs between accuracy, cost, false positives, and reliability hinder practical deployment.
AI.motivation: Identifying new, valuation-relevant information amid growing volumes of AI-generated content is a time-consuming challenge for equity analysts. Existing benchmarks inadequately capture the real-world difficulty of distinguishing genuinely new, material financial information from stale, immaterial, or misleading news.
AI.method: Constructed a benchmark of 656 items combining human-designed, labelled synthetic articles with live news and historical documents. The task requires agents to classify whether news contains genuinely new, valuation-relevant financial information. Evaluated multiple frontier agents (GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and others) against expert analyst labels, measuring accuracy, false-positive rates, cost, and reliability.
AI.result: The best agent matched expert labels in only 52.4% of cases. Estimated false-positive rates ranged dramatically from ~1% (GPT-5.6 Sol) to ~32% (Claude Sonnet 4.6). Substantial trade-offs emerged across accuracy, cost, false positives, and reliability, preventing reliable real-world deployment of news-flow filtering.
AI.conclusion: Current frontier AI agents are insufficiently reliable for automating financial news-flow filtering in real-world equity research contexts. The wide divergence in false-positive rates and accuracy-cost trade-offs underscores the need for continued improvement before practical deployment is viable.

title: STeMP: Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol
summary:
Spatio-temporal machine-learning modelling is an important tool in environmental research. However, machine-learning models are highly sensitive to both the characteristics of the training data, such as its distribution, and methodological choices, including the cross-validation strategy. Each decision has impact and implications on the model itself as well as the estimation of the model quality and applicability for certain purposes. Taking into account the large role of machine-learning based maps of the environment in science and their transfer into practice, transparent reporting of spatio-temporal models, ideally using standardized model protocols, is essential to enable trust, transparency and comparability. However, such protocols are currently lacking for spatio-temporal modelling.
  We propose STeMP (Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol) to fill this gap by serving two purposes: standardized reporting to understand the model functioning as well as providing guidance during the modelling process by pointing at critical decisions and parameters. The protocol is structured in three sections: Overview, Model and Prediction. The Overview section contains metadata, while the Model and Prediction sections go into detail, describing predictors, evaluation and software, and further relevant elements of the modelling workflow.
  The protocol definition is hosted on GitHub and accompanied by an R-package (https://github.com/LOEK-RS/STeMP). The R-package contains a web application that can be used to fill the protocol either manually or in a semi-automated way from provided modelling objects. Warnings are returned from the protocol when common pitfalls are encountered, which may help authors as a guide through the modelling process but also support reviewers in the assessment of modelling studies. Via GitHub, incorporation of contributions and feedback from the community is encouraged.

AI.tldr: STeMP is a standardized Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol that provides both a reporting framework for transparent documentation of spatio-temporal machine-learning models and guidance during the modelling process, accompanied by an R-package with a web application for semi-automated protocol completion and pitfall detection.
AI.motivation: Spatio-temporal machine-learning models are widely used in environmental research but are highly sensitive to training data characteristics and methodological choices (e.g., cross-validation strategies). Despite their significant role in science and practice, no standardized protocol exists for transparent reporting of these models, hindering trust, transparency, reproducibility, and comparability.
AI.method: The authors developed STeMP, a structured protocol organized into three sections: Overview (metadata), Model (predictors, evaluation, software details), and Prediction (modelling workflow elements). The protocol is hosted on GitHub and implemented as an R-package containing a web application that enables manual or semi-automated completion from modelling objects. It includes warning mechanisms that flag common pitfalls to guide authors and aid reviewers.
AI.result: The protocol fills a critical gap in spatio-temporal modelling by providing a standardized reporting framework. The accompanying R-package facilitates adoption through a user-friendly web interface and automated checks against common modelling errors, while the GitHub-based development model encourages community contributions and feedback.
AI.conclusion: STeMP addresses the absence of standardized reporting in spatio-temporal machine-learning modelling by offering both documentation structure and process guidance. It aims to improve model transparency, trustworthiness, and comparability in environmental research, with community-driven evolution via GitHub.

title: Inducing Comparability of Factorised Probability Distributions
summary: To allow for principled comparison between two probabilistic graphical models defined over non-identical variable sets, they have to be lifted to a common measurable space. To this end, we propose an extension scheme for any two given models and establish the formal foundation: Unmatched components are completed using conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions such that the resulting joint distributions differ from the original ones only by multiplicative constants and coincide under projection. This preserves the probabilistic semantics while enabling the application of well-defined distributional discrepancy measures. We establish the invariance of the induced joint under projection and use the extensions to provide a minimal structural extension of two factor graphs to the smalles common measurable space as well as to a common graphical structure by a deterministic algorithm. In addition, we discuss structural and measure-theoretic properties and identify promising criteria for comparison methodologies.

AI.tldr: Proposes a formal extension scheme for comparing two probabilistic graphical models defined over different variable sets, using conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions to lift them to a common measurable space while preserving probabilistic semantics under projection.
AI.motivation: Principled comparison between two probabilistic graphical models is impossible when they are defined over non-identical variable sets; a rigorous method is needed to lift both models to a shared measurable space without distorting their original probabilistic semantics.
AI.method: An extension scheme based on conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions: unmatched components are completed so that the resulting joint distributions differ from the originals only by multiplicative constants and coincide under projection. A deterministic algorithm provides minimal structural extension of two factor graphs to the smallest common measurable space and common graphical structure.
AI.result: The extended joint distributions are invariant under projection, differ from the original distributions only by multiplicative constants, and enable application of well-defined distributional discrepancy measures. The algorithm yields minimal structural extensions to a shared space.
AI.conclusion: The proposed extension framework provides a formal measure-theoretic foundation for comparing probabilistic graphical models with mismatched variable sets, and lays groundwork for future comparison methodologies based on structural and measure-theoretic criteria.

title: From Agent Failures to Text Policies: What Works and What Breaks
summary: TextGrad improves language-model systems by revising text from feedback. Its core thesis is that natural-language feedback can act as a gradient for optimizing text components without changing model weights. Applying it to agents is harder because feedback arrives only after a sequence of actions, making it difficult to identify which decision caused failure. We study this problem by separating the ability to follow a useful policy from the ability to learn that policy from experience. Our main finding is a clear gap between these two abilities. Human-written policies improve two frozen 7B agents on TextWorldExpress by 5.0 success points, showing that useful policy text exists. However, policies generated from agent trajectories do not reliably outperform fixed prompting, even with richer traces, counterfactual evidence, or iterative GEPA search. The main challenge for agent-level TextGrad is therefore not executing textual policy updates, but reliably generating and selecting them from experience.

AI.tldr: TextGrad uses natural language feedback as gradients to optimize text prompts. This paper shows that while human-written policies improve frozen LLM agents, policies automatically generated from agent trajectories fail to reliably outperform fixed prompts—the bottleneck is policy generation/selection from experience, not execution.
AI.motivation: TextGrad's thesis—that natural-language feedback can serve as gradients for textual optimization—works in single-step settings but faces challenges in sequential agent tasks where feedback is delayed. The authors aim to diagnose why: is the problem in executing useful textual policies, or in learning/selecting them from experience?
AI.method: The authors decompose the problem into two capabilities: (1) following a useful textual policy, and (2) learning that policy from experience. They test human-written policies on frozen 7B agents in TextWorldExpress to establish an upper bound, then evaluate policies auto-generated from agent trajectories (varying trace richness, counterfactual evidence, and iterative GEPA search) against fixed prompting baselines.
AI.result: Human-written policies yield a +5.0 success point gain, confirming useful policy text exists and can be executed. However, all automatically generated policies—regardless of trace detail, counterfactual information, or search method—fail to reliably beat fixed prompting, revealing a clear generation/selection gap.
AI.conclusion: The primary bottleneck for agent-level TextGrad is not executing textual policy updates but reliably generating and selecting effective policies from experiential trajectories. This reframes future research toward improving policy proposal and evaluation mechanisms rather than policy implementation.

title: When Does Recurrence Become an Algorithm? Convergence Selection in Weight-Tied Looped Transformers
summary: When does a weight-tied looped transformer -- one block applied T times -- implement an actual algorithm? We answer with four findings from controlled populations on group word problems. (1) The budget law: free training installs a linear computation frontier, a mechanism that solves v positions per loop, whose speed is priced by the training contract: v ~ n_train/T_train (exponent 0.98 +/- 0.04, R^2=0.99), exactly unity under T=n training. SGD selects a frontier matching the minimum the contract demands; granting more test-time loops than ever trained rescues late positions at fixed input length, yielding a principled halting rule T* = ceil(n / v-hat). (2) Architecture prior, not expressivity, picks the algorithm: standard-depth transformers learn parallel scans on this family; weight tying flips the selection to the serial frontier, even when positional addressing for a log-depth scan is supplied. At matched depth and parameters, untied models extrapolate worst and fail to learn A5 at all. (3) The walls are not where circuit complexity says: NC1-completeness costs nothing (A5 generalizes fully), while group order does (S5's 120x120 operator deadlocks joint learning) -- and an operator-first curriculum dissolves the wall in every seed. (4) Mechanisms are portable, not mandatable: warm-starting across budget contracts transfers the algorithm in every seed, re-pricing its speed, while imposing seriality through the input schedule fails where free training succeeds. These results are invisible to standard instruments, which provably saturate at the fixed points trained loops converge to. We introduce a head instrument, the convergence-time scaling tau(n,i), validate it causally via damage cones whose slope reproduces v, and show in-distribution head measurements predict out-of-distribution fate where tail metrics do not. Results replicate on the public easy-to-hard benchmark.

AI.tldr: Analyzes weight-tied looped transformers on group word problems, revealing four findings: a budget law linking training data to computation speed; architecture-driven algorithm selection favoring serial over parallel scans; circuit complexity not predicting learning difficulty (group order does); and portable but non-mandatable algorithmic mechanisms. Introduces a convergence-time scaling instrument that predicts out-of-distribution behavior.
AI.motivation: Understand when and how weight-tied looped transformers implement actual algorithms, moving beyond expressivity arguments to characterize what algorithms emerge under training constraints.
AI.method: Controlled experiments on group word problems (A5, S5) with weight-tied looped transformers. Varies training budget (n_train, T_train), architecture (tied vs untied), and input schedules. Introduces convergence-time scaling τ(n,i) as a head instrument and validates via damage cones.
AI.result: (1) Budget law: computation speed v ≈ n_train/T_train with exponent ~0.98; (2) Weight tying flips algorithm selection from parallel to serial scans; untied models fail on A5; (3) NC1-completeness doesn't hinder learning but group order does; operator-first curriculum resolves deadlock; (4) Algorithms transfer across budget contracts via warm-starting. τ(n,i) predicts OOD fate where tail metrics fail.
AI.conclusion: Weight-tied looped transformers learn serial algorithms governed by a training budget law. Architecture prior, not expressivity, drives algorithm selection. Standard metrics saturate at fixed points, but convergence-time scaling provides a principled instrument for mechanistic analysis and OOD prediction.

title: LeanFlow: A Case Study in Workflow-Driven Lean Autoformalization
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures, ICML 2026: AI for Math Workshop
summary: We present and evaluate LeanFlow, an LLM agent system specialized for translating mathematical papers into buildable Lean projects. Recent verifier-in-the-loop systems show that large formal artifacts can be produced, but it remains unclear which runtime mechanisms affect completion, auditability, or efficiency in document-to-project formalization. We study this question through case studies on two previously unformalized mathematical papers in number theory and measure theory, using model, proof-workflow, and toolset ablations with Kimi2.6 and GPT5.5; we report task outcome, API calls, input tokens, and output tokens. With Kimi2.6, the full workflow completes both document-level projects within the 2000-call budget, while no-queue variants reach the budget limit; with GPT5.5, all document-level variants complete, and the full workflow has the lowest or tied-lowest input-token cost on both sources. As complementary calibration, LeanFlow reaches 75.7% BEq+ on the PFR slice of RLM25 and solves all five ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge projects in our GPT5.5 runs.

AI.tldr: LeanFlow is an LLM agent system that translates mathematical papers into buildable Lean projects. Evaluated on number theory and measure theory papers, the full workflow with Kimi2.6 completes both projects within a 2000-call budget, while GPT5.5 achieves lowest input-token cost. LeanFlow also attains 75.7% BEq+ on the PFR slice of RLM25 and solves all five ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge projects.
AI.motivation: While verifier-in-the-loop systems can produce large formal artifacts, it remains unclear which runtime mechanisms influence completion, auditability, and efficiency in document-to-project formalization. The authors aim to systematically study these factors through controlled ablations.
AI.method: The authors conduct case studies on two previously unformalized mathematical papers (one in number theory, one in measure theory). They perform ablations on model choice (Kimi2.6 vs. GPT5.5), proof-workflow mechanisms (full workflow vs. no-queue variants), and toolset configurations. Metrics include task outcome, API call counts, input tokens, and output tokens. Complementary calibration is done on the PFR slice of RLM25 (measuring BEq+) and the ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge (five projects).
AI.result: With Kimi2.6, the full workflow completes both document-level projects within the 2000-call budget; no-queue variants exhaust the budget. With GPT5.5, all document-level variants complete, and the full workflow achieves the lowest or tied-lowest input-token cost on both sources. LeanFlow reaches 75.7% BEq+ on PFR/RLM25 and solves all five ICML 2026 TCS challenge projects under GPT5.5.
AI.conclusion: Runtime mechanisms such as queuing strategies significantly affect completion and cost-efficiency in LLM-driven formalization. The full LeanFlow workflow, particularly with GPT5.5, provides a strong balance of completion reliability and token efficiency, and generalizes well to benchmark and challenge settings.

title: Learning to Detect UI Principle Violations via Reinforcement Learning
summary:
Small language models and coding agents increasingly generate web front-end code, yet their outputs are typically evaluated primarily for functional correctness. A generated interface may compile, render, and pass unit tests while still violating established interface quality principles, including accessibility barriers, deceptive design patterns, poor visual hierarchy, and excessive decision complexity. Existing auditing approaches face a trade-off between cost, coverage, and scalability: expert human review provides rich judgment but is slow and expensive; frontier vision-language models offer broader reasoning capabilities but remain costly to deploy at scale; and rule-based tools such as axe-core and Lighthouse are inexpensive but primarily capture mechanically checkable accessibility issues.
  We investigate whether a lightweight vision-language model can serve as an effective critic for generated interfaces. We unify 19 interface-quality principles from three complementary sources of HCI knowledge: WCAG 2.2 accessibility standards, deceptive design taxonomies, and established theories of perception, cognition, and interaction. To train this critic, we construct a verified dataset of approximately 10,000 generated web pages by synthetically injecting known violations into clean, LLM-generated Tailwind pages.
  Continued reinforcement learning on a 4B vision-language model improves micro-F1 from 36\% to 84\%, with 13 of 19 principles exceeding 80\% F1. The resulting critic can audit generated interfaces, filter low-quality interface training data, and provide a reward signal for design-aware code generation. We release our data-generation recipe and injection/verification prompts to support reproducible evaluation and future work on scalable interface-quality assessment.

AI.tldr: A 4B vision-language model, fine-tuned via reinforcement learning on synthetically violated web pages, achieves 84% micro-F1 in auditing interface quality across 19 principles spanning accessibility, deceptive design, and visual perception—offering a scalable, low-cost alternative to human review and frontier VLMs.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated web front-end code is evaluated primarily for functional correctness, ignoring critical interface-quality principles (accessibility, deceptive patterns, visual hierarchy, decision complexity). Existing auditing methods are either too expensive (human experts, frontier VLMs) or too narrow (rule-based tools like axe-core/Lighthouse only catch mechanically checkable issues). A scalable, cost-effective, and comprehensive automated critic is needed.
AI.method: The authors unify 19 interface-quality principles from WCAG 2.2, deceptive design taxonomies, and HCI perception/cognition theories. They construct a verified dataset of ~10,000 LLM-generated Tailwind pages with synthetically injected known violations. A 4B vision-language model is then trained via continued reinforcement learning to serve as a critic, using this controlled violation dataset for supervision.
AI.result: Micro-F1 improved from 36% to 84%, with 13 of 19 principles exceeding 80% F1. The resulting critic can audit generated interfaces, filter low-quality training data, and provide a reward signal for design-aware code generation.
AI.conclusion: A lightweight VLM can serve as an effective, scalable critic for interface quality, bridging the gap between cheap-but-narrow rule-based tools and expensive-but-rich human/VLM review. The authors release their data-generation recipe and prompts to support reproducibility and further research.

title: Are Single-Token Sparse Autoencoder Features Causally Necessary? Layer-Depth and SAE-Family Effects
summary: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are used to interpret and steer large language models, yet whether a feature's causal role is stable across SAE families remains untested. Single-token features that activate on one vocabulary item provide the diagnostic case where ground truth permits direct comparison. We analyze 3.9M features across six models and three SAE families using zero-ablation at full layer depth. Single-token features cluster 4.7x tighter in decoder space and concentrate in early layers (Layer 0 in GPT2-Small; L0-L4 in Gemma). Ablating them yields Benjamini-Hochberg-significant logit reductions in 178 of 208 full-layer conditions, with depth controlling whether damage cascades downstream or shapes the output directly. Cross-family causal differences exceed within-family scale effects: on the same base model, GemmaScope and BatchTopK features remain causally anchored, while LlamaScope features are locally redundant. The target token's rank recovers to within 2x baseline 96-98% of the time after the same ablation, and a controlled activation-function comparison reverses sign within the same model, leaving training recipe as the residual candidate. Cross-family interpretability claims are therefore sensitive to training methodology, not just activation function or scale.

AI.tldr: Single-token SAE features show that cross-family causal roles are unstable: training recipe, not activation function or scale, drives interpretability differences across SAE families, even when analyzing the same base model.
AI.motivation: SAE features are widely used for LLM interpretability and steering, but whether a feature's causal role remains consistent across different SAE families (trained on the same base model) has never been empirically tested. Single-token features — those activating on exactly one vocabulary item — provide an ideal diagnostic because ground truth is known.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 3.9 million features across six models and three SAE families (GemmaScope, BatchTopK, LlamaScope), using zero-ablation at full layer depth. They examined single-token features for clustering behavior in decoder space, layer distribution, downstream causal effects (Benjamini-Hochberg-corrected significance testing), target token rank recovery, and performed a controlled activation-function comparison.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Single-token features cluster 4.7× tighter in decoder space and concentrate in early layers. (2) Ablation yields significant logit reductions in 178/208 full-layer conditions. (3) Cross-family causal differences exceed within-family scale effects: GemmaScope and BatchTopK features remain causally anchored, while LlamaScope features are locally redundant. (4) Target token rank recovers to within 2× baseline 96–98% of the time post-ablation. (5) A controlled activation-function comparison reverses sign within the same model.
AI.conclusion: Cross-family interpretability claims are sensitive to training methodology, not merely activation function or model scale. This challenges the assumption that SAE features discovered by one family straightforwardly transfer their causal interpretation to another family, even on identical base models.

title: Optimizing Hypergraph-Based RAG: Toward Better Fact Extraction and Chunk Retrieval
summary: GraphRAG enables deeper reasoning by structuring knowledge as graphs but struggles with n-ary facts. HyperGraphRAG uses hypergraphs for richer semantics, improving accuracy, yet relies on error-prone LLM extraction and inefficient standard chunk retrieval. We address this by employing self-consistency prompting to improve the extraction, and Personalized PageRank algorithm over hypergraph to enhance chunk retrieval.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes improvements to HyperGraphRAG by using self-consistency prompting for more reliable knowledge extraction and Personalized PageRank over hypergraphs for better chunk retrieval, addressing n-ary fact representation limitations in GraphRAG.
AI.motivation: GraphRAG structures knowledge as graphs but cannot adequately represent n-ary facts (facts involving more than two entities). HyperGraphRAG addresses this by using hypergraphs for richer semantics, but suffers from two critical weaknesses: (1) LLM-based knowledge extraction is error-prone, and (2) standard chunk retrieval is inefficient for hypergraph-structured knowledge.
AI.method: Two main techniques are employed: (1) Self-consistency prompting to improve the reliability of LLM-based knowledge extraction from text, reducing errors through multiple sampled reasoning paths; (2) Personalized PageRank algorithm applied over the hypergraph structure to enhance chunk retrieval, leveraging the hypergraph's connectivity to rank and retrieve more relevant information chunks.
AI.result: The abstract does not provide specific quantitative results; it describes the proposed methodological improvements but defers empirical outcomes to the full paper.
AI.conclusion: The abstract does not state an explicit conclusion, but implies that combining self-consistency prompting with Personalized PageRank over hypergraphs can mitigate the extraction and retrieval weaknesses of HyperGraphRAG, thereby improving its overall performance for n-ary fact reasoning.

title: REGARD: Regional Affective Differences in Large Language Models
comment: 17 pages, 11 figures, 3 tables. Includes evaluation of 19 language models, two independent VAD judges, and human validation on 300 items
summary: Large language models trained and aligned within different linguistic and regional ecosystems may frame the same political, cultural, and geopolitical entities in different ways. Such differences are often evaluated through sentiment, favorability, or stance, reducing model attitudes to a single positive-negative axis. We introduce REGARD, a study of what drives affective framing differences across LLMs on post-Soviet entities using target-directed Valence-Arousal-Dominance profiling. We query 19 models on 500 region-specific targets, score their responses with two independent LLM judges, GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and validate the measurements on a 300-item human-annotated subset. Post-hoc Ward-linkage clustering of all 19 models by affective and response-behavior profiles yields three behavioral clusters that cut across model origin, family, and parameter count. Generic-answer rate is strongly associated with lower arousal (r = -0.81) and with cluster placement: models that deflect evaluative prompts with templated responses cluster together at low arousal regardless of origin. These findings show that VAD profiling captures emotional intensity, a dimension of affective framing that is largely invisible to conventional sentiment-based evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces REGARD, a study using Valence-Arousal-Dominance (VAD) profiling to examine how LLMs from different linguistic/regional ecosystems differently frame post-Soviet entities. Testing 19 models on 500 regional targets with dual LLM judges validated against human annotations, the authors find that models cluster into three behavioral groups cutting across origin and size, with generic-answer rate strongly correlated with low arousal (r = -0.81). VAD profiling reveals emotional intensity differences invisible to conventional sentiment-based evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for comparing LLM political and cultural framing rely predominantly on sentiment, favorability, or stance detection — all of which collapse affective framing onto a single positive-negative axis. This overlooks emotional intensity and other dimensions of affective framing. The authors aim to demonstrate that VAD profiling captures richer, sentiment-invisible differences in how LLMs frame geopolitical entities, particularly those in the post-Soviet space where regional model ecosystems may diverge.
AI.method: The authors queried 19 LLMs on 500 region-specific targets related to post-Soviet entities and scored responses using target-directed Valence-Arousal-Dominance profiling. Two independent LLM judges (GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) produced the VAD scores. Measurements were validated against a 300-item human-annotated subset. Post-hoc Ward-linkage clustering was applied to all 19 models based on affective and response-behavior profiles, yielding three behavioral clusters. Correlation analysis examined relationships between generic-answer rate, arousal, and cluster placement.
AI.result: Ward-linkage clustering produced three behavioral clusters that cut across model origin, family, and parameter count — meaning models from different developers and regions can share similar affective behavior patterns. Generic-answer rate showed a strong negative correlation with arousal (r = -0.81): models that deflect evaluative prompts with templated responses consistently cluster at low arousal, regardless of their geographic or organizational origin. This demonstrates that VAD profiling captures emotional intensity differences that sentiment-based evaluation misses.
AI.conclusion: VAD profiling is a valuable complement to sentiment-based evaluation for cross-LLM framing analysis, as it surfaces emotional intensity and dominance dimensions that the positive-negative axis obscures. The clustering results suggest that behavioral response patterns (e.g., generic deflection) may be more predictive of affective framing than model origin or architecture. The authors recommend VAD-based methods for future comparative studies of LLM political and cultural framing.

title: One Round Is All You Need: Analytic Federated Learning for Task-Heterogeneous Multi-Label Medical Image Classification
comment: The 14th IEEE International Conference on Healthcare Informatics
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple clinical institutions to collaboratively train a shared disease classifier without centralizing patient data. In practice, however, each institution annotates only the pathologies within its area of expertise, so the federation operates under task heterogeneity: each client holds labels for a strict subset of the target disease categories while the remaining classes are entirely unobserved at that site. Existing gradient-based FL methods fail under this setting because they require hundreds of communication rounds to converge and because missing class labels introduce systematic false-negative bias that the model cannot correct without a principled mechanism. We propose an analytic federated learning framework for multi-label medical image classification under task heterogeneity.
