The proposed method replaces iterative gradient optimization with three closed-form operations: a balanced label projection that neutralizes class-imbalance bias by normalizing positive and negative contributions to equal total mass; a per-class absolute aggregation law that independently assembles the optimal ridge-regression classifier for each disease category from the sufficient statistics uploaded by its annotating clients; and an optional analytic pseudo-label refinement round that propagates missing-class knowledge from a confidence-filtered teacher classifier to non-annotating clients. The entire procedure requires at most two communication rounds, irrespective of the degree of task heterogeneity or the number of participating clients. Experiments on ChestXray14 under four progressively severe missing-class configurations demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art federated multi-label method FedMLP by up to 18.44 BACC points and 13.24 AUC points, while reducing the communication.

AI.tldr: A communication-efficient analytic federated learning framework for multi-label medical image classification under task heterogeneity (clients label only subsets of disease categories), achieving strong performance in at most two communication rounds via closed-form operations: balanced label projection, per-class absolute aggregation, and optional pseudo-label refinement.
AI.motivation: Federated learning in clinical settings suffers from task heterogeneity — each institution annotates only pathologies in its expertise, leaving many classes unobserved per client. Existing gradient-based FL methods require hundreds of communication rounds and introduce uncorrectable false-negative bias from missing labels.
AI.method: An analytic FL framework replacing iterative optimization with three closed-form steps: (1) balanced label projection normalizing positive/negative contributions to equal total mass to neutralize class-imbalance bias; (2) per-class absolute aggregation law independently assembling optimal ridge-regression classifiers from sufficient statistics of annotating clients; (3) optional analytic pseudo-label refinement using a confidence-filtered teacher classifier to propagate missing-class knowledge. At most two communication rounds needed.
AI.result: On ChestXray14 under four progressively severe missing-class configurations, the method outperforms FedMLP by up to 18.44 BACC points and 13.24 AUC points while dramatically reducing communication rounds.
AI.conclusion: The proposed closed-form, two-round analytic FL framework effectively handles extreme task heterogeneity in multi-label medical image classification, significantly outperforming gradient-based alternatives in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

title: MiniCache: Reusable Program Caching with Small Model Interfaces for Efficient LLM Inference
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for program-aided reasoning, agentic decision making, and structured task execution, but these applications often incur high inference cost. We present MiniCache, a reusable program caching framework that transforms Program-of-Thought (PoT) programs into parameterized cache objects, enabling reusable computation across structurally similar requests. MiniCache reuses the same small model for semantic variable extraction on cache-hit requests and speculative drafting during target-LLM generation, reducing expensive target-LLM invocations while preserving task quality. Experiments on shopping-style request datasets, WebShop, Formula, and CodeTAT-QA demonstrate that MiniCache improves the trade-off between inference latency, cache reuse, and accuracy, achieving up to 3.1x lower latency and 2.8x higher throughput under parallel serving. These results show that small models are most effective not as replacements for large models, but as lightweight interface models that enable reliable and efficient reusable program caching.

AI.tldr: MiniCache introduces a reusable program caching framework that transforms Program-of-Thought outputs into parameterized cache objects, leveraging a small model for semantic variable extraction and speculative drafting to reduce expensive LLM invocations while maintaining task quality, achieving up to 3.1× lower latency and 2.8× higher throughput.
AI.motivation: LLM-based applications for program-aided reasoning, agentic decision-making, and structured task execution suffer from high inference costs due to repeated expensive LLM invocations for structurally similar requests.
AI.method: MiniCache transforms Program-of-Thought (PoT) programs into parameterized cache objects. A small model performs two roles: (1) semantic variable extraction to match incoming requests against cached programs, and (2) speculative drafting during target-LLM generation. On cache hits, cached programs are reused with extracted variables; on misses, the target LLM is invoked. The small model serves as a lightweight interface rather than a replacement for the large model.
AI.result: Evaluated on WebShop, Formula, and CodeTAT-QA shopping-style datasets, MiniCache achieved up to 3.1× lower inference latency and 2.8× higher throughput under parallel serving, while preserving task accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Small models are most effective not as replacements for large models, but as lightweight interface models enabling reliable, efficient reusable program caching. MiniCache demonstrates a favorable accuracy–latency–reuse trade-off.

title: Rushes: A Human Preference Dataset for Pluralistic Alignment
summary: We introduce Rushes, a dataset and benchmark for studying revealed human engagement preferences in interactive narrative environments. Rushes is collected through a game interface where users interact with AI-generated branching narratives and select one choice from a small, explicit candidate set at each decision point. Each interaction logs the full candidate set, the user's choice, and the evolving narrative context, yielding time-ordered trajectories with persistent user-level identifiers. Rushes contains 44,226 decision events from 8,167 unique users across six games, capturing sequential, personalized engagement behavior rather than static judgments. We show that user choices exhibit structured, non-random patterns, quantified by a low choice entropy relative to a uniform baseline. We position Rushes as a diagnostic benchmark for pluralistic alignment and demonstrate a robust Engagement Gap: state-of-the-art LLMs, including GPT-5, fail to outperform simple baselines. While classical Matrix Factorization (SVD) captures measurable personalized signal (37.7%), frontier LLMs (34.23%) struggle to even match the Popularity Baseline (36.4%) on event-level choice prediction. This gap suggests that single, population-level objectives, like those used in modern RLHF, appear insufficient to capture heterogeneous, context-dependent engagement signals. As a result, even highly capable models default to majority preferences rather than adapting to individual trajectories. We release Rushes to support research into pluralistic alignment and sequential decision-making in generative systems. The full code for the platform and dataset will be available here: https://github.com/microsoft/rushes

AI.tldr: Rushes is a benchmark dataset of 44,226 interactive narrative decisions from 8,167 users, designed to study personalized engagement preferences. It reveals an "Engagement Gap" where even GPT-5 underperforms simple baselines at predicting individual user choices, challenging the adequacy of population-level RLHF for capturing heterogeneous preferences.
AI.motivation: Modern LLM alignment techniques like RLHF optimize for population-level, aggregate preferences and may fail to capture heterogeneous, context-dependent, and personalized user engagement. A benchmark is needed to diagnose whether models can adapt to individual sequential decision-making rather than defaulting to majority preferences.
AI.method: The authors built an interactive game platform that logs users' choices among small candidate sets at each narrative branch point, yielding time-ordered trajectories with persistent user IDs. They collected 44,226 decision events from 8,167 users across six AI-generated branching narrative games. They benchmarked several models — including a Popularity Baseline, Matrix Factorization (SVD), and frontier LLMs (e.g., GPT-5) — on event-level choice prediction, measuring choice entropy and personalized prediction accuracy.
AI.result: User choices show structured, non-random patterns with low choice entropy versus uniform baselines. A clear Engagement Gap emerges: SVD achieves 37.7% accuracy, the Popularity Baseline reaches 36.4%, but GPT-5 (the best LLM) only reaches 34.23%, failing to beat simple heuristics. This indicates LLMs default to majority preferences and struggle to leverage individual user history for personalized prediction.
AI.conclusion: Population-level alignment objectives are insufficient for capturing heterogeneous, context-dependent engagement. The Rushes benchmark exposes a significant gap in current LLMs' ability to perform pluralistic alignment and sequential personalization, and the dataset is released to spur research on these challenges.

title: Scaling Interpretable Transformers with Parity Bottleneck Layers
summary: Language models are thought to exhibit the phenomenon of superposition, representing many more features than dimensions in their residual streams. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are designed to recover such features post-hoc, but training models that are interpretable by construction has remained impractical, as a per-layer over-complete bottleneck is prohibitively expensive in both memory and compute. To overcome this issue, we introduce the ParityTransformer, a GPT-2-scale architecture whose intermediate representations are efficient and wide / sparse by design. At each layer, a Deep Parity Bottleneck (DPB) replaces a learned over-complete basis with a parameter-free algebraic dictionary, providing a deterministic incoherence guarantee and eliminating the memory requirements that have prevented per-layer interpretable bottlenecks at scale. A DPB is a hierarchically structured sparse bottleneck which efficiently enforces sparsity using a multi-level mixture-of-experts approach: a hardware-aware implementation that closes the cost gap between activation sparse and dense training to a manageable interpretability tax. Empirically, ParityTransformers perform at least as well as post-hoc SAEs on sparse probing tasks, while out-performing on measures of feature absorption, steering effectiveness, and fine-grained causal interventions. Because subsequent computation acts only on features that survive the sparse bottleneck, the ParityTransformer's features are native to the model's forwards pass by construction, addressing the question of whether SAEs probe features the model actually uses during computation. We see this as a step toward training models whose internal representations are interpretable by design rather than recovered post hoc.

AI.tldr: The ParityTransformer introduces a Deep Parity Bottleneck (DPB) — a parameter-free algebraic dictionary with a hierarchical mixture-of-experts structure — that replaces dense bottlenecks in transformers, enabling per-layer sparse, interpretable representations at scale with manageable compute overhead. The model's features are natively used in the forward pass, outperforming post-hoc SAEs on interpretability metrics.
AI.motivation: Language models exhibit superposition, encoding many more features than dimensions. While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) recover these features post-hoc, training models that are interpretable by construction has been impractical due to the prohibitive memory and compute cost of per-layer over-complete bottlenecks at scale.
AI.method: The authors propose the ParityTransformer with a Deep Parity Bottleneck (DPB) at each layer. The DPB replaces learned over-complete bases with a parameter-free algebraic dictionary that provides deterministic incoherence guarantees. It enforces sparsity via a hierarchically structured, multi-level mixture-of-experts approach, implemented in a hardware-aware manner to close the cost gap between sparse and dense training.
AI.result: ParityTransformers perform at least as well as post-hoc SAEs on sparse probing tasks and outperform them on feature absorption, steering effectiveness, and fine-grained causal interventions. Because computation acts only on features surviving the bottleneck, the features are native to the forward pass — addressing whether SAE-probed features are actually used by the model.
AI.conclusion: This work represents a step toward training models whose internal representations are interpretable by design rather than recovered post hoc, with the DPB making per-layer interpretable bottlenecks practical at scale.

title: Telco-GAIA: Bilingual Benchmark for Agents in Telecom Domain
summary: We introduce Telco-GAIA, a bilingual, multi-modal benchmark for evaluating tool-using agents on the data of a real-world telecommunications operator. Telco-GAIA comprises 100 human-verified question-answering tasks, in English and Arabic, that each demand multi-hop reasoning (4.2 hops on average) over three heterogeneous sources: a static website snapshot (HTML, images, and linked PDFs), a synthetic relational SQL database, and external web archives, spanning text, image, and tabular modalities. The benchmark is delivered as a sandboxed Docker environment and scored by normalized exact string matching, making evaluation objective, deterministic, and reproducible over time without any LLM-as-a-Judge. Evaluating a purpose-built reference agent across twelve commercial and open LLMs, we find Telco-GAIA challenging: even the strongest model solves only 71% of tasks; under a moderate cost budget, this falls to about 40%, and the visually grounded categories remain the weakest, where the average backend scores below 30%, leaving substantial headroom in document and image understanding. Telco-GAIA offers a rigorous, reproducible testbed for enterprise agents and a template for constructing closed-domain benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Telco-GAIA is a bilingual (English/Arabic) multi-modal benchmark with 100 human-verified QA tasks for evaluating tool-using agents on real telecom data, requiring multi-hop reasoning over HTML, SQL, and web archives. Even the strongest LLM solves only 71%, with visually grounded tasks falling below 30%, leaving significant headroom.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of rigorous, reproducible, closed-domain benchmarks for evaluating tool-using AI agents in real-world enterprise settings, particularly those involving multi-modal, multi-hop reasoning across heterogeneous data sources and low-resource languages like Arabic.
AI.method: The authors construct Telco-GAIA: 100 human-verified QA tasks requiring multi-hop reasoning (avg. 4.2 hops) across three heterogeneous sources — a static website snapshot (HTML, images, PDFs), a synthetic relational SQL database, and external web archives — spanning text, image, and tabular modalities. The benchmark is containerized in Docker for sandboxed, deterministic evaluation using normalized exact string matching (no LLM-as-a-Judge). A purpose-built reference agent was evaluated across twelve commercial and open LLMs under both unlimited and moderate cost budgets.
AI.result: Telco-GAIA proves challenging: the strongest LLM solves only 71% of tasks under unlimited budget; under moderate cost constraints this drops to ~40%. Visually grounded categories are the weakest, with average backend scores below 30%, indicating substantial headroom in document and image understanding.
AI.conclusion: Telco-GAIA provides a rigorous, reproducible testbed for enterprise tool-using agents and serves as a template for constructing closed-domain, multi-modal benchmarks. The performance gap, especially in visual understanding and cost-constrained settings, highlights open challenges for real-world agent deployment.

title: Are Diversity Metrics Measuring Diversity? A Capability-Controlled Audit of Majority-Vote Gain in LLM Ensembles
summary: Majority voting over LLMs is widely assumed to benefit from diversity, and diversity measures are used to choose which models to combine. We ask whether five such measures track diversity or mainly re-express capability, auditing them as predictors of majority-vote gain over the best member across 31,900 subsets of 30 LLMs on MMLU-Pro (29 on TruthfulQA) under explicit capability controls. Three findings emerge. First, latent complementarity is ubiquitous: oracle gain is positive in 100% of subsets, yet simple voting beats the strongest member in only 9.98% of all canonical size-3 subsets (18.71% with held-out best selection); the pooled size-2-4 rate is 1.27%, partly reflecting deterministic even-size voting behavior. Second, a joint-correctness proxy (strict diversity) is nearly collinear with one minus mean accuracy (size-3 Spearman rho = +0.991 / +0.988); raw diversity-gain associations are strongly capability-entangled and, with one exception, unstable under control. Third, three linear contingency-table statistics are algebraically non-separable; after capability control, the empirically stable remainder is a modest residual pairwise co-failure association in which more shared error corresponds to lower gain. This direction is robust, but its magnitude is configuration-dependent. Joint rawspace linear regressions treating strict diversity, disagreement, and double-fault as independent predictors are rank-deficient by construction.

AI.tldr: This paper audits five diversity measures for LLM ensembles, finding that apparent diversity-gain correlations are largely artifacts of capability rather than genuine complementarity. When controlling for accuracy, only a weak residual pairwise co-failure association remains predictive of majority-vote gain, and the relationship is negative — more shared errors correlate with lower gain.
AI.motivation: Majority voting over LLMs is commonly believed to benefit from diversity, and diversity metrics are routinely used to select ensemble members. However, it is unclear whether existing diversity measures actually track genuine complementarity or merely re-express model capability (accuracy). The paper aims to disentangle these confounded signals.
AI.method: The authors audit five diversity measures (strict diversity, disagreement, double-fault, Q-statistic, correlation coefficient) as predictors of majority-vote gain over the best ensemble member. They evaluate 31,900 subsets of 30 LLMs on MMLU-Pro and 29 on TruthfulQA, applying explicit capability controls — including partial correlation and stratification by mean accuracy — to isolate diversity's independent contribution. They also analyze algebraic relationships between contingency-table statistics and assess latent complementarity via oracle (best possible) gain.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Oracle gain is positive in 100% of subsets, but simple majority voting beats the strongest member in only 9.98% of size-3 subsets (1.27% pooled for size 2–4). (2) A joint-correctness proxy (strict diversity) is nearly collinear with one minus mean accuracy (Spearman ρ ≈ +0.99); raw diversity-gain associations are capability-entangled and unstable under control. (3) Three linear contingency-table statistics (κ, disagreement, double-fault) are algebraically non-separable; the only stable residual after capability control is a negative pairwise co-failure association — more shared errors predict lower gain — but its magnitude depends on configuration.
AI.conclusion: Existing diversity measures largely recapitulate capability differences rather than measuring true complementarity. Meaningful diversity assessment requires careful capability control. The robust signal is negative co-failure association, not positive diversity-gain correlations. The findings caution against naive use of diversity metrics for LLM ensemble selection.

title: SiGMA: Sign-Guided Merging and Adaptation for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
summary: Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT) is crucial for adapting Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to evolving a sequence of downstream tasks. Prior methods mostly utilize Mixture of Experts or expansion merge approach, primarily focusing on catastrophic forgetting, yet they still suffer from negative interference during inference, where newly learned updates overwrite useful prior knowledge and degrade overall performance. To address this, we propose SiGMA (Sign Guided Merging and Adaptation), a simple yet effective framework that mitigates negative interference with two components: sign guided adaptive tuning during training and sign guided merging at inference. Sign guided adaptive tuning reduces collisions with past knowledge and learns the current task with minimal drift, mitigating severe forgetting. Sign guided merging further improves consolidation by selectively scaling salient parameters to preserve and amplify useful task specific knowledge. Experiments on UCIT and DCL benchmarks show that SiGMA significantly reduces negative interference and outperforms state of the art MCIT methods. Our code is available at SiGMA.

AI.tldr: SiGMA proposes a sign-guided framework for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning that mitigates negative interference during both training (adaptive tuning) and inference (selective merging), outperforming SOTA on UCIT and DCL benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing MCIT methods (MoE, expansion-merge) address catastrophic forgetting but still suffer from negative interference at inference, where new updates overwrite useful prior knowledge. A solution is needed that reduces this interference during both training and inference.
AI.method: SiGMA introduces two components: (1) Sign Guided Adaptive Tuning during training, which reduces collisions with past knowledge and enables learning new tasks with minimal parameter drift; (2) Sign Guided Merging at inference, which selectively scales salient parameters to preserve and amplify task-specific useful knowledge.
AI.result: Experiments on UCIT and DCL benchmarks demonstrate that SiGMA significantly reduces negative interference and achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing MCIT methods.
AI.conclusion: SiGMA effectively addresses the negative interference problem in MCIT by guiding both training and inference with parameter sign information, leading to superior continual adaptation of MLLMs.

title: The Geometry of Personality: Activation Steering with Jungian Cognitive Functions
summary:
Activation steering enables control and interpretation of LLMs, yet existing work primarily models personality through static trait frameworks such as the Big Five. We investigate whether personality can instead be represented and controlled as a set of cognitive processes using the eight Jungian Cognitive Functions. To this end, we introduce a framework comprising a Jungian evaluation protocol and a dataset of over 2,100 role-playing character narrations.
  Activation steering vector extraction and evaluation experiments on Llama-3.1-8B demonstrate effective monotonic control over all eight cognitive functions through activation steering. Beyond controllability, our analysis reveals that: 1. personality information is concentrated in middle transformer layers; 2. steering vectors exhibit structured geometric relationships consistent with distinctions between rational and irrational functions; 3. effective multi-dimensional steering directions cannot be recovered as linear combinations of single-function directions. These findings provide new insights into the representation of personality in LLM activation space and establish a framework for studying interpretable, effective, and multi-dimensional personality control.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes representing personality in LLMs through Jungian Cognitive Functions (eight cognitive processes) rather than static Big Five traits. Using activation steering on Llama-3.1-8B with a 2100+ dataset of role-playing narrations, they demonstrate monotonic control over all eight functions, reveal that personality concentrates in middle layers, find structured geometric relationships between function types, and show multi-dimensional steering cannot be reduced to linear combinations of single-function directions.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering work models personality through static trait frameworks (e.g., Big Five), which overlooks the dynamic, process-oriented nature of personality. The authors aim to investigate whether personality can instead be represented and controlled as a set of cognitive processes using Jung's eight Cognitive Functions.
AI.method: The authors introduce a framework with: (1) a Jungian evaluation protocol to assess the eight cognitive functions; (2) a dataset of over 2,100 role-playing character narrations. They then extract activation steering vectors from Llama-3.1-8B and conduct experiments evaluating controllability, layer-wise concentration of personality information, geometric relationships among steering vectors, and the decomposability of multi-dimensional steering directions.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Activation steering achieves effective monotonic control over all eight cognitive functions. (2) Personality information is concentrated in middle transformer layers. (3) Steering vectors exhibit structured geometric relationships aligning with the rational/irrational function distinction in Jungian theory. (4) Multi-dimensional steering directions cannot be recovered as linear combinations of single-function directions, indicating non-compositional structure.
AI.conclusion: The findings offer new insights into how personality is represented in LLM activation space and establish a framework for interpretable, effective, multi-dimensional personality control grounded in cognitive process theory rather than static trait models.

title: Adaptive Multi-Horizon Reinforcement Learning
summary: Effective decision-making in complex and changing environments requires balancing short-term and long-term consequences. In reinforcement learning (RL), this trade-off is typically controlled through a fixed discount factor, which imposes a single exponentially discounted temporal horizon. However, biological agents exhibit flexible and adaptive temporal discounting, suggesting that effective planning requires multiple timescales. Here, we propose a multi-horizon approach that adaptively selects and combines temporal horizons, enabling robust adaptation to changes in reward structure without manual discount-factor tuning. This flexibility makes the method particularly suitable for continual learning scenarios involving task switches and varying environmental configurations. Empirically, we demonstrate that our approach identifies effective discount factors across a range of MiniGrid environments, including continual settings composed of three sequentially changing tasks. These results suggest that adaptive temporal discounting can improve parameter efficiency and enhance adaptability in both artificial and biologically inspired learning systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multi-horizon reinforcement learning method that adaptively selects and combines multiple discount factors (temporal horizons), enabling robust adaptation to changing reward structures without manual tuning. The approach is validated on MiniGrid environments, including continual learning scenarios with sequential task switches.
AI.motivation: Standard RL uses a fixed discount factor that imposes a single exponential temporal horizon, which is inflexible. Biological agents exhibit adaptive temporal discounting across multiple timescales, suggesting that effective planning requires flexible horizon selection. The authors aim to bridge this gap by enabling RL agents to dynamically adjust their temporal horizons, especially for continual learning where reward structures shift over time.
AI.method: A multi-horizon approach that adaptively selects and combines multiple temporal horizons (discount factors). Instead of relying on a single, manually tuned discount factor, the method dynamically adjusts which horizons to use based on the current task or environment configuration. This facilitates continual learning under task switches and varying reward structures.
AI.result: The method successfully identifies effective discount factors across a range of MiniGrid environments. It demonstrates robust performance in continual learning settings composed of three sequentially changing tasks, showing improved parameter efficiency and adaptability compared to fixed-discount-factor baselines.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive temporal discounting via multi-horizon selection can improve parameter efficiency and adaptability in both artificial and biologically inspired learning systems. The approach eliminates the need for manual discount-factor tuning and supports robust continual learning under environmental non-stationarity.

title: Reliability-Aware LLM Alignment from Inconsistent Human Feedback
summary: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is critical for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences. However, its efficacy is often compromised by the inherent inconsistency and subjectivity of human annotations. Existing preference optimization frameworks, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), typically treat ambiguous pairs with high annotator disagreement identically to those with unanimous consensus, forcing models to overfit to inconsistent supervision signals and leading to suboptimal alignment. In this work, we propose Reliability-Guided Preference Optimization (RGPO), a robust framework designed to mitigate the impact of inconsistent human feedback. RGPO estimates annotator reliability and infers latent ground truth labels from noisy human feedback to identify robust preferences. Furthermore, we introduce a reliability-aware consistency optimization that dynamically modulates the training objective based on the consensus level of annotations, ensuring the model prioritizes high-consensus supervision signals. Extensive experiments on LLM alignment benchmarks demonstrate that RGPO effectively reduces inconsistency and noise in training data and achieves superior performance compared to widely adopted RLHF baselines. Our code and configurations are available at https://github.com/GenieHuang/RGPO.

AI.tldr: RGPO is a framework that estimates annotator reliability and infers latent ground truth from noisy human preferences, then dynamically weights training objectives based on annotation consensus to mitigate the impact of inconsistent human feedback in RLHF.
AI.motivation: Human annotations in RLHF are inherently inconsistent and subjective, yet existing methods like DPO treat all preference pairs equally regardless of annotator disagreement. This forces models to overfit noisy supervision signals, leading to suboptimal alignment with human preferences.
AI.method: RGPO operates in two stages: (1) Reliability Estimation — estimates annotator reliability scores and infers latent ground truth labels from noisy feedback to identify robust preferences; (2) Reliability-Aware Consistency Optimization — dynamically modulates the training objective based on the consensus level of annotations, making the model prioritize high-consensus supervision signals over ambiguous ones.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on LLM alignment benchmarks show that RGPO effectively reduces inconsistency and noise in training data and achieves superior performance compared to widely adopted RLHF baselines.
AI.conclusion: RGPO provides a robust solution for preference optimization under noisy human feedback by explicitly modeling annotator reliability and consensus, yielding better-aligned LLMs than standard RLHF approaches.

title: REFACT: Adaptive Fact Restatement for Compact and Faithful Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
summary: Large language models increasingly rely on long-form reasoning for complex tasks, yet their reasoning traces may drift away from the supplied context when evidence is sparse, noisy, or in conflict with parametric knowledge. Existing grounding methods either attach citations after generation or encourage evidence retrieval inside the trace, but they often do not ensure that cited content is sufficient for the local inference and final answer. We propose REFACT, an adaptive fact-restatement citation framework that trains models to decide when a reasoning step needs contextual grounding and at what granularity source facts should be restated. This design avoids both unsupported inference and indiscriminate fact copying by turning citations into answer-supporting intermediate states. REFACT is optimized with a two-stage SFT-to-RL pipeline in which a citation-utility reward encourages cited facts to be well-formed, source-traceable, and answer-sufficient. Experiments on LongBench, LV-Eval, and ConFiQA show that REFACT improves long-context QA and counterfactual faithfulness while substantially reducing token consumption. Further analysis shows that REFACT preserves more answer-bearing evidence with fewer restated facts, yielding reasoning traces that are denser rather than longer. All code and data are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/REFACT.

AI.tldr: REFACT is a citation framework that trains LLMs to adaptively restate source facts mid-reasoning, using a two-stage SFT-to-RL pipeline with a citation-utility reward to ensure restated evidence is necessary, traceable, and sufficient for answering — improving QA accuracy and faithfulness while reducing token usage.
AI.motivation: LLM reasoning traces can drift from context when evidence is sparse, noisy, or conflicts with parametric knowledge. Existing grounding methods (post-hoc citation or retrieval-augmented generation) fail to guarantee that cited content is sufficient for the local inference step, leading to unsupported conclusions or indiscriminate copying.
AI.method: REFACT trains models to decide (1) when a reasoning step requires contextual grounding, and (2) at what granularity to restate source facts. Citations become intermediate reasoning states. Optimization uses a two-stage pipeline: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning (RL) with a citation-utility reward that scores restated facts on well-formedness, source-traceability, and answer-sufficiency.
AI.result: On LongBench, LV-Eval, and ConFiQA, REFACT improves long-context QA performance and counterfactual faithfulness while substantially reducing token consumption. Analysis shows denser reasoning traces — more answer-bearing evidence preserved with fewer restated facts.
AI.conclusion: REFACT demonstrates that adaptive, utility-driven fact restatement during reasoning yields more faithful, efficient, and evidence-dense traces than existing grounding approaches, without indiscriminate copying or unsupported inference.

title: End-to-End Learning of Safe Optimal Feedback Control in High Dimensions with Control Barrier Function Layers
summary: We consider the problem of learning high-dimensional semi-global feedback controllers under hard safety constraints enforced by control barrier functions (CBFs). Incorporating CBFs into end-to-end policy training requires embedding a quadratic-program-based safety filter as an optimization layer, but computational and differentiation bottlenecks have largely restricted prior approaches to low-dimensional systems, typically with at most 16 state dimensions. We address this limitation by combining operator splitting with the recently developed Jacobian-Free Backpropagation (JFB) method to enable scalable end-to-end training while preserving hard safety guarantees through the CBF safety filter. We justify this training methodology theoretically using nonsmooth analysis techniques and demonstrate its effectiveness on high-dimensional multi-agent nonlinear control problems with state and control dimensions up to 1200 and 400, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a scalable method for training high-dimensional neural network controllers with hard safety constraints via Control Barrier Functions (CBFs), combining operator splitting with Jacobian-Free Backpropagation (JFB) to overcome computational and differentiation bottlenecks. The approach is validated on multi-agent systems with up to 1200 state and 400 control dimensions.
AI.motivation: Prior approaches to embedding CBF-based safety filters (quadratic-program layers) into end-to-end policy training are restricted to low-dimensional systems (≤16 state dimensions) due to computational and differentiation bottlenecks. There is a need for scalable training methods that preserve hard safety guarantees for high-dimensional systems.
AI.method: The authors combine operator splitting techniques with Jacobian-Free Backpropagation (JFB) to bypass the need for differentiating through the implicit QP solver. Operator splitting decomposes the CBF-QP safety filter into simpler subproblems, while JFB avoids expensive Jacobian computations during backpropagation. Theoretical justification is provided via nonsmooth analysis.
AI.result: The proposed method enables end-to-end training of neural controllers with CBF safety filters on high-dimensional multi-agent nonlinear control problems, scaling to 1200 state dimensions and 400 control dimensions — orders of magnitude beyond prior work. Hard safety guarantees are preserved throughout training.
AI.conclusion: Combining operator splitting with JFB is a viable and theoretically justified approach for scaling CBF-based safe policy learning to high-dimensional systems, opening the door to real-world applications involving large-scale multi-agent systems.

title: CANN Bench: Benchmarking Agent Generated Kernels against Real NPU and Algorithmic Limits
summary: AI agents are now capable of writing, compiling, and iteratively optimizing low-level operator kernels on different hardware platforms. Existing benchmarks, however, focus almost exclusively on CUDA and Triton, leaving hardware ecosystems with less-exposed programming models without a common evaluation baseline. We present CANN Bench, an open benchmark for AI-generated operator code on Huawei's Ascend NPU. The current release covers 53 operators and 1060 test cases organized into four difficulty tiers -- from simple elementwise primitives to MoE dispatch and FlashAttention kernels -- spanning FP16, BF16, FP32, and INT8 precision formats. Evaluation adopts a \textbf{three-dimensional weighted composite score} that treats compilation, functional correctness, and performance as independent axes, providing a principled reward signal for kernel-generation agents. Performance is graded against an out-of-the-box PyTorch-on-Ascend baseline and an analytical per-case Hardware-Anchored Performance (HAP) limit on real NPU hardware, ensuring scores reflect genuine optimization headroom rather than measurement artifacts. The evaluation harness is designed to resist reward hacking from the ground up. CANN Bench is versioned within the official CANN repository and is designed for long-term community co-construction, providing the Ascend ecosystem with a quantitative, reproducible, and sustainably maintained yardstick for AI operator-authoring capability.

AI.tldr: CANN Bench is an open benchmark for evaluating AI-generated operator kernels on Huawei's Ascend NPU, covering 53 operators across 1060 test cases with a three-dimensional scoring system (compilation, correctness, performance) designed to resist reward hacking.
AI.motivation: Existing operator-code benchmarks focus almost exclusively on CUDA and Triton, leaving hardware platforms with less-exposed programming models (e.g., Huawei's Ascend NPU) without a standardized evaluation baseline for AI-generated kernels.
AI.method: The benchmark comprises 53 operators and 1060 test cases across four difficulty tiers (elementwise primitives to FlashAttention), four precision formats (FP16, BF16, FP32, INT8), and uses a three-dimensional weighted composite score evaluating compilation success, functional correctness, and performance. Performance is measured against both a PyTorch-on-Ascend baseline and an analytical Hardware-Anchored Performance (HAP) limit on real hardware to quantify genuine optimization headroom.
AI.result: The paper presents the design and structure of CANN Bench, emphasizing its anti-reward-hacking evaluation harness, multi-dimensional scoring, and versioning within the official CANN repository for long-term community co-construction.
AI.conclusion: CANN Bench provides the Ascend ecosystem with a quantitative, reproducible, and sustainably maintained yardstick for AI operator-authoring capability, filling a critical gap in hardware-diverse benchmarking for AI-generated kernels.

title: CSPF: A Constrained Shared-Private Fusion Method for Non-Verifiable Preference Evaluation
summary: At present, reliable evaluation of non-verifiable tasks remains challenging. Existing approaches often fail to adequately capture the diverse evaluative criteria underlying human preferences in such tasks. To this end, we propose Constrained Shared-Private Fusion (CSPF), a fusion method that treats heterogeneous frozen reward models as complementary evaluators and learns to integrate their hidden-state representations under pairwise human-preference supervision. CSPF decomposes each expert signal into shared and expert-private representations, encouraging cross-expert alignment while preserving complementary viewpoints. Across experiments on LM-Arena target-domain adaptation and PPE out-of-distribution preference evaluation, CSPF achieves the best performance on the primary metrics among the evaluated single-expert reward-model, scalar-score multi-expert, and rubric-judge baselines. Overall, CSPF suggests that fusing hidden-state representations provides a more expressive basis for preference assessment, offering a practical route toward integrated evaluative signals for non-verifiable preference tasks.

AI.tldr: CSPF fuses heterogeneous frozen reward models at the hidden-state level under pairwise preference supervision, decomposing signals into shared and expert-private representations. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on LM-Arena adaptation and out-of-distribution preference evaluation.
AI.motivation: Reliable evaluation of non-verifiable tasks (where ground-truth answers are unavailable) is challenging because existing methods fail to capture the diverse, often complementary evaluative criteria underlying human preferences. Simple scalar-score aggregation or single-expert models lose valuable fine-grained information from different reward models.
AI.method: CSPF treats multiple heterogeneous frozen reward models as complementary evaluators. It learns to fuse their hidden-state representations (rather than output scalars) under pairwise human-preference supervision. Each expert's signal is decomposed into a shared representation (encouraging cross-expert alignment) and expert-private representations (preserving complementary, distinctive viewpoints), enabling expressive integration of diverse evaluative signals.
AI.result: On LM-Arena target-domain adaptation and PPE out-of-distribution preference evaluation benchmarks, CSPF achieves the best performance on primary metrics compared to single-expert reward models, scalar-score multi-expert fusion, and rubric-judge baselines.
AI.conclusion: Fusing hidden-state representations rather than output scalars provides a more expressive basis for preference assessment. CSPF offers a practical route toward integrated evaluative signals for non-verifiable preference tasks.

title: Explanation-Based Runtime Verification for Trustworthy ML-driven Optical Networks
comment: 6 Pages, 2 Figures. Accepted and presented at the 30th International Conference on Optical Network Design and Modelling (ONDM 2026), Munich, Germany, 12-15 May 2026
summary: Machine learning (ML) models are increasingly integrated into optical network automation frameworks to support tasks such as failure management, performance monitoring and resource allocation. In these environments, ML-driven predictions may be directly coupled with control-plane actions where incorrect decisions can immediately impact service quality, resource efficiency, and network stability. As automation levels increase, ensuring the reliability of individual decisions at deployment time becomes a critical requirement. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques have emerged to improve transparency by highlighting the factors influencing ML predictions. In addition to identifying influential features, they provide insights into the underlying reasoning process of the model, revealing how different input variables contribute to the final outcome and how feature interactions shape the decision boundary. In this work, we introduce explanation-based runtime verification, an approach that exploits model explanations to assess the soundness of individual ML decisions before they are executed in the network control loop. The proposed approach evaluates explanation coherence and physics grounding consistency at runtime, enabling the system to defer or reject decisions flagged as uncertain. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a representative use case of lightpath quality of transmission classification. Experimental results show that explanation-based verification can intercept a significant fraction of erroneous decisions while preserving high automation rate.

AI.tldr: Introduces explanation-based runtime verification for ML-driven optical network automation, using XAI-derived explanations to assess decision soundness before execution. Demonstrated on lightpath QoT classification, it intercepts erroneous decisions while maintaining high automation rates.
AI.motivation: ML models in optical network automation are increasingly coupled with control-plane actions, where incorrect predictions directly degrade service quality and network stability. As automation levels rise, ensuring the reliability of individual ML decisions at deployment time becomes critical — beyond aggregate metrics like accuracy.
AI.method: Proposes explanation-based runtime verification: at inference time, the system evaluates (1) explanation coherence and (2) physics grounding consistency of model predictions using XAI techniques. Decisions flagged as uncertain or physically implausible are deferred or rejected before entering the network control loop.
AI.result: Experimental validation on lightpath quality of transmission classification shows the approach intercepts a significant fraction of erroneous decisions while preserving a high automation rate (i.e., low false rejection of correct decisions).
AI.conclusion: Explanation-based runtime verification offers a practical mechanism to bridge the gap between ML prediction accuracy and deployment-time decision reliability, enabling safer closed-loop automation in optical networks without sacrificing high levels of operational autonomy.

title: LegalCiteTrust: Benchmarking Citation Trustworthiness in Chinese Long-Form Legal Research Reports
comment: 8 pages, 21 pages with appendix, 26 tables, 4 figures
summary: Long-form legal research reports increasingly rely on LLMs and agentic research systems, but their reliability depends not only on answering the task, but also on whether cited legal authorities are trustworthy. A citation can be risky even when it points to a real source: the report may omit limiting conditions, misdescribe the authority, or use it to support a stronger claim than the source allows. We introduce LegalCiteTrust, a benchmark for evaluating citation trustworthiness in Chinese long-form legal research reports. It contains 72 densely annotated report-level tasks and evaluates reports along three dimensions: Coverage, Support, and Citation Trustworthiness. Citation Trustworthiness is operationalized through citation-level Existence, Fidelity, and Applicability (E/F/A). Experiments on general-purpose LLMs, deep-research systems, and legal-specific systems show that task completion, evidence richness, citation density, and citation reliability expose different system behaviors. Retrieval tools can improve evidence support without reliably improving the Trust score, while E/F/A-based revision improves Trust and Final score more clearly than existence-only filtering. These results suggest that trustworthy legal research generation requires citation-aware evidence governance after retrieval: systems must not only retrieve legal authorities, but also select, describe, and apply them reliably.

AI.tldr: LegalCiteTrust is a benchmark for evaluating citation trustworthiness in Chinese long-form legal research reports, measuring Coverage, Support, and Citation Trustworthiness (Existence, Fidelity, Applicability). Experiments reveal that retrieval tools improve evidence support but not necessarily trust scores, while E/F/A-based revision outperforms existence-only filtering, highlighting the need for citation-aware evidence governance beyond mere retrieval.
AI.motivation: LLM-based legal research systems face a critical reliability problem: even when citations point to real sources, reports may omit limiting conditions, misdescribe authorities, or use sources to support claims stronger than warranted. Existing evaluation focuses on task completion rather than the trustworthiness of cited legal authorities, creating a gap this work addresses.
AI.method: The authors introduce LegalCiteTrust, a benchmark of 72 densely annotated report-level tasks for Chinese long-form legal research. Reports are evaluated along three dimensions — Coverage, Support, and Citation Trustworthiness — with Citation Trustworthiness operationalized via citation-level Existence (does the source exist?), Fidelity (is it described accurately?), and Applicability (does it genuinely support the claim?). Experiments compare general-purpose LLMs, deep-research systems, and legal-specific systems, alongside ablation studies on retrieval tools and E/F/A-based revision strategies.
AI.result: Task completion, evidence richness, citation density, and citation reliability reveal divergent system behaviors. Retrieval tools improve evidence support (Support score) but do not reliably improve the Trust score. E/F/A-based revision produces clearer improvements in both Trust and Final scores compared to existence-only filtering, demonstrating that filtering for mere existence is insufficient for trustworthy legal generation.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy legal research generation requires citation-aware evidence governance after retrieval: systems must not only retrieve legal authorities but also select, describe, and apply them reliably. The E/F/A framework provides a practical scaffold for building and evaluating such systems.

title: Attribution Markets: A Fisher-Market Formulation for Fractional Credit Assignment Between Planned Tasks and Performed Actions
comment: 35 pages, 3 figures. Companion technical report with extended treatment of dynamic/forward-looking markets and reinforcement-learning extensions available separately
summary: Personal and organizational planning systems maintain two records that drift apart: what was planned (a task's effort budget) and what was done (a logged action's duration and description). Existing systems bridge them with an exclusive, all-or-nothing link that strands genuinely related but unlinked effort and reports false stalls on active goals. We formulate the bridge as a quasi-linear Fisher market: planned tasks are budget-constrained buyers, performed actions are divisible goods, and a fused text/structural/temporal signal sets each buyer's valuation. Two market instruments - a seller reserve price and a buyer cash option - yield conservation, a hard budget cap, and a provable junk filter as theorems. We extend the market with a concave completion utility discounting progress as a task nears its plan; standard convergence theory for the market's algorithm does not transfer here, resolved by a satiation-threshold fixed point with existence (Brouwer) and local uniqueness under an explicit diagonal-dominance condition, validated empirically on random and adversarial instances. A de-circularized, multi-seed benchmark - observed affinity corrupted independently of the scored ground truth - surfaces a genuine weak spot: the market's sharp, zero-entropy equilibrium is more sensitive to affinity noise than entropy-regularized optimal transport's permanently smoothed one. We resolve this with a one-parameter entropy-regularized generalization unifying the two, plus a noise-adaptive rule for its regularization strength. We report full reproducibility parameters, discuss limitations candidly, and relate the result to multi-touch attribution, optimal transport, and online Fisher-market algorithms.

AI.tldr: A paper proposing a Fisher market formulation to bridge planning and logging systems, where planned tasks are budget-constrained buyers and logged actions are divisible goods. The market incorporates text/structural/temporal signals, guarantees conservation and a junk filter, addresses convergence issues with a satiation-threshold fixed point, and introduces entropy regularization to improve robustness against affinity noise.
AI.motivation: Existing planning and organizational systems suffer from a fundamental disconnect: planned task effort budgets and logged action records drift apart over time. Current solutions use rigid all-or-nothing links that either miss genuinely related but unlinked effort or falsely report active goals as stalled. A more flexible, principled bridging mechanism is needed.
AI.method: The authors formulate the bridge as a quasi-linear Fisher market where: (1) planned tasks are budget-constrained buyers, (2) performed actions are divisible goods, and (3) a fused text/structural/temporal signal determines each buyer's valuation. Two market instruments (seller reserve price, buyer cash option) yield conservation, a hard budget cap, and a provable junk filter. A concave completion utility function discounts progress near plan completion, with convergence resolved via a satiation-threshold fixed point (Brouwer existence, local uniqueness under diagonal dominance). An entropy-regularized generalization unifies the sharp market equilibrium with entropy-regularized optimal transport, plus a noise-adaptive regularization rule.
AI.result: The satiation-threshold fixed point has guaranteed Brouwer existence and local uniqueness under an explicit diagonal-dominance condition, validated empirically on both random and adversarial instances. Benchmarking reveals the sharp equilibrium's zero-entropy nature is more sensitive to affinity noise than entropy-regularized optimal transport's smoothed alternative. The proposed entropy-regularized generalization with noise-adaptive regularization successfully resolves this sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: The Fisher market formulation provides a theoretically grounded, flexible bridge between planning and logging systems, with provable guarantees (conservation, budget cap, junk filter). The entropy-regularized extension unifies two previously separate approaches and addresses noise sensitivity. Results connect to multi-touch attribution, optimal transport, and online Fisher-market algorithms.

title: Attention Degradation, Function Token Anchoring, and the Limits of Attention-Based Intervention in Large Language Models
summary: Mean cross-positional attention degradation is widely reported in transformer interpretability, yet whether it causally limits contextual retrieval remains untested. We present six coordinated experiments across GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, OPT-1.3B, and distilgpt2. We first characterise short-term (5-100 token) attention degradation, finding a universal exponential-then-plateau pattern whose rate is inversely correlated with depth, with distinct layer-wise entropy signatures per architecture. Function token anchoring proves architecture-dependent: OPT-1.3B (absolute positional encoding) shows distance-dependent preposition specificity, GPT-2 shows uniform non-specific dependence, and LLaMA (RoPE) shows reversal at long distances. Strategic comma insertion at clause boundaries causally reduces prediction degradation in the 40-80 token range, with the benefit tied to syntactic boundary alignment rather than token density. We then test the mechanism causally: Relay-Aware Attention (RAA), which biases attention logits toward function token positions, verifiably increases attention mass by 16-24% yet yields null effects on GPT-2 and LLaMA-1B, preliminary harm on LLaMA-3B, and a mixed effect on OPT-1.3B that nets to approximately zero. Multi-fact retrieval probes further show that degradation rate does not predict retrieval accuracy across models. We conclude that mean attention degradation is largely descriptive rather than prescriptive: function tokens contribute through what their hidden states compute, not through the attention they receive -- with implications for interpretability methodology and attention-score-based inference optimisations such as KV-cache eviction.

AI.tldr: Mean attention degradation is a descriptive, not prescriptive, phenomenon: function tokens contribute to context retrieval through their hidden-state computations, not through the attention weights they receive, challenging attention-score-based interpretability and KV-cache eviction methods.
AI.motivation: While mean cross-positional attention degradation is widely reported in transformer interpretability literature, no prior work has causally tested whether this degradation actually limits contextual retrieval. The paper aims to bridge this gap by distinguishing between descriptive patterns of attention decay and their prescriptive consequences for model behavior.
AI.method: Six coordinated experiments across GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, OPT-1.3B, and distilgpt2: (1) characterization of short-term (5–100 token) attention degradation patterns with layer-wise entropy signatures; (2) analysis of function token anchoring across architectures with different positional encodings (absolute, RoPE); (3) causal intervention via strategic comma insertion at clause boundaries; (4) Relay-Aware Attention (RAA), which biases attention logits toward function token positions to causally manipulate attention mass; (5) multi-fact retrieval probes to relate degradation rate to retrieval accuracy.
AI.result: (1) Universal exponential-then-plateau attention degradation pattern with depth-inverse rate and architecture-specific layer-wise entropy signatures. (2) Function token anchoring is architecture-dependent: OPT-1.3B shows distance-dependent preposition specificity, GPT-2 shows uniform non-specific dependence, LLaMA (RoPE) shows reversal at long distances. (3) Comma insertion causally reduces prediction degradation in the 40–80 token range via syntactic boundary alignment. (4) RAA increases attention mass by 16–24% but yields null effects on GPT-2/LLaMA-1B, harms LLaMA-3B, and shows mixed net-zero effect on OPT-1.3B. (5) Degradation rate does not predict retrieval accuracy across models.
AI.conclusion: Mean attention degradation is largely descriptive rather than prescriptive. Function tokens contribute through hidden-state computations rather than received attention. This has implications for interpretability methodology and questions the validity of attention-score-based inference optimizations such as KV-cache eviction strategies.

title: CEDAR: Causal Edge Discovery for Autoregressive Processes
summary: We propose CEDAR (Causal Edge Discovery for Autoregressive Processes), a constraint-based method for lagged causal edge discovery in sparse autoregressive time series. CEDAR screens candidate cross-variable lags using AR(1)-residualized, U-centered distance correlation, then applies two targeted conditional-independence tests per significant cross-variable lag candidate and accepts at most one lag per ordered pair. A stable MCI pruning step removes indirect edges, and optional deterministic C-nodes adjust for specified trend-like nonstationarity. In sparse regimes where few lags survive screening, CEDAR requires $O(d^2)$ CI tests after screening while retaining edge-level interpretability. CEDAR is most effective when data are scarce and variables exhibit lag-1 self-dynamics; methods with richer conditioning sets become preferable as $T$ grows or when higher-order autoregressive or simultaneous multi-lag effects are common.

AI.tldr: CEDAR is a constraint-based method for discovering lagged causal edges in sparse autoregressive time series. It uses distance correlation screening followed by two targeted conditional independence tests per candidate edge, plus MCI pruning and optional C-nodes for nonstationarity. It is O(d²) efficient post-screening and excels in low-data regimes with lag-1 self-dynamics.
AI.motivation: Existing causal discovery methods for time series either require too many conditional independence tests (scaling poorly with dimensionality) or lack rigorous false-positive control in sparse, high-dimensional settings with limited data. There is a need for a method that balances computational efficiency with statistical rigor, particularly when variables exhibit dominant lag-1 autoregressive dynamics and cross-variable causal effects are sparse.
AI.method: CEDAR proceeds in four stages: (1) Screening: For each ordered pair of variables, it uses AR(1)-residualized, U-centered distance correlation to identify candidate cross-variable lags, filtering out most irrelevancies early. (2) Targeted CI testing: For each surviving candidate, two conditional independence tests are applied, and at most one lag per ordered pair is accepted. (3) MCI pruning: A stable Momentary Conditional Independence step removes indirect edges. (4) Optional C-nodes: Deterministic conditioning nodes can be incorporated to adjust for trend-like nonstationarity.
AI.result: In sparse settings where few lags pass the screening stage, CEDAR requires only O(d²) conditional independence tests after screening while preserving edge-level interpretability. It is most effective when sample size T is small and variables show strong lag-1 self-dynamics. As T grows or when higher-order autoregressive or simultaneous multi-lag effects are prevalent, methods with richer conditioning sets become preferable.
AI.conclusion: CEDAR fills a niche in the causal discovery landscape: sparse, low-T autoregressive settings where lag-1 self-dynamics dominate. Its staged screening plus targeted testing design achieves computational tractability without sacrificing the interpretability of individual edge decisions, though its assumptions limit applicability when richer temporal dynamics are present.

title: Autonomous disproofs of the sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$ with GPT-5.5 Pro
summary: OpenAI's recent disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture marked a milestone for AI in mathematics. It also inspired another breakthrough: a human disproof of the Erdős--Szemerédi sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$. In this paper, we present a simple agent built on GPT-5.5 Pro. Using a problem-agnostic, three-stage prompting pipeline -- proof-plan proposal, proof construction, and review -- the agent autonomously generated correct proofs that the sum-product conjecture is false over $\mathbb R$ in 7 of 8 independent trials; in the remaining trial, it identified an unresolved gap in its argument. The seven proofs are diverse: some are close to existing unit-based constructions, while others avoid units by using $L^p$-type regions of algebraic integers. The system used an average of 132.4k reasoning tokens per trial. We release the code, intermediate outputs, and generated proofs, providing a reproducible, data-contamination-free case study in autonomous proof generation.

AI.tldr: An autonomous agent built on GPT-5.5 Pro, using a three-stage prompting pipeline, generated correct disproofs of the Erdős–Szemerédi sum-product conjecture over ℝ in 7 out of 8 independent trials, producing diverse proofs including both unit-based and novel L^p-type algebraic integer constructions.
AI.motivation: Inspired by OpenAI's recent AI-driven disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture, the authors aim to demonstrate that large language models can autonomously generate novel, correct mathematical proofs — specifically targeting the Erdős–Szemerédi sum-product conjecture over the reals — in a reproducible and contamination-free manner.
AI.method: The system employs a problem-agnostic, three-stage prompting pipeline: (1) proof-plan proposal, (2) proof construction, and (3) review. The agent, built on GPT-5.5 Pro, was run for 8 independent trials, averaging 132.4k reasoning tokens per trial. No problem-specific tuning was used.
AI.result: In 7 of 8 trials, the agent produced correct proofs that the sum-product conjecture is false over ℝ. The remaining trial identified an unresolved gap in its argument. The generated proofs are diverse: some resemble existing unit-based constructions, while others avoid units by using L^p-type regions of algebraic integers.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a reproducible case study in autonomous proof generation, demonstrating that state-of-the-art LLMs can independently discover valid, diverse mathematical disproofs. The authors release code, intermediate outputs, and proofs to ensure transparency and data-contamination-free verification.

title: From a Word-Level Dictionary to Sentence-Level Semantics: Multilingual Grievance Labelling with Contextual Models
summary: Grievance is one of the warning signs analysts look for when assessing threats of violence. It is increasingly measured at scale from online text, most often with word-level lexicons like the Grievance Dictionary that score by matching weighted terms. Such matching is a fast and transparent proxy, but it cannot resolve whether a term is asserted, quoted, negated, or condemned. These lexicons are also often evaluated on pools enriched with the very examples they retrieve, so a high score partly reflects agreement with the lexicon's own selection rule. Examining a five-language, 2{,}000-item evaluation pool, we find its halves separated almost perfectly by the lexicon itself: every item labeled ``random'' is in fact lexicon-negative, so the lexicon's apparent macro-AUROC of 0.686 collapses to a 0.500 floor fixed by construction. We keep the dictionary's 22-construct ontology but replace term matching with context-reading models, evaluated on a non-circular benchmark that separates unconditional-random, lexicon-positive, and lexicon-negative strata across five languages. Reading the full post rather than the target sentence alone helps most where the lexicon is silent, raising average precision on lexicon-negative text from 0.14 to 0.20, with the largest gains on quoted, implicit, and cross-sentence grievance. Together, these results show that grievance is measured more faithfully by reading the surrounding context, and more honestly when tested on text the lexicon did not select. We release our code and benchmark at https://github.com/behavioral-ds/multilingual_grievance.

AI.tldr: Lexicon-based grievance detection suffers from circular evaluation and inability to resolve linguistic context (negation, quotation, implicitness). Using a stratified, non-circular benchmark across five languages, the authors show that context-reading models outperform term-matching lexicons, especially on lexicon-negative text, and that standard evaluation practices inflate apparent performance.
AI.motivation: Grievance detection from online text is critical for violence threat assessment, but existing approaches rely on word-level lexicons (like the Grievance Dictionary) that cannot handle assertion, quotation, negation, or condemnation. Furthermore, standard evaluation pools are constructed by retrieving lexicon-matched examples, creating circularity that artificially inflates performance metrics. The authors aim to expose this circularity and demonstrate that context-aware models yield more faithful measurement.
AI.method: The authors construct a 2,000-item, five-language evaluation pool stratified into three non-overlapping strata: unconditional-random, lexicon-positive, and lexicon-negative. They retain the Grievance Dictionary's 22-construct ontology but replace term matching with context-reading models (transformer-based). The key experimental manipulation is comparing sentence-only vs. full-post context, with evaluation on a non-circular benchmark that prevents lexicon-selection bias from contaminating test data.
AI.result: The lexicon's apparent macro-AUROC of 0.686 collapses to a 0.500 floor under non-circular evaluation, as every "random" item was lexicon-negative by construction. Context-reading models raise average precision on lexicon-negative text from 0.14 to 0.20, with the largest gains on quoted, implicit, and cross-sentence grievance. Reading the full post rather than only the target sentence consistently improves detection where the lexicon is silent.
AI.conclusion: Grievance is measured more faithfully by models that read surrounding context, and more honestly when evaluated on text the lexicon did not select. The work highlights a fundamental methodological flaw in lexicon-based grievance detection and provides a corrected benchmark and codebase for future research.

title: Perspective Latents as an Architectural Condition for Causal Emergence in Active Inference Agents
summary: A recent line of work measures causal emergence in reinforcement learning agents through Integrated Information Decomposition, reporting that $Φ_r$ grows with training and tracks reward improvement. For active inference, this raises the question of how reward-free predictive organization relates to such information-theoretic signatures. I test this within an active inference agent whose architecture separates a fast perception latent $z$ from a slow global latent $g$, where $g$ is driven by prediction error and structurally decoupled from policy gradients. In a reward-free environmental regime-switching protocol, $Φ_r$ concentrates in $g$; its aggregate magnitude is largely architectural and decreases with training. The substantive effect of learning becomes legible only at the atom-compositional level: decoupling flips sign from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant under environmental change, while downward causation carries the regime-dependent adjustment. These results identify $g$ as the architectural locus of $Φ_r$-relevant temporal organization in an active inference agent, and argue against reading scalar $Φ_r$ as a direct index of learned integration.

AI.tldr: An active inference agent with separated latent variables (fast \(z\), slow \(g\)) is studied under reward-free regime-switching. Integrated information decomposition (\(Φ_r\)) concentrates in \(g\), but its magnitude is largely architectural and decreases with training. At the atom-compositional level, decoupling flips from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant, while downward causation adjusts with regime. Scalar \(Φ_r\) is not a direct index of learned integration.
AI.motivation: Prior work shows \(Φ_r\) grows with training in RL agents, correlating with reward. The author asks whether similar information-theoretic signatures emerge in reward-free active inference, and how architectural decoupling of latent variables shapes causal emergence measured by integrated information decomposition.
AI.method: An active inference agent is constructed with two latent levels: a fast perception latent \(z\) and a slow global latent \(g\), where \(g\) is driven purely by prediction error and structurally decoupled from policy gradients. The agent operates under a reward-free environmental regime-switching protocol. Integrated Information Decomposition (\(Φ_r\)) is computed and analyzed at both aggregate and atom-compositional levels, tracking decoupling and downward causation across training and regime changes.
AI.result: \(Φ_r\) concentrates in the \(g\) latent. Its aggregate magnitude is largely architectural and decreases with training. At the atomic level, decoupling flips from negative to positive with learning and becomes invariant to regime switches, while downward causation carries regime-dependent adjustments. Scalar \(Φ_r\) does not directly track learned integration.
AI.conclusion: The slow global latent \(g\) is the architectural locus of \(Φ_r\)-relevant temporal organization in active inference agents. Scalar \(Φ_r\) should not be interpreted as a direct index of learned integration; only atom-compositional analysis reveals the substantive effects of learning, which manifest as a sign flip in decoupling and its regime-invariance.

title: ConfidenceBench: Evaluating Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in settings where fluent but incorrect answers can be costly. In these settings, accuracy alone is insufficient: models must also know when they are likely to be wrong. We present ConfidenceBench, a calibration benchmark that evaluates verbalized confidence estimates in 15 frontier LLMs using the Brier score, a proper scoring rule that incentivises truthful probability reporting. Confidence is elicited via prompting, requiring no access to model logits and making the framework applicable to both closed-source and open-source systems. The benchmark comprises 200 private multiple-choice questions across four categories: spatial reasoning, high-precision mathematics, word lookup, and unknowable questions. Across three independent runs, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve the lowest Brier scores, both reported as 0.103. Both substantially outperform the calibrated-random baseline of 0.1875, while Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite scores 0.367, indicating severe miscalibration. Accuracy and calibration diverge substantially across model families: the most accurate model is not the best-calibrated, and several models perform worse than the calibrated-random Brier baseline despite reasonable accuracy. These results show that verbalized confidence calibration is a distinct and practically important axis of LLM reliability, complementary to standard accuracy-based evaluation.

AI.tldr: ConfidenceBench evaluates verbalized confidence calibration in 15 frontier LLMs using the Brier score on 200 private multiple-choice questions across four categories. Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview tie for best calibration (Brier score 0.103), substantially outperforming the calibrated-random baseline (0.1875). Accuracy and calibration diverge: the most accurate model is not the best-calibrated, establishing verbalized confidence as a distinct, practically important axis of LLM reliability.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings where fluent but incorrect answers are costly. In such contexts, accuracy alone is insufficient — models must also reliably estimate when they are likely to be wrong. The authors argue that verbalized confidence calibration is a neglected but critical dimension of LLM reliability, complementary to standard accuracy benchmarks.
AI.method: The authors introduce ConfidenceBench, a calibration benchmark comprising 200 private multiple-choice questions across four categories: spatial reasoning, high-precision mathematics, word lookup, and unknowable questions. Confidence is elicited purely via prompting (no logit access required), making it applicable to both closed-source and open-source models. Calibration is measured using the Brier score, a proper scoring rule that incentivizes truthful probability reporting. Fifteen frontier LLMs are evaluated across three independent runs.
AI.result: Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve the lowest Brier scores (0.103), substantially outperforming the calibrated-random baseline of 0.1875. In contrast, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite scores 0.367, indicating severe miscalibration. Critically, accuracy and calibration diverge across model families: the most accurate model is not the best-calibrated, and several models perform worse than the calibrated-random baseline despite having reasonable accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Verbalized confidence calibration constitutes a distinct and practically important axis of LLM reliability, orthogonal to standard accuracy metrics. The authors recommend that calibration be routinely evaluated alongside accuracy, particularly for models deployed in cost-sensitive or safety-critical applications.

title: Where Animacy Lives in Large Language Models: Tracing the Circuits of the Animacy Concept
summary: Distinguishing animate from inanimate concepts in written language requires more than shallow text processing, as it involves recognizing complex selectional constraints and contextual cues, such as verb-argument interactions. Yet, current large language models (LLMs) appear to be capable of doing it. We investigate whether this animacy-sensitive behavior of LLMs can be traced to a localized set of causally relevant components and connections. To do so, we construct a controlled dataset of minimal pairs and perform circuit discovery on four open-weight models. Through in-depth experiments and ablations, we show that a causal mechanism responsible for handling animacy in these models does exist, thus discovering an animacy circuit. At the same time, this circuit appears to be less localized compared to other known ones and generalizes only partially across models and animacy tasks, confirming the distributed, context-dependent, and somewhat graded nature of the animacy concept.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether LLMs possess a localized, causally relevant "animacy circuit" for distinguishing animate from inanimate concepts. Using minimal pair datasets and circuit discovery on four open-weight models, the authors find a causal mechanism exists but is less localized than other known circuits, generalizes only partially across models and tasks, and exhibits distributed, context-dependent, graded properties.
AI.motivation: Distinguishing animate from inanimate concepts requires complex linguistic reasoning (e.g., verb-argument selectional constraints) beyond shallow text processing. While LLMs appear capable of this, it is unknown whether this animacy-sensitive behavior can be traced to a localized set of causally relevant components—similar to circuits discovered for other linguistic phenomena.
AI.method: The authors construct a controlled dataset of minimal pairs targeting animacy distinctions and perform circuit discovery (a mechanistic interpretability technique) on four open-weight models. They conduct in-depth experiments and causal ablations to identify components and connections causally responsible for animacy processing.
AI.result: A causal mechanism for animacy handling does exist—an "animacy circuit." However, compared to other known circuits, it is less localized, generalizes only partially across different models and animacy tasks, and exhibits a distributed, context-dependent, and graded nature.
AI.conclusion: Animacy in LLMs is subserved by a genuine but diffuse causal circuit, confirming that the animacy concept is not sharply localized but rather distributed, context-dependent, and graded—mirroring its nuanced linguistic nature.
