title: LLMs Get Lost in Evolving User Intent
summary: As LLMs become more capable, they are increasingly deployed as collaborative agents, taking on user-delegated tasks through iterative interaction. Yet genuine interaction is inherently dynamic: users rarely specify their intent upfront, instead disclosing, revising, and reshaping it as the conversation unfolds. Despite this, LLMs are still predominantly evaluated or trained in single-turn, fully-specified settings, leaving open a fundamental question: how well do LLMs track and act on user intent as it evolves over the course of a conversation? To study this, we introduce a framework that transforms static, single-turn tasks into dynamic multi-turn conversations in which the user's intent evolves across turns--incrementally revealed, revised, and at times redirected mid-conversation--while preserving each task's original evaluation protocol, enabling existing benchmarks to be reused as controlled testbeds without new annotation. Across multiple tasks, we surface a consistent phenomenon: strong static-setting performance does not transfer to the evolving-intent setting, with substantial drops across model families. Our findings point to a fundamental gap: today's LLMs do not yet faithfully track and act on the user's evolving intent, a capability invisible to static evaluation yet critical for future collaborative agents.

AI.tldr: Static single-turn LLM benchmarks fail to capture the dynamic nature of real user interaction where intent evolves over a conversation. The authors introduce a framework converting static tasks into multi-turn conversations with evolving intent, revealing that strong static performance does not transfer — exposing a critical gap in LLMs' ability to track and act on shifting user intent.
AI.motivation: Real user-LLM interaction is inherently dynamic: users disclose, revise, and reshape intent across conversational turns. However, LLMs are predominantly evaluated and trained in single-turn, fully-specified settings. This creates a blind spot: we lack understanding of how well LLMs track evolving user intent, a capability essential for collaborative agents deployed in real-world iterative interactions.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework that algorithmically transforms existing static, single-turn benchmark tasks into dynamic multi-turn conversations. In these conversations, user intent evolves across turns — incrementally revealed, revised, or redirected mid-conversation — while preserving each task's original evaluation protocol. This allows existing benchmarks to be reused as controlled testbeds without requiring new human annotation.
AI.result: Across multiple tasks and model families, the authors find a consistent phenomenon: strong performance in static settings drops substantially in the evolving-intent setting, indicating that static evaluation is a poor proxy for dynamic conversational capability.
AI.conclusion: There is a fundamental gap: today's LLMs do not faithfully track and act on evolving user intent. This capability is invisible to static evaluation yet critical for building future collaborative agents. The proposed framework offers a reusable method for diagnosing and benchmarking this shortcoming.

title: Evaluating and Guarding Citation Faithfulness in Agentic Scientific Synthesis
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures. Includes supplementary material (Appendices S1-S6). Open single-GPU reproducibility kit included
summary:
Agentic LLM systems such as OpenScholar and PaperQA2 read the scientific literature and return cited answers, and both they and their benchmarks already check whether those citations hold, with a fixed attribution model or human graders. Neither audits the reliability of that check itself. We show it is not reliable, and that this matters. On identical agent outputs the measured unsupported-citation rate ranges from about 3% to about 18% depending only on the verifier's strictness, and although verifiers agree on which citations are supported, they disagree on which to flag (negative-specific agreement 0.27 to 0.30), so no single flag set is trustworthy and cross-paper comparison is invalid without a named verifier and protocol.
  We present a gold-anchored evaluation protocol and a deployable guard that make this behavior measurable and bounded. The protocol validates the verifier, measures re-attribution, and calibrates a guarantee against human gold rather than another model's verdict; the verifier is a swappable instrument chosen on cost (recall 0.94 on the supported class, held out), and re-attribution is a commodity step where a deterministic BM25 matches the best open generator. The guard adds a split-conformal layer placing a distribution-free, finite-sample bound on truly unsupported citations that slip past a chosen flagging rule, a guarantee on catch rate rather than conclusion correctness. The bound holds on held-out gold, and we identify and quantify the condition governing its transfer to deployment, calibration-negative difficulty, with a concrete recalibration recipe, left untested by prior conformal-factuality work.
  Validated across four open 27-35B models and three agentic pipelines on public benchmarks (SciFact, QASA, PubMedQA), with confidence intervals on every headline number, the protocol and guard ship as an open single-GPU kit.

AI.tldr: Current LLM-based scientific literature agents check citation support, but the verifiers themselves are unreliable—measured unsupported-citation rates swing from 3% to 18% depending on verifier strictness, with poor agreement on which citations to flag. The authors propose a gold-anchored evaluation protocol and a split-conformal guard that yields distribution-free, finite-sample guarantees on catch rate, validated across multiple models and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic LLM systems for scientific literature (e.g., OpenScholar, PaperQA2) and their benchmarks rely on citation verification—either automated or by human graders—but none audit the reliability of the verification step itself. The authors demonstrate this verification is unreliable: measured unsupported-citation rates vary dramatically with verifier strictness, and verifiers disagree on which specific citations to flag (negative-specific agreement only 0.27–0.30), making cross-paper comparisons invalid and single flag sets untrustworthy.
AI.method: The paper introduces two components: (1) a gold-anchored evaluation protocol that validates the verifier, measures re-attribution, and calibrates guarantees against human gold annotations rather than another model's output—re-attribution uses deterministic BM25 matching the best open generator; (2) a deployable guard based on split-conformal prediction that provides a distribution-free, finite-sample bound on truly unsupported citations slipping past a chosen flagging rule. The bound guarantees catch rate (not conclusion correctness), holds on held-out gold, and includes a recalibration recipe for deployment shift via calibration-negative difficulty.
AI.result: On identical agent outputs, unsupported-citation rates ranged from ~3% to ~18% purely due to verifier strictness. Negative-specific agreement among verifiers was only 0.27–0.30. The BM25 re-attribution matched the best open generator's performance. The split-conformal bound held on held-out gold. Validation spanned four open 27-35B models and three agentic pipelines across SciFact, QASA, and PubMedQA benchmarks, with confidence intervals on all headline numbers.
AI.conclusion: Citation verification in agentic LLM systems is unreliable and must itself be audited. The proposed gold-anchored protocol and split-conformal guard make this behavior measurable and bounded, enabling trustworthy deployment. The complete system ships as an open-source single-GPU kit.

title: CultureTalk-ID: A Multi-Task Dialogue Benchmark for Cultural Commonsense in Indonesian Local Languages
summary: Culture is lived through conversation, yet existing Indonesian cultural commonsense benchmarks evaluate LLMs on short and isolated prompts, stripping away the dialogic context in which cultural nuances actually surface. We introduce CultureTalk-ID, the first dialogue-based benchmark for cultural commonsense in Indonesian and its local languages, comprising 4,496 culturally grounded dialogues across 11 languages and 13 culturally salient topics, curated through a multi-stage human pipeline with native speakers to ensure authenticity. CultureTalk-ID introduces three complementary tasks, namely dialogue-based multiple-choice cultural commonsense reasoning, culturally faithful machine translation, and language steering, which jointly probe whether LLMs can understand, transfer, and generate culturally grounded language.

AI.tldr: CultureTalk-ID is a dialogue-based benchmark for evaluating cultural commonsense in Indonesian and 11 local languages, featuring 4,496 dialogues across 13 cultural topics and three tasks: reasoning, translation, and language steering.
AI.motivation: Existing Indonesian cultural commonsense benchmarks evaluate LLMs using short, isolated prompts that ignore the dialogic context where cultural nuances naturally emerge. There is a need for a benchmark that captures cultural understanding within conversational settings.
AI.method: The authors constructed CultureTalk-ID using a multi-stage human annotation pipeline with native speakers, producing 4,496 culturally grounded dialogues spanning 11 languages and 13 culturally salient topics. They defined three complementary evaluation tasks: (1) dialogue-based multiple-choice cultural commonsense reasoning, (2) culturally faithful machine translation, and (3) language steering, which jointly assess understanding, transfer, and generation of culturally grounded language.
AI.result: The paper introduces the benchmark and its construction methodology; specific experimental results on LLM performance are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: CultureTalk-ID provides a first-of-its-kind resource for evaluating whether LLMs can understand, transfer, and generate culturally grounded Indonesian language in realistic conversational contexts, addressing a critical gap in multilingual and multicultural NLP evaluation.

title: PromptPack: Scaling LLM Annotation Agents for Online Recommendation
summary: Online recommendation platforms increasingly use Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract structured features from ad creatives. While deploying a single-call LLM annotation agent yields significant Click-Through Rate (CTR) improvements in our live production environment, per-creative prompting is prohibitively expensive to scale. The redundant system instructions sent in every request account for 94% of billed input tokens. To break this cost bottleneck, we introduce PromptPack, a scalable, high-throughput LLM annotation agent. PromptPack achieves this scale via in-context batching, combining a shared system prompt, a strict XML structural envelope, and an output correction layer to ensure deterministic, pipeline-ready feature extraction across multiple creatives simultaneously. We evaluate PromptPack via an offline retrieval benchmark using a downstream logistic-regression ranker. To deeply profile the agent's behavior, we measure AUC and introduce Volume-Weighted Absolute Lift (VWAL), a novel metric capturing the signal quality of the generated features. Compared to our live, unbatched production baseline, PromptPack at batch size 20 cuts our LLM costs by 89% and accelerates throughput by 2.5x while fully preserving AUC.

AI.tldr: PromptPack is a batched LLM annotation system that cuts costs by 89% and boosts throughput 2.5× by sharing system prompts and using structured XML output, all while preserving downstream CTR ranking performance.
AI.motivation: Single-call LLM annotation for ad creative feature extraction is effective for CTR prediction but prohibitively expensive: per-creative prompts waste 94% of input tokens on redundant system instructions, making scaling infeasible in production.
AI.method: PromptPack uses in-context batching with three components: (1) a shared system prompt sent once per batch, (2) a strict XML structural envelope for deterministic multi-creative output parsing, and (3) an output correction layer to ensure pipeline-ready features. A logistic-regression ranker evaluates extracted features via offline retrieval. The paper also introduces Volume-Weighted Absolute Lift (VWAL) as a novel metric for signal quality.
AI.result: At batch size 20, PromptPack reduces LLM costs by 89%, increases throughput by 2.5×, and fully preserves AUC compared to the unbatched production baseline.
AI.conclusion: In-context batching with structured output enforcement is a practical, cost-effective strategy for scaling LLM-based feature extraction in industrial recommendation systems without sacrificing downstream model quality.

title: Sample-Efficient Learning from Agent Experience
summary: Real-world agent learning is often constrained by costly environment interactions, such as running time-consuming experiments or obtaining human feedback. In-context learning offers a highly sample-efficient way for agents to learn from their own interaction histories, but its gains disappear once that experience is removed from the context. Separately, context distillation provides a mechanism for internalizing contextual information into model weights. However, applying it to agents' interaction histories without sacrificing environment sample efficiency remains underexplored. We term this problem Experience Distillation and develop an implementation that requires no further environment interaction beyond the collected experience. Experiments on 749 curated software-engineering tasks and six text-adventure games show that it retains at least 64.8\% of the gains from in-context learning across both domains, whereas direct supervised fine-tuning on the collected experience recovers only 3.8\%. Compared with classical reinforcement-learning baselines, in-context learning from trial-and-error experience followed by Experience Distillation matches their performance with at least \(9.6\times\) fewer environment samples.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses "Experience Distillation," a method for internalizing agents' interaction histories into model weights without requiring additional environment interactions. It retains 64.8% of in-context learning gains versus only 3.8% for direct supervised fine-tuning, and matches RL baselines with at least 9.6× fewer environment samples.
AI.motivation: In-context learning (ICL) enables sample-efficient learning from interaction history but loses all benefits once context is removed. Context distillation can internalize context into weights, but applying it to agent experiences without sacrificing sample efficiency is underexplored. The authors aim to bridge this gap.
AI.method: The authors propose Experience Distillation, which distills an agent's collected interaction history (trial-and-error experiences) into model weights without requiring further environment samples. This contrasts with direct supervised fine-tuning on the same collected experience.
AI.result: On 749 software-engineering tasks and six text-adventure games, Experience Distillation retains at least 64.8% of ICL gains, while direct SFT recovers only 3.8%. Compared to classical RL baselines, ICL followed by Experience Distillation matches their performance with ≥9.6× fewer environment samples.
AI.conclusion: Experience Distillation effectively preserves the benefits of in-context learning in model weights without extra environment interaction, offering a sample-efficient alternative to both pure ICL and classical reinforcement learning for agent training.

title: Adaptive Confidence-weighted Expansion for Trustworthy Multi-Omics Multimodal Fusion
comment: Accepted for publication in the proceedings of the International Conference on Pattern Recognition (ICPR 2026)
summary: Multimodal learning is a robust approach to improve predictive performance in applications such as medical prognosis. However, the clinical applicability of models that use multimodal learning is hampered by their poor performance under noisy or uninformative data streams. Present fusion approaches often lack robust mechanisms for the dynamic assessment of data quality and for the provision of a trustable confidence score on the final prediction. This dissuades their deployment in safety-critical settings. To address these limitations, we introduce Adaptive Confidence-weighted Expansion (ACE), a novel framework to enhance the trustworthiness of multimodal fusion models. ACE first enhances the multimodal space by generating new, complementary modalities from intra-modality correlations. It then employs a dual-level confidence mechanism that (1) adaptively reweighs all modalities by their reliability before fusion and (2) estimates a global trust score over the fused, final decision. To evaluate ACE, we used four challenging multi-omics datasets (BRCA, KIPAN, LGG, and ROSMAP). ACE significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms in both classification performance and confidence calibration. Our framework provides a more stable and robust data fusion method that facilitates the use of multimodal learning in addressing high-stakes problems.

AI.tldr: ACE is a multimodal fusion framework that improves trustworthiness by generating complementary modalities and employing dual-level confidence mechanisms (adaptive reweighting + global trust scoring), outperforming SOTA on four multi-omics datasets in both accuracy and calibration.
AI.motivation: Multimodal learning improves medical prognosis but suffers under noisy/uninformative data streams. Existing fusion methods lack dynamic data quality assessment and reliable confidence scores, making them unsuitable for safety-critical clinical deployment.
AI.method: ACE operates in two stages: (1) modality expansion — generating new complementary modalities from intra-modality correlations to enrich the multimodal space; (2) dual-level confidence — adaptively reweighting each modality by its reliability before fusion, then computing a global trust score over the fused decision for overall prediction confidence.
AI.result: Evaluated on four multi-omics datasets (BRCA, KIPAN, LGG, ROSMAP), ACE significantly outperformed state-of-the-art algorithms in both classification performance and confidence calibration.
AI.conclusion: ACE provides a more stable and robust data fusion method that enables safer deployment of multimodal learning in high-stakes clinical applications by ensuring reliable predictions with well-calibrated confidence estimates.

title: DynamicMCPBench: A Trace-Grounded, Effect-Scored Benchmark for LLM Agents over Live MCP Servers
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed over Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, yet the benchmarks used to evaluate them score the final answer or a fixed "ground-truth" list of tools, both of which are fragile once the underlying data is live and stateful. We present DynamicMCPBench, a reusable framework rather than a fixed dataset. A practitioner can run it on their own MCP servers to test models on their own tasks, or let it collect servers automatically to measure a model's general ability to solve agentic tasks. Given the servers and any set of models, it generates realistic goals, pursues each one live to record a successful trajectory, distills that trajectory into path-agnostic effect checkpoints, and scores an agent on whether it reproduces those effects, never on the final answer. To show what the framework reveals, we run it at scale: 24 models over 121 servers and 750 tasks spread evenly over 15 task categories (50 each), where each category targets a distinct tool-use challenge of the generated questions. Each task is scored by pass^3: it counts as solved only if all three independent attempts succeed. Even the strongest agents solve only about half of the tasks, 31% of tasks are solved by no model at all, and accuracy collapses as the required tool chain grows longer (from 39% on the shortest chains to 13% on the longest). A human validation study confirms the automatic scoring is reliable (chance-corrected agreement of 0.76). DynamicMCPBench thus turns benchmark construction into something practitioners can rerun on their own servers and models, while exposing a consistent inability of current agents to handle long, multi-step agentic tasks.

AI.tldr: DynamicMCPBench is a reusable, live benchmarking framework for LLM agents operating over MCP servers. Instead of scoring fixed ground-truth answers, it generates tasks, records successful trajectories, distills them into path-agnostic effect checkpoints, and scores agents on whether they reproduce those effects. At scale (24 models, 121 servers, 750 tasks across 15 categories), even the strongest agents solve only ~50% of tasks, 31% remain unsolved by any model, and accuracy drops sharply with longer tool chains (39% → 13%).
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM agents over MCP servers evaluate final answers or fixed tool-call lists, both of which become fragile and unreliable when underlying server data is live and stateful. There is a need for a reusable, self-contained evaluation framework that practitioners can run on their own servers with their own tasks, and that scores agents based on reproducible effects rather than brittle answer matching.
AI.method: DynamicMCPBench is a framework, not a fixed dataset. Given MCP servers and models, it: (1) generates realistic goals using an LLM, (2) pursues each goal live to record a successful trajectory, (3) distills that trajectory into path-agnostic effect checkpoints (observable state changes), and (4) scores an agent by whether it reproduces those effects, not the final answer. Scoring uses pass³ (all three independent attempts must succeed). The framework was run at scale across 24 models, 121 servers, 750 tasks (50 per category × 15 categories), where each category targets a distinct tool-use challenge. Human validation assessed scoring reliability (chance-corrected agreement: 0.76).
AI.result: Even the strongest agents solve only ~50% of tasks. 31% of tasks are solved by no model at all. Accuracy declines sharply as required tool-chain length increases: from 39% on the shortest chains to 13% on the longest. Human validation confirmed automatic scoring is reliable (chance-corrected agreement of 0.76).
AI.conclusion: DynamicMCPBench transforms benchmark construction into a process practitioners can rerun on their own servers and models, while exposing a consistent inability of current LLM agents to handle long, multi-step agentic tasks. The framework's effect-based, path-agnostic scoring and pass³ metric provide a more robust evaluation paradigm than answer-matching approaches.

title: GaugeQuant: Online Learning of Quantization-Optimal Bases from LLM Symmetries
summary: Transformers are known to have internal continuous symmetries that leave outputs invariant, while modifying quantization. GaugeQuant leverages this in-training by introducing a LogSumExp term to the loss that breaks the symmetries, thus selecting a basis that minimizes activation outliers. A stop-gradient operator ensures that only rotation matrices are updated, yielding the language modeling objective completely unaltered. Our requires no specific calibration data, no quantization simulation, and adds negligible training overhead. With the LLaMA-2 7B model under W4A4 quantization with group size 128, perplexity drops from 8.22 to 6.73, competing with post-training methods that require frozen models and calibration datasets. Under W4A16, perplexity drops from 11.16 to 5.45. Code is available at https://github.com/MPedraBento/gauge-quant.

AI.tldr: GaugeQuant leverages internal continuous symmetries of Transformers to select a basis that minimizes activation outliers during training, using a LogSumExp regularizer with stop-gradient, achieving significant perplexity improvements under low-bit quantization without calibration data or quantization simulation.
AI.motivation: Transformers possess internal continuous symmetries that leave outputs invariant but affect quantization behavior. Existing quantization methods typically require post-training calibration on frozen models. GaugeQuant aims to exploit these symmetries during training to inherently produce models more amenable to quantization, eliminating the need for calibration data or quantization-aware training.
AI.method: GaugeQuant introduces a LogSumExp regularization term added to the standard language modeling loss that breaks the continuous symmetries of the Transformer. A stop-gradient operator ensures that only rotation matrices (gauge transformations) are updated by this regularizer, leaving the forward pass and the original LM objective completely unaltered. This selects a basis that minimizes activation outliers during training, with negligible overhead and no quantization simulation.
AI.result: On LLaMA-2 7B: W4A4 quantization (group size 128) perplexity improved from 8.22 to 6.73; W4A16 quantization perplexity improved from 11.16 to 5.45. The method competes with post-training quantization methods that require frozen models and calibration datasets.
AI.conclusion: GaugeQuant demonstrates that in-training gauge-fixing via symmetry-breaking regularization is an effective and efficient alternative to post-training quantization methods, achieving strong perplexity recovery under aggressive quantization regimes with minimal training overhead and no calibration data.

title: PrefReward: Learning User Preference Matrix for Personalized Text Generation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable ability in generating personalized content by leveraging user histories and contextual cues. However, most existing personalization approaches rely on implicit representations within model parameters, making it difficult to interpret user-specific preferences or effectively handle long-context dependencies. To address these challenges, we propose PrefReward, a novel preference-aware generative framework that explicitly models user styles through a structured preference matrix and integrates it into the decoding process as a reward signal. PrefReward consists of two stages: (1) extracting a user-specific preference matrix that summarizes individual stylistic tendencies, and (2) using the matrix to guide generation via a KL-divergence-based reward function. Experiments on the LongLaMP dataset show that PrefReward outperforms non-personalized and retrieval-based baselines in both generation quality and personalization interpretability.

AI.tldr: PrefReward is a two-stage framework that explicitly models user stylistic preferences via a structured preference matrix and guides LLM decoding with a KL-divergence-based reward signal, outperforming baselines on generation quality and interpretability.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM personalization approaches rely on implicit preference representations within model parameters, which lack interpretability and struggle with long-context dependencies. There is a need for explicit, interpretable user preference modeling that can effectively guide personalized generation.
AI.method: PrefReward consists of two stages: (1) Extraction of a user-specific structured preference matrix that summarizes individual stylistic tendencies from user history; (2) Integration of this matrix into the decoding process as a reward signal using a KL-divergence-based reward function to guide generation toward user-aligned outputs.
AI.result: On the LongLaMP dataset, PrefReward outperforms both non-personalized and retrieval-based baselines in terms of generation quality and personalization interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Explicit preference modeling via a structured matrix combined with reward-guided decoding offers a promising direction for interpretable, high-quality personalized text generation with LLMs.

title: Memory-Computation Tradeoffs in Semi Amortized Parametric Optimization
summary: Learning-enabled decision systems often use offline data or computation to reduce online compute cost. Despite the empirical success of such approaches, there is limited general understanding of how much offline information is needed to achieve a desired accuracy under a fixed online computation budget. We study this question through the lens of amortized parametric optimization: an offline phase stores a finite memory of solved problem instances, and an online phase produces a solution to a new instance by retrieving a warm start and applying $K$ steps of projected gradient descent. We analyze this setup for smooth convex parametric optimization over a compact domain, using a nonparametric predictor built from the stored offline solutions. For $μ$-strongly convex objectives, we establish matching upper and lower bounds on the memory required to guarantee $\varepsilon$-accuracy under a fixed online iteration budget $K$. For convex objectives satisfying a $β$-growth condition ($β>2$), we obtain near-matching bounds and identify a phase transition in $K$ beyond which additional memory provides no benefit. We further provide a general proof framework that (i) explicitly quantifies the memory cost of acceleration---how much offline memory is required to achieve a prescribed speedup over the unaided online optimizer---and (ii) identifies two key quantities driving this cost: the convergence rate of the online optimizer and the Lipschitz sensitivity of the solution map to the problem parameter. Experiments on parameterized ridge regression confirm the predicted memory--computation--accuracy tradeoffs.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes fundamental memory–computation–accuracy tradeoffs in amortized parametric optimization, providing matching (or near-matching) upper and lower bounds on the offline memory required to guarantee ε-accuracy under a fixed online gradient descent budget K, for both strongly convex and growth-conditioned convex objectives.
AI.motivation: Despite widespread empirical use of offline precomputation to accelerate online decision-making (e.g., warm-starting, learned optimizers), there is no general theory quantifying how much offline memory/storage is necessary to achieve a target accuracy given a fixed online computation budget.
AI.method: The authors formalize the problem as amortized parametric optimization: an offline phase stores a finite set of solved instances; online, a nonparametric predictor retrieves a warm start and applies K steps of projected gradient descent. They derive minimax bounds on required memory size by analyzing covering/packing of the parameter space, leveraging convergence rates of gradient descent and Lipschitz sensitivity of the solution map. A general proof framework is introduced that decouples the roles of the optimizer's convergence rate and the solution map's parametric smoothness.
AI.result: For μ-strongly convex objectives, matching upper and lower bounds on memory are established. For convex objectives under a β-growth condition (β > 2), near-matching bounds are obtained, revealing a phase transition in K beyond which additional memory yields no benefit. The framework explicitly quantifies the memory cost of acceleration, i.e., how much offline storage is needed to achieve a prescribed speedup over the unaided online optimizer. Experiments on parameterized ridge regression validate the theoretical tradeoffs.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides the first general characterization of minimal offline memory requirements for amortized parametric optimization, identifying convergence rate and solution-map sensitivity as the two key quantities governing the memory–computation–accuracy tradeoff, with practical implications for designing learned optimizers and warm-start strategies.

title: One More Turn, Less Regret: A Regret-Based Multi-Turn Benchmark for LLMs' Clarification Policies
summary: Ambiguous user requests make clarification a sequential decision problem for conversational LLM assistants: they must decide whether to ask, what to ask, when to stop, and when to answer. We introduce RegretBench, a multi-turn benchmark that evaluates clarification as policy behavior rather than isolated question quality. RegretBench provides a hidden-intent formulation of ambiguity, supports free-form interaction grounded in semantic-state tracking, and introduces a regret-based objective that measures how much value a model loses relative to a reference clarification policy. Experiments on open-domain QA and product recommendation scenarios show that final success alone is insufficient, as models with similar accuracy can differ substantially in efficiency, robustness to user behaviors, and stopping decisions. By jointly measuring intent resolution, interaction cost, ineffective clarification, and regret, RegretBench reveals whether models clarify usefully and efficiently. Our results show that effective clarification requires more than plausible questions: models must ask the right question at the right time and stop once the user's intended meaning is clear.

AI.tldr: RegretBench is a multi-turn benchmark that evaluates conversational LLMs' clarification behavior as a sequential decision-making process, using a regret-based metric to measure how much value is lost relative to an optimal clarification policy. It reveals that models with similar accuracy can differ significantly in efficiency, robustness, and stopping decisions, and that effective clarification requires asking the right question at the right time and knowing when to stop.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation paradigms treat clarification as isolated question quality, failing to capture that handling ambiguous user requests is fundamentally a sequential decision problem: deciding whether to ask, what to ask, when to stop, and when to answer. A benchmark is needed that evaluates clarification as a policy, accounting for the full trajectory of interaction rather than single-turn question relevance.
AI.method: The authors introduce RegretBench with three core design elements: (1) a hidden-intent formulation where the user's true intent is known to the evaluator but not the model, grounding ambiguity in semantic-state tracking; (2) free-form multi-turn interaction with automated state-based evaluation; and (3) a regret-based objective that quantifies how much value (measured via intent resolution and interaction cost) a model loses compared to a reference clarification policy. Experiments span open-domain QA and product recommendation scenarios.
AI.result: Models with similar final accuracy exhibit substantial divergence in efficiency, robustness to varied user behaviors, and stopping decisions. Final success rate alone is an insufficient metric. Joint measurement of intent resolution, interaction cost, ineffective clarification, and regret reveals which models clarify both usefully and efficiently.
AI.conclusion: Effective clarification is not simply a matter of generating plausible clarifying questions. Models must learn to ask the right question at the right time and stop once the user's intended meaning is sufficiently resolved. RegretBench provides the framework to measure and optimize these sequential decision-making aspects of conversational clarification.

title: Toward Mechanistic Interpretability of an AI Foundation Model Fine-Tuned for Atmospheric Chemistry
summary: Weather forecasting foundation models (FMs) are increasingly fine-tuned to predict air quality, offering fast global pollution forecasts at lower computational cost than conventional chemical transport models. These FMs are typically trained on reanalysis data and generate forecasts through autoregressive rollout. They do not explicitly represent governing physical or chemical processes. Therefore, high forecast skill does not reveal whether a model has learned physical mechanisms or exploits statistical regularities in its training data. Here, we present the first study of what a FM fine-tuned for atmospheric chemistry has learned by examining Microsoft's Aurora model. We impose controlled chemical perturbations on its forecasts and test them against known photochemical relationships. We then examine the internal representations that generate these forecasts. We find that Aurora captures a first-order ozone response to reactive nitrogen but does not enforce the chemical constraints that a process-based model encodes. It generates chemically inconsistent combinations of related species and relaxes localized emission features such as wildfire plumes toward background. Internally, its representations remain largely organized around the meteorology inherited during pretraining, with little structure specific to chemistry. Using sparse autoencoders, we identify internal components that causally control the chemical forecast but do not map cleanly onto individual atmospheric processes. This work provides a framework for testing whether AI forecasting systems learn atmospheric chemistry from reanalysis data. As these models are increasingly positioned to inform environmental policy decisions, we argue that composition forecasts should also be judged by their internal mechanisms rather than by benchmark skill alone.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether a fine-tuned weather foundation model (Microsoft's Aurora) has genuinely learned atmospheric chemistry or simply exploits statistical patterns. Through controlled chemical perturbations and internal representation analysis, the authors find Aurora captures some first-order ozone-NOx relationships but produces chemically inconsistent species combinations and lacks process-specific internal structure, arguing that composition forecasts should be evaluated by internal mechanisms, not just benchmark skill.
AI.motivation: Foundation models fine-tuned for air quality prediction achieve high forecast skill without explicitly encoding physical/chemical processes. This raises a critical epistemological question: does high skill indicate that the model has learned genuine photochemical mechanisms, or merely that it exploits statistical regularities in reanalysis training data? With these models increasingly positioned to inform environmental policy, understanding what they have actually learned is essential for trustworthy deployment.
AI.method: The authors apply a two-pronged approach to Microsoft's Aurora model: (1) controlled chemical perturbation experiments that test whether forecasts respect known photochemical relationships (e.g., ozone-NOx-VOC sensitivity, wildfire plume evolution), and (2) interpretability analysis of internal representations using sparse autoencoders to identify components that causally control chemical forecasts and examine whether these map onto distinct atmospheric processes.
AI.result: Aurora captures a first-order ozone response to reactive nitrogen perturbations but fails to enforce deeper chemical constraints: it generates chemically inconsistent combinations of related species and spuriously relaxes localized emission features (e.g., wildfire plumes) toward background levels. Internal representations remain primarily organized around pretrained meteorology, with little chemistry-specific structure. Sparse autoencoders reveal components that causally influence the chemical forecast, but these do not cleanly correspond to individual atmospheric processes.
AI.conclusion: High forecast skill alone is insufficient evidence that an AI model has learned atmospheric chemistry. The authors argue that composition forecasts from foundation models should also be evaluated by internal mechanistic fidelity — not merely benchmark performance — especially as these systems are increasingly used to inform environmental policy decisions.

title: CMI-Mem: Toward Generalizable Long-Term Memory Management via CMI-Augmented Reinforcement Learning
summary: Memory Manager models are pivotal in agent systems. Existing methods rely predominantly on LLM-judged synthetic question-answer (QA) pairs, making memory valuation dependent on sampled queries and the downstream reader. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{CMI-Mem}, a reinforcement learning(RL)-based lightweight memory manager model with a hybrid reward that combines downstream QA correctness and intrinsic Conditional Mutual Information (CMI). CMI evaluates the information contributed by new conversational inputs relative to the current memory state without conditioning on a sampled QA query, thereby complementing rather than replacing QA grounding. Our codes are available at: https://github.com/Wyb0627/CMIMem , and the CMI-Mem-4B model checkpoint is available at: https://www.modelscope.cn/models/wyb0627/CMIMem-4B

AI.tldr: CMI-Mem is a lightweight RL-based memory manager that learns memory valuation using a hybrid reward combining downstream QA correctness with intrinsic Conditional Mutual Information (CMI), where CMI measures the information gain of new inputs relative to current memory state without relying on sampled QA pairs.
AI.motivation: Existing memory manager models depend on LLM-generated synthetic QA pairs for memory valuation, which introduces dependency on sampled queries and the downstream reader model. This makes the valuation brittle and query-conditioned. The authors aim to introduce a query-agnostic information-theoretic signal (CMI) to complement QA-based grounding.
AI.method: The proposed CMI-Mem model uses a lightweight architecture trained via reinforcement learning with a hybrid reward function. The reward jointly optimizes two signals: (1) downstream QA correctness (task grounding) and (2) intrinsic Conditional Mutual Information (CMI), which quantifies the information contributed by new conversational inputs relative to the current memory state without conditioning on any sampled QA query, thereby serving as a complementary, query-agnostic valuation signal.
AI.result: The paper does not provide explicit quantitative results in the abstract. The contribution is primarily methodological, with model checkpoints (CMI-Mem-4B) and code released publicly.
AI.conclusion: CMI-based intrinsic reward complements QA-grounded rewards for training memory manager models, offering a more robust and query-independent approach to memory valuation in agent systems. The approach is validated through open-source release of the 4B-parameter model and codebase.

title: Progressive Cramming: Reliable Token Compression and What It Reveals
summary: Token cramming compresses sequences into learned embeddings with near-perfect reconstruction, but fixed token budgets and 99\% accuracy thresholds leave it unclear whether residual errors reflect optimization failures or fundamental limits. We introduce progressive cramming, which grows the target prefix token-by-token, stopping only when reconstruction is no longer achievable within a fixed optimization budget. Progressive trajectories occupy low-dimensional structure in embedding space. Prepending a crammed embedding causes a moderate but consistent accuracy drop on multiple-choice benchmarks even with the original prefix in context, and collapses capability almost entirely under generative evaluation. Causal attention-knockout interventions trace this degradation to the embedding's interactions in the model's early layers. These results position progressive cramming as a tool for studying compression limits and show that perfect reconstruction - achievable through brittle steering rather than transferable semantics - is insufficient for meaningful compression.

AI.tldr: Progressive cramming grows compressed token prefixes stepwise until reconstruction fails, revealing that near-perfect reconstruction quality does not preserve model utility — the compressed embeddings cause significant performance drops, especially in generative tasks, due to brittle early-layer interactions rather than transferable semantic content.
AI.motivation: Prior token cramming work achieves near-perfect reconstruction at fixed token budgets and 99% accuracy thresholds, but it remains ambiguous whether residual errors stem from optimization shortcomings or fundamental compression limits. The authors aim to disentangle these possibilities and assess whether reconstruction fidelity translates to preserved downstream capability.
AI.method: The authors propose progressive cramming, which incrementally grows a prefix embedding token-by-token, halting when reconstruction becomes infeasible under a fixed optimization budget. They analyze the resulting trajectory structure in embedding space, evaluate crammed embeddings on multiple-choice and generative benchmarks (with and without the original prefix in context), and apply causal attention-knockout interventions to localize the source of performance degradation to specific early transformer layers.
AI.result: Progressive cramming trajectories exhibit low-dimensional structure in embedding space. Prepending a crammed embedding yields moderate but consistent accuracy drops on multiple-choice tasks and near-total capability collapse on generative evaluation, even when the original prefix is provided in context. Causal attention-knockout experiments trace this degradation to the embedding's interactions within the model's early layers.
AI.conclusion: Perfect reconstruction is achievable through brittle steering mechanisms rather than transferable semantic compression, and reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient for meaningful compression. Progressive cramming serves as a principled tool for probing fundamental compression limits in language models.

title: Synthetic minority data is redundant or invalid: a data-dependent validity theory and a de-biased test
comment: 45 pages, 7 figures; Supplementary Information included as appendix
summary: For two decades, the standard remedy for class-imbalanced learning has been to fabricate synthetic minority examples, and the standard evidence of their validity has been a check that cannot fail: synthetic points are scored against the very data that generated them. We de-bias the check. Validity becomes a population quantity -- the probability that a synthetic point truly belongs to the minority class -- with a consistent estimator that scores synthetic points against withheld real data. Where held-out ground truth is available, the classical test underestimates true invalidity in 96-99% of method-by-imbalance-ratio cells, while the de-biased estimator tracks it closely. We prove validity is a property of the data, not the method: class overlap sets an invalidity floor no faithful generator escapes, making oversampling redundant where classes separate and invalid where they overlap. Across 91 methods, three classifiers, and datasets spanning medicine and finance -- including a generator engineered to pass the classical check -- none clears both bars: gains over the best trivial baseline are noise-thin (median below 0.01 F1, a decision threshold's reach), and most damage calibration. We release the audit as a pip-installable test and flip the burden of proof: synthetic minority data must now demonstrate, on the data at hand, both validity and information gain.

AI.tldr: The paper audits two decades of class-imbalanced learning research, showing that the standard validity check for synthetic minority examples is circular (testing on generating data). It introduces a de-biased population estimator, proves that validity is fundamentally limited by class overlap, and demonstrates across 91 methods that synthetic oversampling provides negligible gains over trivial baselines while damaging calibration.
AI.motivation: For 20 years, the standard approach to class imbalance has been SMOTE-style synthetic minority oversampling, validated by a circular test that scores synthetic points against the same data used to generate them. This paper aims to de-bias this evaluation, establish what validity actually means in a population sense, and systematically audit whether synthetic oversampling methods genuinely add value beyond trivial baselines.
AI.method: The authors (1) redefine validity as a population quantity — the probability a synthetic point truly belongs to the minority class — and propose a consistent estimator using withheld real data; (2) prove theoretically that class overlap sets a hard invalidity floor no generator can escape; (3) conduct a large-scale empirical audit across 91 oversampling methods, three classifiers, and real-world medical/finance datasets, comparing against trivial baselines (e.g., no resampling, random oversampling); and (4) engineer a generator deliberately designed to pass the classical check, demonstrating its failure under the de-biased test.
AI.result: The classical validity check underestimates true invalidity in 96–99% of method-by-imbalance-ratio cells. No method clears both validity and information-gain bars: median F1 gain over the best trivial baseline is below 0.01, and most methods harm calibration. The engineered generator passes the classical check easily but fails the de-biased test, confirming the circularity problem.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic minority oversampling is redundant where classes are separable and invalid where they overlap. The burden of proof must shift: future methods must demonstrate both validity (via the de-biased estimator) and information gain on the data at hand. The authors release the audit as a pip-installable package.

title: AI-Driven Multi-Hop Relay Selection for Smart Urban NR-V2X Networks via Learning-to-Optimize Graph Neural Networks
summary:
Reliable and low-latency NR-V2X communications are essential for smart mobility in dense urban environments. However, limited Road-Side Unit (RSU) density, frequent non-line-of-sight conditions, and highly dynamic vehicular topologies often prevent many Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) from maintaining stable single-hop connectivity. Although multi-hop relay-assisted communication can extend infrastructure coverage, selecting relay links in real time under practical flow, capacity, and connectivity constraints remains challenging.
  Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) yields optimal multi-hop relay decisions, but its computational complexity scales sharply with network density, limiting real-time applicability. To address this, we propose a Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for real-time NR-V2X relay selection. Vehicular communication states are modeled as attributed graphs, where CAVs and RSUs are nodes and candidate radio links are enriched with propagation-aware features. An offline MILP oracle provides optimal supervision, while an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network (GINE) approximates oracle decisions with near-constant inference latency. Experiments on large-scale urban datasets generated by an integrated SUMO--GEMV2 simulation pipeline show that the proposed approach achieves connectivity comparable to that of the MILP oracle while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude. The framework enables cost-effective enhancement of urban V2X connectivity by leveraging existing vehicular assets and supporting scalable, real-time NR-V2X operation in smart city environments.

AI.tldr: A GNN-based Learning-to-Optimise framework is proposed for real-time multi-hop relay selection in NR-V2X networks, achieving near-optimal connectivity with drastically reduced computation time compared to MILP.
AI.motivation: Dense urban V2X scenarios suffer from limited RSU density, NLOS conditions, and dynamic topologies, preventing stable single-hop connectivity. While MILP provides optimal multi-hop relay decisions, its computational complexity scales poorly with network density, making real-time operation infeasible.
AI.method: Vehicular communication states are modeled as attributed graphs (nodes = CAVs/RSUs, edges = radio links with propagation-aware features). An offline MILP oracle generates optimal supervision labels. An edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network (GINE) is trained to approximate the oracle's relay selection decisions, enabling near-constant inference latency. Evaluation uses a SUMO–GEMV2 co-simulation pipeline on large-scale urban datasets.
AI.result: The proposed GNN-based L2O approach achieves connectivity performance comparable to the MILP oracle while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables cost-effective, scalable, real-time NR-V2X relay selection by leveraging existing vehicular assets, supporting enhanced urban V2X connectivity in smart city deployments.

title: slang.gr as a Large-Scale Crowdsourced Resource for Non-Standard Greek
comment: Preprint of a paper accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 14th EETN Conference on Artificial Intelligence (SETN 2026)
summary: Slang is a central component of everyday language, reflecting linguistic creativity, social identity, and cultural change, yet its dy- namic and non-standard nature makes it difficult to model computationally. We present the first large-scale computational study of slang.gr, a crowdsourced lexicon of Greek non-standard language, combining lexical content, user-generated tags, and interaction data. To enable the systematic analysis, we map noisy folksonomic tags to a structured multi-layer taxonomy capturing both semantic categories and sociolinguistic metadata. Using this representation, we analyze the linguistic structure of Greek slang and the behavior of its contributor community. We find that slang is strongly centered on person-related and evaluative language, exhibits high morphological creativity, and is shaped by highly skewed participation with short user lifespans and overlapping communities. Building on these signals, we introduce a community-based confidence score for definitions that integrates user roles, interaction patterns, and moderation signals. Our results show that taxonomy-based representations improve interpretability while retaining meaningful aspects of behavioral structure, enabling a more structured and interpretable analysis of confidence signals. Overall, this work establishes slang.gr as a computational resource for non-standard Greek and provides a foundation for sociolinguistic NLP, bias analysis, and the study of informal language in LLMs.

AI.tldr: First large-scale computational study of slang.gr, a crowdsourced Greek slang lexicon. Authors map noisy folksonomic tags to a structured multi-layer taxonomy, analyze linguistic patterns and contributor behavior, and introduce a community-based confidence score for definitions, establishing a resource for Greek sociolinguistic NLP.
AI.motivation: Slang is central to everyday language but difficult to model computationally due to its dynamic, non-standard nature. Existing resources for non-standard Greek are scarce, and there is no structured framework for analyzing crowdsourced slang data that captures both semantic and sociolinguistic dimensions.
AI.method: The authors take slang.gr — a crowdsourced lexicon with lexical entries, user-generated tags, and interaction data — and map its noisy folksonomic tags to a structured multi-layer taxonomy covering semantic categories and sociolinguistic metadata. They then analyze the linguistic structure (e.g., morphological creativity, semantic focus) and contributor community behavior (participation skew, user lifespans, community overlap). Finally, they introduce a community-based confidence score integrating user roles, interaction patterns, and moderation signals.
AI.result: Greek slang is strongly centered on person-related and evaluative language, exhibits high morphological creativity, and is shaped by highly skewed participation with short user lifespans and overlapping communities. The taxonomy-based representations improve interpretability while retaining behavioral structure, and the community-based confidence score enables structured analysis of definition reliability.
AI.conclusion: slang.gr is established as a computational resource for non-standard Greek. The taxonomy-based approach and confidence scoring framework provide a foundation for sociolinguistic NLP, bias analysis, and the study of informal language in LLMs.

title: Memoir: Should a Model Write to Its Memory While It Thinks?
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables, 1 algorithm. Code: https://github.com/RightNow-AI/Memoir
summary: Memoir combines per-sample fast memory, shared slow parameters, variable-depth latent recurrence, and a future-latent energy objective. We test its riskiest coupling: each pondering iteration may rewrite the fast tier that the same iteration reads. On procedural associative recall with key interference, we compare a coupled arm against an otherwise identical read-only pondering arm. Both arms contain 81,738 parameters, including 76,362 trainable parameters, and use matched declared forward multiply-accumulate counts, data, optimizer, schedule, and seeds. After 240 training steps across 12 seeds, coupled recall is 0.5203 with a 95 percent interval of [0.4522, 0.5883], while read-only recall is 0.6557 with [0.5953, 0.7160]. The arms are paired per seed, and the read-only lead of 0.1354 gives a paired t of 3.23 on 11 degrees of freedom with a 95 percent interval of [0.0431, 0.2277] on the difference, winning on 10 of 12 seeds. After 960 steps across 8 seeds, both arms reach 1.0000, so the measured effect is a learning-speed penalty at a fixed budget, not a demonstrated capability penalty. That longer control is ceiling limited, leaving convergence on a non-saturating task unmeasured. A predicted failure in which memory rewriting corrupts the energy signal did not occur: the energy margin grew and held. Kernel restructuring also reduced delta-rule forward time from 0.907 ms to 0.351 ms on the stated device. Code and evidence are available at https://github.com/RightNow-AI/Memoir

AI.tldr: Memoir introduces a coupled read-write pondering mechanism where each iteration rewrites the same fast memory it reads. On an associative recall task, coupling incurs a learning-speed penalty (lower recall at 240 steps) compared to a read-only variant, but both converge to perfect recall by 960 steps. The feared corruption of the energy signal did not materialize. A kernel optimization also reduced delta-rule forward time significantly.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates Memoir, an architecture combining per-sample fast memory with shared slow parameters and variable-depth latent recurrence. The core motivation of this experiment is to test the riskiest design choice: allowing each pondering iteration to rewrite the fast memory tier that the same iteration reads, which could potentially corrupt the future-latent energy objective used for learning.
AI.method: Two arms are compared on a procedural associative recall task with key interference: a coupled arm (read-write pondering) and a read-only pondering arm, otherwise identical. Both arms have 81,738 parameters (76,362 trainable), matched multiply-accumulate counts, identical data, optimizer, schedule, and seeds. Performance is measured at 240 training steps (12 seeds) and 960 steps (8 seeds), with paired statistical tests across seeds. A kernel restructuring optimization for the delta-rule forward pass is also evaluated.
AI.result: At 240 steps, coupled recall is 0.5203 [0.4522, 0.5883] vs. read-only 0.6557 [0.5953, 0.7160], a significant read-only lead of 0.1354 (paired t=3.23, df=11, p<0.01, winning on 10/12 seeds). By 960 steps, both arms reach 1.0000 recall, so the effect is a learning-speed penalty, not a capability ceiling. The energy margin grew and held, refuting the predicted corruption failure. Kernel restructuring reduced delta-rule forward time from 0.907ms to 0.351ms.
AI.conclusion: The coupled read-write pondering mechanism is viable: it incurs only a transient learning-speed penalty at fixed budget and does not corrupt the energy signal. However, the ceiling-limited control leaves convergence behavior on non-saturating tasks unmeasured, and further work is needed to characterize the coupling's effect on harder problems where perfect recall may not be attainable.

title: KeySI: An Interaction Framework for Tuning Text Embeddings Based on Human Feedback
summary: In large-scale text analysis tasks, pre-trained language models are often used to embed text corpora for downstream analysis. However, such models may struggle to capture domain-specific semantics and adapting them typically requires large amounts of labeled data and technical expertise to implement training pipelines. Recent approaches have demonstrated how visual interactions in document projections can capture human feedback as training signals for model tuning. However, these methods operate on document-level feedback, which requires users to open and assess individual documents in order to provide effective feedback. In this paper, we propose KeySI, an interaction framework that enables feature-level feedback through keyword-based concept specification. Users specify feedback by organizing extracted keywords into groups representing concepts, which KeySI translates into document-level supervision for subsequent tuning. By operating on keywords as the primary interaction medium, KeySI reduces the need for manual document inspection and labeling and lowers the barrier to adapting embedding models. We present a prototype implementation that, given a corpus, curates representative keywords, visualizes keywords and document embeddings via dimensionality reduction, allows interactive specification of keyword groups, and supports iterative refinement through system feedback. We evaluate KeySI through a user study, usage scenarios, and quantitative experiments demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing user intent and improving embedding alignment.

AI.tldr: KeySI is an interaction framework that enables users to adapt pre-trained language model embeddings through feature-level feedback by organizing extracted keywords into concept groups, reducing the need for manual document inspection compared to prior document-level feedback approaches.
AI.motivation: Pre-trained language models struggle with domain-specific semantics, and adapting them typically requires substantial labeled data and technical expertise. While prior work uses visual interactions with document projections for feedback-driven tuning, these methods operate at the document level, forcing users to open and assess individual documents — a labor-intensive bottleneck. There is a need for a more efficient, lower-barrier interaction paradigm for embedding model adaptation.
AI.method: KeySI introduces feature-level feedback via keyword-based concept specification. Users organize extracted keywords into groups representing semantic concepts. The system translates these keyword groupings into document-level supervision signals for model tuning. A prototype implementation curates representative keywords from a corpus, visualizes both keywords and document embeddings using dimensionality reduction, supports interactive keyword group specification, and provides iterative refinement through system feedback.
AI.result: The authors evaluate KeySI through a user study, usage scenarios, and quantitative experiments, demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing user intent and improving embedding alignment.
AI.conclusion: KeySI lowers the barrier to adapting embedding models by shifting interaction from document-level to keyword-level feedback, enabling efficient domain-specific tuning without requiring extensive labeled data or deep technical expertise.

title: A Comparative Evaluation of Embeddings and LLMs in a Greek Book Publisher Setting - The CUP Dataset
comment: Preprint of a manuscript submitted to the 14th EETN Conference on Artificial Intelligence (SETN 2026)
summary: We present CUP, a Greek book retrieval benchmark consisting of 868 catalog records and 104 expert-annotated queries with graded relevance judgments. We evaluate sparse (BM25), dense (sentence-transformers), hybrid, and LLM-assisted retrieval methods in this book-search setting. Multilingual embeddings outperform Greek-specific models, while hybrid retrieval performs best overall. A query-level analysis shows that BM25 excels at named-entity queries, while dense and hybrid methods improve natural-language, noisy, cross-lingual, and concept queries. Field-aware prompting has model-specific effects, while LLM TOC summarization improves TOC-only retrieval and LLM post-filtering improves early-stage retrieval at a high cost. Overall, CUP enables real-world evaluation of Greek retrieval across lexical, semantic, noisy, and cross-lingual queries.

AI.tldr: CUP is a Greek book retrieval benchmark with 868 records and 104 annotated queries. The study finds hybrid retrieval performs best overall, with BM25 excelling at named-entity queries and dense methods better on natural-language and cross-lingual queries. LLM-based techniques (TOC summarization, post-filtering) offer gains but at higher cost.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of real-world retrieval benchmarks for the Greek language, particularly in the book-search domain, which involves diverse query types (lexical, semantic, noisy, cross-lingual). Existing resources do not adequately evaluate how different retrieval paradigms handle the linguistic and practical challenges of Greek book catalog search.
AI.method: The authors construct CUP, a benchmark of 868 Greek book catalog records with 104 expert-annotated queries and graded relevance judgments. They evaluate four retrieval paradigms: sparse (BM25), dense (sentence-transformers, including multilingual and Greek-specific models), hybrid (sparse + dense), and LLM-assisted methods (field-aware prompting, TOC summarization, post-filtering). A query-level analysis categorizes queries by type (named-entity, natural-language, noisy, cross-lingual, concept) to understand per-method strengths.
AI.result: Multilingual embeddings outperform Greek-specific models. Hybrid retrieval achieves the best overall performance. BM25 is strongest on named-entity queries. Dense and hybrid methods improve results on natural-language, noisy, cross-lingual, and concept queries. Field-aware prompting shows model-specific effects. LLM-based TOC summarization improves table-of-contents-only retrieval. LLM post-filtering boosts early-stage retrieval but incurs high computational cost.
AI.conclusion: CUP provides a realistic evaluation platform for Greek book retrieval across diverse query types. No single retrieval method dominates all scenarios — BM25 remains valuable for entity-heavy queries, while dense and hybrid approaches better handle semantic and noisy queries. LLM-assisted techniques offer marginal gains at significant cost, suggesting careful cost-benefit analysis is needed for production deployment.

title: External Clustering Validation by the Homogeneity-Parsimony Trade-off
summary: Scalar metrics are often used to evaluate clusterings against known classes, but they can obscure a fundamental trade-off: clusterings should be informative about class labels while avoiding unnecessary fragmentation. Here we describe normalized scores of cluster homogeneity and parsimony that quantify this trade-off. These scores build on the information bottleneck principle, modified to not reward lossy compression. We show by example and mathematical proof that our definitions of these scores have the intuitive property of varying monotonically under cluster refinement in contrast to related proposals. Extending the information-theoretic framework beyond Shannon entropies, we furthermore derive set-matching and pair-based counterparts of the homogeneity and parsimony scores. These unify commonly used evaluation criteria and show that, in the pair-based setting, the homogeneity-parsimony trade-off recovers the receiver operating characteristic of binary classifiers. We demonstrate the framework's utility for feature selection and algorithm comparison, illustrating how considering scores jointly can clarify clustering operating points and identify Pareto-optimal solutions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces normalized homogeneity and parsimony scores for clustering evaluation based on the information bottleneck principle, modified to avoid rewarding lossy compression. The scores vary monotonically under cluster refinement (unlike prior proposals), unify set-matching and pair-based evaluation criteria, and reveal that the homogeneity-parsimony trade-off recovers the ROC of binary classifiers in the pair-based setting.
AI.motivation: Scalar clustering metrics obscure a fundamental trade-off: clusterings should be informative about class labels (homogeneity) while avoiding unnecessary fragmentation (parsimony). Existing evaluation criteria fail to capture this trade-off cleanly, and related information-theoretic proposals lack the desirable monotonicity property under cluster refinement.
AI.method: The authors extend the information bottleneck principle, removing its tendency to reward lossy compression, to define normalized homogeneity and parsimony scores. They prove these scores vary monotonically under cluster refinement. Beyond Shannon entropy, they derive set-matching and pair-based counterparts, unifying common evaluation criteria. In the pair-based case, they show the trade-off curve recovers the ROC of binary classifiers.
AI.result: The proposed scores are proven mathematically to vary monotonically under cluster refinement, unlike related proposals. The framework unifies set-matching and pair-based evaluation criteria. The pair-based homogeneity-parsimony trade-off is shown to recover the ROC curve. Practical utility is demonstrated through feature selection and algorithm comparison, where joint score analysis clarifies clustering operating points and identifies Pareto-optimal solutions.
AI.conclusion: The homogeneity-parsimony framework provides a principled, information-theoretic foundation for clustering evaluation that respects the trade-off between informativeness and fragmentation, unifies disparate evaluation criteria, and offers practical benefits for model selection, feature selection, and algorithm comparison.

title: WaveformQA: Benchmarking LLM Temporal Reasoning on Digital Waveforms
comment: 10 pages; abridged version published in IEEE International Conference on LLM-Aided Design (ICLAD), 2026
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation and reasoning, yet their ability to perform temporal reasoning over digital waveform data remains largely unexplored. Although reasoning over digital waveforms is a critical bottleneck in design verification, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate hardware description language (HDL) code generation and use waveforms only as supplementary context. This paper presents WaveformQA, an open-source question-answering benchmark for evaluating LLM temporal reasoning over digital waveforms. The benchmark comprises 360 questions with programmatically generated ground truths across eight categories of varying difficulty, including questions targeting multi-signal correlation and event ordering. Waveforms are generated from open-source design implementations, ensuring reproducibility and grounding the benchmark in real hardware behavior. Evaluation of frontier LLMs reveals that while models achieve reasonable accuracy on simple queries, performance degrades due to context window limitations and reasoning difficulties on complex temporal and multi-step questions. In addition, we show that an event-time JSON representation of waveforms improves LLM reasoning accuracy versus the standardized value change dump (VCD) format. The open-source framework supports extending to new question categories and importing new waveform sources, enabling researchers to rapidly prototype temporal reasoning experiments.

AI.tldr: WaveformQA is an open-source QA benchmark with 360 questions across 8 categories for evaluating LLM temporal reasoning over digital waveforms. Frontier LLMs perform well on simple queries but degrade on complex temporal/multi-step questions; an event-time JSON representation outperforms the standard VCD format.
AI.motivation: LLMs have shown strong code generation and reasoning capabilities, but temporal reasoning over digital waveform data — a critical bottleneck in hardware design verification — remains unexplored. Existing benchmarks focus on HDL code generation with waveforms only as supplementary context, leaving a gap in evaluating how well LLMs can reason about temporal signal behavior.
AI.method: The authors introduce WaveformQA, an open-source benchmark with 360 programmatically generated QA pairs across 8 difficulty-graded categories (including multi-signal correlation and event ordering). Waveforms are sourced from open-source hardware designs for reproducibility. Frontier LLMs are evaluated using both the standard VCD format and a proposed event-time JSON representation, with ground truth answers generated programmatically.
AI.result: Frontier LLMs achieve reasonable accuracy on simple temporal queries but performance significantly degrades on complex, multi-step, and temporally intricate questions due to context window limitations and reasoning difficulties. The event-time JSON representation consistently yields higher reasoning accuracy compared to the standardized VCD format.
AI.conclusion: WaveformQA fills a critical evaluation gap for LLM temporal reasoning in digital design verification. The findings highlight current LLM limitations in multi-signal correlation and event ordering tasks, while the open-source framework enables rapid prototyping of new question categories and waveform sources for future research.

title: A Unified Moral-Value Dataset for Instruction Tuning
comment: Accepted at the 4th International Workshop on Value Engineering in AI (VALE 2026), co-located with IJCAI-ECAI 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have developed rapidly and become valuable tools in everyday life. However, how to align LLMs to a particular set of human values is still an open problem. Recent studies show that instruction tuning has strong potential for zero-shot tasks and may serve as an effective approach to addressing value alignment. Nevertheless, although many datasets for instruction tuning already exist, they are not specifically designed around moral scenarios and behaviors. We construct a unified moral-value dataset that can be directly used for instruction tuning. This dataset is built upon existing moral-value datasets by merging them into a unified corpus and converting them into an instruction-response format. We show that training on a mixed dataset combining general task datasets with our dataset preserves general-task performance, and we report preliminary observations on how the mixing ratio affects value-oriented task performance. Our work provides a moral-value dataset for instruction tuning and offers a useful resource for further alignment research. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/teohzzh/value-for-instruction-tuning.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs a unified moral-value dataset in instruction-response format by merging and converting existing moral datasets, enabling instruction tuning of LLMs for value alignment while preserving general-task performance through mixed-dataset training.
AI.motivation: Aligning LLMs with specific human values remains an open problem. While instruction tuning shows promise for zero-shot tasks and value alignment, existing instruction-tuning datasets lack focus on moral scenarios and behaviors, creating a gap in resources for training morally-aligned models.
AI.method: The authors constructed a unified moral-value dataset by merging multiple existing moral-value datasets into a single corpus and converting them into an instruction-response format suitable for instruction tuning. They then trained models on a mixed dataset combining general task datasets with their moral-value dataset, and analyzed how different mixing ratios affect performance.
AI.result: Training on the mixed dataset preserves general-task performance, and the mixing ratio between general and moral-value data influences value-oriented task performance.
AI.conclusion: The paper delivers a ready-to-use moral-value dataset for instruction tuning and establishes it as a useful resource for future research on value alignment of LLMs.

title: New Complexity-Theoretic Frontiers of Tractability for Neural Network Training
comment: Appeared in the proceedings of NeurIPS 2023
summary: In spite of the fundamental role of neural networks in contemporary machine learning research, our understanding of the computational complexity of optimally training neural networks remains incomplete even when dealing with the simplest kinds of activation functions. Indeed, while there has been a number of very recent results that establish ever-tighter lower bounds for the problem under linear and ReLU activation functions, less progress has been made towards the identification of novel polynomial-time tractable network architectures. In this article we obtain novel algorithmic upper bounds for training linear- and ReLU-activated neural networks to optimality which push the boundaries of tractability for these problems beyond the previous state of the art. In particular, for ReLU networks we establish the polynomial-time tractability of all architectures where hidden neurons have an out-degree of $1$, improving upon the previous algorithm of Arora, Basu, Mianjy and Mukherjee. On the other hand, for networks with linear activation functions we identify the first non-trivial polynomial-time solvable class of networks by obtaining an algorithm that can optimally train network architectures satisfying a novel data throughput condition.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes new polynomial-time algorithmic upper bounds for optimally training neural networks with linear and ReLU activations. For ReLU networks, it proves tractability when hidden neurons have out-degree 1. For linear networks, it identifies the first non-trivial polynomially solvable class via a data throughput condition.
AI.motivation: Despite neural networks' central role in ML, computational complexity of optimal training remains poorly understood. Recent work has focused on lower bounds for linear/ReLU networks, but identifying tractable architectures has lagged behind. This paper aims to push the boundary of polynomial-time trainable architectures.
AI.method: Algorithmic design and complexity-theoretic analysis. For ReLU networks, leverages the out-degree-1 constraint on hidden neurons to devise a polynomial-time optimal training algorithm, improving on Arora et al.'s prior result. For linear networks, introduces a novel data throughput condition that enables polynomial-time solvability.
AI.result: (1) ReLU networks: Polynomial-time tractability established for all architectures where hidden neurons have out-degree 1. (2) Linear networks: First non-trivial polynomial-time solvable class identified via the data throughput condition.
AI.conclusion: The results expand the frontier of tractable neural network training, demonstrating that beyond known hardness results, meaningful polynomial-time algorithms exist for architecturally constrained ReLU and linear networks.

title: NVIDIA-labs OO Agents: Native Python Object-Oriented Agents
summary:
Traditional agent development is split across prompt templates, tool schemas, callback code, and workflow graphs.
