We present NVIDIA Object-Oriented Agents (NOOA), a model-agnostic Python framework for building reliable AI agents. NOOA takes a simpler approach: an agent is a Python object. Its methods are the actions the model can take, fields are its state, docstrings are its prompts, and its type annotations are contracts. A method whose code body consists of "..." is completed at runtime by an LLM-driven agent loop, while methods with normal bodies remain standard deterministic Python. This gives developers and agents the same interface, so agent behavior can be tested, traced, refactored, and improved just like other software.
  This paper makes three contributions. (1) We present the agent-as-a-Python-object programming model and the design principles behind it. Where Python has existing abstractions, we adopt them directly. Agent-specific capabilities--context, events, state rendering, long-term memory, and validated LLM loops--are exposed through simple Pythonic APIs, so both developers and agents share one familiar programming model. (2) We identify six model-facing ideas that NOOA is, to our knowledge, the first to combine on a single surface: typed input/output, pass-by-reference over live objects, code as action, programmable loop engineering, explicit object state, and model-callable harness APIs for context and events. We find the community already converging on several of these ideas--often as experimental or partial features--and present the comparison to encourage further adoption. (3) We demonstrate that current models use this interface effectively, both in targeted capability tests and on agentic and reasoning benchmarks such as SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 and ARC-AGI-3.

AI.tldr: NOOA is a Python framework where agents are plain Python objects—methods are actions, docstrings are prompts, type annotations are contracts, and ellipsis-bodied methods are LLM-completed at runtime. This unifies developer and agent interfaces, enabling standard software practices like testing and refactoring for agent behavior.
AI.motivation: Traditional agent development fragments logic across prompt templates, tool schemas, callback code, and workflow graphs. NOOA aims to collapse this complexity by making an agent indistinguishable from a regular Python object, so both humans and LLMs interact through the same interface, reducing friction in building, testing, and maintaining reliable AI agents.
AI.method: NOOA models an agent as a Python object where: methods with `...` bodies are dynamically completed by an LLM agent loop at runtime; methods with normal bodies remain deterministic Python; fields hold state; docstrings serve as prompts; type annotations enforce contracts. It surfaces six model-facing primitives: typed I/O, pass-by-reference over live objects, code-as-action, programmable loop engineering, explicit object state, and model-callable harness APIs for context/events. Standard Python abstractions are reused wherever possible.
AI.result: Current LLMs use the NOOA interface effectively, demonstrated through targeted capability tests and on benchmarks including SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.0, and ARC-AGI-3. The six model-facing ideas—several of which the community is independently converging on—are, to the authors' knowledge, combined on a single surface for the first time.
AI.conclusion: The agent-as-a-Python-object model simplifies agent development by unifying human and model interfaces. By adopting existing Python abstractions and combining six key model-facing design ideas, NOOA enables agents to be developed, tested, and improved like conventional software, with empirical results supporting its effectiveness.

title: news-crawler-LM: A Small Long-Context Model For High-Quality News Crawling
summary: Extracting structured content from news pages remains challenging due to heterogeneous HTML layouts, inconsistent markup, and substantial boilerplate such as navigation elements and advertisements. Rule-based news crawlers can achieve high extraction accuracy by encoding site-specific structure, but require manual configuration in order to generalize to new publishers. Large language models provide a more flexible alternative by reducing the need for handcrafted rules, but their high computational cost limits practical deployment. In this paper, we introduce news-crawler-LM, a small long-context language model fine-tuned on high-quality, human-validated extractions from the Fundus news-crawling library. Our model converts raw HTML into plaintext and structured JSON, including fields such as headline, author, publication date, and article body. In our experiments, news-crawler-LM outperforms strong baselines in HTML-to-Markdown and HTML-to-JSON extraction, improving performance by +4.8 BLEU and +6.1 METEOR in the HTML-to-Markdown task, and by +2.2 BLEU and +4.1 METEOR in the HTML-to-JSON task. However, we also observe that our model only slightly better compared to other rule-based parsing libraries on the HTML-to-plaintext task in evaluations on previously unseen publishers. We release all models and artifacts to the research community.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces news-crawler-LM, a small long-context language model fine-tuned for extracting structured content (headline, author, date, body) from raw HTML news pages. It outperforms strong baselines in HTML-to-Markdown and HTML-to-JSON extraction but shows only marginal gains over rule-based parsers on plaintext extraction from unseen publishers.
AI.motivation: News content extraction is hindered by heterogeneous HTML layouts, inconsistent markup, and boilerplate (ads, navigation). Rule-based crawlers achieve high accuracy but require manual, site-specific configuration. LLMs offer flexibility but are computationally expensive. The authors aim to bridge this gap with a small, fine-tuned LM that balances accuracy and efficiency.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune a small long-context language model on high-quality, human-validated extraction examples sourced from the Fundus news-crawling library. The model takes raw HTML as input and outputs either plaintext or structured JSON containing headline, author, publication date, and article body.
AI.result: news-crawler-LM achieves +4.8 BLEU and +6.1 METEOR over baselines on HTML-to-Markdown, and +2.2 BLEU and +4.1 METEOR on HTML-to-JSON extraction. However, on HTML-to-plaintext for unseen publishers, it only slightly outperforms rule-based parsing libraries.
AI.conclusion: A small, fine-tuned long-context LM can effectively extract structured news content from raw HTML, outperforming baselines on structured output tasks. However, its advantage over rule-based methods is limited for plaintext extraction on unseen domains, suggesting complementary strengths. All models and artifacts are released publicly.

title: Robust Asynchronous Q-Learning under Reward and State Corruption via Batching
comment: To appear at the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC) 2026
summary: Motivated by reinforcement learning in harsh environments, we consider the problem of learning an optimal policy subject to adversarially corrupted feedback. Specifically, at each time-step, an adversary can perturb both the reward and state observations of the learner following the Huber contamination model. To defend against such data corruption, we propose {\texttt{BR-Async-Q}}: a novel, epoch-based, robust \(Q\)-learning algorithm built upon two key ideas: (i) partitioning the online data stream into batches to reduce variance, and (ii) constructing robust estimates of the Bellman optimality operator using such batched data. We prove a high-probability $\ell_\infty$ error bound for {\texttt{BR-Async-Q}} that matches that for vanilla \(Q\)-learning, up to a small additive term that scales with the fraction of corrupted samples. To our knowledge, this provides the first robustness guarantee for asynchronous \(Q\)-learning subject to both reward and state corruption. Furthermore, when only rewards are corrupted, the dependence of our algorithm's bound on the corruption fraction is minimax optimal.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes BR-Async-Q, the first robust asynchronous Q-learning algorithm that defends against adversarial corruption of both reward and state observations under the Huber contamination model, achieving near-optimal error bounds.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning deployed in harsh, real-world environments faces adversarial data corruption. Prior robust RL work either assumes synchronous updates or only handles reward corruption. The gap is providing robustness guarantees for asynchronous Q-learning under both state and reward corruption simultaneously.
AI.method: BR-Async-Q is an epoch-based robust Q-learning algorithm with two core mechanisms: (1) partitioning the online data stream into batches to reduce variance, and (2) constructing robust estimates of the Bellman optimality operator from batched data to mitigate the effect of corrupted samples, following the Huber contamination model where an adversary can perturb both rewards and state observations at each time step.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves a high-probability ℓ∞ error bound matching vanilla Q-learning, plus a small additive term scaling with the corruption fraction. For reward-only corruption, the dependence on the corruption fraction is minimax optimal. This represents the first robustness guarantee for asynchronous Q-learning under joint reward and state corruption.
AI.conclusion: BR-Async-Q demonstrates that robust asynchronous Q-learning is possible under both reward and state corruption with near-optimal theoretical guarantees, closing a significant gap in the robust reinforcement learning literature.

title: ArbiGraph: Arbitrarily Scalable Verifiable Task Graphs for Evaluating Context Management
summary: We introduce ARBIGRAPH, a benchmark generator for evaluating whether tool-assisted language agents can retain, update, compose, and discard task-relevant context across extended reasoning workflows. ARBIGRAPH represents each task as a natural-language problem with an executable Python solver, and composes tasks through typed intermediate states, instantiated here as scalar and list values. This design enables controllable task graphs whose length, dependency structure, distractor count, and value type can be varied while preserving exact automatic verification. We instantiate ARBIGRAPH with math, GSM-style word-problems, and Python-tracing task categories, and evaluate a Qwen3.5-27B tool-assisted agent across four topologies. The results show high accuracy on isolated tasks but substantial degradation on more complex dependent tasks: accuracy drops by up to 33.3% on branching chains of dependent math tasks. This shows that ARBIGRAPH exposes failures that are not visible from single-task evaluation alone. Our code, generated datasets, and evaluation results are available at https://github.com/pavelgolikov/ArbiGraph.git

AI.tldr: ARBIGRAPH is a benchmark generator for testing whether tool-assisted language agents can manage task-relevant context (retain, update, compose, discard) across long reasoning chains. It generates controllable task graphs with typed intermediate states, enabling automatic verification. Evaluation of a Qwen3.5-27B agent reveals up to 33.3% accuracy degradation on complex dependent tasks versus isolated tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate language agents on isolated tasks, failing to capture failures that emerge only when agents must manage context across extended, interdependent reasoning workflows. There is a need for a controllable, automatically verifiable benchmark that systematically tests context retention, updating, composition, and discarding.
AI.method: ARBIGRAPH represents each task as a natural-language problem paired with an executable Python solver. Tasks are composed into directed graphs via typed intermediate states (scalar and list values). The generator allows control over graph length, dependency structure, distractor count, and value types, while ensuring exact automatic verification of correctness. Tasks span math problems, GSM-style word problems, and Python-tracing categories across four topologies.
AI.result: A Qwen3.5-27B tool-assisted agent achieves high accuracy on isolated tasks but suffers substantial degradation on complex dependent tasks — up to 33.3% accuracy drop on branching chains of dependent math tasks. This demonstrates that ARBIGRAPH exposes context-management failures invisible to single-task evaluation.
AI.conclusion: ARBIGRAPH reveals that current tool-assisted language agents struggle with maintaining and composing context across extended reasoning chains, highlighting a critical weakness not captured by existing single-task benchmarks. The framework provides a flexible, automatically verifiable testbed for advancing agent context-management capabilities.

title: Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs
comment: Accepted by ICIC 2026. 12 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong generation and reasoning performance, but the Transformer architecture incurs high inference cost. Existing acceleration methods often rely on task-specific fine-tuning or training from scratch, increasing adaptation cost and limiting cross-task usability. We present an Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework (AdaDSF) that converts off-the-shelf pre-trained LLMs into depth-sparse models without full retraining. Our key insight is that layers contribute unequally to representation transformation, characterized by the cosine similarity between layer input and output hidden states. Based on this, AdaDSF assigns layer-wise token retention ratios from similarity statistics, uses a lightweight router to select informative tokens at each layer, and introduces a feature-preserving alignment objective to match intermediate and final representations between sparse and dense models. On GPT-NeoX and Qwen2.5 over language modeling and commonsense reasoning, AdaDSF substantially reduces inference FLOPs while preserving performance close to dense counterparts. Under comparable sparsity, AdaDSF consistently yields smaller accuracy degradation than strong baselines including MoD, D-LLM, and DLO.

AI.tldr: AdaDSF converts pre-trained LLMs into depth-sparse models without retraining by using layer-wise token retention based on hidden state cosine similarity, a lightweight router, and a feature-preserving alignment objective, achieving substantial inference FLOP reduction with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based LLMs suffer from high inference cost, and existing acceleration methods require task-specific fine-tuning or training from scratch, which is expensive and limits cross-task generalization. A plug-and-play, retraining-free sparsification method is needed.
AI.method: AdaDSF (Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework) leverages the observation that layers contribute unequally to representation transformation, quantified by cosine similarity between layer input and output hidden states. It assigns layer-wise token retention ratios from similarity statistics, employs a lightweight router to select informative tokens at each layer, and uses a feature-preserving alignment objective to match intermediate and final representations between sparse and dense models — all without full retraining.
AI.result: On GPT-NeoX and Qwen2.5 across language modeling and commonsense reasoning, AdaDSF substantially reduces inference FLOPs while maintaining performance close to dense baselines. Under comparable sparsity, it consistently achieves smaller accuracy degradation than MoD, D-LLM, and DLO.
AI.conclusion: AdaDSF offers an effective, retraining-free approach to convert off-the-shelf LLMs into efficient depth-sparse models, enabling significant inference cost reduction with minimal performance drop, and outperforming existing sparse inference baselines.

title: The Human-AI Substitution Principle: When will you be replaced by AI in your organization?
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming organizations, raising a fundamental organizational and economic question: when will a human employee be replaced by AI? We present an analytical model for studying Human--AI Task Allocation (HAT) in hierarchical organizations. A central feature of the HAT model is that it formally encodes the economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI capability scaling. The HAT model allows us to derive how risk-adjusted costs, skills, organizational depth, deployment scale, strategic adaptation, and risk jointly determine when, where, why, and under what structural conditions human--AI replacement occurs. A key result is the Human--AI Substitution Principle, which provides a precise condition --- grounded in the formal asymmetry assumption --- under which AI replaces human labor. Building on this result, we show that AI adoption can produce abrupt workforce transitions, hybrid human--AI organizations, including cases where risk heterogeneity sustains human and AI roles without requiring a minimum-human-fraction constraint, and flatter managerial hierarchies with wider spans of control. The HAT model identifies structural conditions under which middle-management roles exhibit elevated vulnerability to automation, and shows that the vulnerability of highly skilled workers depends on a skill threshold shaped by organizational depth, baseline costs, and risk differentials. More broadly, the paper connects automation economics, organizational design, AI governance, and workforce planning into a unified theory of AI-driven organizational transformation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the Human-AI Task Allocation (HAT) model, an analytical framework for understanding when and how AI replaces human labor in hierarchical organizations. The model formalizes the economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI capability scaling, yielding a precise Human-AI Substitution Principle, predictions about abrupt workforce transitions, hybrid organizations, flatter hierarchies, and elevated automation vulnerability in middle management.
AI.motivation: As AI rapidly transforms organizations, a fundamental question arises: under what conditions does AI replace human employees? Existing frameworks lack a formal model that captures the structural asymmetry between how humans acquire skills (through costly learning) and how AI scales capabilities (through investment in computation/data). The authors seek to fill this gap with a rigorous analytical model that identifies the precise economic and organizational conditions governing human-AI replacement decisions.
AI.method: The authors develop the Human-AI Task Allocation (HAT) model, an analytical framework set within hierarchical organizations. The model's central feature is its formal encoding of the economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI capability scaling. Using this model, they derive how risk-adjusted costs, skills, organizational depth, deployment scale, strategic adaptation, and risk jointly determine replacement outcomes. From this, they derive key results including the Human-AI Substitution Principle.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) The Human-AI Substitution Principle, a precise condition grounded in formal asymmetry that determines when AI replaces human labor. (2) AI adoption can produce abrupt workforce transitions. (3) Hybrid human-AI organizations can emerge, with risk heterogeneity sustaining both roles without a minimum-human-fraction constraint. (4) AI leads to flatter managerial hierarchies with wider spans of control. (5) Middle-management roles show elevated vulnerability to automation. (6) Highly skilled workers' vulnerability depends on a skill threshold shaped by organizational depth, baseline costs, and risk differentials.
AI.conclusion: The paper synthesizes automation economics, organizational design, AI governance, and workforce planning into a unified theory of AI-driven organizational transformation. The HAT model provides a formal foundation for predicting and understanding the structural conditions under which AI substitutes for human labor across hierarchical levels.

title: GRADRAG: Cross-Component Prompt Adaptation for Coordinated Multi-Agent RAG
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems increasingly employ multiple LLM agents. Yet, most prior work optimizes components in isolation rather than coordinating improvements across the pipeline. We introduce GRADRAG, a framework for cross-component prompt adaptation that models the RAG pipeline as a computational graph and propagates structured evaluation feedback to update upstream agents. An Evaluator critiques downstream answers and supporting evidence, producing actionable feedback that a Prompt Optimizer uses to iteratively update adaptive agents, such as retrievers, graph constructors, and answerers. The Evaluator also triggers early stopping when the output is deemed satisfactory. We evaluate GRADRAG on the SQUALITY and QMSUM benchmarks under two retrieval paradigms: flat chunk-based retrieval using IRCoT-style query refinement (Trivedi et al., 2023), and graph-based retrieval that constructs and iteratively enriches an entity-relation graph from the document. Across both settings, GRADRAG consistently outperforms one-step refinement baselines that update only the final generator, achieving a 12-15 percentage point net preference margin in LLM-judged pairwise comparisons, with most gains realized within two refinement iterations.

AI.tldr: GRADRAG introduces a cross-component prompt optimization framework for multi-agent RAG systems that models the pipeline as a computational graph, propagates evaluation feedback upstream, and achieves 12–15 pp gains over single-step refinement baselines within two iterations.
AI.motivation: Most prior work on RAG systems optimizes individual components (retrievers, graph constructors, answer generators) in isolation, failing to coordinate improvements across the entire pipeline. This leaves significant performance gains unrealized due to a lack of cross-component feedback propagation.
AI.method: GRADRAG models the RAG pipeline as a computational graph where adaptive upstream agents (retrievers, graph constructors, answerers) are iteratively refined. An Evaluator critiques downstream answers and supporting evidence, producing structured, actionable feedback. A Prompt Optimizer then uses this feedback to update upstream agent prompts. The Evaluator also implements early stopping when outputs are satisfactory. The framework is evaluated under two retrieval paradigms: flat chunk-based retrieval with IRCoT-style query refinement, and graph-based retrieval that builds and enriches entity-relation graphs from documents.
AI.result: On SQUALITY and QMSUM benchmarks, GRADRAG consistently outperforms one-step refinement baselines that update only the final generator, achieving a 12–15 percentage point net preference margin in LLM-judged pairwise comparisons, with most gains realized within two refinement iterations.
AI.conclusion: Cross-component, iterative prompt adaptation via structured feedback propagation is highly effective for multi-agent RAG systems, yielding substantial gains over isolated component optimization with minimal iteration overhead.

title: Offline RL with Hierarchical Action Chunking
summary: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of learning general-purpose policies from static datasets. However, scaling these methods to long-horizon tasks remains a challenge due to the curse of horizon, where value estimation errors can compound through long chains of bootstrapped Bellman backups. Existing hierarchical approaches mitigate this by decomposing tasks into subgoals, yet they often rely on low-level controllers that suffer from myopic execution and biased value estimates. In this work, we propose Hierarchical Implicit Q-Chunking (HiQC), an offline goal-conditioned RL algorithm that combines high-level latent planning with low-level action chunking. By conditioning the low-level critic on temporally extended action sequences, HiQC enables unbiased k-step value backups, compressing the horizon at both the planning and execution levels. We theoretically demonstrate that this dual decomposition results in a tighter bound on value error under a bounded per-backup error model compared to standard hierarchy or flat chunking alone. Empirically, HiQC achieves the highest aggregate performance among the compared methods on the OGBench suite, with its largest gains on long-horizon navigation tasks such as humanoid-giant.

AI.tldr: HiQC combines high-level latent planning with low-level action chunking for offline goal-conditioned RL, reducing value estimation errors in long-horizon tasks through unbiased k-step backups and dual horizon compression.
AI.motivation: Scaling offline goal-conditioned RL to long-horizon tasks is hindered by the curse of horizon — value estimation errors compound through long chains of bootstrapped Bellman backups. Existing hierarchical methods using subgoal decomposition suffer from myopic low-level controllers and biased value estimates.
AI.method: HiQC integrates hierarchical latent planning with action chunking at the low level. The low-level critic is conditioned on temporally extended action sequences (chunks), enabling unbiased k-step value backups. This dual decomposition compresses the effective horizon at both planning and execution levels.
AI.result: Theoretically, HiQC yields a tighter bound on value error under bounded per-backup error compared to standard hierarchy or flat chunking. Empirically, HiQC achieves the highest aggregate performance on OGBench, with largest gains on long-horizon tasks like humanoid-giant.
AI.conclusion: Dual decomposition via hierarchical planning plus action chunking is an effective strategy for offline goal-conditioned RL, substantially mitigating horizon-induced value error accumulation in long-horizon settings.

title: Refusal-Gated Decoding: Preserving Refusal Behavior Under High-Temperature Sampling
summary: High-temperature sampling is one of the primary mechanisms for increasing diversity in LLMs. Recent advances in truncation-based sampling techniques have helped mitigate drawbacks of high-temperature sampling such as neural text degeneration, thereby enabling greater diversity in LLM outputs without sacrificing coherence. However, increasing the entropy of the token probability distribution via high temperatures has also been shown to weaken model guardrails by reducing the model's refusal response in the presence of harmful prompts. Despite the potential benefits of high-temperature sampling and the importance of maintaining model safety, there is a lack of existing solutions for maintaining the refusal behavior of LLMs under a higher entropy regime. To address this gap, we systematically study how temperature influences refusal behavior in LLMs and propose an efficient sequential decoding approach which preserves a model's greedy decoding refusal response at high temperatures while incurring minimal additional latency. Through extensive experiments, we show that our approach preserves 91-99% of the greedy decoding refusal behavior across three benchmark datasets without compromising the model's high-temperature response for safe prompts. Our work demonstrates how refusal behavior can be maintained in an efficient manner for applications which require high-temperature sampling.

AI.tldr: High-temperature sampling increases LLM output diversity but weakens safety guardrails by reducing refusal responses to harmful prompts. The authors systematically study this phenomenon and propose an efficient sequential decoding method that preserves 91-99% of greedy decoding refusal behavior at high temperatures with minimal latency overhead, without degrading safe-prompt responses.
AI.motivation: High-temperature sampling improves diversity in LLM generation, and truncation-based techniques have mitigated coherence issues. However, elevated temperature also raises the entropy of token probability distributions, which inadvertently weakens model guardrails — specifically reducing the model's likelihood of refusing harmful prompts. Despite the practical importance of both diversity and safety, no prior work addresses how to maintain refusal behavior under high-temperature regimes.
AI.method: The authors first conduct a systematic study of how temperature affects refusal behavior in LLMs. They then propose a sequential decoding approach that operates efficiently: during autoregressive generation, the method detects when the model would refuse under greedy decoding and intervenes to preserve that refusal response even at high temperatures, while otherwise allowing the high-temperature distribution to govern generation for safe prompts.
AI.result: The proposed approach preserves 91-99% of the greedy decoding refusal behavior across three benchmark datasets. Importantly, this is achieved without compromising the quality or diversity of model responses to safe prompts, and with minimal additional latency.
AI.conclusion: Refusal behavior can be effectively and efficiently maintained at high sampling temperatures, enabling applications that require both diverse outputs and robust safety guardrails. This work fills a critical gap at the intersection of LLM diversity and safety.

title: Phonetic forced alignment for low-resource language varieties: Model training and evaluation on Chengdu Mandarin
summary: Phonetic forced alignment is a key technique in phonetic research, yet existing alignment systems lack specialized models for low-resource language varieties. We address this by training text-dependent and text-independent aligners for Chengdu Mandarin using a 17-hour corpus and a custom G2P dictionary. We trained a text-dependent GMM-HMM model (Chengdu-MFA) and fine-tuned a pretrained audio encoder on frame classification with Chengdu-MFA's pseudo label for text-independent alignment (Chengdu-FC). Evaluation on an expert-annotated test set show that both methods significantly outperform Standard Mandarin baselines. Chengdu-MFA reduced average phone boundary differences by 31.8%, while Chengdu-FC achieved a 61.2% reduction. This work establishes a practical bootstrapping pipeline for developing accurate aligners for under-resourced varieties without labor- and time-intensive manual annotation.

AI.tldr: This paper develops two phonetic forced alignment systems—one text-dependent (GMM-HMM) and one text-independent (fine-tuned encoder)—for the low-resource Chengdu Mandarin variety, achieving substantial boundary error reductions (31.8% and 61.2%) over Standard Mandarin baselines using a bootstrapping pipeline that minimizes manual annotation.
AI.motivation: Existing phonetic forced alignment systems lack specialized models for low-resource language varieties, and manual annotation for such varieties is labor- and time-intensive. The authors aim to fill this gap for Chengdu Mandarin.
AI.method: The authors used a 17-hour Chengdu Mandarin corpus and a custom grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) dictionary. They trained a text-dependent GMM-HMM aligner (Chengdu-MFA) and then used its pseudo-labels to fine-tune a pretrained audio encoder on frame classification, producing a text-independent aligner (Chengdu-FC). Both were evaluated against expert-annotated test data and compared with Standard Mandarin baselines.
AI.result: Chengdu-MFA reduced average phone boundary differences by 31.8% relative to Standard Mandarin baselines. Chengdu-FC achieved a 61.2% reduction, substantially outperforming both the baseline and the text-dependent model.
AI.conclusion: The proposed bootstrapping pipeline—training a text-dependent model and distilling its outputs into a text-independent model—enables accurate forced alignment for under-resourced language varieties without requiring extensive manual annotation.

title: Multilevel Graph Wavelet Compressed Sensing with Scale-Aware Neural Recovery
summary: Scientific machine learning methods such as neural operators and physics-informed neural networks have advanced engineering applications and inverse problems, but their training typically requires large volumes of simulated data. This makes data preparation and model training expensive. We propose Graph Wavelet Compressed Sensing (GWCS), a learning-based framework for offline compression of graph signals by representing them as sparse, interpretable wavelet-domain representations using the spectral graph wavelet transform. The framework combines a nonparametric multilevel importance sampler, which retains high-energy wavelet coefficients within each scale for a given compression ratio, with a scale-aware graph neural network that reconstructs the signal from the sparse coefficients. We evaluate the proposed framework on synthetic approximately band-limited graph signals over random graphs and four PDE simulation datasets over meshes, which include Turbulent Radiative Layer, Viscoelastic Instability, Kolmogorov Flow, and Dynamic Stall. We compare against graph signal sampling methods and graph autoencoder baselines. Results demonstrate that the framework achieves high reconstruction fidelity and substantial data compression compared to existing benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Proposes GWCS, a framework that compresses graph signals offline by sparsely representing them in the spectral graph wavelet domain, using importance sampling for coefficient selection and a scale-aware GNN for reconstruction, achieving high fidelity on PDE simulation data.
AI.motivation: Training neural operators and physics-informed neural networks requires large volumes of simulated data, making data preparation and model training expensive. There is a need for effective offline compression of graph-structured simulation data to reduce storage and transmission costs while preserving reconstruction quality.
AI.method: GWCS uses the spectral graph wavelet transform to represent graph signals sparsely in the wavelet domain. A nonparametric multilevel importance sampler retains high-energy wavelet coefficients within each scale for a given compression ratio. A scale-aware graph neural network then reconstructs the original signal from the sparse wavelet coefficients.
AI.result: Evaluated on synthetic band-limited graph signals over random graphs and four PDE simulation datasets (Turbulent Radiative Layer, Viscoelastic Instability, Kolmogorov Flow, Dynamic Stall) over meshes. GWCS achieves high reconstruction fidelity and substantial data compression compared to graph signal sampling methods and graph autoencoder baselines.
AI.conclusion: GWCS provides an effective offline compression framework for graph signals, combining wavelet-domain sparsity with learned reconstruction, and outperforms existing benchmarks in both compression ratio and reconstruction quality on PDE simulation data.

title: Capital Markets LLM Reliability Score (CM-LRS): From Plausible to Bankable
comment: 23 pages. Resubmission of submit/7557765, which expired due to an arXiv system bug (confirmed in support ticket AH-199019); the overfull-box correction requested by moderators has been applied. Original submission held in moderation since 14 May 2026. Therefore, request priority review/approval
summary:
In capital-markets workflows the question is rarely whether a large language model can produce a fluent draft, but whether the draft is bankable: defensible in front of a counter-party or a regulator, with the documents in hand. Existing methods address parts of that gap: open-domain QA benchmarks reward surface accuracy, and finance benchmarks (FinanceBench, FinQA, ConvFinQA) advance document-grounded and numerical QA but evaluate at the question-answer layer rather than the workflow outputs practitioners defend.
  We introduce CM-LRS, a Capital Markets LLM Reliability Score, evaluating outputs at the workflow-output layer across seven dimensions: factual accuracy, evidence traceability, numerical consistency, workflow completeness, source discipline, decision usefulness, and reviewability/auditability. Each is scored 0-5 against a rubric anchored on signals reviewers in regulated settings use; the aggregate is tunable to the workflow.
  We demonstrate CM-LRS on five workflows (DCM transaction-terms extraction, precedent retrieval, issuer profile synthesis, M&A transaction-comparable reasoning, ECM transaction-terms extraction) over public SEC EDGAR filings, a public UK takeover release, and fictional synthetic supplements, scoring four models against four independent LLM judges spanning three model families.
  Three findings. First, the frontier closed-source models cluster within 0.22 points on four-judge averaged CM-LRS (Sonnet 4.6 = 4.31, Opus 4.7 = 4.30, GPT-5.5 = 4.09); all four judges place the open-weights baseline (Llama 3.3 70B = 3.15) last. Second, that gap concentrates on retrieval (2.23) and synthesis (2.15), not extraction (0.84). Third, Decision Usefulness shows the widest cross-model dispersion of any dimension (4.0 points on issuer profiling) and top-tier inter-judge agreement (mean r = 0.52).
  Plausibility is cheap. Bankability is the bar.

AI.tldr: CM-LRS introduces a Capital Markets LLM Reliability Score that evaluates LLM outputs at the workflow-output layer across seven dimensions (factual accuracy, evidence traceability, numerical consistency, workflow completeness, source discipline, decision usefulness, reviewability/auditability), finding frontier models cluster closely while the gap with open-weights models concentrates on retrieval and synthesis rather than extraction tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM evaluation methods (open-domain QA, FinanceBench, FinQA, ConvFinQA) assess surface accuracy or question-answer performance but fail to evaluate whether outputs are "bankable" — defensible to counterparties or regulators with supporting documentation. Capital markets workflows demand a higher standard than mere fluency or plausibility.
AI.method: The authors propose CM-LRS, scoring LLM outputs on a 0-5 rubric across seven dimensions anchored on signals used by reviewers in regulated settings. The aggregate score is tunable per workflow. Evaluation covers five capital markets workflows (DCM transaction-terms extraction, precedent retrieval, issuer profile synthesis, M&A transaction-comparable reasoning, ECM transaction-terms extraction) using public SEC EDGAR filings, a UK takeover release, and synthetic supplements, with four models scored by four independent LLM judges from three model families.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Frontier closed-source models cluster within 0.22 points (Sonnet 4.6=4.31, Opus 4.7=4.30, GPT-5.5=4.09), while Llama 3.3 70B (3.15) ranks last across all judges. (2) The performance gap concentrates on retrieval (2.23 gap) and synthesis (2.15 gap), not extraction (0.84 gap). (3) Decision Usefulness shows the widest cross-model dispersion (4.0 points on issuer profiling) with top-tier inter-judge agreement (mean r=0.52).
AI.conclusion: Plausibility is cheap; bankability is the bar. CM-LRS provides a structured, multi-dimensional framework for evaluating LLM reliability in capital markets workflows, revealing that frontier models converge on reliability while open-weights models lag primarily in retrieval and synthesis capabilities.

title: Position Bias is Hidden Behind Ceiling Effects: A Permutation Diagnostic for LLM Benchmarks
comment: 25 pages, 4 figures, 2 appendices. Code, data, and preregistration verification at https://github.com/TambaClan/inspect_permute. Companion paper: arXiv:2606.26185
summary: Position bias in multiple-choice LLM evaluation is widely cited as a confound in capability comparisons, but published measurements rely on single answer-order shuffles whose results confound the bias signal with content-level noise and sampling stochasticity. I introduce inspect_permute, an open-source extension to the inspect_ai evaluation framework that runs exhaustive answer-order permutations per question and reports the chi-squared / Cramer V signature of position bias with bootstrap confidence intervals. I apply the tool across four vendors (gpt-4o-mini, claude-haiku-4-5, gemini-2.5-flash, grok-3) on five MMLU subjects, 24,000 API calls under temperature-0 generation, with falsifier predictions pre-registered via a public SHA-256 hash before half the data was observed. Position bias turns out to be statistically detectable only within a roughly 60-95% base-accuracy Goldilocks zone. Below it, processing-load dominance swamps subject-specific signal; above it, ceiling effects compress the variance below the chi-squared test resolution. Detectable cells separate into two mechanism types: monotone A-to-D decrease (processing_load, in low-tier models) and non-monotone D-drop (content_ambiguity, in a narrow capability band). Standard MMLU places every frontier-tier model above the detection band, so absence of signal there should be read as not measurable, not unbiased. Together with the ceiling-effect characterisation in arXiv:2606.26185, this work brackets the detectable region of position-bias measurement and makes the field central question askable in a verifiable form. Package, data, preregistration under MIT.

AI.tldr: Position bias in LLM multiple-choice evaluation is only statistically detectable within a 60-95% accuracy "Goldilocks zone"; outside it, processing-load dominance (low accuracy) or ceiling effects (high accuracy) mask the signal. The author introduces inspect_permute, a tool for exhaustive permutation testing, and identifies two bias mechanisms: monotone A-to-D decrease and non-monotone D-drop.
AI.motivation: Existing measurements of position bias in LLM multiple-choice evaluations are confounded — they use single answer-order shuffles that mix genuine bias signal with content-level noise and sampling stochasticity. The field lacks a methodologically rigorous, statistically grounded way to detect and characterize position bias, and lacks understanding of the conditions under which such bias is measurable at all.
AI.method: The author developed inspect_permute, an open-source extension to the inspect_ai framework that performs exhaustive answer-order permutations per question (rather than single shuffles). Bias detection uses chi-squared tests and Cramér's V effect sizes with bootstrap confidence intervals. The study evaluates four models (GPT-4o-mini, Claude-Haiku-4.5, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Grok-3) across five MMLU subjects, totaling 24,000 API calls under temperature-0. A pre-registration protocol was used: falsifier predictions were hashed (SHA-256) and published before half the data was collected.
AI.result: Position bias is statistically detectable only in a 60–95% base-accuracy Goldilocks zone. Below this band, processing-load dominance overwhelms subject-specific signal; above it, ceiling effects compress variance below chi-squared test resolution. Two mechanistic types of bias emerged: (1) monotone A-to-D decrease associated with processing load, found in lower-tier models; (2) non-monotone D-drop associated with content ambiguity, found in a narrow capability band. Frontier-tier models on standard MMLU sit above the detection band, so absence of signal there indicates non-measurability rather than genuine unbiasedness.
AI.conclusion: Together with prior ceiling-effect characterization work (arXiv:2606.26185), this study brackets the detectable region of position-bias measurement. The absence of position-bias signal in frontier models on standard benchmarks should be interpreted as "not measurable" rather than evidence of unbiased behavior. The work enables the central question of position bias to be asked in a verifiable, statistically principled form. All artifacts are released under MIT license.

title: Profiling Lightweight Large Language Models
summary: Lightweight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed locally on personal computers and are expected to play a growing role in resource-constrained edge and mobile environments. In such settings, energy consumption, execution time, and memory usage directly affect practical usability, yet existing evaluations of LLM efficiency largely rely on proxy descriptors such as parameter count or FLOPs, often decoupled from task precision. This paper introduces a PTME-based experimental framework for the precision-aware profiling of lightweight LLM inference, jointly measuring Precision, execution Time, peak Memory usage, and Energy consumption through direct hardware-level measurements. The methodology is applied to a representative set of lightweight LLMs executed locally under edge-class resource envelopes on a controlled desktop platform, using benchmarks spanning code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-task understanding. We find that static proxy descriptors approximate inference cost well but fail to predict precision. Tightening the resource envelope increases cost without affecting precision, amplifying execution time more strongly than energy and penalizing larger models the most. Moreover, no single model dominates across all PTME dimensions, and a Pareto analysis reveals non-dominated configurations that would be hidden by accuracy-only or efficiency-only assessments, providing practical guidance for selecting models under different resource envelopes. These results show that selecting lightweight LLMs by size, FLOPs, latency, or accuracy alone can select the wrong deployment candidate; PTME profiling exposes configurations that preserve useful accuracy at lower physical cost.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PTME, a hardware-level profiling framework that jointly measures Precision, execution Time, peak Memory, and Energy for lightweight LLMs deployed locally. Applied to edge-class settings, results show that static metrics (parameter count, FLOPs) approximate cost but not accuracy; tightening resource constraints amplifies time more than energy; and Pareto-optimal configurations exist that are invisible to accuracy-only or efficiency-only evaluations.
AI.motivation: Lightweight LLMs are increasingly deployed on edge/mobile devices where energy, time, and memory directly impact usability. However, existing efficiency evaluations rely on proxy descriptors (parameter count, FLOPs) decoupled from task precision, failing to capture the real physical trade-offs between accuracy and resource consumption under constrained local execution.
AI.method: The authors propose PTME — an experimental framework for precision-aware profiling combining four directly measured hardware-level metrics: Precision (task accuracy), execution Time, peak Memory usage, and Energy consumption. The framework is applied to a representative set of lightweight LLMs running locally on a controlled desktop platform under edge-class resource envelopes, using benchmarks covering code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-task understanding.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) static proxies (size, FLOPs) correlate with inference cost but fail to predict precision; (2) tightening resource envelopes increases cost without improving precision, with execution time penalized more than energy, and larger models disproportionately affected; (3) no single model dominates all PTME dimensions; (4) Pareto analysis reveals non-dominated configurations hidden by accuracy-only or efficiency-only assessments.
AI.conclusion: Selecting lightweight LLMs based solely on size, FLOPs, latency, or accuracy risks choosing suboptimal deployment candidates. PTME profiling exposes configurations that retain useful accuracy at lower physical cost, providing practical guidance for model selection under diverse resource constraints.

title: Word meaning co-determines vowel-inherent spectral change. A corpus-based investigation of conversational Mandarin
summary: This study investigates vowel-inherent spectral change (VISC) in spontaneous conversational Mandarin. Using the generalized additive model and word embeddings from distributional semantics, we show that, when controlling for variables such as vowel duration, gender, speaker identity, co-articulation, vowel identity, and utterance position, vowel formant trajectory dynamics have word-specific components that are tied to their meaning in context: The F1 and F2 trajectories of words can be predicted from their contextualized embeddings with an accuracy that substantially exceeds a permutation baseline. Challenging modular cognitive models of speech production, these results indicate that, words' semantics co-determine the fine details of their articulation.

AI.tldr: Vowel formant trajectories in spontaneous Mandarin conversation carry word-specific information predictable from contextualized word embeddings, demonstrating that lexical semantics co-determines fine phonetic detail in articulation.
AI.motivation: To test whether vowel-inherent spectral change (VISC) — the dynamic formant trajectories within vowels — contains word-specific information tied to meaning, thereby challenging strictly modular cognitive models of speech production that separate phonetics from semantics.
AI.method: Generalized additive models (GAMs) were applied to acoustic data from spontaneous conversational Mandarin to control for vowel duration, gender, speaker identity, co-articulation, vowel identity, and utterance position. Word embeddings from distributional semantics were then used to predict F1 and F2 formant trajectories, with accuracy evaluated against a permutation baseline.
AI.result: F1 and F2 trajectory dynamics contain word-specific components predictable from contextualized embeddings at accuracy substantially exceeding a permutation baseline, even after controlling for all major phonetic and speaker-related confounds.
AI.conclusion: The results challenge modular cognitive models of speech production by showing that word meaning co-determines the fine articulatory details of vowels, supporting an integrated, non-modular relationship between semantics and phonetics.

title: TwistedMerge: Certified Higher-Order Diagnostics and Abstention for Model Merging
summary: Model merging combines independently trained or fine-tuned models, but pairwise alignability does not imply globally consistent alignment. We formulate merging as a finite descent problem in which checkpoints are local objects, alignment maps are transitions, and cycle products are residuals. TwistedMerge is a conservative certification pipeline that separates fixed-chart averaging, synchronization-removable gauge inconsistency, a certified central obstruction on a specified comparison complex, and nonabelian holonomy. A residual is promoted to a cohomology class only after inverse-consistency, coefficient-identification, centrality, and closure tests; otherwise the method abstains and returns an ordinary or synchronized fallback. We prove a constant-edge no-go result, frozen-complex three-way and predeclared-family error-control theorems, and a refinement test for comparison-complex sensitivity. A planted neural alignment defect is removed by cycle-consistent synchronization, showing that a nonzero cycle score alone is not a higher obstruction. Controlled central systems recover the predicted non-coboundary and projective-rank behavior, while noisy estimates move from certification to abstention without false lifts on the tested controls. A trained low-rank-adapter audit shows that naive factor averaging depends on the chosen GLr representative, whereas global factor synchronization and dense-delta SVD are stable. On natural checkpoint collections, cycle residuals do not predict merge degradation and no natural central or period-index class is certified. The results position descent theory as a falsifiable certification and abstention framework.

AI.tldr: TwistedMerge is a certification pipeline for model merging that uses descent theory to detect and classify obstructions to globally consistent alignment. It separates gauge inconsistency from genuine central obstructions, employs conservative tests before lifting residuals to cohomology classes, and demonstrates that cycle residuals in natural checkpoints do not predict merge degradation.
AI.motivation: Pairwise alignability between model checkpoints does not guarantee globally consistent alignment across multiple models. Existing merging methods lack a principled framework for detecting when merging will fail due to fundamental obstructions beyond simple gauge inconsistency. The work aims to provide a falsifiable certification and abstention framework grounded in descent theory.
AI.method: Model merging is formulated as a finite descent problem where checkpoints are local objects, alignment maps are transitions, and cycle products are residuals. TwistedMerge separates four components: (1) fixed-chart averaging, (2) synchronization-removable gauge inconsistency, (3) a certified central obstruction on a comparison complex, and (4) nonabelian holonomy. A residual is promoted to a cohomology class only after passing inverse-consistency, coefficient-identification, centrality, and closure tests; otherwise the method abstains with a fallback.
AI.result: The paper proves a constant-edge no-go result, frozen-complex three-way and predeclared-family error-control theorems, and a refinement test for sensitivity. A planted neural alignment defect is removed by cycle-consistent synchronization, demonstrating that a nonzero cycle score alone is not a higher obstruction. Controlled central systems recover predicted non-coboundary and projective-rank behavior. Noisy estimates trigger abstention without false lifts. A low-rank-adapter audit shows naive factor averaging is GLr-representation dependent, whereas global factor synchronization and dense-delta SVD are stable. On natural checkpoints, cycle residuals do not predict merge degradation and no natural central or period-index class is certified.
AI.conclusion: Descent theory provides a sound falsifiable certification and abstention framework for model merging. The conservative pipeline prevents false obstruction claims, and the empirical findings suggest that genuine higher-order obstructions may be rare in practice, positioning TwistedMerge as a diagnostic tool rather than a universal predictor of merge quality.

title: Enhancing Explainable Cardiac Diagnosis with Guide-Grounded Multimodal LLMs
summary: The electrocardiogram (ECG) is a cornerstone of cardiac as- sessment, yet clinical deployment of deep learning models remains con- strained by limited interpretability and the hallucination risk of large language models (LLMs). Existing CNN+Grad-CAM+multimodal LLM frameworks can generate ECG reports, but their explanations are often only weakly grounded in established diagnostic criteria, reducing trust- worthiness and reproducibility. We propose a guide-grounded multimodal framework that explicitly anchors report generation in curated clinical knowledge. A convolutional neural network (CNN) and Grad-CAM first produce class probabilities and class-specific heatmaps from 12-lead ECG images. In parallel, authoritative ECG textbooks and guideline materials are distilled offline into a structured ECG Interpretation Guide, which is injected as a fixed knowledge block for every sample. Conditioned on the ECG image, Grad-CAM overlay, CNN-derived fact pack, and the in- jected guide, a multimodal LLM generates structured diagnostic reports with guideline-consistent terminology and criteria usage. Experiments on the full PTB-XL test set demonstrate that guide grounding improves se- mantic quality and perceived consistency of generated reports while pre- serving competitive classification performance. In particular, our method increases the average BERTScore of generated impressions from 0.818 to 0.953 relative to a strong CNN+Grad-CAM+MLLM baseline, indicat- ing closer alignment with reference reports. These findings suggest that injecting a distilled interpretation guide into the multimodal prompting pipeline offers a practical pathway to reduce hallucinations and enhance the clinical plausibility of LLM-based ECG explanations, bringing ex- plainable cardiac diagnosis closer to real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: A guide-grounded multimodal framework for ECG report generation that injects distilled clinical knowledge into an LLM pipeline, improving BERTScore from 0.818 to 0.953 and reducing hallucinations.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models for ECG interpretation suffer from limited interpretability and LLM hallucination risks. Existing CNN+Grad-CAM+multimodal LLM frameworks produce weakly grounded explanations that lack alignment with clinical diagnostic criteria, undermining trustworthiness and reproducibility in real-world deployment.
AI.method: A CNN with Grad-CAM extracts class probabilities and heatmaps from 12-lead ECG images. In parallel, authoritative ECG textbooks and guidelines are distilled offline into a structured ECG Interpretation Guide, injected as a fixed knowledge block. A multimodal LLM, conditioned on the ECG image, Grad-CAM overlay, CNN-derived fact pack, and injected guide, generates structured diagnostic reports with guideline-consistent terminology.
AI.result: On the full PTB-XL test set, guide grounding increased average BERTScore from 0.818 to 0.953 compared to a CNN+Grad-CAM+MLLM baseline, while preserving competitive classification performance and improving semantic quality and perceived consistency.
AI.conclusion: Injecting a distilled interpretation guide into the multimodal prompting pipeline offers a practical pathway to reduce hallucinations and enhance clinical plausibility of LLM-based ECG explanations, bringing explainable cardiac diagnosis closer to real-world deployment.

title: MemTools: A Unified Research Framework for Interoperable Agent Memory
summary: While memory systems are essential for agent architectures, pervasive architectural fragmentation restricts systematic research. Existing implementations typically couple different stages of the memory lifecycle, entangle evaluation logic with specific datasets, and provide limited support for the management of heterogeneous memory types. We introduce MemTools, an interoperability research framework that decouples memory system components from their underlying deployment environments. MemTools standardizes the memory lifecycle through declarative data contracts, enabling the interchangeable assembly of components across different systems. It orthogonally separates benchmark datasets from execution protocols to facilitate controlled assessments. Furthermore, MemTools provides a unified computational interface for coordinating symbolic, neural, and multimodal memory representations within a shared runtime. Empirical evaluations on cross-system component integration, evaluation protocol reconfiguration, and heterogeneous memory coordination demonstrate that MemTools enables systematic isolation and analysis of memory design variables. These findings suggest that MemTools provides a practical and extensible infrastructure for advancing principled research on agent memory.

AI.tldr: MemTools is an interoperability framework that decouples agent memory system components via declarative data contracts, enabling modular assembly, standardized benchmarking, and unified coordination of symbolic, neural, and multimodal memory representations.
AI.motivation: Pervasive architectural fragmentation in agent memory systems restricts systematic research. Existing implementations couple memory lifecycle stages together, entangle evaluation with specific datasets, and offer limited support for heterogeneous memory types, making controlled experimentation difficult.
AI.method: MemTools introduces declarative data contracts to standardize the memory lifecycle, orthogonally separates benchmark datasets from execution protocols for controlled evaluation, and provides a unified computational interface for coordinating symbolic, neural, and multimodal memory within a shared runtime.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations demonstrate MemTools enables systematic isolation and analysis of memory design variables across three dimensions: cross-system component integration, evaluation protocol reconfiguration, and heterogeneous memory coordination.
AI.conclusion: MemTools provides a practical and extensible infrastructure that advances principled research on agent memory by enabling modular, interoperable, and systematically evaluable memory architectures.

title: Information-Theoretically Secure Aggregation for Lightweight Federated Learning: Resilient to Dropouts and Adversaries
summary: On-device federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving and personalized model training on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones and IoT nodes. To reduce communication cost, sign-based methods (e.g., signSGD) transmit one-bit gradients. However, exposing gradient signs makes them vulnerable to inference attacks, while existing secure aggregation schemes are often incompatible with such methods or incur significant computational and communication overhead. We propose a lightweight and information-theoretically secure aggregation framework tailored for sign-based FL. The framework securely computes the majority vote (MV) polynomial through single-round secure multiplication, ensuring end-to-end information-theoretic security under the honest-majority assumption while revealing only the final aggregated sign to the server. To enhance efficiency and scalability, we introduce two key techniques. First, inverse-form exponent reduction halves the effective MV polynomial degree, reducing both communication and computation costs. Second, we propose single-round secure multiplication, achieving linear offline complexity and storage with only a single online communication. Together, these techniques reduce online communication by up to 99.5% and latency by up to 85.7% compared to conventional approaches. Also, by leveraging inherent MDS-code-based decoding, the framework achieves robustness against both dropouts and adversarial behaviors, yielding accuracy gains of up to 20.65% and 10.74%, respectively. Overall, the proposed framework establishes a practical foundation for large-scale, low-latency, and information-theoretically secure aggregation in sign-based FL.

AI.tldr: A lightweight, information-theoretically secure aggregation framework for sign-based federated learning that uses single-round secure multiplication and inverse-form exponent reduction to achieve up to 99.5% communication reduction and robustness against dropouts and adversaries.
AI.motivation: Sign-based FL methods (e.g., signSGD) reduce communication by transmitting one-bit gradients, but exposing gradient signs enables inference attacks. Existing secure aggregation schemes are either incompatible with sign-based methods or impose heavy computational/communication overhead. There is a need for a lightweight, secure aggregation framework compatible with sign-based FL.
AI.method: The framework securely computes the majority vote (MV) polynomial via single-round secure multiplication under the honest-majority assumption, providing end-to-end information-theoretic security with only the final aggregated sign revealed. Two key innovations: (1) inverse-form exponent reduction that halves the effective MV polynomial degree, and (2) single-round secure multiplication with linear offline complexity/storage and only one online communication round. Robustness against dropouts and adversaries is achieved through inherent MDS-code-based decoding.
AI.result: Online communication reduced by up to 99.5% and latency by up to 85.7% versus conventional approaches. Accuracy gains of up to 20.65% under dropout conditions and 10.74% under adversarial behaviors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework establishes a practical foundation for large-scale, low-latency, information-theoretically secure aggregation in sign-based federated learning.

title: Efficient and Interpretable Body-Based Emotion Recognition with Lightweight Temporal Convolutional Networks
comment: Accepted at the 14th International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII 2026)
summary: Body-based emotion recognition is important for real-time affective systems, but graph-based skeleton models can be computationally expensive. This paper studies whether lightweight temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) can provide an efficient and interpretable alternative for body-based emotion classification. We evaluate a family of TCN models on DIEM-A and compare them with a graph-based time-series graph (G-TSG) baseline using accuracy, macro-F1, parameter count, and inference latency. Although G-TSG achieves the highest mean performance, TCN-Base remains within $1.58$ accuracy points and $1.25$ macro-F1 points while using $79.18\%$ fewer parameters and reducing classifier latency by approximately $12.5\times$. We also analyze body-region contributions using region-specific TCN models, zero-based occlusion, and G-TSG gradient saliency. The results show that upper-body motion provides the strongest standalone regional cue, that the usefulness of body regions varies across emotions, and that different interpretability methods capture distinct aspects of model behavior. These findings suggest that lightweight TCNs can support efficient body-based emotion recognition while also providing practical insight into how motion cues contribute to classification.

AI.tldr: Lightweight TCNs achieve competitive body-based emotion recognition accuracy (~1.5 points below graph-based baselines) while using ~79% fewer parameters and ~12.5× faster inference, with interpretability analyses revealing upper-body dominance and emotion-specific regional contributions.
AI.motivation: Graph-based skeleton models for body-based emotion recognition are computationally expensive, limiting real-time deployment. The authors investigate whether lightweight temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) can serve as an efficient, interpretable alternative without substantial performance degradation.
AI.method: A family of TCN architectures is evaluated on the DIEM-A dataset and compared against a graph-based time-series graph (G-TSG) baseline. Metrics include accuracy, macro-F1, parameter count, and inference latency. Interpretability is assessed via region-specific TCN models, zero-based occlusion analysis, and G-TSG gradient saliency to quantify body-region contributions per emotion.
AI.result: G-TSG achieves the highest mean accuracy and macro-F1, but TCN-Base trails by only 1.58 accuracy points and 1.25 macro-F1 points while using 79.18% fewer parameters and reducing classifier latency by ~12.5×. Upper-body motion is the strongest standalone regional cue. The informativeness of body regions varies by emotion, and different interpretability methods reveal distinct aspects of model behavior.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight TCNs offer a viable, efficient alternative for body-based emotion recognition with practical interpretability benefits. The emotion-dependent utility of body regions and method-specific interpretability insights provide actionable guidance for designing efficient affective computing systems.

title: Anti-Periodic Positional Encoding: Möbius Boundary Conditions Make In-Context Retrieval Reliable
summary: Möbius RoPE is a rotary positional encoding built on the anti-periodic frequency ladder $θ_i=π(2i+1)/N$: every rotation plane advances by an odd multiple of $π$ across the training context, so the positional holonomy is $-1$ and the two ends of the sequence are deterministically coupled through a closed-form Dirichlet "dipole"; to our knowledge this is the first anti-periodic boundary condition in positional encoding. We verify the theory numerically to $\sim 10^{-6}$ and pretrain 48 models spanning six 160M-class and three 410M-class arms (2B FineWeb-Edu tokens each; the hybrid arm puts Möbius frequencies on 25% of heads). Hybrid perplexity is unchanged (29.66 vs. 29.72), but needle-in-a-haystack retrieval becomes reliable: $90.3\pm5.7\%$ versus $63.3\pm31.4\%$ at context 512 ($n=6$ seeds), observed worst seed 86% versus 14%, robust variance tests $p=0.013$-$0.029$ (unadjusted), recurring at 410M (Levene $p=0.040$). Matched controls isolate the mechanism: an aperiodic ladder in the same frequency band reproduces none of the effect, and a periodic (holonomy $+1$) ladder only a fraction. Swapping trained models' frequency table back to standard RoPE (weights frozen) collapses retrieval, with damage concentrated on far needles: trained models depend on this long-range geometry. A NoPE arm is even more reliable at short context but pays a 13% perplexity tax and extrapolates worst; only the anti-periodic hybrid pairs baseline perplexity with a high reliability floor. The effect is scoped to single-needle retrieval within the training window; a one-line frequency swap thus provides zero-cost insurance against the retrieval seed lottery.

AI.tldr: Möbius RoPE introduces an anti-periodic positional encoding where rotation frequencies are odd multiples of π over the context length (holonomy −1), coupling sequence ends via a Dirichlet "dipole." A hybrid variant (25% Möbius heads) matches standard RoPE perplexity while dramatically stabilizing needle-in-a-haystack retrieval (90.3% vs. 63.3%), eliminating the "seed lottery" with a one-line frequency swap.
AI.motivation: Standard RoPE exhibits high variance in long-range retrieval tasks, where performance depends heavily on random seed — a "retrieval seed lottery." The authors seek a principled positional encoding modification that provides deterministic long-range coupling without degrading language modeling perplexity, effectively providing zero-cost insurance against retrieval failures.
AI.method: The authors propose Möbius RoPE, which uses an anti-periodic frequency ladder θᵢ = π(2i+1)/N, giving positional holonomy of −1 (a Möbius-like twist). This creates deterministic coupling between sequence ends via a closed-form Dirichlet "dipole" boundary condition. They pretrain 48 models (160M and 410M parameters, 2B tokens each) across six architecture arms: standard RoPE, Möbius RoPE, hybrid (25% Möbius heads), NoPE, aperiodic controls, and periodic (holonomy +1) controls. Evaluation uses needle-in-a-haystack retrieval with multiple seeds and statistical variance tests (Levene's test). They also perform ablation via post-hoc frequency table swapping.
AI.result: The hybrid arm achieves baseline perplexity (29.66 vs. 29.72 for standard RoPE) while increasing retrieval reliability from 63.3±31.4% to 90.3±5.7% at context 512 (n=6 seeds), with worst-seed performance improving from 14% to 86%. Variance reduction is statistically significant (p=0.013–0.029, unadjusted; Levene p=0.040 at 410M). Control arms confirm the anti-periodic mechanism is essential: aperiodic ladders show no effect, periodic ladders only partial. Swapping trained Möbius models back to standard frequencies collapses far-needle retrieval. NoPE excels at short context but suffers 13% perplexity degradation and poor extrapolation.
AI.conclusion: A one-line frequency swap to Möbius RoPE on a subset of attention heads provides zero-cost insurance against the retrieval seed lottery, matching baseline perplexity while establishing a high reliability floor for long-range retrieval within the training window. The effect is specific to anti-periodic boundary conditions (holonomy −1).

title: HierarchicalDAEW: Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted Graph Convolution with Evidential Uncertainty for Multi-Section Spatial Gene Expression Prediction from H&E Histology
summary: Spatial transcriptomics assays remain costly and technically demanding, restricting transcriptome-wide profiling to specialist settings and preventing routine clinical deployment. Predicting spatially resolved gene expression from H&E histology could close this gap, yet current methods largely ignore the underlying tissue architecture and rarely quantify how their predictions can be trusted. We introduce HierarchicalDAEW, a dual-graph architecture that addresses both gaps. On the spot graph, a Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted convolutional operator learns separate projections for inter-domain, intra-domain, and boundary edges derived from Leiden clustering, allowing the model to treat tissue heterogeneity as an explicit structural signal rather than an implicit one. A second gene-level graph then fuses protein-protein interaction priors from STRING-DB with tissue-specific co-expression through learned attention gating, propagating predictions from a landmark gene set to a broader gene panel. Reliability is handled through evidential uncertainty estimation, which produces far better calibrated confidence intervals than Monte Carlo dropout under identical conditions. Across six human Visium sections spanning breast, colorectal, prostate, and cerebellar tissue, and against thirteen published baselines, HierarchicalDAEW achieves the strongest correlation with ground-truth expression, with gains that hold up under multi-seed reproducibility checks and negative controls that rule out positional shortcuts. Ablations further confirm that both the domain-aware edge typing and the hierarchical depth are necessary to this improvement, and calibrated uncertainty estimates identify low-confidence predictions for pathologist review before clinical action.

AI.tldr: HierarchicalDAEW is a dual-graph architecture that predicts spatially resolved gene expression from H&E histology by explicitly modeling tissue heterogeneity via domain-aware edge-weighted convolutions and propagating predictions through a gene-level graph fusing PPI priors with co-expression, while providing calibrated uncertainty estimates via evidential deep learning.
AI.motivation: Spatial transcriptomics is costly and technically demanding, limiting clinical deployment. Predicting gene expression from routine H&E histology could bridge this gap, but existing methods (1) ignore underlying tissue architecture by treating all spatial relationships uniformly, and (2) lack calibrated uncertainty quantification, making predictions untrustworthy for clinical decision-making.
AI.method: HierarchicalDAEW employs a dual-graph architecture: (1) A spot-level graph where a Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted (DAEW) convolutional operator learns separate projections for inter-domain, intra-domain, and boundary edges derived from Leiden clustering, encoding tissue heterogeneity as explicit structural signal. (2) A gene-level graph that fuses STRING-DB protein-protein interaction priors with tissue-specific co-expression via learned attention gating, propagating predictions from landmark genes to a broader panel. Reliability is quantified through evidential uncertainty estimation, producing well-calibrated confidence intervals.
AI.result: Across six human Visium sections (breast, colorectal, prostate, cerebellar tissue) and against thirteen published baselines, HierarchicalDAEW achieved the strongest correlation with ground-truth expression. Gains persisted under multi-seed reproducibility checks and negative controls ruling out positional shortcuts. Ablations confirmed that domain-aware edge typing and hierarchical depth are both necessary, and calibrated uncertainty estimates successfully identified low-confidence predictions for pathologist review.
AI.conclusion: HierarchicalDAEW demonstrates that explicitly encoding tissue architecture via domain-aware graph convolutions and propagating through a hierarchically structured gene graph, combined with evidential uncertainty estimation, substantially improves both predictive accuracy and reliability of H&E-to-transcriptome prediction, advancing clinical feasibility.

title: Auditing Provenance Sensitivity in LLM Agent Action Selection
summary: LLM agents choose tools and arguments from context that mixes user requests, tool outputs, retrieved records, memory, and untrusted text. Evidence can be relevant without being authorized to determine a decision, so a correct action need not be grounded only in permitted evidence. We introduce a target-specific authorization audit that labels context factors separately for each tool and argument target. Its primary test holds the task, proposition, position, and policy fixed while changing only the proposition's source authority. We then test behavior when valid evidence is weakened and use context-subset interactions as a secondary localization diagnostic. Across 450 controlled next-action tasks and multiple open-weight LLM families, trusted and untrusted variants produce different actions in 5.4 percent of competing cases versus 1.7 percent of supporting cases. Under controlled degradation, unauthorized competition is retained in a full-correct, mixed-error, clean-correct pattern in 2.4 percent of comparisons, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 2.1 to 3.0 percent. These are controlled stress-set rates, not deployment prevalence. The models respond to textual source-authority cues, but this does not prevent untrusted evidence from influencing their actions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a target-specific authorization audit to test whether LLM agents improperly rely on untrusted evidence when choosing tools and arguments, finding that untrusted sources influence actions in ~5.4% of competing cases and that source-authority cues alone are insufficient to prevent this influence.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly operate in contexts where evidence comes from heterogeneous sources (user requests, tool outputs, retrieved records, memory, untrusted text), but not all evidence is authorized to determine decisions. The authors identify a critical gap: existing evaluations do not test whether agents respect source authorization when making tool and argument selections, opening the door to adversarial manipulation via untrusted inputs.
AI.method: The authors propose a target-specific authorization audit with: (1) a primary test that fixes task, proposition, position, and policy while varying only the proposition's source authority (trusted vs. untrusted); (2) a controlled degradation test where valid evidence is weakened; and (3) context-subset interactions as a secondary localization diagnostic. The study spans 450 controlled next-action tasks across multiple open-weight LLM families.
AI.result: Key findings: trusted and untrusted variants produce different actions in 5.4% of competing cases vs. 1.7% of supporting cases. Under controlled degradation, unauthorized competition persists in a full-correct, mixed-error, clean-correct pattern in 2.4% of comparisons (95% CI: 2.1–3.0%). The models respond to textual source-authority cues, but this does not prevent untrusted evidence from influencing their actions.
AI.conclusion: LLM agents exhibit measurable vulnerability to unauthorized evidence influence despite responding to source-authority cues. The proposed audit framework provides a systematic method for evaluating and diagnosing authorization failures in agentic systems, highlighting that textual labeling of trustworthiness is an insufficient safeguard.

title: An Evaluation Framework for Structured Audio Captions Validated by Controlled Perturbations
summary: Recent advancements in automated audio captioning (AAC) have shifted from monolithic sentence generation toward structured formats that explicitly disentangle distinct acoustic and semantic properties.
