However, evaluating this heterogeneous data remains a significant challenge. Existing caption metrics focus on flat textual outputs and fail to reliably assess multimodal attributes. To bridge this gap, we propose a multi-axis evaluation framework tailored for structured audio descriptions. Building on the AudioCards dataset, we evaluate outputs across five orthogonal axes: tag-sets, descriptions, logical reasoning, numeric measurements, and spectral profiles. Our approach combines Large Language Model (LLM) judges to capture semantic nuance with deterministic computational metrics to precisely measure acoustic deviations. To rigorously validate the reliability of this framework, we introduce a controlled perturbation testing protocol that injects typed, graded errors into groundtruth annotations. Our results demonstrate that this framework successfully distinguishes meaning-preserving paraphrases from genuine semantic and acoustic corruptions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-axis evaluation framework for structured audio captioning that combines LLM judges with deterministic metrics to assess outputs across five orthogonal axes, validated through a controlled perturbation testing protocol.
AI.motivation: Existing AAC evaluation metrics are designed for monolithic sentence-level captions and cannot reliably assess structured, multi-modal outputs that disentangle acoustic and semantic properties. There is a critical gap in evaluation methodology for heterogeneous audio descriptions.
AI.method: The authors propose a multi-axis evaluation framework operating over five orthogonal axes: tag-sets, descriptions, logical reasoning, numeric measurements, and spectral profiles. The framework pairs LLM-based judges (for semantic nuance) with deterministic computational metrics (for precise acoustic deviation measurement). Validation employs a controlled perturbation testing protocol that injects typed, graded errors into ground-truth annotations.
AI.result: The framework successfully distinguishes meaning-preserving paraphrases from genuine semantic and acoustic corruptions, demonstrating its reliability and discriminative power for structured audio caption evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-axis framework effectively bridges the evaluation gap for structured AAC outputs, offering a validated, reliable approach that captures both semantic subtlety and acoustic precision across heterogeneous description formats.

title: Multi-turn RL with Structural and Performance Aware Rewards for CUDA Kernel Generation
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful technique to enhance the reasoning capacity of LLMs for optimized code generation. However, existing RLVR approaches primarily rely on outcome-based signals such as correctness and speedup, overlooking performance-critical structural properties of programs that are essential for generating optimized code. In this work, we propose CudaPerf, a reflective RL framework that incorporates both verifiable execution rewards and structural code-aware rewards derived from parallelization features (e.g., memory coalescing, occupancy, Arithmatic Intensity, and synchronization patterns). CudaPerf operates in two stages: (1) an offline pairwise ranking module that learns to distinguish strong and weak program candidates via contrastive comparisons, and (2) an online RL training phase that jointly optimizes for correctness, performance, and structural efficiency through a unified reward signal. To further enhance learning, CudaPerf utilizes iterative refinement using execution feedback enabling progressive improvement of generated candidates. We also introduce a dataset comprising 2.9k C to CUDA and 1k PyTorch to CUDA programs, each paired with diverse input configurations and multiple CUDA implementations encompassing diverse optimization strategies. CudaPerf is evaluated across multiple benchmarks comprising both C to CUDA and PyTorch to CUDA transformations. Empirical findings suggest that CudaPerf significantly outperforms strong baselines, including Qwen-3-32B (for C to CUDA) and CUDA Agent (for PyTorch to CUDA) by achieving up to 5X & 3.32X improvements in speedup, and 17% & 7% improvements in correctness, respectively.

AI.tldr: CudaPerf is a reflective reinforcement learning framework for optimized CUDA code generation that combines verifiable execution rewards with structural code-aware rewards (memory coalescing, occupancy, arithmetic intensity, synchronization). It outperforms baselines like Qwen-3-32B and CUDA Agent by up to 5× speedup and 17% correctness gains.
AI.motivation: Existing RLVR approaches for code generation rely solely on outcome-based signals (correctness, speedup) and ignore performance-critical structural properties of programs (memory coalescing, occupancy, arithmetic intensity, synchronization patterns), limiting their ability to generate truly optimized code.
AI.method: CudaPerf uses a two-stage reflective RL framework: (1) an offline pairwise ranking module that learns to distinguish strong vs. weak program candidates through contrastive comparisons, and (2) an online RL training phase that jointly optimizes for correctness, performance, and structural efficiency via a unified reward signal. It also employs iterative refinement with execution feedback. A new dataset of 2.9k C→CUDA and 1k PyTorch→CUDA programs with diverse input configurations and multiple CUDA implementations is introduced.
AI.result: CudaPerf achieves up to 5× speedup improvement over Qwen-3-32B on C→CUDA and 3.32× over CUDA Agent on PyTorch→CUDA, along with 17% and 7% correctness improvements, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating structural code-aware rewards alongside verifiable execution rewards significantly enhances RL-based code optimization. The reflective RL design with pairwise contrastive ranking and iterative execution-feedback refinement proves effective for generating high-performance CUDA kernels.

title: Auditing Evidence Use in Medical LLM Diagnosis
summary: Medical LLMs are often evaluated by whether they select the correct diagnosis, but diagnostic accuracy alone does not show whether the model used the case evidence appropriately. We present a behavioral audit of evidence use in medical diagnosis. For each case, we decompose patient information into evidence units, score candidate diagnoses under controlled evidence subsets, and mine low-order interactions in diagnostic margins. Because medical evidence is diagnosis-relative, the audit separates interaction discovery from failure assignment: large or negative interactions can reflect plausible differential diagnosis, while suspicious interactions require robustness checks and clinical review. We evaluate five open-weight LLMs on DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase. Across datasets, faithful support and differential conflict or cancellation account for most interaction strength, showing that many evidence interactions are clinically plausible rather than failures. In a DDXPlus-focused blinded five-reviewer 130-item enriched review sample, invalid or shortcut-like cases concentrate in negated or absent findings and clinically local evidence. These results show that accuracy can hide candidate evidence-use failures and motivate role-aware audits for medical LLM evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a behavioral audit framework that decomposes medical LLM reasoning into evidence-unit interactions, revealing that diagnostic accuracy can mask inappropriate evidence use. The audit distinguishes clinically plausible differential-diagnosis interactions from genuine failures, finding that most interactions are faithful, while invalid/shortcut cases concentrate in negated/absent findings and localized clinical evidence.
AI.motivation: Diagnostic accuracy alone is insufficient for evaluating medical LLMs because it does not reveal whether the model arrives at the correct diagnosis through appropriate use of clinical evidence. A model may be right for the wrong reasons, relying on spurious shortcuts or ignoring critical findings. There is a need for auditing methods that assess the quality and plausibility of evidence use, not just correctness of the final output.
AI.method: The authors propose a behavioral audit framework with three components: (1) decomposing each case's patient information into atomic evidence units; (2) scoring candidate diagnoses under systematically controlled subsets of evidence to measure marginal contributions; (3) mining low-order (pairwise and three-way) interactions among evidence units in diagnostic margins. Crucially, the audit separates interaction discovery from failure assignment: large or negative interactions may reflect valid differential diagnosis reasoning, while suspicious interactions undergo robustness checks and blinded clinical review. Five open-weight LLMs are evaluated on DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase. A DDXPlus-focused blinded five-reviewer study on 130 enriched items provides expert validation.
AI.result: Across all three datasets, faithful support and differential conflict/cancellation account for the majority of interaction strength, indicating that most evidence interactions are clinically plausible rather than failures. Invalid or shortcut-like cases are concentrated in two categories: negated or absent findings, and clinically local evidence. The five-reviewer blinded assessment of the enriched sample confirms these patterns.
AI.conclusion: Accuracy-based evaluation of medical LLMs can conceal failures in evidence use. The proposed role-aware audit framework provides a complementary evaluation paradigm that distinguishes clinically valid interactions from genuine reasoning failures, enabling more rigorous assessment of model behavior in medical diagnosis.

title: Token Budget Saturation and Mechanistic Early Detection of Reasoning Non-Convergence in Chain-of-Thought Models
summary: Chain-of-thought reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B exhibit a bimodal convergence pattern: generations either terminate within a token budget (converged) or exhaust it without reaching a conclusion (non-converged). We characterize this phenomenon empirically, showing that converged generations achieve 90.3% accuracy on AIME 1983-2024 while non-converged ones achieve only 6.6%, with an overall convergence rate of 62.0%. We then ask whether this outcome is detectable early in the thinking chain using internal model representations. Training linear probes on hidden-state activations at token positions 50-300, we find that layer-20 activations at token 150 achieve AUC 0.608 (+-0.080, 5-fold CV), reliably above chance even at token 50. Activation probes consistently outperform behavioral baselines derived from token entropy and repetition statistics. A sweep-level permutation test yields p=0.063 (100,000 permutations), consistent with a modest signal that our sample size cannot confirm at conventional thresholds. These findings suggest that convergence fate is partially encoded in intermediate representations well before the generation ends, opening a path toward early-exit inference and adaptive compute allocation.

AI.tldr: Chain-of-thought reasoning models show a bimodal convergence pattern where "converged" generations are highly accurate (90.3%) and "non-converged" ones fail (6.6%). Linear probes on hidden-state activations can detect whether a generation will converge as early as token 50, with layer-20 activations at token 150 achieving AUC 0.608. This enables potential early-exit inference strategies.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B waste significant compute on generations that will never converge to a correct answer. The authors aim to determine whether the fate of a generation (converged vs. non-converged) is detectable early in the thinking process, which could enable adaptive compute allocation and early termination of doomed trajectories.
AI.method: The authors first empirically characterize the bimodal convergence pattern on AIME 1983-2024, measuring accuracy and convergence rates. They then train linear probes on hidden-state activations from token positions 50–300 to classify whether a generation will ultimately converge. These activation probes are compared against behavioral baselines (token entropy, repetition statistics). Statistical significance is assessed via a sweep-level permutation test (100,000 permutations).
AI.result: Converged generations achieve 90.3% accuracy vs. 6.6% for non-converged, with a 62.0% overall convergence rate. Layer-20 activations at token 150 yield AUC 0.608 (±0.080, 5-fold CV), above chance even at token 50. Activation probes consistently outperform behavioral baselines. The permutation test yields p=0.063, suggesting a modest but not conventionally significant signal.
AI.conclusion: Convergence fate is partially encoded in intermediate model representations well before generation ends. This opens the door to early-exit inference mechanisms and more adaptive compute allocation strategies for chain-of-thought reasoning models.

title: Three-Pronged Spectral Control for Federated Parameter Efficient Fine Tuning
summary: Federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables communication-efficient adaptation of large pretrained models on decentralized edge data, but it remains fragile under non-IID client heterogeneity. In low-rank adaptation (LoRA), different clients may learn locally useful but spectrally misaligned update subspaces, causing high-variance aggregation and poor global transfer. We propose TRISHUL, a spectral-control framework for robust federated PEFT. TRISHUL follows the FL no-raw-data-sharing setting but does not itself provide formal privacy guarantees. TRISHUL uses shared frozen multi-head low-rank bases to obtain algebraically exact aggregation of compact core updates, applies nuclear norm proximal shrinkage to suppress client-specific high-rank spectral components before upload, and allocates adaptation heads non-uniformly across layers using a concave water filling budget rule derived from pretrained layer capacity. Because shrinkage is performed only on small core matrices, TRISHUL adds negligible computation and no extra per-round communication over the underlying multi-head PEFT protocol. Across vision and language benchmarks, including CIFAR-100, SVHN, 20 Newsgroups, MRQA, and GLUE with LLaMA3.2-1B, TRISHUL improves convergence, stability, and final performance over federated LoRA baselines, with greater gains under stronger heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: TRISHUL proposes a spectral-control framework for robust federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) that uses shared frozen multi-head low-rank bases with algebraically exact aggregation, nuclear norm proximal shrinkage to suppress high-rank client-specific components, and a concave water-filling budget rule for non-uniform head allocation across layers.
AI.motivation: Federated PEFT with LoRA suffers under non-IID client heterogeneity because clients learn locally useful but spectrally misaligned update subspaces, leading to high-variance aggregation and poor global transfer. Existing approaches lack spectral regularization to control this misalignment.
AI.method: TRISHUL introduces three components: (1) shared frozen multi-head low-rank bases enabling algebraically exact aggregation of compact core updates; (2) nuclear norm proximal shrinkage applied to small core matrices before upload to suppress client-specific high-rank spectral components; (3) a concave water-filling budget rule derived from pretrained layer capacity that allocates adaptation heads non-uniformly across layers. Shrinkage operates only on small core matrices, adding negligible computation and zero extra per-round communication.
AI.result: TRISHUL improves convergence, stability, and final performance over federated LoRA baselines across vision (CIFAR-100, SVHN) and language benchmarks (20 Newsgroups, MRQA, GLUE with LLaMA3.2-1B), with greater gains under stronger data heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: Spectral control via shared bases, nuclear norm shrinkage, and capacity-aware head allocation effectively mitigates the fragility of federated PEFT under non-IID conditions, achieving robust performance without additional communication overhead.

title: Code Monitor Red Teaming for Public-Test-Passing Code
summary: Visible tests are a common gate for LLM-generated code, but passing them does not certify specification correctness. We study a deployment-like monitoring problem: after code has passed public tests, can a weaker LLM verifier identify the residual hidden bugs? We introduce Code Monitor Red Teaming, a monitor-red-teaming protocol that fixes a public-check information boundary while varying generator pressure, verifier scaffolding, and weak-to-strong capability. We instantiate it as CodeMonitorBench, spanning function-level, data-science, and workflow code. Across 71,000 generated candidates, 43,677 pass public tests and 23,081 of those fail hidden tests. Weak verifiers improve with scaffolding and model family, but still miss most hidden bugs at 5% false-positive rate. As a robustness stress test, adversarial public-test-overfit pressure lowers verifier AUROC and raises low-FPR miss rates in most cells. A GLM-5.1 verifier recovers part of the gap under the same evidence boundary; an inferability audit shows that remaining misses mix verifier failures with M1 evidence limits.

AI.tldr: Code Monitor Red Teaming evaluates whether weaker LLMs can detect hidden bugs in LLM-generated code that already passed public tests. Across 71K candidates, weak verifiers miss most hidden bugs at low false-positive rates, and adversarial overfitting to public tests further degrades performance.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated code that passes visible (public) tests may still contain hidden bugs that violate the full specification. Current evaluation practices rely on public test passing as a quality signal, but this does not guarantee correctness. The paper investigates a realistic deployment monitoring scenario: after code has cleared public tests, can a weaker, cost-effective LLM verifier identify residual bugs that only hidden tests would reveal?
AI.method: The authors introduce Code Monitor Red Teaming, a protocol that fixes a public-check information boundary and systematically varies three dimensions: (1) generator pressure (including an adversarial public-test-overfit condition), (2) verifier scaffolding (prompting strategies), and (3) weak-to-strong capability gaps between generator and verifier models. They instantiate this as CodeMonitorBench, covering function-level programming, data science, and workflow code. The evaluation spans 71,000 generated candidates, with monitoring performance measured via AUROC and miss rates at a 5% false-positive rate. An inferability audit further distinguishes verifier failures from fundamental evidence limits (M1).
AI.result: Of 71,000 generated code candidates, 43,677 passed public tests, yet 23,081 of those failed hidden tests — confirming the monitoring problem is substantial. Weak verifiers improved with better scaffolding and stronger model families but still missed most hidden bugs at the 5% FPR threshold. Under adversarial public-test-overfit pressure, verifier AUROC dropped and low-FPR miss rates increased across most experimental cells. A stronger GLM-5.1 verifier recovered part of the performance gap under the same evidence boundary. The inferability audit revealed that remaining misses stem from both verifier failures and genuine M1 evidence limits where public-test information alone is insufficient to deduce the hidden bug.
AI.conclusion: Passing public tests is an insufficient signal for code correctness, and current weak-verifier approaches cannot reliably detect hidden bugs at operationally acceptable false-positive rates. The Code Monitor Red Teaming framework provides a systematic methodology for stress-testing code monitoring pipelines, revealing that both verifier capability and fundamental information-boundary constraints limit detection. Stronger verifiers help but do not fully close the gap.

title: When Trivia Is Not Trivial: Everyday Knowledge Failures in Multilingual LLMs
summary: Quiz rooms, trivia nights, and quiz shows challenge human knowledge across a wide range of topics, from canonical facts to everyday culture. In this paper, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can perform competitively in such settings, using quiz-style questions to test them on both common and niche topics. We introduce TriviaRoomQA, a multilingual benchmark designed to evaluate everyday, culturally grounded, and long-tail knowledge across 288 topics. The benchmark contains 3,300 parallel multiple-choice questions in six European languages and additional 5,340 French-only questions for a more fine-grained case study. We evaluate 30 open-weight LLMs from European, Asian, and North American providers, covering models from 7 to 70B parameters. We find that models are strong on knowledge-intensive topics such as history, geography, and mathematics, but substantially weaker on everyday popular-culture topics such as celebrities, music, movies, and news. Moreover, model performance varies across languages even for the same underlying questions, suggesting that access to factual knowledge is not always language-independent. In sum, our dataset and experiments demonstrate an important knowledge gap which is not captured by existing academic-based saturated benchmarks.

AI.tldr: TriviaRoomQA is a multilingual benchmark of 3,300 parallel quiz-style questions across 6 European languages (plus 5,340 French-only questions) covering 288 topics. Evaluating 30 open-weight LLMs (7–70B), the study finds models excel on knowledge-intensive topics (history, geography, math) but struggle with popular culture (celebrities, music, movies). Performance varies across languages for identical questions, indicating factual knowledge access is not language-independent, revealing gaps missed by saturated academic benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks are academically oriented and saturated; they fail to capture everyday, culturally grounded, and long-tail knowledge that humans routinely demonstrate in quiz and trivia settings. The authors aim to test whether LLMs can perform competitively on such broad, practical knowledge across multiple languages.
AI.method: The authors introduce TriviaRoomQA, a multilingual multiple-choice benchmark spanning 288 topics with 3,300 parallel questions in six European languages and an additional 5,340 French-only questions for fine-grained analysis. They evaluate 30 open-weight LLMs (ranging from 7B to 70B parameters) from European, Asian, and North American providers, comparing performance across topics, languages, and model scales.
AI.result: LLMs perform well on knowledge-intensive topics (history, geography, mathematics) but significantly underperform on everyday popular-culture topics (celebrities, music, movies, news). Critically, model accuracy varies across languages for the same underlying questions, indicating that factual knowledge retrieval is not language-independent. This reveals a knowledge gap unaddressed by existing saturated academic benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: TriviaRoomQA exposes a critical weakness in current LLMs: their inability to consistently access factual knowledge across languages and their poor handling of popular-culture, everyday knowledge. The benchmark provides a more ecologically valid assessment of LLM knowledge, complementing traditional academic benchmarks and highlighting directions for improvement in multilingual and culturally grounded knowledge representation.

title: Best-of-Evidence: Best-of-N Selection under Partial Verification
summary: BoN improves model outputs by sampling several candidates and selecting one with a proxy score, but it assumes that complete candidates can be evaluated reliably. Many vision-language tasks instead provide only partial verification: a finding, span, value, region, or relation may be checkable even when no dependable whole-response verifier exists. Moreover, the same claim may recur across candidates with opposing stances, allowing one observation to support part of the pool and contradict another. We introduce Best-of-Evidence (BoE), an inference-time selection framework that keeps the BoN candidate pool fixed, represents reusable claims with a signed candidate--factor graph, and allocates a limited budget to evidence actions that can change the final choice. BoE formalizes selection under partial verification and provides a practical score-based controller, with the zero-budget case recovering the underlying BoN decision. Theoretically, we show that residual evidence capacity limits any evidence-driven improvement and that shared factor queries can achieve an O(log K) versus Θ(K) query separation in a factor-code model. Common-ledger experiments on four medical VQA settings show that BoE can improve fixed-pool selection and rescue some BoN failures when evidence is reliable, contrastive, and decision-relevant, while also revealing the channel-quality and candidate-generation limits that prevent universal gains.

AI.tldr: BoE extends Best-of-N sampling by introducing a signed candidate-factor graph and budgeted evidence actions, enabling inference-time selection under partial verification when whole-response evaluators are unavailable.
AI.motivation: Standard BoN assumes reliable whole-response evaluation, but many vision-language tasks only support partial verification (e.g., checking individual claims, spans, or relations). Furthermore, claims recur across candidates with opposing stances, meaning evidence can simultaneously support and contradict parts of the candidate pool. Existing methods cannot exploit this partial, reusable evidence structure during inference-time selection.
AI.method: BoE formalizes selection with a signed candidate-factor graph where claims are reusable factors linking candidates. A limited budget is allocated to "evidence actions" — queries that verify specific factors. A practical score-based controller decides which factors to probe. The framework nests BoN as the zero-budget special case. Theoretically, the authors prove residual evidence capacity bounds improvement and demonstrate an O(log K) vs. Θ(K) query separation using shared factor queries in a factor-code model.
AI.result: Experiments on four medical VQA settings show BoE improves fixed-pool selection and recovers some BoN failures when evidence is reliable, contrastive, and decision-relevant. However, gains are not universal — performance is bounded by channel quality and candidate-generation limits.
AI.conclusion: BoE offers a principled way to leverage partial, reusable verification signals during inference when global verifiers are absent. Its effectiveness depends critically on evidence quality and the diversity of the candidate pool, revealing fundamental limits that prevent uniform improvement.

title: Is Deep Research Reliable? Misleading Knowledge Induces False Conclusions
summary: Deep Research agents extend LLM-based assistants into long-horizon workflows involving planning, retrieval, evidence synthesis, and report generation, yet their reliability in open information environments remains underexplored. A key concern is whether apparently credible but factually misleading knowledge encountered in such environments can propagate through these workflows and be adopted as false conclusions in final reports. To study this failure mode, we introduce MisKnow-Agent, a framework for constructing and validating misleading knowledge for Deep Research tasks. MisKnow-Agent generates misleading instances with controllable authority levels and styles, yielding 5,933 quality-controlled instances built on DeepResearch Benchmark tasks. Extensive experiments across open-source and closed-source Deep Research agents show that even limited exposure to misleading knowledge can induce false-conclusion adoption in final reports, revealing a broad reliability vulnerability in current Deep Research agents. Although search-enabled verifier models consistently identify the retained instances as misleading during focused corpus validation, the same instances can still be adopted during long-horizon research, revealing a disconnect between focused verification and workflow-level evidence use. Finally, we evaluate pre- and post-research defenses, both individually and in combination, finding that all three configurations mitigate but do not fully prevent false-conclusion adoption. Our findings suggest that reliable Deep Research requires evidence verification and correction capabilities at both the model and framework levels, beyond improvements in planning, retrieval, evidence integration, or report-generation abilities.

AI.tldr: Introduces MisKnow-Agent, a framework to evaluate how misleading knowledge propagates through Deep Research agents' long-horizon workflows. Experiments on 5,933 instances across open and closed-source agents reveal a systemic vulnerability: apparently credible but false information is readily adopted into final reports, and existing defenses only partially mitigate this failure mode.
AI.motivation: Deep Research agents are increasingly deployed for complex, long-horizon tasks involving planning, retrieval, synthesis, and report generation. However, their reliability in open information environments—specifically their susceptibility to adopting and propagating misleading knowledge—remains underexplored. The authors aim to systematically characterize this failure mode.
AI.method: The authors propose MisKnow-Agent, a framework that generates controllable misleading knowledge instances (varying authority levels and stylistic properties) grounded in the DeepResearch Benchmark. They produce 5,933 quality-controlled instances and test them across multiple open-source and closed-source Deep Research agents. They also introduce search-enabled verifier models for focused corpus validation, and evaluate three defense configurations (pre-research, post-research, and combined) against false-conclusion adoption.
AI.result: Even limited exposure to misleading knowledge induces false-conclusion adoption in final reports across all tested agents. Search-enabled verifiers reliably identify misleading instances during focused validation, yet the same instances are still adopted during full long-horizon research—indicating a disconnect between focused verification and workflow-level evidence use. All three defense configurations mitigate but fail to fully prevent false-conclusion adoption.
AI.conclusion: Reliable Deep Research requires evidence verification and correction capabilities at both the model and framework levels, beyond incremental improvements in planning, retrieval, evidence integration, or report generation alone.

title: RUMBA: Russian User Memory Benchmark
summary: The ability to handle long-term memory in LLMs is becoming increasingly critical, yet existing benchmarks remain English-centric and rely on aggregate retrieval metrics, failing to capture interactions between long-range context, temporal information, and reasoning. To address this, we introduce RUMBA (Russian User Memory BenchmArk) - a new benchmark for long-term conversational memory that provides a fine-grained taxonomy of memory-centric question types and a unified methodology accounting for semantic type, session scope, temporal reasoning, and the explicitness of temporal expressions. RUMBA consists of timestamped user-assistant dialogues with QA pairs requiring retrieval, combination, and reasoning across sessions. While designed for Russian, we also provide an aligned English subset under the same methodology. We evaluate contemporary memory systems and long-context models, and show how RUMBA serves as a diagnostic tool to analyze model behavior across benchmark slices and identify strengths and failure modes of different memory mechanisms.

AI.tldr: RUMBA is a new benchmark (Russian + English) for evaluating long-term conversational memory in LLMs, featuring timestamped multi-session dialogues and a fine-grained taxonomy of memory-centric question types that captures semantic type, session scope, temporal reasoning, and temporal expression explicitness.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term memory benchmarks are English-centric and rely on coarse aggregate retrieval metrics, failing to capture the nuanced interplay between long-range context, temporal information, and reasoning. There is a need for a diagnostic tool that provides fine-grained analysis of model memory capabilities across multiple dimensions.
AI.method: The authors construct RUMBA, a benchmark of timestamped user-assistant dialogues spanning multiple sessions, paired with QA items. Questions are categorized along a unified taxonomy covering semantic type, session scope, temporal reasoning, and explicitness of temporal expressions. The benchmark is natively Russian but includes an aligned English subset. Contemporary memory systems and long-context models are evaluated against RUMBA, with performance analyzed across benchmark slices to diagnose strengths and failure modes.
AI.result: RUMBA serves as an effective diagnostic tool, revealing distinct performance patterns across different memory mechanisms when evaluated on fine-grained slices. The benchmark exposes specific strengths and failure modes of contemporary memory systems and long-context models that aggregate metrics would otherwise obscure.
AI.conclusion: RUMBA provides a more granular, linguistically diverse framework for evaluating long-term memory in LLMs, highlighting the importance of moving beyond aggregate metrics and English-only evaluation to understand how models handle temporal reasoning and cross-session information retrieval.

title: The Weight of Silence: A Causal Case for Weights Over the Scratchpad in Latent Chess Reasoning
comment: 28 pages, 5 figures, preprint also available at Zenodo: https://zenodo.org/records/21454434
summary: Latent, or silent, reasoning lets language models carry out intermediate computation in continuous vector space instead of words, and is widely assumed to function as an internal scratchpad the model actively consults during inference. Whether that assumption survives reinforcement learning has not been tested directly: existing causal analyses of latent reasoning are confined to math and logic tasks, and compare a model's reliance on its thoughts within a single checkpoint, never before and after an RL stage. We train a chess-playing model through a staged latent-reasoning curriculum followed by reinforcement learning, and find legality climbs monotonically to 61% (from a 48% pre-RL baseline) while checkmate confabulation is eliminated entirely. To locate this gain, we run a six-condition causal intervention suite on the same model before and after RL: substituting or adding matched noise to the latent thought vectors leaves performance unchanged, ablating them causes only mild degradation, and only exact-zero vectors cause collapse. This robustness gap is itself the finding: under exact-zero corruption, legality collapses to 1% pre-RL versus 9% post-RL, a gap that survives correction for testing across the full battery; milder conditions trend similarly without independently reaching significance. RL appears to add robustness to disruption, not reliance on thought content. These results push back against the field's default assumption that latent thoughts function as an actively consulted inference-time scratchpad, and instead indicate latent reasoning's principal effect here is shaping the model's parameters during training. We also demonstrate a working RL gain in chess, a domain outside the math and logic settings where multiple groups report the same latent-reasoning-plus-RL recipe failing to improve accuracy over SFT.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the prevailing assumption that latent reasoning serves as an actively consulted internal scratchpad during inference. Through a chess-playing experiment with RL, the authors find that RL improves performance but makes the model robust to latent thought disruption — suggesting latent reasoning primarily shapes parameters during training rather than functioning as a runtime workspace.
AI.motivation: The field widely assumes latent (continuous vector space) reasoning acts as an internal scratchpad that models actively consult during inference. However, existing causal analyses are limited to math/logic tasks and compare only within a single checkpoint, never before and after reinforcement learning. The authors aim to test whether this "active scratchpad" assumption survives RL training.
AI.method: The authors train a chess-playing language model using a staged latent-reasoning curriculum followed by reinforcement learning (RL). They then apply a six-condition causal intervention suite both before and after RL: substituting latent thought vectors, adding matched noise, ablating them, and injecting exact-zero vectors. Performance is measured via legality rate and checkmate confabulation.
AI.result: RL improves legality from 48% to 61% and eliminates checkmate confabulation. Under causal interventions: substituting or adding noise leaves performance unchanged; ablation causes only mild degradation; only exact-zero corruption causes collapse (1% pre-RL vs 9% post-RL). RL thus adds robustness to disruption rather than increasing reliance on thought content. The authors also demonstrate a working RL gain in chess — a domain where others have reported the latent-reasoning-plus-RL recipe failing.
AI.conclusion: The results push back against the default assumption that latent thoughts function as an actively consulted inference-time scratchpad. Instead, latent reasoning's principal effect appears to be shaping model parameters during training. The findings also establish chess as a domain where latent reasoning plus RL yields measurable gains, in contrast to prior negative reports in math/logic settings.

title: Source-Prior-Driven Selective Adaptation for Efficient Diffusion Model Finetuning
summary: Fine-tuning large diffusion models for new domains or styles involves a trade-off: improving target-specific generation often degrades the pretrained model's broad generative capability. Existing full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods typically handle this trade-off only implicitly. In this work, we propose a novel source-prior-driven selective adaptation method to efficiently fine-tune diffusion models, achieving a favorable trade-off. Our method relies on two key observations: (1) the loss of general generative capability is highly inconsistent across pretrained parameters, and (2) parameters that have a relatively small impact on the model's general generative capability remain structurally inconsistent across layers and parameter types. Motivated by these observations, we first learn a static mask to explicitly identify parameters better suited for downstream adaptation, and then construct structured update strategies for the selected subset. Experiments show that our method achieves a better adaptation-retention trade-off than existing strong baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a selective adaptation method for fine-tuning diffusion models that uses a learned static mask to identify which parameters to update, achieving a better trade-off between target-domain adaptation and retention of general generative capability.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning large diffusion models for new domains involves a fundamental trade-off: improving target-specific generation while preserving the pretrained model's broad generative capability. Existing full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods handle this trade-off only implicitly, without explicitly identifying which parameters should be adapted.
AI.method: A source-prior-driven selective adaptation method based on two key observations: (1) the loss of general generative capability varies significantly across pretrained parameters, and (2) parameters with minimal impact on general capability are structurally inconsistent across layers and types. The method first learns a static mask to explicitly identify parameters suited for downstream adaptation, then applies structured update strategies to the selected subset.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves a better adaptation-retention trade-off compared to existing strong baselines in experiments.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly identifying and selectively updating parameters via a learned static mask, the method effectively balances domain adaptation with preservation of pretrained generative capabilities, outperforming both full fine-tuning and existing parameter-efficient approaches.

title: What, Where, and How: Disentangling the Roles of Task, Language, and Model in Code Model Representations
comment: 16 pages, 11 figures, 6 tables. Code: https://github.com/piotrwilam/Atlas2x2 ; dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/piotrwilam/Atlas2x2
summary:
Do independently trained language models come to represent the same thing in the same way? We answer for code, extending a recently introduced concept-circuit extraction method to a 2x2 design -- Python and Rust crossed with Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and DeepSeek-Coder-V1-6.7B -- and measuring a complete inventory of grammatical concepts (58 Python, 57 Rust) identically in all four cells: the smallest design that separates what depends on the task, the language, and the model.
  The answer splits into three parts. What earns dedicated circuitry is set by the task: the models agree on which concepts receive circuits (Spearman $ρ$ = 0.638 for Python, 0.673 for Rust, both p < $10^{-7}$). Where those circuits sit is set by the model: Qwen processes concepts in a late band (~L17-19), DeepSeek at L6-7, for both languages. How circuits grow across layers is also set by the model: Qwen gives its atomic concepts an early spike that DeepSeek does not. "Are circuits universal?" thus has no single answer: yes for What, no for Where and How -- universality is a property of representational content, not of computational organisation.
  None of this structure was fixed in advance. The agreement could have landed anywhere between independence and identity; it lands at $ρ\approx 0.65$. Rust constructs receive 2-3x more concept-specific circuitry than their Python equivalents, in both models. Both models share neurons between the languages (6/7 and 7/7 paired constructs), DeepSeek 1.94x more than Qwen -- a direction no prior result predicts. And Qwen binds nine keywords of Rust's type-and-trait machinery into one tight neuron cluster (Jaccard 0.535 vs null 0.112, p < 0.001), a semantic dimension invisible in surface syntax. Ablation and linear probes confirm the circuits are functional.
  All claims are scoped to this 2x2; whether the per-model profile predicts a third model is the designed next test.

AI.tldr: A 2x2 study (Python/Rust × Qwen/DeepSeek code LMs) finds that which grammatical concepts get circuits is task-driven and universal across models, but where and how these circuits develop is model-specific. Rust concepts receive 2-3x more dedicated circuitry, models share neurons cross-linguistically, and Qwen clusters Rust's type-trait keywords into a semantic dimension absent from surface syntax.
AI.motivation: To determine whether independently trained language models converge on identical internal representations for the same concepts, specifically decomposing "universality of circuits" into three separable questions: What concepts are represented (content), Where in the network they are represented (layer location), and How they develop across layers (growth trajectory).
AI.method: A concept-circuit extraction method applied to a 2×2 factorial design: two programming languages (Python, Rust) × two code language models (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, DeepSeek-Coder-V1-6.7B). A complete inventory of grammatical concepts (58 Python, 57 Rust) is measured identically across all four cells. Ablation studies and linear probes validate circuit functionality. Cross-linguistic neuron sharing and Jaccard clustering analyses are performed.
AI.result: The "What" — which concepts earn circuits — shows strong cross-model agreement (Spearman ρ = 0.638 Python, 0.673 Rust, both p < 10⁻⁷). The "Where" — layer location — is model-dependent: Qwen uses a late band (~L17-19), DeepSeek at L6-7. The "How" — growth trajectory — is also model-specific: Qwen gives atomic concepts an early spike. Rust constructs receive 2-3× more concept-specific circuitry than Python equivalents. Both models share neurons across languages (6/7 and 7/7 paired constructs), with DeepSeek sharing 1.94× more. Qwen clusters nine Rust type-and-trait keywords into a tight neuron cluster (Jaccard 0.535 vs null 0.112, p < 0.001).
AI.conclusion: Circuit universality is not monolithic: it holds for representational content (What) but not for computational organization (Where and How). The findings reveal a previously unrecognized semantic dimension in Rust's type system and demonstrate that cross-linguistic neuron sharing is substantial and asymmetric between models. The next planned test is whether a model's profile predicts behavior in a third model.

title: ADABORD: a novel AdaBoost approach for ordinal classification
comment: 42 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Submitted to CS top tier journal
summary: Ordinal Classification (OC) deals with classification tasks where the classes follow a natural order. Despite the progress in OC, many existing approaches fail to fully leverage the ordinal information, treating the problem as nominal classification and thereby losing performance potential. In this work, ADABORD, an AdaBoost framework specifically designed for ordinal classification problems, is introduced. The ordinal nature of the classes is incorporated into two key components of the well-known AdaBoost algorithm: 1) the base estimator, where decision trees with the ordinal Gini splitting criterion are proposed; 2) the error function used to update sample weights at each stage and the weights of the classifier in the final ensemble model, given by the absolute ranked probability score, a measure that accounts for both the ordering and the distance between classes. ADABORD is extensively compared against seven state-of-the-art methods on the TOC-UCO repository, the largest benchmark collection for OC to date. The experimental results, supported by statistical analysis, show that ADABORD significantly outperforms competing methods, particularly on datasets with five or more classes, where the ordinal structure becomes more pronounced. Source code, along with all experimental protocols, is publicly available to ensure reproducibility and facilitate future research in OC.

AI.tldr: ADABORD is an AdaBoost framework tailored for ordinal classification that integrates ordinal information through a novel ordinal Gini splitting criterion for decision trees and an absolute ranked probability score for weight updates. It significantly outperforms seven state-of-the-art methods on the TOC-UCO benchmark, especially on datasets with five or more classes.
AI.motivation: Many existing ordinal classification methods treat the problem as nominal classification, failing to fully exploit the natural order among classes, which leads to suboptimal performance.
AI.method: ADABORD adapts AdaBoost with two ordinal-aware components: (1) decision tree base estimators using an ordinal Gini splitting criterion, and (2) sample and classifier weighting via the absolute ranked probability score, which captures both class ordering and inter-class distances.
AI.result: Extensive evaluation on the TOC-UCO repository (the largest OC benchmark) with statistical analysis shows ADABORD significantly outperforms seven competing state-of-the-art methods, with gains most pronounced on datasets having five or more classes.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating ordinal information directly into both the base learner and the ensemble weighting mechanism yields substantial performance improvements, and the public release of code and protocols aims to ensure reproducibility and spur further OC research.

title: Traceable Scholarship: Page Anchors and Ariadne's Thread for Humanistic Inquiry in the Age of Generative AI
comment: 33 pages, 8 tables. This paper proposes a normative and infrastructural framework for traceable, AI-assisted humanistic research and presents an auditable Kant case study
summary: Generative AI lets large language models produce scholarly-looking text within seconds, yet fluency does not equal valid explanation. The deepest risk is not factual error alone but the appearance that an explanation is already established without clear sources, page numbers, editions, or evidence. We liken the page anchor to Ariadne's thread: within the labyrinth of generative fluency, it is the thread that leads the scholar back to the source. This paper proposes Traceable Scholarship as the minimum normative condition for AI-assisted humanistic research, situating it across the three revolutions of knowledge infrastructure: print, digital, and generative AI. We introduce page anchors, dual page numbers, citation-first generation, NO_EVIDENCE, human verification, four-level compliance, and Scope Contract, and present AIH-Infra as a three-layer reference implementation: Contexture (document structuring), Open WebUI AIH-Infra (traceable knowledge base), and AIH-Infra MCP Server (agent gateway). A case study on a 29-volume Kant Akademie-Ausgabe knowledge base illustrates how traceability supports retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading. Traceability is not a software feature; it is the condition under which humanistic research can remain public and refutable in the age of generative AI.

AI.tldr: Proposes "Traceable Scholarship" as the minimum normative standard for AI-assisted humanities research, introducing page anchors, dual page numbers, citation-first generation, and a three-layer reference implementation (AIH-Infra), tested on a 29-volume Kant corpus to ensure scholarly work remains public, verifiable, and refutable.
AI.motivation: Generative AI produces fluent scholarly text rapidly, but fluency masks a critical failure: explanations appear authoritative without traceable sources, page numbers, editions, or evidence. The core risk is not mere factual error but the erosion of scholarly refutability — the appearance of established explanation without demonstrable provenance. The authors argue that without explicit traceability mechanisms, humanistic research loses its public, contestable character in the generative AI era.
AI.method: The paper develops "Traceable Scholarship" conceptually by situating it across three knowledge infrastructure revolutions (print, digital, generative AI), then operationalizes it through concrete mechanisms: page anchors (linking claims to specific source locations), dual page numbers (original + digital edition), citation-first generation (citations precede claims), NO_EVIDENCE markers (explicitly flagging unsupported statements), human verification protocols, four-level compliance grading, and a Scope Contract defining system boundaries. A three-layer reference implementation (AIH-Infra) is presented: Contexture (document structuring layer), Open WebUI AIH-Infra (traceable knowledge base), and AIH-Infra MCP Server (agent gateway). Validation uses a 29-volume Kant Akademie-Ausgabe knowledge base to demonstrate retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading.
AI.result: The Kant Akademie-Ausgabe case study (29 volumes) demonstrates that the traceability framework supports three key functions: (1) retrieval correction — identifying and remedying misattributed or hallucinated citations; (2) evidence grading — assigning confidence levels based on source proximity and verification status; and (3) judgment downgrading — explicitly reducing the epistemic status of claims lacking adequate anchors. The AIH-Infra implementation shows feasibility of the page anchor mechanism across a substantial humanities corpus.
AI.conclusion: Traceability is not a software feature but the foundational condition for humanistic research to remain public and refutable under generative AI. The page anchor, analogized to Ariadne's thread, provides the essential path back to sources within the labyrinth of machine fluency. Traceable Scholarship is proposed as the minimum normative condition for AI-assisted humanistic work, ensuring that scholarship retains its defining characteristic: the capacity for others to contest claims by following evidence back to its origin.

title: Artificial Epanorthosis: Why large language models overuse a classical rhetorical figure, and how to mitigate it
summary: A rhetorical figure that Cicero and Quintilian catalogued two thousand years ago reappears, systematically, in the text of large language models: epanorthosis, the self-correction of the specimen «This is not a course. It is a journey of transformation». This essay argues that the overuse is a trained disposition, driven mainly by a training distribution rich in promotional prose and by preference tuning (RLHF) that rewards confident, emphatic phrasing; the left-to-right nature of generation is an amplifier rather than the root cause. Building on evidence that models diverge from human rhetorical style, and on Fontanier's classification of epanorthosis as a figure of thought, it sets out a programme that scores the figure against genre-specific human baselines through an Epanorthosis Index (density relative to the human rate). A first measurement, on three sizes of one instruction-tuned model family, finds mis-calibration by register in both directions: the models overshoot in oratory (about twofold, near threefold in Italian, concentrated in the larger tiers) and undershoot in informal question-and-answer writing, while matching humans in argument, journalism, and encyclopedic prose. Three constructive contributions follow: a survey of mitigation techniques centred on lightweight LoRA adapters; a demonstration, in Italian, that a one-line instruction cuts the figure by half to nearly three-quarters and that a supervised-fine-tuning adapter removes it almost entirely, with a scaling coefficient that dials the reduction back onto the human rate; and the argument that the target is calibration to the human rate for each genre, not elimination. It closes on the stakes: the real risk is that we begin to write like the machines.

AI.tldr: LLMs systematically overuse epanorthosis (rhetorical self-correction, e.g., "This is not X. It is Y."), a figure catalogued by Cicero and Quintilian. The overuse stems from training on promotional prose and RLHF rewarding confident phrasing, not from left-to-right generation. The paper introduces an Epanorthosis Index to measure density against genre-specific human baselines, finding miscalibration (overshoot in oratory, undershoot in informal Q&A). Mitigation via LoRA adapters and instruction-based prompting is demonstrated, with the goal of calibration to human rates per genre, not elimination.
AI.motivation: The observation that LLMs systematically overuse the rhetorical figure of epanorthosis, diverging from human rhetorical style. The concern is not merely stylistic but substantive: the real risk is that humans begin to write like machines, losing authentic rhetorical diversity.
AI.method: 1) Identifying the phenomenon and arguing its root causes (training distribution rich in promotional prose + RLHF preference tuning, with left-to-right generation as amplifier). 2) Drawing on Fontanier's classification of epanorthosis as a figure of thought. 3) Proposing an Epanorthosis Index (density relative to human rate) and measuring it across three model sizes in one instruction-tuned family against genre-specific human baselines (oratory, informal Q&A, argument, journalism, encyclopedic prose). 4) Surveying mitigation via lightweight LoRA adapters. 5) Demonstrating in Italian that a one-line instruction reduces the figure by 50–75% and that supervised fine-tuning adapters remove it almost entirely, with a scaling coefficient to dial back to human rates.
AI.result: Miscalibration by register: models overshoot in oratory (~2×, ~3× in Italian, concentrated in larger tiers) and undershoot in informal Q&A writing, while matching human rates in argument, journalism, and encyclopedic prose. Mitigation results: one-line instruction cuts epanorthosis by half to nearly three-quarters; SFT adapter removes it almost entirely; a scaling coefficient enables dialing reduction back onto the human rate for each genre.
AI.conclusion: The target should be calibration to the human rate per genre, not elimination of the figure. The stakes are cultural and linguistic: overuse of epanorthosis in LLM output risks shaping human writing toward machine-like rhetorical patterns, eroding authentic stylistic diversity.

title: Weight-norm Criticality: A Mechanism for Loss Spikes Induced by the Normalization and Weight Decay
summary: Most explanations of training instability focus on \emph{learning-rate criticality}, typically characterized by the Edge of Stability, beyond which optimization becomes unstable. We argue that, in practical deep neural network training, there is an additional and often overlooked \emph{weight-norm criticality}. This criticality is induced by the interaction between normalization (which introduces scale-invariant components) and weight decay (which persistently shrinks parameter norms). As the weight decay coefficient increases, the norms of scale-invariant weights are progressively driven toward zero. Meanwhile, the sharpness of the loss landscape increases rapidly, destabilizing the optimization dynamics and resulting in abrupt loss spikes. This perspective provides a rationale for why weight penalties can improve generalization yet cannot be made arbitrarily strong: excessive decay drives scale-invariant weight norms past a critical boundary and destabilizes training. Our work provides a new mechanistic understanding of loss spikes through the lens of \emph{weight-norm criticality}. Moreover, \emph{weight-norm criticality} yields testable predictions that we validate empirically in networks with scale-invariant components, providing empirical support for the proposed mechanism.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a novel "weight-norm criticality" as a cause of training instability, distinct from learning-rate criticality. It arises from the interplay between normalization layers (scale invariance) and weight decay, where strong decay pushes scale-invariant weights toward zero, rapidly increasing loss landscape sharpness and causing abrupt loss spikes.
AI.motivation: Existing explanations of training instability focus on learning-rate criticality (Edge of Stability). The authors argue this is incomplete: practical DNN training exhibits instability driven by weight decay interacting with normalization layers, a mechanism that is overlooked and not well understood.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of how normalization introduces scale-invariant weight components, combined with the persistent shrinking effect of weight decay. As the weight decay coefficient increases, scale-invariant weight norms cross a critical boundary, rapidly increasing loss sharpness. The authors derive testable predictions from this framework and validate them empirically in networks with scale-invariant components (e.g., BatchNorm, LayerNorm).
AI.result: Weight-norm criticality provides a mechanistic explanation for abrupt loss spikes: excessive weight decay drives scale-invariant weight norms past a critical threshold, causing sharpness to spike and optimization to destabilize. This also explains why weight decay improves generalization but cannot be made arbitrarily strong. Empirical validation supports the proposed mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Training instability in deep networks has a dual origin: learning-rate criticality and weight-norm criticality. The latter emerges from normalization–weight decay interactions, offering a new lens to understand and predict loss spikes. This insight can guide practical choices of weight decay strength in training.

title: OPOD: On-Policy Omni Distillation
summary: Omni-modal models can handle text, images, and audio in one system, but improving all of these abilities together remains difficult. Training a single model on pooled multimodal data often fails to match models specialized for individual modalities. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a way to combine such specialists: the student generates a response, and a teacher evaluates that same response, so the student learns directly from behaviors it actually produces. Yet using several teachers can introduce competing guidance and improve one modality at the expense of another. We present On-Policy Omni Distillation (OPOD), which routes each student response to the matching text, image, or audio teacher. OPOD keeps teacher guidance only on tokens where the teacher assigns a higher probability than the student, adjusts the influence of each modality teacher independently during training, and asks the routed teacher to assess both the final answer and whether the reasoning supports the correct answer. Across twelve benchmarks and three backbone sizes, OPOD achieves the best average score at every scale, reaching 70.8, 51.7, and 46.2 and exceeding the strongest comparator by 2.1, 1.8, and 1.7 points. On the 30B model, it outperforms both the base model and a counterpart post-trained jointly on pooled multimodal data on all twelve benchmarks, and ranks first or second on eleven even when the individual specialists are included. The specialists are discarded after training, leaving one deployable omni-modal model. These results show that coordinating modality-specific teachers is an effective way to improve a shared model while maintaining cross-modal balance.

AI.tldr: OPOD introduces a training strategy for omni-modal models that routes student-generated responses to modality-specific teachers (text, image, audio), applies selective token-level guidance where the teacher outperforms the student, and independently modulates each teacher's influence. The resulting single model surpasses joint-training baselines and approaches specialist-level performance across all three modalities without retaining the teachers at deployment.
AI.motivation: Training a unified omni-modal model on pooled multimodal data typically underperforms modality-specific specialists. While on-policy distillation can leverage specialist teachers, using multiple teachers simultaneously introduces competing guidance that degrades cross-modal balance — improving one modality often harms others. The core problem is how to integrate multiple specialist teachers into a single student without destructive interference.
AI.method: OPOD has three key mechanisms: (1) **Response routing** — each student-generated response is routed to the corresponding modality-matched teacher (text→text teacher, image→image teacher, audio→audio teacher). (2) **Selective token-level distillation** — teacher guidance is applied only on tokens where the teacher assigns higher probability than the student, preventing the teacher from overwriting already-strong student predictions. (3) **Independent modality weighting** — the influence of each modality teacher is adjusted independently during training. Additionally, the teacher evaluates both the correctness of the final answer and whether the reasoning chain supports that answer.
AI.result: Across 12 benchmarks and 3 backbone sizes, OPOD achieves the best average scores at every scale: 70.8, 51.7, and 46.2, exceeding the strongest comparator by 2.1, 1.8, and 1.7 points respectively. On the 30B model, OPOD outperforms both the base model and a jointly post-trained counterpart on all 12 benchmarks, and ranks 1st or 2nd on 11 of 12 even when individual specialists are included in the comparison.
AI.conclusion: Coordinating modality-specific teachers via targeted routing, selective distillation, and independent weighting is an effective strategy for improving omni-modal models while preserving cross-modal balance. The specialists are discarded after training, yielding a single deployable model that approaches or exceeds specialist-level performance across text, image, and audio tasks.

title: DONDO: Open w2v-BERT Speech-Recognition Base Models for African Languages
summary: We present DONDO, a family of open, permissively licensed automatic speech recognition (ASR) base models for African languages, built on the w2v-BERT 2.0 self-supervised speech encoder. DONDO comprises twenty-one monolingual models and five multilingual models spanning twenty-seven language varieties across Ghana, Sierra Leone, Nigeria, Senegal, Kenya and Zimbabwe. Models are fine-tuned primarily on read speech drawn from religious texts, which offer broad, license-clear and orthographically consistent coverage for languages that otherwise lack transcribed audio. We describe a two-step (and, for one family, three-step) learning-rate-annealed fine-tuning procedure that first adapts a shared multilingual model at a high learning rate and then anneals it to recover, and in several cases surpass, strong monolingual baselines. We further describe a lightweight language-conditioning mechanism that injects a one-hot language identity as a sequence of prefix frames prepended to the acoustic features, allowing a single multilingual checkpoint to be steered to a target language at inference. Across the five multilingual families the annealed models reach average word error rates (WER) of 10-13%, closing most of the gap to monolingual models while covering many languages in a single checkpoint. All models are released on the Hugging Face KhayaAI organisation under the Apache-2.0 license (attribution only) so that others may fine-tune them freely, including for commercial use. We provide a conservative estimate that the languages covered are spoken by on the order of one hundred million first-language speakers, and by substantially more when second-language use is included.

AI.tldr: DONDO is a family of open-source ASR models for 27 African language varieties, built on w2v-BERT 2.0. Using read religious speech data, a two-step annealed fine-tuning procedure, and a lightweight language-conditioning mechanism, the multilingual models achieve 10-13% WER while approaching monolingual performance in a single checkpoint. All models are released under Apache-2.0.
AI.motivation: African languages suffer from a severe lack of transcribed audio data for ASR development. Existing resources are scarce, and licensing restrictions often limit commercial use. The authors leverage read speech from religious texts, which provide broad, license-clear, orthographically consistent coverage, to build openly licensed ASR models for under-resourced African languages.
AI.method: The work uses w2v-BERT 2.0 as the self-supervised speech encoder. A two-step (and in one case three-step) learning-rate-annealed fine-tuning procedure is employed: first adapting a shared multilingual model at a high learning rate, then annealing to recover monolingual performance. A lightweight language-conditioning mechanism injects a one-hot language identity as prefix frames prepended to acoustic features, enabling a single multilingual checkpoint to be steered to a target language at inference. Models include 21 monolingual and 5 multilingual variants across 27 language varieties from six African countries.
AI.result: The annealed multilingual models achieve average word error rates of 10-13% across the five multilingual families, closing most of the performance gap to monolingual baselines while covering many languages in a single checkpoint. In several cases, the annealed multilingual models surpass strong monolingual baselines. The languages covered are spoken by an estimated 100 million first-language speakers and substantially more including second-language use.
AI.conclusion: DONDO demonstrates that open, permissively licensed ASR models for under-resourced African languages can be built using religious-domain read speech. The annealed fine-tuning strategy with language conditioning enables compact multilingual models that rival monolingual performance. All models are publicly released under Apache-2.0 on Hugging Face, enabling both research and commercial downstream fine-tuning.

title: Regularized Optimization on Grassmann Manifold: Theory, Algorithm and Applications
summary: Spectral methods are among the most widely used techniques for community detection, clustering, and graph learning. Their performance, however, critically depends on the accurate estimation of the underlying spectral subspace and can deteriorate substantially in the presence of noise, outliers, or model perturbations. To address this limitation, we propose a Regularized Projection Matrix Approximation (RPMA) framework for robust estimation of rank-$K$ projection matrices. RPMA extends classical spectral projection by incorporating a regularization term, producing projection estimates that are more robust, sparse, and interpretable. We formulate the proposed model as an optimization problem on the manifold of rank-$K$ projection matrices and exploit its geometric equivalence to the Grassmann manifold. Based on this manifold characterization, we derive the first- and second-order optimality conditions, establish the local stability of the regularized leading eigenspace, and characterize the stability of the critical-point landscape under sufficiently small regularization. To efficiently solve the resulting nonconvex optimization problem, we develop a Riemannian gradient projection algorithm with backtracking line search, together with a more efficient Cayley--Sherman--Morrison--Woodbury (Cayley--SMW) gradient method that avoids repeated eigendecompositions. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that RPMA substantially improves the recovery accuracy of projection matrices and consistently outperforms conventional spectral projection methods for community detection and clustering under noisy environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RPMA, a regularized framework for robust rank-K projection matrix estimation on the Grassmann manifold, solved via Riemannian optimization with a Cayley-SMW gradient method, demonstrating superior performance in noisy community detection and clustering.
AI.motivation: Spectral methods for community detection and clustering rely heavily on accurate spectral subspace estimation, but their performance degrades significantly under noise, outliers, or model perturbations. Existing methods lack robustness in these challenging regimes.
AI.method: RPMA augments classical spectral projection with a regularization term and formulates the problem as optimization on the manifold of rank-K projection matrices (geometrically equivalent to the Grassmann manifold). The authors derive first- and second-order optimality conditions, establish local stability of the regularized leading eigenspace, and characterize the critical-point landscape under small regularization. Two algorithms are developed: a Riemannian gradient projection with backtracking line search, and a more efficient Cayley-Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury (Cayley-SMW) gradient method that avoids repeated eigendecompositions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that RPMA substantially improves projection matrix recovery accuracy and consistently outperforms conventional spectral projection methods for community detection and clustering under noisy conditions.
AI.conclusion: RPMA provides a theoretically grounded, computationally efficient approach to robust spectral subspace estimation, with strong empirical performance in noisy settings. The manifold-based formulation and Cayley-SMW algorithm make it both principled and practical.

title: Representing Entity Importance in AI Knowledge Systems: A Dual-Signal Framework of Audience Evaluation and Structural Authority
summary:
AI knowledge systems require representations of entity importance for retrieval, recommendation, evidence selection, and knowledge-intensive reasoning. Yet importance is often reduced to a single score derived from either human response or graph structure. Such compression may discard distinctions that matter when an AI system must choose among entities for different tasks. This study introduces an interpretable dual-signal representation in which each entity is characterized by an audience-evaluation dimension and a structural-authority dimension.
  The framework is evaluated using movie entities as an empirical validation domain. IMDb non-commercial datasets provide a rating-based audience ranking, Wikidata supports entity alignment, and English Wikipedia hyperlinks form the knowledge network on which PageRank estimates structural authority. Experiments on 482 entities and 13,690 directed relationships reveal a statistically significant but weak association between the two dimensions (Spearman rho = 0.2275, p < 0.001). Their overlap is only 10% in the top 10 and 34% in the top 100, while entity-level divergence occurs in both directions.
  The results show that audience evaluation and structural authority are non-redundant signals and should not automatically be collapsed into a single scalar notion of importance. The contribution is not a new ranking algorithm or learned embedding, but a minimal knowledge-representation framework and an empirical test of its dimensional necessity. The findings support task-aware AI knowledge systems that preserve distinct importance signals before applying context-specific selection or aggregation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a dual-signal importance representation for AI knowledge systems, separating audience evaluation from structural authority, and empirically demonstrates that these two dimensions are statistically distinct and should not be collapsed into a single importance score.
AI.motivation: Current AI knowledge systems typically reduce entity importance to a single scalar score (from human ratings or graph structure), but this compression discards meaningful distinctions needed when systems must select entities for different tasks. The authors argue that importance is multidimensional and that conflating audience-driven and structure-driven signals leads to information loss.
AI.method: The authors construct an interpretable dual-signal framework: (1) audience evaluation derived from IMDb ratings, and (2) structural authority estimated via PageRank on English Wikipedia hyperlink networks, with Wikidata for entity alignment. They evaluate 482 movie entities with 13,690 directed relationships, measuring association via Spearman rank correlation and analyzing overlap proportions in top-k rankings.
AI.result: The two dimensions show a statistically significant but weak correlation (Spearman rho = 0.2275, p < 0.001). Overlap between the dimensions is only 10% in the top 10 entities and 34% in the top 100. Entity-level divergence occurs bidirectionally, confirming the signals are largely non-redundant.
AI.conclusion: Audience evaluation and structural authority are non-redundant signals that should not be collapsed into a single scalar. The contribution is a minimal knowledge-representation framework and empirical evidence supporting task-aware AI systems that preserve distinct importance dimensions before downstream context-specific aggregation.

title: Counterfactual Explainability Framework With CycleGAN And Counterfactual-Classifier Alignnment Score for Retinal Disease Classification
summary: Automated detection of vision impairing retina-based ocular conditions from fundus images is important for early screening, timely referral and reducing dependency on specialist-only assessment, for which neural network-based deep learning (DL) models have been widely utilized. However, explainability of the DL frameworks remains a major bottleneck for clinical adoption, particularly when model decisions are not linked to retinal regions that are clinically meaningful. To address this issue, this study presents CounterFundus, a novel CycleGAN-driven counterfactual explainability framework, integrating EfficientNet-B5-based retinal disease detection with visually interpretable disease-to-normal fundus image translation. For each pathological image, the counterfactual yielded by the CycleGAN generator represents an estimated healthy counterpart and the resultant difference map is utilized to localize disease-associated retinal changes. Unlike conventional post-hoc saliency methods, CounterFundus provides counterfactual explanations through visually plausible disease-to-normal retinal translation. Thereafter, to quantify the spatial agreement between counterfactual difference maps and classifier saliency, the Counterfactual-Classifier Alignment Score (CCAS) is introduced, embedding Spearman correlation, binary IoU and pointing accuracy into a single assessment protocol. To this end, EigenCAM-aligned evaluation demonstrates that the generated counterfactual explanations remain spatially consistent with classifier-relevant retinal evidence across all CCAS dimensions. Along with that, ablation studies further confirm that CCAS-filtered counterfactual augmentation improves the downstream classification performance in fundus images, establishing CounterFundus as a clinically-grounded, explainable artificially intelligence (XAI) framework for retinal disease detection.

AI.tldr: CounterFundus is a CycleGAN-based counterfactual explainability framework for retinal disease detection that translates pathological fundus images to healthy counterparts, generating difference maps to localize disease regions. A novel Counterfactual-Classifier Alignment Score (CCAS) quantifies spatial agreement between counterfactual explanations and classifier saliency, with ablation studies confirming that CCAS-filtered counterfactual augmentation improves downstream classification performance.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models for retinal disease detection from fundus images lack explainability, as model decisions are not linked to clinically meaningful retinal regions. Post-hoc saliency methods are insufficient. There is a need for counterfactual explanations that show what a pathological image would look like if healthy, enabling clinically interpretable localization of disease-associated changes.
AI.method: CounterFundus integrates two components: (1) an EfficientNet-B5 classifier for retinal disease detection, and (2) a CycleGAN-based generator that translates pathological fundus images to estimated healthy counterparts (counterfactuals). Difference maps between original and counterfactual images localize disease-associated regions. The Counterfactual-Classifier Alignment Score (CCAS) is introduced as a unified metric combining Spearman correlation, binary IoU, and pointing accuracy to assess spatial agreement between counterfactual difference maps and EigenCAM classifier saliency maps. Ablation studies use CCAS-filtered counterfactual augmentation to improve classification.
AI.result: The generated counterfactual explanations are spatially consistent with classifier-relevant retinal evidence across all CCAS dimensions, as validated by EigenCAM-aligned evaluation. CCAS-filtered counterfactual augmentation improves downstream classification performance in fundus images.
