AI.conclusion: CounterFundus establishes a clinically-grounded explainable AI framework for retinal disease detection, offering visually plausible counterfactual explanations with validated spatial alignment to classifier evidence, thereby addressing a key barrier to clinical adoption of deep learning in ophthalmology.

title: SciExplore: Evaluating Autonomous Agents from Scientific Navigation to Information Integration
summary: Scientific research involves complex information-seeking and reasoning workflows across heterogeneous sources. However, existing benchmarks primarily emphasize general-domain retrieval or static scientific question answering, and therefore fail to assess key capabilities required in realistic scientific research workflows. We introduce SciExplore, a benchmark designed to evaluate scientific information-seeking and reasoning capabilities of LLMs and agents. SciExplore comprises four task types covering 103 expert-curated tasks across more than ten scientific disciplines: scientific database navigation, ambiguous literature retrieval, missing reference completion, and cross-source structured knowledge synthesis, which probe progressively higher-level abilities from entity-level reasoning and document-level identification to evidence-level grounding and domain-level synthesis. We evaluate over ten state-of-the-art LLMs and autonomous agents on SciExplore, revealing substantial performance gaps with performance degrading sharply as task complexity increases and extremely low accuracy on the most challenging structured synthesis tasks. These results highlight significant limitations of current models and agents in realistic scientific information-seeking scenarios.

AI.tldr: SciExplore is a benchmark with 103 expert-curated tasks across four task types that evaluate LLMs and agents on realistic scientific information-seeking and reasoning, revealing sharp performance degradation as task complexity increases and near-zero accuracy on the hardest structured synthesis tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks focus on general-domain retrieval or static scientific QA, failing to capture the complex, multi-source information-seeking and reasoning workflows inherent to real scientific research. There is a need for a benchmark that probes progressively higher-level capabilities required in authentic scientific workflows.
AI.method: The authors construct SciExplore, a benchmark spanning 10+ scientific disciplines with 103 expert-curated tasks across four hierarchical task types: (1) scientific database navigation (entity-level reasoning), (2) ambiguous literature retrieval (document-level identification), (3) missing reference completion (evidence-level grounding), and (4) cross-source structured knowledge synthesis (domain-level synthesis). Over ten state-of-the-art LLMs and autonomous agents are evaluated on this benchmark.
AI.result: Performance degrades sharply as task complexity increases across all evaluated models. On the most challenging cross-source structured knowledge synthesis tasks, models achieve extremely low accuracy, revealing substantial limitations of current LLMs and agents in realistic scientific information-seeking scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs and autonomous agents exhibit significant capability gaps in realistic scientific information-seeking and reasoning workflows, particularly as tasks demand higher-level synthesis and cross-source grounding. SciExplore provides a rigorous evaluation framework to guide future research toward addressing these deficiencies.

title: Surprisal Theory is Tautological (without Rational Grounding)
summary: Surprisal theory holds that the human processing difficulty of a linguistic unit in context is an affine function of its surprisal under some language model. I argue this claim is a tautology without further constraint: for any non-negative difficulty measure over units in context, there exists a language model whose surprisal is an affine function of it under mild technical conditions. Therefore, because any pattern of difficulty is consistent with some language model, without an additional constraint on the language model, surprisal theory makes no falsifiable predictions. The tautology was long obscured by an assumption implicit in two decades of psycholinguistic work---that the relevant language model is the distribution that generated the training corpus, so that improving corpus fit improves predictions of human behavior. Recent empirical work has undermined this assumption, demonstrating that better corpus models can be worse predictors of processing difficulty. I conclude that breaking the tautology requires a rationalist intervention, i.e., the relevant language model must be derived from a non-empirically motivated model of the comprehender, which could be based on, for instance, memory constraints or processing goals, and that, thus, does not depend on the behavioral data surprisal theory is meant to explain.

AI.tldr: Surprisal theory is tautological unless the language model is constrained by rational principles independent of the behavioral data it aims to explain; merely improving corpus fit is insufficient and can even worsen predictions.
AI.motivation: The author aims to expose a fundamental logical flaw in surprisal theory as commonly applied in psycholinguistics: without an a priori constraint on the language model, the theory is unfalsifiable because any difficulty pattern can be accommodated by some model.
AI.method: This is a theoretical argument. The author formally demonstrates that for any non-negative difficulty measure, there exists a language model whose surprisal is an affine function of it (under mild technical conditions). The argument then traces how an implicit assumption—that the relevant model is the corpus-generating distribution—obscured this tautology, and cites recent empirical evidence showing that better corpus models can predict human difficulty worse, undermining that assumption.
AI.result: The paper establishes that surprisal theory, without additional constraints, is a tautology. The empirical finding that improved language models can yield poorer fits to human processing data is presented as evidence against the corpus-as-ground-truth assumption, reinforcing the need for a non-empirical constraint.
AI.conclusion: To become falsifiable, surprisal theory requires a "rationalist intervention": the language model must be derived from theory-driven principles about the comprehender (e.g., memory constraints, processing goals) that are independent of the behavioral data the theory seeks to explain.

title: From Evaluation to Optimisation: Hierarchy-Aware Training Signals for CWE Prediction in Python
summary: The original ALPHA benchmark introduced a taxonomy-aware penalty for evaluating CWE-level vulnerability prediction in Python and proposed that the penalty could theoretically also serve as a training signal. This paper provides that validation. We compare three delivery mechanisms: supervised fine-tuning, a dual-head classification loss, and reinforcement learning with a dense reward derived from the normalised penalty. We find that supervised approaches consistently regress below the zero-shot baseline under distribution shift, while GRPO succeeds. Our best policy reduces the cumulative ALPHA penalty of Qwen2.5-Coder-7B on Security Hardening and Adversarial Testing (SVEN) dataset by 27.9% under greedy decoding, and by 25.5% under sampled decoding(p = 0.005, Welch's t-test), reaching statistical parity with its 4.5x larger zero-shot teacher. We conclude that the value of a hierarchical penalty as a training signal depends largely on the directness of its delivery.

AI.tldr: Validates the ALPHA benchmark's hierarchical CWE taxonomy penalty as a training signal for vulnerability prediction. Supervised fine-tuning and dual-head loss underperform zero-shot baselines under distribution shift, while GRPO reinforcement learning with a dense penalty-derived reward succeeds, reducing cumulative penalty by up to 27.9% and matching a 4.5× larger teacher model.
AI.motivation: The original ALPHA benchmark proposed that its taxonomy-aware CWE penalty could serve as a training signal, but this was never empirically validated. This paper aims to test whether the hierarchical penalty can effectively guide model training for improved vulnerability prediction.
AI.method: Three delivery mechanisms are compared for incorporating the ALPHA penalty as a training signal: (1) supervised fine-tuning, (2) a dual-head classification loss, and (3) Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) reinforcement learning using a dense reward derived from the normalized ALPHA penalty. Evaluation uses the Qwen2.5-Coder-7B model on the Security Hardening and Adversarial Testing (SVEN) dataset, with both greedy and sampled decoding, assessed via Welch's t-test.
AI.result: Supervised approaches consistently perform worse than the zero-shot baseline under distribution shift. GRPO succeeds: the best policy reduces cumulative ALPHA penalty by 27.9% (greedy decoding) and 25.5% (sampled decoding) with statistical significance (p = 0.005). This matches the performance of a 4.5× larger zero-shot teacher model.
AI.conclusion: The value of a hierarchical penalty as a training signal depends primarily on the directness of its delivery. Indirect methods (supervised losses) fail, while direct optimization via GRPO yields statistically significant gains, validating the penalty's utility when applied through reinforcement learning.

title: Clustered Edge Intelligence: Beyond Just Convergence of Edge Computing and AI
comment: This is not survey or position paper. 28 Pages, 10 figures, 4 Tables, 108 references, Under review, submitted to Information Fusion
summary: We are moving from an information age to the age of intelligence. A decade, or possibly less than that, data will not be the gold anymore rather the derived intelligence out of the data and the information we posses from the edge of the network. Existing Edge Intelligence research focuses mainly on two directions: using AI for edge resource management and deploying lightweight AI models on edge devices. However, existing edge computing research lacks an intelligence-centric framework in which derived intelligence is treated as a first-class, independently manageable entity that can be described, discovered, observed, shared, reused, and dynamically clustered across heterogeneous edge devices and applications. To address these research gaps, we introduced Clustered Edge Intelligence, a visionary intelligence-centric approach. The aim of CEI is to make intelligence a shareable and reusable first-class entity that can be independently represented, discovered, observed, exchanged, and managed across the distributed edge-cloud continuum. We present a three layer CEI architecture and examine enabling technologies and research dimensions, including intelligence inventories, semantic knowledge representation, communication, discoverability, observability, lifecycle automation, clustering mechanisms, marketplaces, interoperability, and standardization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Clustered Edge Intelligence (CEI), a novel framework that elevates derived intelligence to a first-class, independently manageable entity across the edge-cloud continuum, enabling it to be described, discovered, shared, reused, and dynamically clustered. A three-layer architecture is presented alongside key enabling technologies and research dimensions.
AI.motivation: Existing Edge Intelligence research is limited to two narrow directions — using AI for edge resource management and deploying lightweight AI models on devices. There is no framework that treats derived intelligence itself as a first-class, shareable, and reusable entity with independent lifecycle management across heterogeneous edge environments.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Clustered Edge Intelligence (CEI) vision and propose a three-layer architecture. They systematically examine enabling technologies and research dimensions including intelligence inventories, semantic knowledge representation, communication, discoverability, observability, lifecycle automation, clustering mechanisms, marketplaces, interoperability, and standardization.
AI.result: The paper delivers a conceptual architecture and a structured research agenda for CEI, identifying key technological enablers and open research dimensions required to realize intelligence as an independently manageable, first-class entity across the edge-cloud continuum.
AI.conclusion: Clustered Edge Intelligence represents a necessary paradigm shift toward an intelligence-centric edge ecosystem, where derived intelligence becomes a reusable, discoverable, and dynamically clusterable asset, moving beyond data-centric computing to true intelligence-driven distributed systems.

title: Spectral Transformation for Layer-wise Global Rank Discovery in Federated LoRA for Vision Transformers
comment: Accepted at ECML-PKDD 2026 (Research Track). This is the submitted version, prior to peer review. Code: https://github.com/DASS-Lab-Group/SpecTraL
summary: Fine-tuning Vision Transformers (ViTs) with low-rank adapters (LoRA) promises better communication efficiency under federated setup, yet existing aggregation strategies face fundamental limitations. Independently averaging these LoRA factors is mathematically inconsistent, introducing cross-term aggregation error. In contrast, approaches that preserve heterogeneous client ranks by concatenating local adapters on the server substantially increase download cost and often require merging global LoRA updates into pretrained weights on the clients, causing reinitialization lag and unstable convergence. Other approaches further increase server-side overhead by reconstructing dense weight updates or training auxiliary models to refine aggregation error. In this work, we propose SpecTraL, spectral transformation for layer-wise global rank discovery, that resolves these challenges within a unified design. SpecTraL stacks local LoRA modules from clients and performs orthonormal Householder Transformation of the stacked adapters directly in the low-rank latent space, eliminating dense reconstruction of the global update and any auxiliary refinement on the server. By leveraging the Spiked Covariance Model from Random Matrix Theory, SpecTraL analytically separates the global consensus signal from non-IID noise, discovering optimal layer-wise global ranks without manual hyperparameter tuning. To match local ranks in subsequent rounds, we introduce a padding-aware initialization framework that lets clients incorporate residual LoRA dimensions without re-merging them into the pre-trained base model. Experiments on federated fine-tuning of ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 over DomainNet and NICO++ demonstrate improved accuracy-communication trade-offs, reduced server computation, and elimination of hyperparameter search for rank selection. Our code is available at https://github.com/DASS-Lab-Group/SpecTraL

AI.tldr: SpecTraL proposes a federated LoRA fine-tuning method for ViTs that uses Householder transformations in low-rank latent space and Random Matrix Theory to discover optimal global ranks, eliminating aggregation errors and manual rank tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing federated LoRA aggregation strategies suffer from: (1) mathematically inconsistent averaging of LoRA factors causing cross-term errors; (2) concatenation-based approaches increasing download cost and causing reinitialization lag; (3) server-side overhead from dense reconstruction or auxiliary models. A unified solution is needed.
AI.method: SpecTraL stacks local LoRA modules and applies orthonormal Householder Transformation directly in low-rank latent space, avoiding dense reconstruction. It uses the Spiked Covariance Model from Random Matrix Theory to analytically separate global consensus signal from non-IID noise, discovering optimal layer-wise global ranks without hyperparameter tuning. A padding-aware initialization framework allows clients to incorporate residual LoRA dimensions without re-merging into pretrained weights.
AI.result: Experiments on federated fine-tuning of ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 over DomainNet and NICO++ show improved accuracy-communication trade-offs, reduced server computation, and elimination of hyperparameter search for rank selection.
AI.conclusion: SpecTraL delivers a unified, principled solution to federated LoRA aggregation that is both mathematically consistent and communication-efficient, removing the need for manual rank tuning through spectral analysis grounded in Random Matrix Theory.

title: From Scalars to Time Series: Rethinking Implicit Neural Representations for Time-Varying Volumetric Data
summary: Implicit neural representations (INRs) for time-varying volumetric data are typically trained using dense sampling over spatiotemporal coordinates, where each observation corresponds to a single point in space and time. This coordinate-wise formulation requires extensive sampling during optimization, leading to high computational cost and inefficient use of temporal structure. In this work, we revisit this design choice and show that dense spatiotemporal sampling is not necessary for learning time-varying fields. Instead, we represent the data as a collection of spatially indexed time series and train INRs using sequence-level supervision over each spatial location, rather than coordinate-wise scalar samples. This reformulation eliminates the need for dense spatiotemporal sampling and instead learns each spatial location from its full temporal evolution in a structured manner. We demonstrate that this representation is compatible with a range of existing INR architectures and consistently improves reconstruction quality, while significantly reducing training cost. Furthermore, we show that this formulation can be combined with mixture-of-experts architectures, and that our MoE instantiation further improves reconstruction quality compared to both the base reformulation and existing MoE-based INR methods, providing a stronger capacity allocation under heterogeneous temporal dynamics.

AI.tldr: The authors propose reformulating implicit neural representations (INRs) for time-varying volumetric data by using sequence-level supervision over spatially indexed time series instead of dense spatiotemporal point-wise sampling. This reduces training cost, improves reconstruction quality, and integrates effectively with mixture-of-experts architectures.
AI.motivation: Traditional INRs for time-varying volumetric data rely on coordinate-wise dense spatiotemporal sampling, which is computationally expensive during optimization and inefficiently exploits temporal structure. The authors aim to eliminate this inefficiency.
AI.method: Instead of sampling individual (x, y, z, t) points, the data is represented as a collection of spatially indexed time series. INRs are trained with sequence-level supervision over the full temporal evolution at each spatial location. This approach is compatible with existing INR architectures and is extended to a mixture-of-experts (MoE) instantiation for handling heterogeneous temporal dynamics.
AI.result: The sequence-level reformulation consistently improves reconstruction quality across various INR architectures while significantly reducing training cost. The MoE instantiation further improves quality over both the base reformulation and existing MoE-based INR methods through better capacity allocation.
AI.conclusion: Dense spatiotemporal sampling is unnecessary for learning time-varying fields. Sequence-level supervision over spatial locations is a more efficient and higher-quality alternative, and it synergizes well with MoE architectures for handling heterogeneous temporal dynamics.

title: Nipping the Butterfly Effect in the Bud: Self-Output Fine-Tuning for Autoregressive Weather Prediction
summary: Long-horizon weather forecasting is a fundamental challenge in atmospheric science, for which autoregressive Deep Learning Weather Prediction (DLWP) has emerged as the primary paradigm. Although the autoregressive pipeline is highly scalable and flexible, its prediction errors grow rapidly over long forecasting horizons. In this work, we study this error growth phenomenon from both theoretical and empirical perspectives. Our analysis reveals that the growth is driven by a feedback loop between output errors and input distribution shifts. Specifically, the autoregressive process amplifies small initial output errors, which progressively corrupt subsequent input distributions, echoing the butterfly effect in atmospheric science and ultimately deteriorating forecasting accuracy over longer horizons. Furthermore, we show that this distributional shift originates at the earliest stage of inference, with out-of-distribution signatures detectable as early as the first autoregressive step. To mitigate this issue, we propose \textbf{Self-Output Fine-Tuning (SOFT)}, a plug-and-play strategy that leverages the model's own one-step predictions to calibrate the biased input distribution encountered at the first step. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, despite its simplicity, SOFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon forecasting tasks and substantially reduces both prediction errors and distributional discrepancy. The success of SOFT highlights the importance of reexamining the fundamental pipeline of deep learning weather prediction, representing a critical pipeline advance for atmospheric science.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates why autoregressive deep learning weather prediction models accumulate errors over long horizons, identifying a feedback loop between output errors and input distribution shifts (akin to the butterfly effect). The authors propose Self-Output Fine-Tuning (SOFT), a simple plug-and-play method that uses the model's own one-step predictions to calibrate the biased input distribution, achieving state-of-the-art long-horizon forecasting performance.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive DLWP models are scalable and flexible, but their prediction errors grow rapidly over long forecasting horizons. The underlying mechanism of this error growth is not well understood, limiting progress in long-horizon weather prediction.
AI.method: The authors first analyze the error growth phenomenon theoretically and empirically, revealing a feedback loop: small initial output errors amplify through the autoregressive process, progressively corrupting input distributions (distribution shift), analogous to the butterfly effect. They show this distributional shift is detectable as early as the first autoregressive step. To address this, they propose Self-Output Fine-Tuning (SOFT), a plug-and-play strategy that uses the model's own one-step predictions to calibrate the biased input distribution encountered at the first inference step.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that SOFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon forecasting tasks, substantially reducing both prediction errors and distributional discrepancy.
AI.conclusion: The success of SOFT highlights the importance of reexamining the fundamental autoregressive pipeline in deep learning weather prediction, representing a critical advance for atmospheric science.

title: CASC: Causal Adversarial Subspace Clustering for Multivariate Spatiotemporal Data
summary: Deep subspace clustering plays a critical role in applications involving multivariate spatiotemporal data, such as sea ice monitoring, disease spread analysis, and tracking neuro-degeneration over time. Despite recent advances, existing methods primarily rely on geometric self-expressiveness, assume static subspace structures, and often fail to capture causal dependencies, local spatial interactions, and long-range temporal dynamics inherent in complex spatiotemporal systems. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Causal Adversarial Subspace Clustering (CASC) framework for discovering evolving latent regimes in high-dimensional spatiotemporal data. CASC integrates a U-Net-inspired deep adversarial clustering architecture with stacked FAConvLSTM layers to preserve spatial and temporal structure while learning robust latent representations. A graph attention transformer-based self-expressive network is introduced to jointly model local spatial relationships, global dependencies, and long-range temporal interactions. Furthermore, we propose two new learning objectives: (1) a Causal Subspace Preservation Loss that aligns self-expression coefficients with latent causal relationships, encouraging clusters to reflect underlying causal processes rather than simple feature similarity, and (2) a Dynamic Temporal Subspace Evolution Loss that captures evolving subspace structures and temporal regime transitions in nonstationary environments. Together, these components transform deep subspace clustering from a correlation-driven paradigm into a causal-temporal regime discovery framework.

AI.tldr: CASC introduces a causal-temporal framework for deep subspace clustering in spatiotemporal data, integrating U-Net adversarial architecture with graph attention transformers, and proposing two novel losses — Causal Subspace Preservation and Dynamic Temporal Subspace Evolution — to shift from correlation-based to causality-driven regime discovery.
AI.motivation: Existing deep subspace clustering methods rely on geometric self-expressiveness, assume static subspace structures, and fail to capture causal dependencies, local spatial interactions, and long-range temporal dynamics in complex spatiotemporal systems (e.g., sea ice monitoring, disease spread, neurodegeneration tracking).
AI.method: CASC combines: (1) a U-Net-inspired deep adversarial clustering architecture with stacked FAConvLSTM layers for preserving spatial-temporal structure; (2) a graph attention transformer-based self-expressive network for jointly modeling local spatial relationships, global dependencies, and long-range temporal interactions; (3) a Causal Subspace Preservation Loss aligning self-expression coefficients with latent causal relationships; and (4) a Dynamic Temporal Subspace Evolution Loss capturing evolving subspace structures and regime transitions in nonstationary environments.
AI.result: The abstract does not report specific quantitative results; the contribution is methodological, framing the approach as transforming deep subspace clustering from a correlation-driven paradigm into a causal-temporal regime discovery framework for evolving latent regimes.
AI.conclusion: By integrating causal reasoning and temporal evolution modeling into subspace clustering, CASC enables more meaningful discovery of latent regimes in nonstationary spatiotemporal data, moving beyond static geometric similarity to capture causal processes and dynamic transitions.

title: Beyond Independent Optimization: Compression, MoE Routing, and Quantization Interactions in Multimodal Edge Intelligence
summary: Efficient multimodal inference is increasingly constrained not only by model quality or FLOP count, but also by the cost of preserving, moving, routing, caching, and quantizing multimodal representations under latency, memory, and energy constraints. This paper reviews recent advances in efficient vision-language and multimodal large language models, covering visual token compression, video token management, KV-cache optimization, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing, low-bit quantization, edge deployment, and hardware-aware benchmarking. We argue that these techniques cannot be treated as independent optimizations. Visual token compression alters downstream feature distributions and MoE routing decisions, routing behavior affects expert utilization and quantization sensitivity, quantized router logits influence expert assignment, KV-cache policies determine retained multimodal evidence, and hardware constraints often transform computational savings into memory and communication bottlenecks. We organize the literature around these interactions and identify key design trade-offs, including accuracy versus token budget, static versus adaptive compression, sparse routing efficiency versus expert collapse, and low-bit inference versus modality-specific degradation. Finally, we introduce Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic for video MoE models and highlight open research directions in routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, hardware-aware co-design, and unified benchmarking for multimodal edge intelligence.

AI.tldr: This paper surveys recent advances in efficient multimodal inference, arguing that techniques like visual token compression, KV-cache optimization, MoE routing, and quantization are deeply interdependent and must be co-designed rather than independently optimized. It organizes the literature around these interactions, identifies key trade-offs, and introduces Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic for video MoE models.
AI.motivation: Efficient multimodal inference faces a bottleneck beyond FLOP count and model quality: the cost of preserving, moving, routing, caching, and quantizing multimodal representations under real-world latency, memory, and energy constraints. Current research treats optimizations (compression, routing, quantization, caching) as isolated techniques, but these components interact in non-trivial ways that can undermine overall system efficiency. A holistic understanding of these interactions is missing.
AI.method: The paper is a survey/review that organizes the literature around the interactions among key efficiency techniques: (1) visual token compression and its downstream effects on feature distributions and MoE routing; (2) KV-cache optimization and its impact on retained multimodal evidence; (3) MoE routing behavior affecting expert utilization and quantization sensitivity; (4) quantized router logits influencing expert assignment; and (5) hardware constraints transforming computational savings into memory and communication bottlenecks. It also proposes a new diagnostic metric called Temporal Routing Consistency for video MoE models.
AI.result: The survey identifies key design trade-offs: accuracy versus token budget, static versus adaptive compression, sparse routing efficiency versus expert collapse, and low-bit inference versus modality-specific degradation. It introduces Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic for evaluating routing stability in video MoE models and highlights open research directions in routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, hardware-aware co-design, and unified benchmarking for multimodal edge intelligence.
AI.conclusion: Efficient multimodal inference requires a holistic, co-design approach where compression, routing, quantization, caching, and hardware constraints are jointly optimized. Treating them independently leads to cascading inefficiencies. Future work should focus on routing-aware compression, cross-modal KV-cache policies, hardware-aware co-design, and standardized multimodal edge benchmarks.

title: Training Large Language Models for Self-Explanation Faithfulness
comment: To appear at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on Representational Alignment (Re-Align), 10 pages (long paper)
summary: We propose a Reinforcement Learning (RL) method to directly optimize the faithfulness of self-explanations - the extent to which a model's generated reasoning accurately reflects its internal decision-making process. While existing work focuses on evaluating faithfulness or using inference-time prompting frameworks to improve an LLM's self-explanation's tractability, these approaches do not provide a mechanism to directly optimize a model's parameters to generate faithful self-explanations. We bridge this gap by modifying existing faithfulness metrics into an RL training objective. We investigate (1) if models can be trained to accurately detect factors that affect their decisions, and (2) whether RL can directly optimize for the disclosure of these factors thereby improving LLM self-explanations' faithfulness. We experiment with two intervention types: random-word insertions and user-bias insertions, using a per-sample reward derived from the Phi-CCT correlation metric. RL fine-tuned Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B show substantial improvements on the Phi-CCT faithfulness metric, with in-distribution scores rising from near-zero to as high as 0.664, and out-of-distribution scores reaching up to 0.691 on held-out tasks such as StrategyQA. Cross-intervention generalization is weaker but more interesting: a priori we would not expect a model trained only on random word insertions to generalize to user-bias phrases, yet Llama3.1-8B shows non-zero transfer in this direction. The reverse direction and Qwen3-8B do not replicate this, indicating model-dependent and setup-dependent effects we cannot yet explain. Lastly we analyze model behavior to rule out reward gaming behaviors that often plague RL training. Ultimately, we show that models can be trained to implicitly identify influential factors and disclose them, offering a scalable path toward reducing unfaithful reasoning in LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using Reinforcement Learning to directly optimize the faithfulness of LLM self-explanations by converting faithfulness metrics into training rewards, demonstrating substantial improvements on Phi-CCT scores with Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B, though cross-intervention generalization remains limited and model-dependent.
AI.motivation: Existing work on LLM self-explanation faithfulness either evaluates it or uses inference-time prompting, but lacks a mechanism to directly optimize model parameters for generating faithful explanations. The authors aim to bridge this gap by enabling models to learn to accurately detect and disclose factors influencing their decisions.
AI.method: The authors modify the Phi-CCT faithfulness metric into a per-sample RL reward function. They fine-tune Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B using RL with two intervention types (random-word insertions and user-bias insertions), then evaluate faithfulness improvements both in-distribution and out-of-distribution (e.g., StrategyQA), and analyze cross-intervention generalization and potential reward gaming.
AI.result: RL fine-tuning dramatically improved Phi-CCT scores: in-distribution from near-zero to 0.664, out-of-distribution to 0.691. Cross-intervention generalization was limited — Llama3.1-8B showed non-zero transfer from random-word to user-bias interventions, but the reverse and Qwen3-8B did not, suggesting model- and setup-dependent effects. No evidence of reward gaming was found.
AI.conclusion: Models can be trained via RL to implicitly identify and disclose influential decision factors, offering a scalable path toward reducing unfaithful reasoning in LLMs. The mixed cross-intervention generalization results highlight open questions about model-specific behaviors that warrant further investigation.

title: GuardianAgentBench: Where Agents Fail and How to Guard Them
summary: As large language model agents increasingly operate autonomously with access to tools and external environments, ensuring their safe and reliable behavior becomes critical. We present GuardianAgentBench (GABench), a benchmark of 580 scenarios across six domains evaluated on three production-ready frameworks: LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Vectara. The benchmark incorporates rigorous multi-stage validation and five adversarial attack modes. Experiments with six state-of-the-art models reveal that even the strongest configuration achieves only 74.8% overall accuracy and expose two distinct failure regimes: stronger models under-call required tools, while weaker models mis-select and over-call tools. Performance degrades monotonically with both tool-set size and sequential turn depth, with long-horizon planning proving the steeper bottleneck. Our guardrail implementation consistently outperforms system-prompt-based defenses across all models, recovering 19.9% of failures at a false positive rate of just 0.5%. These results demonstrate that execution-time structural intervention improves safety without disrupting correct agent behavior.

AI.tldr: GABench is a benchmark of 580 safety scenarios for LLM agents across 6 domains and 3 frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, Vectara). Testing 6 SOTA models reveals only 74.8% max accuracy, with distinct failure regimes (under-calling vs. over-calling tools) and performance degrading with tool-set size and turn depth. A guardrail implementation recovers 19.9% of failures at 0.5% false positive rate, outperforming prompt-based defenses.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents gain autonomous access to tools and external environments, ensuring their safe and reliable behavior becomes critical. No existing benchmark systematically evaluates agent safety across multiple frameworks, adversarial conditions, and failure modes with execution-time interventions.
AI.method: The authors construct GuardianAgentBench with 580 scenarios spanning 6 domains, validated through rigorous multi-stage validation, and test across 3 production frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, Vectara) under 5 adversarial attack modes. Six SOTA models are evaluated. A structural guardrail mechanism operating at execution time is compared against system-prompt-based defenses, measuring accuracy, false positive rates, and failure recovery.
AI.result: The best model configuration achieves only 74.8% overall accuracy. Two distinct failure regimes emerge: stronger models under-call required tools, while weaker models mis-select and over-call tools. Performance degrades monotonically with both tool-set size and sequential turn depth, with long-horizon planning as the steeper bottleneck. The guardrail recovers 19.9% of failures at a 0.5% false positive rate, consistently outperforming system-prompt defenses across all models.
AI.conclusion: Execution-time structural intervention (guardrails) improves LLM agent safety without disrupting correct behavior, outperforming prompt-based defenses. The benchmark reveals fundamental limitations in current agent architectures regarding tool selection and long-horizon planning, highlighting critical areas for future improvement.

title: A Polynomial Architecture-Attribution Co-Design Framework for Exact Aumann-Shapley Attribution in GNNs
summary: We study feature-level and node-level explanations for graph neural networks (GNNs) through the lens of Aumann-Shapley attribution. Path-integral methods such as Integrated Gradients provide an axiomatic formulation of attribution, but their practical use in deep GNNs typically relies on finite-sample numerical approximations to the path integral, requiring a trade-off between quadrature error and computational cost. This paper proposes APEX, a model-attribution co-design framework that makes the attribution integral exactly computable under a polynomial GNN architecture. The key component is PolyGIN, a GIN-style graph network whose message-passing, normalization, and transformation operations preserve a bounded multivariate polynomial form for scalar model scores, such as pre-softmax logits. We show that, for a PolyGIN with $L$ polynomial transformation blocks, the derivative along the attribution path has degree at most $2^L-1$. Therefore, Gauss--Legendre quadrature can evaluate the Aumann--Shapley path integral exactly, up to floating-point precision, with $2^{L-1}$ deterministic evaluation points. The resulting attributions can be computed at the feature level and then aggregated into node-level scores while preserving completeness. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graph benchmarks show that PolyGIN maintains competitive predictive performance, while the complete APEX framework achieves higher attribution fidelity than the compared baselines and substantially reduces the number of evaluations required for path integration.

AI.tldr: APEX is a co-designed framework combining a polynomial GNN architecture (PolyGIN) with exact Aumann-Shapley attribution computation via Gauss-Legendre quadrature, eliminating the approximation-error vs. cost trade-off in path-integral attribution methods like Integrated Gradients.
AI.motivation: Path-integral attribution methods (e.g., Integrated Gradients) for GNNs rely on numerical approximation of integrals, forcing a trade-off between quadrature error and computational cost. There is a need for exact, axiomatically sound attribution without finite-sample approximation.
AI.method: The authors propose APEX: (1) PolyGIN, a GIN-style GNN where message-passing, normalization, and transformation operations preserve a bounded multivariate polynomial form for scalar outputs; (2) Proof that PolyGIN's derivative along the attribution path has degree at most 2^L-1 for L blocks; (3) Exact evaluation of the Aumann-Shapley path integral using Gauss-Legendre quadrature with only 2^{L-1} deterministic points, producing feature-level attributions aggregable to node-level scores with guaranteed completeness.
AI.result: PolyGIN maintains competitive predictive accuracy on synthetic and real-world graph benchmarks. APEX achieves higher attribution fidelity than baselines and substantially reduces the number of integration evaluations required.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing model architecture with attribution computation enables exact, efficient Aumann-Shapley attribution for GNNs without sacrificing predictive performance, offering a principled alternative to approximate path-integral methods.

title: Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning: Attribution-Guided Repair and Knowledge Reuse for Structured Agent Skills
summary: Agent Skills package reusable procedural knowledge as external artifacts for frozen language-model agents, yet existing optimizers do not jointly resolve where a failure occurs in a workflow, which mechanism caused it, and how relevant knowledge from third-party Skills should be reused locally. We introduce Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning (WML). Its Node--Mechanism Attribution identifies the failed workflow node, implicated mechanisms, and smallest valid edit target, routing single-mechanism defects to L3 resources and relational defects across mechanisms to L2 composition protocols. A six-module Workflow-Guided Skill Optimization (WGSO) loop then selects provenance- and scope-aware third-party knowledge, applies bounded patches, evaluates candidates, and stores verified outcomes in optimizer-side memory. On SpreadsheetBench, WML reaches 90.33 +/- 1.53 and 74.67 +/- 3.51 Hard Accuracy with DeepSeek and Qwen3.6-Flash, respectively; without additional optimization, the learned Skills transfer to WikiTableQuestions with 84.00 +/- 2.00 and 83.00 +/- 2.00 Denotation Accuracy. On Compiler-Supported50, WML attains both the highest hard-PASS rate and the lowest cost per successful task; compiled execution sharply reduces tokens and calls relative to a direct SkillAgent while retaining most of its successful tasks. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/xiaolin9595/workflow-localized-mechanism-learning.

AI.tldr: WML introduces a two-stage framework for optimizing frozen LM agents' skills: first, Node-Mechanism Attribution pinpoints where and why a workflow fails (single-mechanism vs. relational defects), then a Workflow-Guided Skill Optimization loop reuses third-party knowledge with provenance awareness, applies bounded patches, and stores verified fixes. The approach achieves strong performance on SpreadsheetBench and transfers zero-shot to WikiTableQuestions, while also excelling on Compiler-Supported50 with high pass rates and low cost.
AI.motivation: Existing skill optimizers for frozen language-model agents treat failures opaquely — they do not jointly localize which workflow node failed, which mechanism caused the failure, and how to appropriately reuse third-party Skill knowledge. This leads to imprecise edits and missed opportunities for compositional repair.
AI.method: WML comprises two core components: (1) Node–Mechanism Attribution (NMA), which identifies the failed node, the implicated mechanism(s), and the smallest valid edit target, routing single-mechanism defects to L3 (skill-level) resources and relational cross-mechanism defects to L2 (composition protocol) resources; (2) a six-module Workflow-Guided Skill Optimization (WGSO) loop that selects provenance- and scope-aware third-party knowledge, applies bounded patches, evaluates candidates, and caches verified outcomes in optimizer-side memory.
AI.result: On SpreadsheetBench, WML achieves 90.33±1.53 (DeepSeek) and 74.67±3.51 (Qwen3.6-Flash) Hard Accuracy. Without further optimization, skills transfer to WikiTableQuestions at 84.00±2.00 and 83.00±2.00 Denotation Accuracy. On Compiler-Supported50, WML achieves the highest hard-PASS rate and lowest cost per successful task; compiled execution drastically reduces tokens and API calls versus direct SkillAgent while preserving most successful tasks.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained failure attribution combined with provenance-aware, scoped skill reuse enables both stronger in-domain optimization and zero-shot skill transfer. The compiler-backed execution further demonstrates practical efficiency gains, making WML a promising direction for maintaining and evolving agent skill libraries.

title: Smooth Neural Point Processes via B-Splines
summary: Temporal point processes (TPPs) provide a general and flexible framework for modeling sequences of events in continuous time. Neural networks have been successfully employed to model TPPs in a highly expressive and data-driven way. Neural TPPs are typically trained via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) by minimizing the negative log-likelihood (NLL), which depends on both the conditional intensity function (CIF) and its integral over time, the compensator. Recent neural TPP approaches enable exact evaluation of the NLL without numerical integration. However, these methods typically model the compensator rather than the CIF directly, impose constraints on the neural network architecture, and are computationally expensive during training, as event contributions to the NLL are evaluated sequentially rather than in parallel. In this work, we propose a novel neural TPP model that directly parametrizes the CIF as a non-negative combination of B-spline basis functions, whose coefficients are predicted by a neural network. This formulation enables exact evaluation of the NLL, preserves full flexibility in the neural architecture, allows efficient parallelization during training, and naturally supports CIF smoothness regularization through the integrated squared second derivative. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show improved computational efficiency and predictive accuracy compared to the reference neural TPP baseline.

AI.tldr: Proposes a neural TPP that parametrizes the conditional intensity function directly via B-spline basis functions with neural network-predicted coefficients, enabling exact NLL evaluation, parallel training, architectural flexibility, and built-in smoothness regularization.
AI.motivation: Existing neural TPPs either require numerical integration for NLL, or when exact evaluation is possible, they model the compensator rather than the CIF, constrain network architecture, and require sequential (non-parallel) event evaluation during training.
AI.method: Models the CIF as a non-negative linear combination of B-spline basis functions, where coefficients are output by a neural network. This yields an analytical integral (compensator) for exact NLL computation, imposes no architectural constraints, and supports parallel event processing plus integrated squared second derivative regularization for smoothness.
AI.result: Improved computational efficiency and predictive accuracy over the reference neural TPP baseline on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed B-spline-based neural TPP successfully addresses key limitations of prior work—architectural constraints, sequential training, and indirect CIF modeling—while maintaining exact NLL evaluation and delivering superior empirical performance.

title: Naju: A Native Discrete State-Space Model with Independent Retention and Writing for Long-Sequence Memory
summary: Long-sequence memory tracking places two opposing demands on a recurrent state: near-lossless retention of stored bindings over long horizons, and active overwriting of stale ones. In our diagnostic suite, the strongest efficient baselines tend to solve only one side well. Continuous-time-parameterized state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba obtain their discrete recurrence by zero-order-hold discretization of a continuous-time system; we argue that this detour is unnecessary for memory tracking and parameterize the discrete transition directly. Naju (Native Adaptive Junction Unit) factorizes the recurrent update, schematically $x_n = f_n\odot x_{n-1} + i_n\odot(B_n u_n)$, into an explicit discrete pole (a learned forget gate $f_n$), an independent write gain $i_n$, and input-dependent write/read maps. Since the sigmoid pole satisfies $0<f_n<1$, each frozen local coordinate is Schur-stable by construction, and the full time-varying recurrence satisfies a fading-memory/BIBO bound under uniform boundedness assumptions, with no stability regularizer. We formalize the key structural limitation of coupled designs: any non-expansive complementary single-gate recurrence ties the effective retention $r$ and write gain $w$ through $|r|+w\le 1$, so near-complete retention forces weak writing; decoupling $f_n$ from $i_n$ removes this constraint. Empirically, Naju is the only evaluated model that remains strong on both retention and overwriting at 4x the training length. Beyond the diagnostic suite, we evaluate Naju on WikiText-103 language modeling, Long Range Arena, and multi-query associative recall. Across these settings, Naju consistently combines strong long-range memory with competitive or superior performance, outperforming the Mamba baselines in the principal comparisons while remaining competitive with the Transformer and preserving linear-time, linear-memory scaling.

AI.tldr: Naju proposes a decoupled discrete recurrence for SSMs that separates the forget gate from the write gain, overcoming a fundamental constraint in coupled single-gate designs where near-complete retention forces weak overwriting. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on both long-sequence retention and active overwriting tasks while preserving linear complexity.
AI.motivation: Long-sequence memory tracking requires simultaneously retaining old bindings near-losslessly and actively overwriting stale ones. Existing efficient baselines (including Mamba-style SSMs) tend to solve only one side of this trade-off. The authors argue that the continuous-time discretization detour in SSMs is unnecessary, and identify a structural limitation: coupled single-gate recurrences impose a binding constraint between retention and write gain, preventing simultaneous strong performance on both.
AI.method: The method, Naju (Native Adaptive Junction Unit), directly parameterizes a discrete recurrence: x_n = f_n ⊙ x_{n-1} + i_n ⊙ (B_n u_n). It factorizes the update into three components: (1) an explicit learned forget gate f_n (sigmoid, 0<f_n<1) ensuring per-coordinate Schur stability without regularizers; (2) an independent write gain i_n; and (3) input-dependent write/read maps B_n. Decoupling f_n from i_n removes the single-gate constraint |r|+w≤1, enabling both near-complete retention and strong overwriting simultaneously.
AI.result: In the diagnostic suite, Naju is the only model strong on both retention and overwriting at 4× training length. On WikiText-103 language modeling, Long Range Arena, and multi-query associative recall, Naju consistently combines strong long-range memory with competitive or superior performance, outperforming Mamba baselines while matching the Transformer and preserving linear-time, linear-memory scaling.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling the forget gate from the write gain removes a fundamental limitation of coupled recurrent designs, enabling simultaneous strong retention and overwriting. The resulting Naju model matches or exceeds Mamba and Transformer baselines across diverse long-sequence benchmarks while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: TOUR: A Trajectory-Level Unlearning Benchmark for Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents are trained on fixed behavioral trajectories, which makes trajectory-level deletion important when selected data must be removed after training. Evaluating such deletion is difficult because a lower membership score can reflect trajectory removal, residual memorization visible to another attack, or policy collapse that destroys useful behavior. We introduce Trajectory-level memOrization and Unlearning in offline RL (TOUR), a benchmark that combines trajectory-level partitioning, matched non-member controls, retraining references, retained-performance anchors, and multi-attack privacy auditing. Across D4RL locomotion experiments and an exploratory AntMaze extension, TOUR shows that common deletion baselines have environment-dependent privacy-utility behavior. Retraining and fine-tuning often provide stronger retained-utility references than uniform GA+Refit, while TrajDeleter remains a useful comparator but is not uniformly stronger under the same audit. Reference-model, threshold, deviation, equivalence, action-error, representation-based, and query-limited attacks further show that a single likelihood-based membership score can overstate deletion quality. In the evaluated settings, conclusions about offline RL unlearning are therefore not stable under single-score auditing. They depend on matched non-member construction, retraining-relative calibration, attack family, retained utility, and explicit scope for diagnostic architecture or component-level evidence.

AI.tldr: TOUR introduces a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating trajectory-level unlearning in offline RL, revealing that single-score membership auditing overstates deletion quality and that conclusions depend on matched controls, retraining calibration, attack diversity, and retained utility.
AI.motivation: Trajectory-level data deletion in offline RL is critical when selected training data must be removed post-training. Existing evaluation methods are unreliable because a low membership score can falsely indicate successful deletion when it actually reflects residual memorization detectable by other attacks or policy collapse. A systematic, multi-faceted benchmark is needed.
AI.method: TOUR integrates five components: (1) trajectory-level partitioning for deletion requests, (2) matched non-member controls for calibration, (3) retraining-from-scratch references as gold-standard unlearning targets, (4) retained-performance anchors to detect policy collapse, and (5) multi-attack privacy auditing spanning reference-model, threshold, deviation, equivalence, action-error, representation-based, and query-limited attacks. Evaluated on D4RL locomotion tasks with an AntMaze extension.
AI.result: Common deletion baselines exhibit environment-dependent privacy-utility trade-offs. Retraining and fine-tuning provide stronger retained-utility references than uniform GA+Refit. TrajDeleter is a useful comparator but not uniformly stronger under consistent auditing. Multiple attack types reveal that single likelihood-based membership scores overstate deletion quality, making unlearning conclusions unstable without diverse auditing.
AI.conclusion: Conclusions about offline RL unlearning are unstable under single-score auditing. Reliable evaluation requires matched non-member construction, retraining-relative calibration, multiple attack families, retained-utility measurement, and explicit scope for diagnostic architecture or component-level evidence.

title: Reexamining zero-shot summarization: Empirical investigation of trustworthiness of LLM-summarizers
comment: 28 pages, Under review in a journal
summary:
Zero-shot summarization using Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly advanced the abstractive summarization task by producing coherent and fluent summaries. However, underlying stochasticity of the large language models raises concerns about the stability and trustworthiness of the LLM-generated summaries. This issue has become increasingly important due to proliferation of LLM-generated summaries in educational settings, where students and researchers summarize complex academic materials in zero-shot manner.
  We propose a novel two-level diagnostic protocol for benchmarking LLM-summarizers based on the stability of the generated summaries. At the lower level, document-level stability analysis is performed over multiple LLM-summaries generated under controlled environment, and the stability coefficient is computed. Each generated summary is scored for semantic and factual alignment with the original document, enabling estimation of stability along more than one dimensions. At the next level, observations from a stratified sample of documents drawn from the corpus are consolidated to estimate the stability index of the LLM-summarizer, which is the proxy for its trustworthiness.
  Our empirical investigation of three LLM-summarizers across three genres of documents reveals statistically significant differences in the generation-level variability among LLMs across summary evaluation metrics. This study advances the LLM-summarization research by evidential recognition of the stability problem in LLM-summaries and motivates further research towards development of robust, reliable and trustworthy LLM-summarizers.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a two-level diagnostic protocol to benchmark LLM summarizers based on summary stability, computing document-level stability coefficients across semantic and factual dimensions, then aggregating them into a corpus-level trustworthiness index. Empirical evaluation across three LLMs and three genres reveals statistically significant variability in generation stability.
AI.motivation: The stochastic nature of LLMs raises concerns about the stability and trustworthiness of generated summaries, particularly as LLM-based summarization becomes prevalent in educational settings where students and researchers summarize complex academic materials in a zero-shot manner. Existing work lacks systematic methods to diagnose and quantify this instability.
AI.method: A two-level diagnostic protocol: (1) Lower level — document-level stability analysis where multiple summaries are generated under controlled conditions for the same document, a stability coefficient is computed, and each summary is scored for semantic and factual alignment with the source; (2) Upper level — observations from a stratified document sample are consolidated to estimate a global stability index serving as a proxy for trustworthiness. Empirical validation uses three LLM summarizers across three document genres.
AI.result: Statistically significant differences in generation-level variability were found among LLMs across summary evaluation metrics. The protocol successfully reveals instability patterns that vary by LLM and document genre, confirming that stability is a measurable and discriminating property of LLM summarizers.
AI.conclusion: The study provides evidential recognition of the stability problem in LLM-generated summaries and establishes a replicable benchmarking framework. It calls for further research toward robust, reliable, and trustworthy LLM summarizers, particularly for high-stakes educational applications.

title: GlucoTune: A Unified Framework for Blood Glucose Preprocessing, Forecasting, and Benchmarking in Diabetes
summary: Preprocessing blood glucose time-series data is a critical yet often overlooked step in developing data-driven methods for diabetes management, particularly for type 1 diabetes. The lack of standardized preprocessing workflows and evaluation protocols hinders reproducibility and complicates fair comparison across studies. These challenges are further exacerbated by data-sharing restrictions, as privacy and licensing constraints often prevent the redistribution of preprocessed medical datasets. To address these limitations, we present GlucoTune, a comprehensive and extensible framework for reproducible experimentation with blood glucose time-series data. The framework standardizes the entire experimental workflow, from preprocessing to model evaluation, enabling reproducible experiments directly from the original datasets. Reproducible preprocessing is achieved through configurable pipelines defined in portable YAML configuration files, ensuring consistent data handling without distributing sensitive preprocessed data. Beyond preprocessing, GlucoTune provides a unified interface for implementing, training, and evaluating blood glucose prediction models. The framework integrates public datasets through standardized wrappers and provides a curated collection of state-of-the-art blood glucose prediction and general time-series forecasting methods, while remaining readily extensible to additional datasets, preprocessing strategies, and forecasting models. To promote transparent and consistent evaluation, GlucoTune includes a benchmarking leaderboard that reports results across datasets, preprocessing configurations, and forecasting methods, enabling systematic comparison of experimental settings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GlucoTune through comprehensive experiments and assess its usability in a user study.

AI.tldr: GlucoTune is a standardized, extensible framework for reproducible blood glucose time-series preprocessing and prediction model benchmarking, addressing the lack of standardization and data-sharing restrictions in type 1 diabetes research through YAML-configured pipelines and a unified evaluation interface.
AI.motivation: Blood glucose time-series research for diabetes management suffers from (1) no standardized preprocessing workflows, (2) inconsistent evaluation protocols that hinder fair comparison, and (3) data-sharing restrictions due to privacy/licensing that prevent redistribution of preprocessed datasets. These issues collectively undermine reproducibility in the field.
AI.method: The authors propose GlucoTune, a framework that: (1) standardizes preprocessing via configurable YAML pipelines, enabling reproducible data handling without sharing sensitive preprocessed data; (2) provides a unified interface for training and evaluating glucose prediction models; (3) integrates public datasets through standardized wrappers; (4) curates state-of-the-art prediction and time-series forecasting methods; and (5) implements a benchmarking leaderboard for systematic comparison across datasets, preprocessing configs, and models.
AI.result: The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments, and its usability is validated via a user study.
AI.conclusion: GlucoTune successfully addresses key reproducibility challenges in blood glucose time-series research by providing a standardized, extensible, and privacy-conscious experimental framework, enabling fair benchmarking and reproducible experimentation from original datasets.

title: EmoAgent-R1: Towards Multimodal Emotion Understanding with Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Agent Specialization
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance in multimodal emotion recognition (MER) tasks and lifted MER to a new level that is complex emotion understanding with advanced video understanding abilities and natural language description. However, existing MLLM-based methods often use a fixed prompt to perceive the emotions, ignoring the dynamicity and complexity of the emotion source in the multimodal inputs. To address these issues, we propose a novel Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Agent Specialization framework (\textbf{EmoAgent-R1}) to optimize the emotion recognition, reasoning, and generalization abilities of an MLLM with dynamic agent specialization based on reinforcement learning. Specifically, we first adopt a cold start strategy to endow an MLLM with preliminary emotion recognition, reasoning, and agent routing ability by training with synthetic answer-conditioned chain-of-thought data and agent routing data. Then, we further train the MLLM with reinforcement learning to perceive emotions in a two-step agentic workflow with agent selection and agent specialization. To effectively train EmoAgent-R1, we propose a novel Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO) to combine group-based relative advantages with a PMI-inspired progressive token-level modulation to transform sparse rewards into fine-grained learning signals, mitigating the coarse-grained uniform credit assignment issue in GRPO. Extensive experiments on MER benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our EmoAgent-R1 in stronger emotion reasoning performance and improved optimization stability.

AI.tldr: EmoAgent-R1 proposes a reinforcement learning framework with dynamic agent specialization for multimodal emotion recognition, using a novel P-GRPO algorithm to convert sparse rewards into fine-grained signals, achieving superior emotion reasoning and optimization stability.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM-based MER methods use fixed prompts that ignore the dynamic and complex nature of emotion sources in multimodal inputs, limiting performance.
AI.method: A cold-start phase trains the MLLM with synthetic answer-conditioned chain-of-thought and agent routing data. Then reinforcement learning employs a two-step agentic workflow: agent selection followed by agent specialization. A novel Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO) combines group-relative advantages with PMI-inspired progressive token-level modulation to transform sparse rewards into fine-grained learning signals.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on MER benchmarks show superior emotion reasoning performance and improved optimization stability compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: The EmoAgent-R1 framework effectively addresses the dynamic nature of multimodal emotion recognition through reinforcement learning-based dynamic agent specialization, outperforming fixed-prompt approaches.

title: Relative Value Learning
comment: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026
summary: In reinforcement learning, critics typically estimate absolute state values $V(s)$, estimating how good a particular situation is in isolation. However, it turns out that only differences in value are relevant for control. Motivated by this, we propose Relative Value Learning (RV), a framework that learns value differences directly via an antisymmetric function $Δ(s_i, s_j) = V(s_i) - V(s_j)$. We introduce a pairwise Bellman operator and prove it is a $γ$-contraction with a unique fixed point equal to the true value differences, derive well-posed $1$-step, $n$-step and $λ$-return targets and reconstruct generalized advantage estimation from pairwise differences to obtain an unbiased policy-gradient estimator (R-GAE). Beyond theoretical results, we integrate RV with PPO and achieve competitive performance on the Atari benchmark (49 ALE games) compared to standard PPO, indicating that relative value estimation is an effective alternative to absolute critics.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Relative Value Learning (RV), a reinforcement learning framework that learns value differences between state pairs using an antisymmetric function, rather than estimating absolute state values. The authors prove theoretical properties (contraction, fixed point), derive multi-step targets and an unbiased policy-gradient estimator (R-GAE), and show competitive Atari benchmark performance when integrated with PPO.
AI.motivation: In reinforcement learning, only value differences matter for control, yet standard critics learn absolute state values V(s). This work is motivated by the insight that explicitly modeling pairwise value differences may be more natural and efficient, avoiding learning irrelevant absolute value information.
AI.method: The authors propose an antisymmetric function Δ(s_i, s_j) = V(s_i) - V(s_j) to directly model value differences. They introduce a pairwise Bellman operator, prove it is a γ-contraction with a unique fixed point equal to true value differences, derive well-posed 1-step, n-step, and λ-return targets, and reconstruct Generalized Advantage Estimation from pairwise differences to produce an unbiased policy-gradient estimator called R-GAE. The method is integrated with PPO for empirical evaluation.
AI.result: RV integrated with PPO achieves competitive performance against standard PPO across 49 Atari 2600 games (ALE benchmark), demonstrating that relative value estimation serves as an effective alternative to absolute critics in practice.
AI.conclusion: Relative Value Learning offers a theoretically sound and practically effective alternative to absolute value function estimation in RL, with the key insight that modeling value differences directly is both sufficient for control and empirically competitive.

title: Demographically-Informed Heat-Mortality Risk Curves via Risk Graph Neural Networks
summary: Estimating heat-related mortality risk is a core task in environmental epidemiology, typically addressed with Distributed Lag Non-linear Models (DLNMs); interpretable exposure-response surfaces fitted to temperature-mortality time series. DLNMs are effective but ignore demographic and geographic context, despite well-established relevance to heat vulnerability. We propose Risk Graph Neural Networks (RGNNs), a hierarchical GNN encoder that uses granular census features to optimise DLNM coefficient vectors, preserving interpretable risk curve outputs while substantially improving predictive calibration. Evaluated across 10 regions of England and Wales on two unprecedented heat years, RGNN variants maintain both lower point-errors and near-nominal uncertainty coverage during the 2022 heatwave where baselines collapse.

AI.tldr: RGNNs enhance traditional DLNMs for heat-related mortality estimation by incorporating granular census-based demographic and geographic features via a hierarchical GNN encoder, maintaining interpretable risk curves while significantly improving predictive calibration, particularly during extreme heat events like the 2022 UK heatwave.
AI.motivation: Existing DLNMs for heat-mortality risk estimation are effective but ignore demographic and geographic context, which is well-established as critical to heat vulnerability. This omission limits predictive calibration, especially during unprecedented extreme heat events where baseline models fail.
AI.method: Proposes Risk Graph Neural Networks (RGNNs), a hierarchical GNN encoder architecture that leverages granular census-derived features to optimise the coefficient vectors of DLNMs. The model preserves the interpretable exposure-response surface output of DLNMs while incorporating spatial and demographic context.
AI.result: Evaluated across 10 regions of England and Wales over two unprecedented heat years, RGNN variants demonstrated lower point-prediction errors and maintained near-nominal uncertainty coverage during the 2022 heatwave, where baseline models collapsed.
AI.conclusion: RGNNs successfully bridge the gap between interpretable epidemiological modelling and context-aware machine learning, offering a robust framework for heat-mortality risk estimation that remains calibrated under extreme, out-of-distribution heat events.

title: Faster IndexTTS-2: Accelerating and Streaming Autoregressive Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech Synthesis on GPUs
summary: Autoregressive text-to-speech models achieve strong naturalness but suffer from slow inference due to sequential token generation, limiting their deployment in production applications that require low latency. IndexTTS-2 is a state-of-the-art autoregressive TTS model consisting of a GPT, a flow-matching Diffusion Transformer, and a vocoder. Despite its high synthesis quality, its inference speed barely reaches real-time without streaming or batching support. We present Faster IndexTTS-2, which accelerates all neural network components of IndexTTS-2 for production deployment on GPUs using NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM. Faster IndexTTS-2 also enables streaming synthesis for latency-sensitive interactive applications, and batched inference across all components to maximize GPU utilization. Experiments on the Seed-TTS benchmark for both English and Chinese demonstrate up to 5.0$\times$ speedup on the autoregressive GPT and 3.6$\times$ end-to-end, with minimal degradation in word error rate, speaker similarity, and naturalness. Our methodology provides a practical reference for efficiently accelerating similar autoregressive speech models on GPUs.

AI.tldr: Faster IndexTTS-2 accelerates the IndexTTS-2 autoregressive TTS model using NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM, achieving up to 5.0× speedup on the GPT component and 3.6× end-to-end, while enabling streaming and batched inference with minimal quality degradation.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive TTS models like IndexTTS-2 have high synthesis quality but suffer from slow sequential inference, barely reaching real-time speed. This limits deployment in production applications requiring low latency, streaming, and high GPU utilization.
AI.method: The authors optimize all neural network components (GPT, flow-matching Diffusion Transformer, vocoder) of IndexTTS-2 using NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM. They further enable streaming synthesis for low-latency interactive use and batched inference across all components to maximize GPU utilization.
AI.result: On the Seed-TTS benchmark for both English and Chinese, Faster IndexTTS-2 achieves up to 5.0× speedup on the autoregressive GPT and 3.6× end-to-end speedup, with minimal degradation in word error rate, speaker similarity, and naturalness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed optimization methodology provides a practical reference for efficiently accelerating autoregressive speech models on GPUs, making high-quality TTS viable for production deployment.

title: Can Generative Recommendation Reach Cold Items? A Temporal Perspective on Semantic-ID Generation
summary: Semantic-ID-based generative recommendation represents items as sequences of shared semantic tokens, enabling token recombination beyond isolated item IDs. However, closed-world recombination does not necessarily imply temporal open-token cold-start induction, where new items enter the item catalog with unseen atomic tokens or weakly supported SID paths. In this work, we revisit SID-based generative recommendation under an absolute-time temporal protocol that separates seen and unseen targets and diagnoses the cold item reachability at the token level. Through seen/unseen-hit analysis, coldness taxonomy, and oracle-prefix probing, we show that current SID-based models can occasionally reach future items supported by observed tokens and prefixes, but struggle with unseen atomic tokens and unsupported SID paths. We further explain this boundary by interpreting SID generation as hierarchical semantic bucketing: early tokens select coarse semantic regions, while later tokens refine item-specific paths. These findings show that SID generation is compositional but not fully open-ended, and suggest future directions in more independent SID spaces, scoring-based interfaces, and dynamic textual context.

AI.tldr: Current SID-based generative recommenders can reach future items using observed tokens/prefixes but fail with unseen atomic tokens and unsupported SID paths. The authors diagnose this boundary by interpreting SID generation as hierarchical semantic bucketing and suggest improvements via independent SID spaces, scoring interfaces, and dynamic text.
AI.motivation: Existing Semantic ID (SID) generative recommenders rely on closed-world token recombination, but real-world catalogs evolve over time with new items introducing unseen atomic tokens or weakly supported SID paths. The paper aims to systematically diagnose whether and when current SID models can induce cold-start items under a strict temporal protocol.
AI.method: The authors adopt an absolute-time temporal protocol that cleanly separates seen (training) and unseen (future) item targets. They conduct three diagnostic analyses: (1) seen/unseen-hit analysis measuring whether models can generate both seen and unseen items; (2) coldness taxonomy categorizing cold-start failures by token-level causes; and (3) oracle-prefix probing, which supplies ground-truth prefixes to isolate where generation breaks down.
AI.result: SID-based models can occasionally generate future items when those items rely on tokens and prefixes already observed during training. However, performance degrades sharply for items involving unseen atomic tokens or entirely unsupported SID paths. The analysis reveals SID generation functions as hierarchical semantic bucketing: early tokens determine coarse semantic regions, while later tokens refine item-specific paths — making the process compositional but not fully open-ended.
AI.conclusion: SID generation is compositional but bounded by token observability. The cold-start reachability boundary is explained by the hierarchical bucketing interpretation. Future work should explore more independent SID spaces, scoring-based interfaces instead of autoregressive generation, and dynamic incorporation of textual context to improve open-ended item induction.

title: Automated Synthesis and Adversarial Validation of Executable Causal Research Pipelines
summary: While automated research systems promise to accelerate empirical analysis, they are prone to silent failures: instances in which analysis code executes successfully yet relies on invalid causal assumptions. We present the Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Epidemiology Research Assistant (ARA), a framework that makes these failures visible by explicitly encoding causal design principles, study-specific assumptions, and methodological constraints. ARA integrates protocol construction, synthetic data generation, and adversarial validation into a unified pipeline. The framework translates natural language research questions into structured causal protocols and executable analysis code by first constructing a protocol and then generating synthetic datasets using Structural Causal Models (SCMs) with known ground-truth effects. This synthetic-data step can also support pipeline development when access to confidential data, such as medical data, is restricted. The generated analysis is then evaluated under controlled violations of identification assumptions. We evaluate ARA on the Automated Causal Reasoning Benchmark, assessing recovery of identification strategies, causal quantities, treatment and outcome variables, and consistency between generated code and approved protocol. Protocol construction and adversarial validation did not consistently improve numerical agreement with benchmark estimates compared with standard LLM-based generation. However, they changed the failure mode: instead of silently returning causal estimates, ARA often surfaced protocol concerns, diagnostic failures, incomplete inference, or downgraded non-causal interpretations. These findings suggest that validity-first automated science systems should be evaluated not only by answer accuracy, but also by whether they indicate when causal claims are unwarranted.
