The workflow decomposes the design task into constrained code-generation steps: plant-interface construction, normalization, manipulated-variable controlled-variable (MV-CV) pairing, controller specification, closed loop simulation, scenario generation, performance evaluation and Bayesian-optimization (BO) based tuning. Generated artifacts are executed and validated before downstream tasks proceed, and failed artifacts are repaired using validation feedback. The proposed approach is demonstrated on a nonlinear gas-preheater benchmark with coupled pressure and temperature dynamics. The generated workflow produces a physically consistent decentralized PI (proportional-integral) feedback-feedforward control structure and an executable tuning environment. Bayesian optimization reduces the closed loop performance objective, which aggregates set-point tracking and disturbance-rejection errors for the controlled variables, by approximately 26.5% relative to the initial controller generated by the workflow, mainly through improved pressure-loop transient performance. This figure quantifies the automated tuning stage rather than a comparison against a manually designed controller. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using structured large-language-model-based code generation to construct executable control-design workflows, while also highlighting the need for broader validation on larger plantwide-control benchmarks.

AI.tldr: A structured LLM-driven workflow automates multi-variable control design from dynamic process models, demonstrated on a nonlinear gas-preheater. The workflow spans plant interfacing, MV-CV pairing, controller specification, simulation, and Bayesian optimization tuning, achieving ~26.5% improvement in closed-loop performance over the initial generated controller.
AI.motivation: To explore the feasibility of using structured large language model (LLM)-based code generation to automate the entire multi-variable control design pipeline from dynamic process models, reducing manual engineering effort while maintaining physical consistency and executability of the generated artifacts.
AI.method: The workflow decomposes control design into constrained code-generation stages: plant-interface construction, normalization, MV-CV pairing, controller specification, closed-loop simulation, scenario generation, performance evaluation, and Bayesian optimization (BO)-based tuning. Each stage's outputs are validated before downstream tasks; failures trigger repair using validation feedback. The approach is demonstrated on a nonlinear gas-preheater benchmark with coupled pressure and temperature dynamics, producing a decentralized PI feedback-feedforward structure.
AI.result: The workflow generated a physically consistent decentralized PI feedback-feedforward controller and executable tuning environment. Bayesian optimization reduced the closed-loop performance objective (aggregating set-point tracking and disturbance-rejection errors) by approximately 26.5% relative to the initial controller, driven primarily by improved pressure-loop transient performance.
AI.conclusion: Structured LLM-based code generation is feasible for constructing executable control-design workflows. However, broader validation on larger plantwide-control benchmarks is needed to assess generalizability and robustness.

title: Error Certificates for KV-Cache Eviction via Randomized Design
summary: Deterministic KV-cache eviction keeps the top-$k$ tokens under an importance score and deletes the rest. We prove that this design cannot know what it destroyed: evicted values can be altered so that everything the serving system retains is unchanged while the true attention-output error grows arbitrarily, so no serving-time estimator of that error is consistent. Randomized eviction restores identifiability. With a Poisson-sampled tail at known inclusion probabilities, one logit offset performs the Hájek correction inside the softmax, and a survey-sampling variance estimator over the retained set becomes a per-step error certificate with 0.97 empirical coverage at no accuracy cost. On real workloads we pre-registered seven claims and lost three: question-aware eviction at 25--50\% budgets is nearly free; output log-probability predicts failure better than the certificate; certificate-gated budget escalation adds nothing. What survives is attribution: the certificate separates cache-induced from inherent failures (AUC 0.73--0.75, against 0.47--0.54 for output confidence) and schedules recomputation better than random or confidence gating. Randomization buys attribution, not prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges deterministic KV-cache eviction by proving it cannot reliably estimate its own error. The authors propose randomized eviction with Poisson sampling, enabling a Hájek-corrected softmax and a survey-sampling variance estimator that serves as an error certificate. Empirical results show the certificate excels at attribution (separating cache-induced from inherent errors) and scheduling recomputation, but underperforms output log-probability for failure prediction.
AI.motivation: Deterministic top-k KV-cache eviction is widely used to reduce memory footprint in LLM serving, but it operates blindly—it cannot know what information was destroyed. The authors prove a fundamental non-identifiability result: evicted values can be adversarially perturbed without changing any retained state, yet the true attention-output error can be made arbitrarily large. This means no consistent error estimator can exist at serving time under deterministic eviction.
AI.method: The authors propose randomized eviction: instead of deterministically dropping the lowest-scored tokens, they use Poisson sampling with known inclusion probabilities. This enables two key mechanisms: (1) a Hájek correction—a single logit offset applied inside the softmax that corrects for the sampling bias—and (2) a Horvitz-Thompson-style survey-sampling variance estimator computed over the retained KV-cache set, which yields a per-step error certificate. They pre-registered seven claims and tested them on real workloads with budget-constrained (25–50%) KV-cache eviction.
AI.result: Three of seven pre-registered claims failed: question-aware eviction at moderate budgets is nearly cost-free; output log-probability outperforms the certificate for failure prediction; and certificate-gated budget escalation provides no benefit. However, the certificate succeeds at attribution, achieving AUC 0.73–0.75 for separating cache-induced failures from inherent ones, versus 0.47–0.54 for output confidence. It also schedules recomputation better than random or confidence-based gating. The core takeaway: randomization buys attribution, not prediction.
AI.conclusion: Randomized KV-cache eviction with Poisson sampling restores statistical identifiability to the error estimation problem. The resulting variance-based certificate is not a good predictor of failure, but it reliably attributes errors to cache eviction versus inherent model uncertainty, and effectively gates recomputation. The negative results (log-probability as a better predictor, no benefit from budget escalation) are informative for future work in efficient LLM serving.

title: KroQuant: Kronecker-Structured Block Transforms for Efficient Post-Training Quantization of Diffusion Transformers
summary:
Post-training quantization (PTQ) of diffusion transformers (DiTs) to W4A4 severely degrades output quality, because activations entering each linear layer contain outliers that 4-bit formats cannot represent. The standard fix applies an invertible linear transform to the activations and its inverse to the weights before quantizing both. Normalization layers between blocks force this transform to run online at every denoising step, making its inference computation cost the binding design constraint. Existing options trade quantization quality for inference cost: per-channel scaling (SmoothQuant) is computationally cheap but impacts the magnitude of the channels, which can harm quantization accuracy; fixed Hadamard transforms yield better quantization accuracy but require large block sizes that incur a high online cost; learned full-$d$ invertible transforms calibrate best but entail a prohibitive dense $d \times d$ matrix multiplication (GEMM) per layer per step.
  We propose KroQuant, a PTQ method that applies a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform to each 32-element block of the activation, storing less than half the parameters of per-channel scaling. The block-local structure runs as small tensor-core GEMMs, and on an MI350 GPU the KroQuant quantizer kernel is up to $14\%$ faster than the SmoothQuant kernel. Offline LoRaQ weight calibration then absorbs the residual per-weight quantization error. On PixArt-$Σ$, SANA, and FLUX.1-schnell at W4A4 (MXFP4e2), KroQuant produces outputs closer to the FP reference than SVDQuant and LoRaQ on MJHQ-30K and SDCI, while preserving or improving image quality.

AI.tldr: KroQuant introduces a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform for W4A4 post-training quantization of diffusion transformers, operating on 32-element activation blocks. It reduces quantization error while running faster than SmoothQuant, and combined with LoRaQ weight calibration, outperforms SVDQuant and LoRaQ on image generation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: W4A4 PTQ of DiTs suffers from severe quality degradation due to activation outliers. Existing solutions trade off quantization quality against inference cost: SmoothQuant is fast but harms accuracy; fixed Hadamard transforms are accurate but computationally expensive; learned full-rank transforms are optimal but require prohibitive per-layer per-step dense matrix multiplications. A method that balances these trade-offs is needed.
AI.method: KroQuant applies a learned Kronecker-structured invertible linear transform to each 32-element block of activations before quantization, with the inverse applied to weights. The Kronecker structure uses fewer parameters than per-channel scaling. Block-local transforms execute as small tensor-core GEMMs. Offline LoRaQ weight calibration then absorbs residual per-weight quantization error.
AI.result: On an MI350 GPU, the KroQuant quantizer kernel is up to 14% faster than SmoothQuant. At W4A4 (MXFP4e2) on PixArt-Σ, SANA, and FLUX.1-schnell, KroQuant produces outputs closer to the FP reference than SVDQuant and LoRaQ on MJHQ-30K and SDCI benchmarks, while preserving or improving image quality.
AI.conclusion: KroQuant demonstrates that learned Kronecker-structured transforms effectively bridge the gap between cheap per-channel scaling and expensive full-rank transforms for DiT quantization, achieving both computational efficiency and high fidelity in W4A4 image generation.

title: Expert Behavior Prior Reinforcement Learning
summary: Behavior prior reinforcement learning (BPRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm to improve sample efficiency in online reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging policy priors derived from offline demonstrations. However, most existing BPRL methods rely on static offline datasets, which often suffer from low data diversity and suboptimal trajectory quality. This reliance restricts the effectiveness of policy priors, hindering both policy exploitation and stability during online training. Consequently, agents are prone to inefficient exploration and unstable learning dynamics. To address these limitations, we deviate from existing offline pre-training methods and propose an Expert Behavior Prior (EBP) algorithm. Specifically, we introduce a Q-guided conditional variational autoencoder (Q-CVAE) that learns to generate expert policy priors directly from the online replay buffer. This enables the generation of high-value actions for guiding policy updates without relying on pre-collected expert trajectories. To further enhance policy exploitation, we propose an expert policy guidance (EPG) mechanism that selects expert actions from a generative support set, and we integrate a policy gradient correction (PGC) module to harmonize Q-guidance with expert supervision, promoting stable and consistent policy improvement. Extensive experiments conducted on robotic control (Gym, PyBullet) and industrial control (DMControl) benchmarks demonstrate that EBP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art online RL algorithms, achieving higher sample efficiency and more stable convergence.

AI.tldr: EBP introduces a Q-guided conditional VAE to generate expert policy priors directly from the online replay buffer, bypassing static offline datasets, and combines expert policy guidance with policy gradient correction for stable, sample-efficient online RL.
AI.motivation: Existing BPRL methods depend on static offline datasets with low diversity and suboptimal trajectories, which limit the effectiveness of policy priors and cause inefficient exploration and unstable learning during online training.
AI.method: EBP uses a Q-guided conditional variational autoencoder (Q-CVAE) to generate expert priors from the online replay buffer, an expert policy guidance (EPG) mechanism that selects high-value actions from a generative support set, and a policy gradient correction (PGC) module that aligns Q-guidance with expert supervision for consistent policy updates.
AI.result: On Gym, PyBullet, and DMControl benchmarks, EBP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art online RL algorithms in both sample efficiency and convergence stability.
AI.conclusion: Generating expert behavior priors online via Q-CVAE, rather than relying on static offline data, effectively improves exploration, exploitation, and training stability in online reinforcement learning.

title: Agentic coding without the cloud: evaluating open-weight large language models on longitudinal data preparation tasks
summary: Large language models (LLMs) and agents are now widely used tools in code development, with data typically sent to third-party cloud-based models. Their adoption in research using personal data is constrained by governance requirements that typically prohibit data transmission to external services. Locally deployable open-weight models offer an alternative since sensitive data never leave the local environment. We introduce an open-source framework for evaluating the efficacy of AI agents powered by open-weight LLMs on one of the most persistent bottlenecks in research on longitudinal population studies: data preparation. The framework comprises: a curated ground-truth dataset (cleaning scripts preparing six sweeps of data from a British cohort study), task definitions encompassing tasks such as category harmonization and multi-wave merging, and automated routines for evaluating the LLM-produced R code and outputted data. We benchmark LLMs across the (consumer grade) deployment spectrum to assess their efficacy in 20 data preparation tasks (creation of 102 variables). Current state-of-the-art, 31-35B parameter models almost saturated our benchmark ("average task completion" up to 87.9%). The performance of open-weight LLMs running on consumer-grade hardware shows promise of a viable path toward AI-assisted data preparation in governance-restricted research settings. Our framework is publicly available at: https://github.com/UCL-ARC/RRBench.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RRBench, an open-source framework for evaluating how well locally-deployable open-weight LLMs can automate data preparation tasks in longitudinal population studies. Using a curated benchmark of 20 real-world tasks from a British cohort study, the authors find that 31-35B parameter models achieve up to 87.9% task completion on consumer-grade hardware, demonstrating a viable privacy-compliant path to AI-assisted data preparation.
AI.motivation: Researchers working with sensitive longitudinal population data face a critical bottleneck in data preparation (harmonization, merging waves, etc.) but cannot use cloud-based LLMs due to governance and data protection regulations. The authors aim to determine whether locally-deployable open-weight LLMs can serve as an effective, privacy-compliant alternative for automating these tedious data preparation tasks.
AI.method: The authors constructed RRBench, a benchmark framework with three components: (1) a curated ground-truth dataset comprising cleaning scripts for six sweeps of a British cohort study; (2) defined task specifications covering category harmonization, multi-wave merging, and other data preparation operations; (3) automated evaluation routines that assess both the correctness of LLM-generated R code and the resulting output data. They then benchmarked various open-weight LLMs across the consumer-grade deployment spectrum on 20 data preparation tasks involving the creation of 102 variables.
AI.result: Current state-of-the-art open-weight models in the 31-35B parameter range nearly saturated the benchmark, achieving up to 87.9% average task completion. This demonstrates that models runnable on consumer-grade hardware can effectively assist with data preparation tasks in governance-restricted research environments.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight LLMs deployed locally on consumer-grade hardware represent a promising and viable solution for AI-assisted data preparation in research contexts where data governance restrictions prohibit cloud-based services. The publicly available RRBench framework provides a standardized means for ongoing evaluation and comparison of models on these domain-specific tasks.

title: Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization
summary: Scaling inference-time computation has emerged as a reliable method to improve the performance of large language models on complex reasoning and programming tasks. However, standard approaches such as independent sampling and sequential multi-turn refinement operate without token-level credit assignment, resulting in computational inefficiency, since valid reasoning prefixes are frequently discarded. In this work, we introduce Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization (TTEL), an inference-time algorithm that utilizes fixed or environment feedback to perform token-level error localization. By comparing conditional probabilities under informed feedback against a null-context baseline, TTEL isolates the step at which an error occurred. The algorithm then truncates the trajectory and branches a new generation, maximally reusing the valid prefix. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that TTEL establishes strictly dominating Pareto frontiers across sequential reasoning domains, measured by pass-at-k vs. generated-token cost. With Qwen3-8B on LiveCodeBench, TTEL attains a pass@64 of 71.0% while generating approximately half as many tokens as independent sampling (360.4k vs. 735.0k). Generalizing to math benchmarks AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025, TTEL cleanly outperforms competing test-time baselines across both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507.

AI.tldr: TTEL introduces token-level error localization using conditional probability comparison against a null-context baseline to identify where errors occur in LLM reasoning chains, then truncates and re-samples from the valid prefix. It achieves superior pass@k efficiency, halving token costs while matching or exceeding independent sampling performance.
AI.motivation: Standard inference-time scaling methods (independent sampling, sequential multi-turn refinement) lack token-level credit assignment, causing valid reasoning prefixes to be inefficiently discarded. The authors aim to improve computational efficiency by localizing errors at the token level and reusing correct prefixes.
AI.method: TTEL compares conditional probabilities under two conditions: (1) informed feedback (e.g., execution results or ground-truth verification) and (2) a null-context baseline. Significant divergence in these probability distributions pinpoints the token step where an error occurred. The trajectory is then truncated at the last correct step, and a new generation is branched from that valid prefix, maximizing reuse of correct reasoning.
AI.result: TTEL establishes strictly dominating Pareto frontiers across sequential reasoning benchmarks. On LiveCodeBench with Qwen3-8B, it achieves pass@64 of 71.0% using 360.4k tokens versus 735.0k for independent sampling (~51% reduction). On math benchmarks AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025, TTEL outperforms competing test-time baselines with both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507.
AI.conclusion: Error localization via token-level credit assignment significantly improves the computational efficiency of inference-time scaling. TTEL provides a practical, feedback-driven method that reuses valid reasoning prefixes, yielding strong empirical gains across both code and math domains.

title: Regulating autonomous and agentic AI
summary: Regulating activities where regulatees use autonomous and agentic AI is challenging. Regulatory assumptions about regulatee knowledge and control no longer hold true; much of that lies elsewhere in the AI supply chain which thus needs to be brought within the scope of regulation. Governance systems for autonomous AI cannot replicate existing governance models, but need a fresh approach. Retrospective supervisory oversight becomes ineffective as a risk management tool, and AI autonomy generates new systemic risks which require new solutions. This paper investigate four regulatory systems: UK regulation of content platforms, data protection, UK financial services, and the EU AI Act\'92s cross-sectoral regime. It analyses the challenges posed by autonomous and agentic AI and proposes potential solutions which regulators might adopt. These will transform regulation from a reactive process to an active one, and assist it in adapting to the challenges of AI autonomy.

AI.tldr: Traditional regulatory models fail under autonomous AI because assumptions about regulatee knowledge and control break down. The paper examines four regulatory systems (UK content platforms, data protection, UK financial services, EU AI Act) and proposes shifting regulation from reactive oversight to active, supply-chain-wide governance to address new systemic risks.
AI.motivation: Autonomous and agentic AI disrupts foundational regulatory assumptions: regulatees may lack knowledge of or control over AI systems they deploy, as critical decisions and capabilities reside upstream in the AI supply chain. Retrospective supervisory oversight becomes ineffective, and new systemic risks emerge that existing governance models cannot address.
AI.method: Comparative doctrinal analysis of four regulatory systems — UK content platform regulation, data protection law, UK financial services regulation, and the EU AI Act's cross-sectoral regime — examining how each system is challenged by autonomous/agentic AI and identifying regulatory gaps.
AI.result: Across all four regimes, the analysis reveals common failures: retrospective oversight cannot manage real-time autonomous decision-making; regulatees lack sufficient knowledge and control; and the AI supply chain must be brought within regulatory scope. The paper identifies potential solutions for transforming regulation from a reactive to an active process.
AI.conclusion: Governance of autonomous AI requires a fresh approach: extending regulation across the AI supply chain, adopting active rather than reactive supervisory mechanisms, and developing new tools to address systemic risks unique to AI autonomy.

title: Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by having a cheap draft propose tokens that a target verifies in parallel. Frontier models increasingly ship a built-in Multi-Token-Prediction (MTP/NEXTN) draft head under the assumption that the draft is negligibly cheap. At million-token context this breaks: an MTP draft head typically runs full attention over the entire KV cache at every draft step, so its read grows linearly with context and comes to dominate the draft cost -- precisely where speculation is most valuable. The effect compounds with draft length (a deep native draft can turn net-negative, slower than no speculation) and sharpens under hybrid/linear-attention targets, where cheaper verification leaves the draft's full-attention read exposed. We apply a StreamingLLM-style sliding window plus attention sink to the draft's attention only (Windowed-MTP), leaving full-attention verification intact. It is training-free, drop-in, and lossless by construction: the full-attention target still decides every accepted token, so windowing changes only which tokens are proposed, never which are accepted. It bounds the draft's KV working set to a constant, dropping ~99% of KV entries at 1M. Across three architecture families (Qwen GDN-MoE 35B/122B and a Mamba2-hybrid NoPE 120B) at 1M context on a single GPU in SGLang, windowing cuts the per-decode-step cost over the shipping native MTP draft by +28% to +44%, an input-invariant margin that widens with context. Since per-token latency is this cost divided by acceptance length, at matched acceptance end-to-end decode latency improves by the same amount, and more where windowing also lifts acceptance, while preserving the target's verified output distribution. Finally, the unread draft KV -- 7.7-11% of total KV at 1M -- is reclaimed via a compact ring buffer at no acceptance or quality cost.

AI.tldr: Multi-Token Prediction draft heads in speculative decoding become a performance bottleneck at long contexts due to full-attention KV cache reads scaling linearly with context length. The authors propose Windowed-MTP, a training-free method that applies a StreamingLLM-style sliding window + attention sink exclusively to the draft model's attention, bounding its KV working set to a constant size and recovering 28–44% per-decode-step cost at 1M-token contexts.
AI.motivation: Frontier LLMs increasingly ship with built-in MTP/NEXTN draft heads for speculative decoding, based on the assumption that the draft is negligibly cheap relative to the target model. However, at million-token contexts, this assumption fails: the draft head runs full attention over the entire KV cache at every draft step, causing its read cost to grow linearly with context length and dominate overall latency. This is especially acute with deep native drafts (which can become net-negative vs. no speculation) and with hybrid/linear-attention targets where cheaper verification exposes the draft's full-attention cost. The problem compounds with draft length.
AI.method: Windowed-MTP applies StreamingLLM's sliding-window attention plus attention sink mechanism exclusively to the draft model's attention layers, while the target model retains full-attention verification. This is: (1) training-free — no fine-tuning required; (2) drop-in — no architectural changes; and (3) lossless by construction — the full-attention target still verifies every accepted token, so windowing changes only which tokens are proposed, never which are accepted. The method bounds the draft's KV working set to a constant, dropping ~99% of KV entries at 1M context. Additionally, the unread draft KV (7.7–11% of total KV) is reclaimed via a compact ring buffer.
AI.result: Evaluated across three architecture families (Qwen GDN-MoE 35B/122B and a Mamba2-hybrid NoPE 120B) at 1M context on a single GPU in SGLang, Windowed-MTP reduces per-decode-step cost by +28% to +44% compared to the shipping native MTP draft. This margin is input-invariant and widens with context length. End-to-end decode latency improves proportionally at matched acceptance rates, with further gains where windowing also lifts acceptance. The KV reclamation via ring buffer incurs no acceptance or quality cost.
AI.conclusion: Windowing the draft attention in speculative decoding is a simple, training-free, and lossless optimization that eliminates the context-length scaling bottleneck of native MTP draft heads, delivering substantial latency improvements at long contexts while fully preserving the target model's verified output distribution.

title: SPORD: A Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose Approach for Supply Chain Planning
summary: For years, supply chain planning at e-commerce firms has operated as a collection of isolated projects. Each planning task from static network planning to dynamic warehouse assortment planning requires analysts to spend weeks building models from scratch, calibrating and persuading executives to act on outputs they cannot verify. Three barriers drive this: bespoke models proliferate because standardization is difficult (operational fragmentation); once unified, the combinatorial scale of millions of SKUs, thousands of nodes, and intricate routing logic exceeds what solvers can handle within a tight window (computational intractability); and a mathematically optimal solution still fails to be implemented if the executives do not trust it (implementation hurdle). To bridge this gap, we propose and implement the Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose method, deployed as JD.com's NetSim platform. The central insight is decoupling: simulation proposes by generating and evaluating the full set of operationally valid candidate paths-absorbing all idiosyncratic business logic, while an integer program disposes by selecting the globally optimal subset. Computationally, matrix-vectorized CPU/GPU accelerated simulation achieves a 10-100 times speedup over serial methods, and a list scheduling algorithm reduces coupled-order processing from hours to minutes. Operationally, we establish a closed loop via an intelligent diagnosis engine. Since 2025, NetSim has optimized end to-end services for over 20,000 suppliers, the cross-regional fulfillment rate dropped from 6.1% to 4.9%, and the average monthly carbon reduction is approximately 5,745 tCO2e. SPORD moves simulation from monitoring to active planning. The transparent outputs turn skeptical executives into engaged collaborators, and the modular architecture ensures that the next planning requires just configuration, not reconstruction.

AI.tldr: JD.com's NetSim platform uses a Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose (SPORD) method that decouples supply chain planning into simulation-based candidate generation and integer programming-based global optimization, achieving 10-100x speedups, reducing cross-regional fulfillment rates from 6.1% to 4.9%, and cutting ~5,745 tCO₂e monthly.
AI.motivation: Supply chain planning at e-commerce firms suffers from three barriers: (1) operational fragmentation — bespoke models proliferate because standardizing diverse planning tasks is difficult; (2) computational intractability — the combinatorial scale of millions of SKUs, thousands of nodes, and complex routing logic exceeds solver capacity within time constraints; (3) implementation hurdle — mathematically optimal solutions go unused when executives lack trust in unverifiable outputs.
AI.method: The SPORD method decouples planning into: (a) Simulation-Propose phase, where matrix-vectorized CPU/GPU accelerated simulation generates and evaluates all operationally valid candidate paths, absorbing idiosyncratic business logic; (b) OR-Dispose phase, where an integer program selects the globally optimal subset from these candidates. A list scheduling algorithm reduces coupled-order processing from hours to minutes. An intelligent diagnosis engine provides a closed-loop feedback mechanism to build executive trust.
AI.result: Matrix-vectorized simulation achieves 10-100x speedup over serial methods. List scheduling reduces coupled-order processing from hours to minutes. Deployed in 2025 at JD.com, NetSim optimized end-to-end services for 20,000+ suppliers. Cross-regional fulfillment rate dropped from 6.1% to 4.9%, and average monthly carbon reduction reached ~5,745 tCO₂e. Executives became engaged collaborators due to transparent outputs.
AI.conclusion: SPORD elevates simulation from passive monitoring to active planning. The decoupled, modular architecture ensures future planning tasks require only configuration rather than reconstruction, overcoming fragmentation, intractability, and trust barriers simultaneously.

title: Finite-Sample Coverage Audits for High-Recall Candidate Generation: Certification and Learning-Theoretic Design
summary: An initial high-recall stage in an empirical pipeline decides which items pass to later review, labelling, or modelling, and relevant items it misses are lost to every subsequent stage. We study how many audit labels are needed to certify, with finite-sample validity, that this missed relevant mass is small, and our main results characterise the label complexity of this problem. We first show that no procedure using only labels from inside the candidate set can certify any non-trivial bound on the missed mass: the audit must sample the excluded pool, the only region where unrecovered relevant items can lie. We then prove a matching finite-corpus lower bound. Any valid audit that certifies fewer than $m$ missed relevant items with high probability when none are present, even if adaptive and permitted to label the entire included pool, must inspect on the order of $N_0/m$ excluded-pool labels. Excluded-pool auditing is therefore minimax rate-optimal, not merely convenient, for missed-mass certification in the zero-miss regime. Building on this characterisation, we develop an exact finite-sample toolkit, using binomial and hypergeometric inversion rather than asymptotic approximation, that certifies missed mass, converts it to recall through a two-pool design, certifies pre-specified families of nested candidate generators simultaneously, and produces stress-test certificates against declared perturbation mechanisms. These certificates can be paired with observable review burden to select the least burdensome pre-specified candidate generator meeting a missed-mass target. Every guarantee holds under one discipline: the candidate generator, or the pre-specified family from which it is selected, and the audit rule are fixed before the certification labels are examined.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes that certifying a small missed-relevant-mass in high-recall pipelines requires auditing the excluded pool, proves a minimax lower bound showing excluded-pool sampling is rate-optimal, and provides exact finite-sample tools using binomial/hypergeometric inversion for certification, recall conversion, and stress-testing.
AI.motivation: High-recall screening stages (e.g., in systematic reviews, e-discovery) determine which items proceed to downstream processing. Items missed at this stage are permanently lost. Practitioners need finite-sample valid certificates that the missed relevant mass is small, but the label complexity required to obtain such certificates was not previously characterized.
AI.method: The authors formalize the missed-mass certification problem, prove that auditing only the candidate (included) set yields no non-trivial bound, and derive a finite-corpus minimax lower bound showing order N₀/m excluded-pool labels are necessary. They then develop finite-sample exact confidence procedures based on binomial and hypergeometric inversion, supporting two-pool designs, simultaneous certification over nested families, and stress-testing against perturbation mechanisms.
AI.result: Key results: (1) Auditing only the candidate set cannot certify any non-trivial missed-mass bound. (2) Any valid audit that certifies fewer than m missed items with high probability requires Ω(N₀/m) labels from the excluded pool, establishing excluded-pool auditing as minimax rate-optimal. (3) The proposed finite-sample toolkit provides exact certificates without asymptotic approximation, handles simultaneous family-wise certification, and pairs with review-burden estimates for model selection.
AI.conclusion: Excluded-pool auditing is not merely convenient but statistically necessary for missed-mass certification. The finite-sample toolkit enables rigorous, distribution-free certification in practical high-recall pipelines, with all guarantees holding under the discipline that candidate generators and audit rules are pre-specified before label examination.

title: Towards Faithful Graph Explanations with Synergistic Edge Effects via Granular Balls
summary: Instance-level explanations aim to reveal the rationale behind a model's decisions for a specific graph. Previous methods explain graph neural networks (GNNs) by selecting important edges to induce subgraphs, where edge importance is assessed by perturbing each edge and observing changes in the model predictions. However, they often neglect the synergistic effects among edges, which are crucial for accurately characterizing edge importance. To address this issue, we propose SeeExplainer, a parameter-free explainer to interpret GNNs. Specifically, we first introduce a granular-ball graph refinement mechanism that decomposes a graph into several disjoint granular-balls with no fixed size, and utilize them as nodes to construct a structural graph. This process can better capture the synergistic effects among edges. Then, we perturb nodes and edges in the structural graph to generate explanatory subgraphs based on their respective contributions. Experiments on several graph classification datasets of different networks show that SeeExplainer outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: SeeExplainer is a parameter-free GNN explainer that introduces granular-ball graph refinement to capture synergistic edge effects, then perturbs structural graph elements to generate superior explanatory subgraphs for graph classification.
AI.motivation: Previous instance-level GNN explanation methods assess edge importance via isolated perturbation, neglecting synergistic effects among edges that are critical for accurately characterizing edge contributions to model predictions.
AI.method: A parameter-free approach called SeeExplainer with two stages: (1) granular-ball graph refinement that decomposes the original graph into disjoint, variable-sized granular-balls and uses them as nodes to build a structural graph, capturing edge synergies; (2) perturbation of nodes and edges in this structural graph based on their contributions to generate explanatory subgraphs.
AI.result: SeeExplainer outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on several graph classification datasets across different network architectures.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling synergistic edge effects via granular-ball refinement significantly improves the fidelity of GNN explanations over perturbation-based methods that treat edges independently.

title: OpenForgeRL: Train Harness-native Agents in Any Environment
summary: Modern AI agents rely on elaborate inference harnesses such as Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw to drive multi-turn reasoning, tool use, and access to external systems. While powerful, these complex harnesses also make agents hard to train end-to-end with open infrastructure, whose SFT/RL stacks cannot natively express stateful, multi-process harness inference. To address this, we present OpenForgeRL, an open-source framework for training harness-based agents end-to-end in diverse environments. OpenForgeRL achieves this with a lightweight proxy that serves the harness's model calls while recording them as training data for a standard RL codebase (e.g., veRL), and a Kubernetes orchestrator that runs each rollout in its own remote container, together enabling training on any harness in any environment at scale. By decoupling training and inference, OpenForgeRL allows researchers to easily train, study, and improve agents directly in the real harnesses and environments they are deployed with. We validate our framework across diverse, complex harnesses and environments, spanning tool/claw-based agents and multimodal GUI browser- and computer-use agents. Using only hundreds to a few thousand tasks, OpenForgeClaw reaches 31.7 pass^3 and 55.9 pass@3 on ClawEval and 33.7 on QwenClawBench. OpenForgeGUI reaches 37.7 on OSWorld-Verified, 63.0 on Online-Mind2Web, and 72.3 on WebVoyager. Both outperform open baselines of similar size on nearly all benchmarks, and in the GUI setting match or surpass models several times larger. Beyond benchmarks, we analyze how harness choice (e.g., ZeroClaw, OpenClaw, Codex) and RL shape agent behavior. We find that some harnesses are substantially harder to learn than others, and that RL improves agentic reliability, such as self-verification, tool coverage, and completing multi-step plans, though critical abilities such as error recovery remain weak.

AI.tldr: OpenForgeRL is an open-source framework that enables end-to-end RL training of agent harnesses by decoupling inference from training via a proxy layer and Kubernetes-based orchestration. The framework demonstrates strong results across tool-use and GUI agents, and provides analysis on how RL and harness choice shape agent behavior.
AI.motivation: Modern AI agents depend on complex, stateful, multi-process inference harnesses (e.g., Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw) for tool use and environment interaction. However, existing open-source SFT/RL training stacks cannot natively handle such harnesses, making end-to-end training infeasible. There is a need for infrastructure that bridges production-grade agent harnesses with standard RL training pipelines.
AI.method: OpenForgeRL introduces two key components: (1) a lightweight proxy that intercepts and serves the harness's model calls while simultaneously recording them as training data for a standard RL codebase like veRL, and (2) a Kubernetes orchestrator that executes each rollout in a separate remote container, enabling scalable training across arbitrary harnesses and environments. The framework decouples training from inference, allowing researchers to train agents directly in their deployment harnesses.
AI.result: OpenForgeClaw achieves 31.7 pass^3 and 55.9 pass@3 on ClawEval, and 33.7 on QwenClawBench. OpenForgeGUI reaches 37.7 on OSWorld-Verified, 63.0 on Online-Mind2Web, and 72.3 on WebVoyager. Both outperform open baselines of comparable size on nearly all benchmarks; the GUI agent matches or surpasses models several times larger. Analysis reveals some harnesses are harder to learn than others, and RL improves self-verification, tool coverage, and multi-step planning, though error recovery remains weak.
AI.conclusion: OpenForgeRL demonstrates that decoupling training from complex agent harnesses via proxy-based data capture and containerized orchestration is a viable, scalable approach for end-to-end RL training. The framework enables practical research on agent behavior under different harnesses and reveals both the gains and remaining limitations of RL for agentic capabilities.

title: Multimodal Pretraining for Generalizable EEG Representation Learning
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) models used for epilepsy are often limited to specific datasets and tasks. This limited approach can make it challenging to apply these models across different datasets or in various situations. However, recent studies in foundation models and self-supervised learning suggest that an adaptable EEG backbone could support a range of EEG related tasks. In this study, we have developed a multimodal EEG foundation model that combines a raw signal encoder based on the Mamba architecture, a Vision Transformer (ViT)-style encoder for time-frequency data, and a lightweight encoder for text, all within a shared embedding space. The pretraining process relies on several innovative techniques, such as masked modeling, cross-view contrastive alignment, and temporal consistency losses. These methods are designed to create rich, seizure-relevant representations without requiring labeled data. To assess the efficacy and generalization of our pretrained model, we fine-tuned it on the canonical CHB-MIT seizure detection benchmark and additional seizure detection datasets, and conducted extensive experiments comparing different model variants. On the standard CHB-MIT split, our best single model achieved an AUROC of 0.874, and an ensemble variant reached 0.878 AUROC, representing state-of-the-art performance on this benchmark. In addition to standard train-test splits, we evaluated performance under a leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocol, which is rarely reported in prior EEG seizure modeling work and highlights the difficulty of patient-independent seizure detection, with a mean LOSO balanced accuracy of 0.558 across 19 subjects. Across datasets and evaluation settings, our multimodal foundation model enabled robust seizure detection and straightforward adaptation to new seizure detection scenarios, while also supporting interpretable seizure localization.

AI.tldr: A multimodal EEG foundation model combining Mamba-based raw signal encoding, ViT-based time-frequency encoding, and text encoding in a shared embedding space achieves state-of-the-art seizure detection (0.874–0.878 AUROC on CHB-MIT) via self-supervised pretraining with masked modeling, cross-view contrastive alignment, and temporal consistency losses.
AI.motivation: Current EEG models for epilepsy are typically constrained to specific datasets and tasks, limiting cross-dataset generalization. There is a need for an adaptable EEG backbone—inspired by foundation models and self-supervised learning—that can support diverse EEG-related tasks without reliance on labeled data.
AI.method: A multimodal EEG foundation model with three encoders sharing a common embedding space: (1) a Mamba-based raw signal encoder, (2) a Vision Transformer (ViT)-style encoder for time-frequency representations, and (3) a lightweight text encoder. Pretraining employs masked modeling, cross-view contrastive alignment, and temporal consistency losses. Evaluation includes fine-tuning on CHB-MIT and additional seizure detection datasets under both standard train-test splits and leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocols.
AI.result: Best single model: 0.874 AUROC on CHB-MIT; ensemble variant: 0.878 AUROC (state-of-the-art). LOSO evaluation yielded a mean balanced accuracy of 0.558 across 19 subjects, highlighting the difficulty of patient-independent seizure detection. The model demonstrated robust cross-dataset seizure detection, straightforward adaptation to new scenarios, and interpretable seizure localization.
AI.conclusion: The multimodal EEG foundation model provides a flexible, generalizable framework for EEG-based seizure detection, achieving SOTA results while revealing the substantial challenges of patient-independent detection via LOSO evaluation. Its design supports interpretability and easy adaptation to new datasets and tasks.

title: MSBraM: A Multi-scale Self-supervised Brain Foundation Model for Hierarchical EEG Dynamics Learning
summary: Self-supervised foundation models have recently shown strong potential for electroencephalogram (EEG)-based analysis. However, existing approaches struggle to capture the inherently multi-scale temporal structure of EEG signals, where local neural patterns and long-range dependencies jointly encode task-relevant information. This limitation hampers cross-scale representation learning and generalization across diverse downstream tasks. To address this challenge, we propose MSBraM, a Multi-Scale self-supervised Brain foundation Model designed to learn hierarchical EEG representations. MSBraM follows a two-stage pretraining framework. First, a multi-scale neural tokenizer discretizes raw EEG signals into semantic codes at different temporal resolutions via vector-quantized reconstruction. Second, the model is pretrained to predict masked codes using a curriculum multi-scale masking strategy, progressively integrating fine-grained local patterns with global temporal context. We pretrain MSBraM on over 2,400 hours of EEG data and evaluate it across 10 downstream tasks on 12 public datasets. Extensive experiments show that MSBraM achieves superior performance on other state-of-the-art pretrained models, demonstrating strong generalization and transferability. These results indicate that explicitly modeling multi-scale temporal dynamics is critical for effective EEG foundation models.

AI.tldr: MSBraM is a multi-scale self-supervised foundation model for EEG that uses a two-stage pretraining framework (vector-quantized multi-scale tokenization + curriculum masked prediction) to capture hierarchical temporal dynamics, achieving SOTA on 10 downstream tasks across 12 public datasets with 2,400+ hours of pretraining.
AI.motivation: Existing EEG foundation models fail to capture the multi-scale temporal structure inherent in EEG signals, where both local neural patterns and long-range dependencies are essential. This limits cross-scale representation learning and generalization across diverse downstream tasks.
AI.method: MSBraM uses a two-stage pretraining framework: (1) A multi-scale neural tokenizer discretizes raw EEG into semantic codes at different temporal resolutions via vector-quantized reconstruction. (2) The model is pretrained with a curriculum multi-scale masking strategy that predicts masked codes, progressively integrating fine-grained local patterns with global temporal context.
AI.result: MSBraM outperforms state-of-the-art pretrained models on 10 downstream tasks evaluated across 12 public datasets, demonstrating strong generalization and transferability.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling multi-scale temporal dynamics is critical for building effective EEG foundation models, as evidenced by MSBraM's superior performance and robust cross-task generalization.

title: Zero-Flow Two-Sample Tests
summary: We propose a new approach to two-sample testing for deciding whether two sets of samples are drawn from the same distribution. The test is built on a statistical discrepancy based on the zero-flow criterion, termed zero-flow discrepancy (ZFD). We prove the validity of ZFD and propose a practical testing procedure, termed the zero-flow two-sample test (ZF2ST). The key idea is to learn how samples from the two distributions are locally misaligned and use the resulting directional pattern as evidence of distributional difference. By separating witness learning from hypothesis evaluation, ZF2ST can use flexible neural networks while maintaining valid statistical calibration. We develop both regression-based and power-maximized approaches for learning the witness. Experiments on synthetic and image datasets demonstrate that ZF2ST can achieve strong testing power for structured distributional changes while maintaining well-calibrated type-I error.

AI.tldr: Proposes ZF2ST, a two-sample test using a zero-flow discrepancy criterion. It learns local misalignment patterns between distributions via flexible neural networks while maintaining valid statistical calibration through separation of witness learning and hypothesis evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing two-sample tests often struggle to balance flexibility (using deep learning) with valid statistical guarantees. The authors aim to design a test that can leverage expressive neural networks for detecting complex distributional differences while preserving rigorous type-I error control.
AI.method: The test is based on the zero-flow discrepancy (ZFD), a statistical discrepancy derived from the zero-flow criterion. The approach separates witness function learning from hypothesis evaluation: a neural network learns how samples from two distributions are locally misaligned, producing a directional pattern. This witness is then evaluated via a calibrated statistical test. Two learning strategies are developed: regression-based and power-maximized approaches.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and image datasets show ZF2ST achieves strong testing power for structured distributional changes while maintaining well-calibrated type-I error rates.
AI.conclusion: ZF2ST provides a principled framework that combines neural network flexibility with valid statistical inference for two-sample testing, effectively detecting structured distributional shifts.

title: X$^3$-OPD: Distilling Reasoning into Large Audio-Language Models via On-Policy Alignment
summary: While large audio-language models have achieved remarkable progress in auditory perception, they still lag behind text-based large language models in deep logical reasoning, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data. To bridge this gap, we propose X$^3$-OPD, a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that transfers reasoning capabilities from a powerful text teacher to an audio-language student. During training, the student generates reasoning trajectories conditioned on its own acoustic perception, while the teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers. We further construct a three-tier symmetric corpus covering textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning grounded in complex acoustic scenes, and spoken-dialogue reasoning involving paralinguistic cues. This design extends cross-modal distillation beyond textually recoverable content to reasoning grounded in non-linguistic events, prosody, and conversational context. Experiments on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR demonstrate that X$^3$-OPD substantially improves audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality while largely preserving the model's existing capabilities under domain shift.

AI.tldr: X³-OPD is a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that transfers logical reasoning capabilities from a text-based LLM teacher to an audio-language student model. It uses a three-tier symmetric corpus (textual reasoning as speech, audio-event reasoning, spoken-dialogue reasoning) and token-level teacher guidance to substantially improve audio-grounded chain-of-thought reasoning while preserving existing capabilities.
AI.motivation: Audio-language models lag behind text-based LLMs in deep logical reasoning due to a scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data. The authors aim to bridge this gap by transferring reasoning capabilities from a powerful text teacher to an audio-language student without requiring extensive curated audio reasoning datasets.
AI.method: X³-OPD employs cross-modal on-policy distillation: the audio-language student generates reasoning trajectories from its own acoustic perception, while a text-based teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers. A three-tier symmetric corpus is constructed: (1) textual reasoning rendered into speech, (2) audio-event reasoning grounded in complex acoustic scenes, and (3) spoken-dialogue reasoning involving paralinguistic cues. This extends distillation beyond textually recoverable content to non-linguistic events, prosody, and conversational context.
AI.result: Experiments on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR show substantial improvements in audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality, while largely preserving existing model capabilities under domain shift.
AI.conclusion: Cross-modal on-policy distillation with a diverse, symmetric corpus is an effective strategy for imbuing audio-language models with deep reasoning capabilities, overcoming data scarcity without sacrificing generalization.

title: Logical Regression for Planning with Axioms
summary: In automated planning, logical regression is an operation that returns the most general condition necessary for an action to achieve a particular formula. It has many applications, such as allowing for more robust plan execution and providing compact policies for non-deterministic planning. Although relatively simple to calculate in basic planning settings, logical regression becomes significantly more complex when additional factors, such as axioms, are present. We introduce a methodology for approximating the logical regression of an action in a domain that includes axioms; an approximation that limits conditions to partial states. Our method produces minimal partial states while avoiding the recalculation of axioms. To demonstrate the impact of our methods, we embed our form of regression in an execution monitoring context, a well-established setting that can benefit greatly from logical regression. Our results show that this form of regression can dramatically generalize partial states across multiple domains, reducing the number of variables considered for execution monitoring by up to 70%, and demonstrate that the resulting execution monitor is robust enough to recover frequently in an environment with unexpected changes: several domains recover over 50% of the time in our tests.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an approximation method for logical regression in planning domains with axioms, producing minimal partial states without axiom recalculation. Applied to execution monitoring, it reduces variables by up to 70% and enables robust recovery (over 50% in several domains) from unexpected environmental changes.
AI.motivation: Logical regression is valuable for robust plan execution and compact policy generation in non-deterministic planning, but becomes significantly more complex when axioms are present. Existing approaches struggle with this added complexity, creating a need for practical approximation methods that can handle axiom-rich domains while maintaining computational feasibility.
AI.method: The authors introduce a methodology for approximating logical regression that restricts conditions to partial states. The method computes minimal partial states as regression results while deliberately avoiding the costly recalculation of axioms, thereby balancing expressiveness with computational efficiency.
AI.result: The regression method dramatically generalizes partial states across multiple domains when embedded in execution monitoring. It reduces the number of variables needed for monitoring by up to 70%. In environments with unexpected changes, the resulting execution monitor recovers over 50% of the time across several tested domains.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approximate logical regression effectively handles axiom-equipped domains, producing compact partial states that significantly improve execution monitoring performance — both in terms of variable reduction and recovery robustness under dynamic, unexpected conditions.

title: Graph Learning on Ensembles of Cyclic Peptides: An Investigation of Molecular Ensemble Modeling
comment: Accepted to Graph Foundation Models workshop at ICML '26. Contains 8 pages, 4 figures
summary: Molecular property prediction from structure often uses a single representative conformation, even though many molecules exist as conformational ensembles in solution. We introduce EnsembleEGNN, a molecular ensemble foundation model that encodes an ensemble by first encoding each conformer with shared Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN) layers, then pooling the resulting conformer representations with a Set Attention Block. We pretrain the model on CREMP, a cyclic peptide ensemble dataset, using a multi-task self-supervised objective combining masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, and pairwise distance reconstruction. On the CREMP-CycPeptMPDB dataset, training EnsembleEGNN from scratch fails entirely ($R^2=0.005$). However, the pretrained model reaches $R^2=0.477$ and Pearson $r=0.699$, outperforming the sequence-only BERT baseline ($R^2=0.439$, Pearson $r=0.667$). When EnsembleEGNN is co-trained end-to-end with the BERT sequence encoder, the hybrid model improves further to $R^2=0.538$ and Pearson $r=0.737$. These results demonstrate that encoding conformational ensembles into a single thermodynamically informed embedding improves cyclic-peptide property prediction.

AI.tldr: EnsembleEGNN is a pretrained molecular ensemble model that encodes conformational ensembles using shared EGNN layers and Set Attention pooling. Pretrained on a cyclic peptide dataset with multi-task self-supervised learning, it significantly outperforms sequence-only baselines for property prediction, with further gains when co-trained with a BERT sequence encoder.
AI.motivation: Most molecular property prediction methods use a single representative conformation, ignoring that molecules in solution exist as conformational ensembles. This work aims to capture the thermodynamic distribution of conformers to improve property prediction, particularly for flexible molecules like cyclic peptides.
AI.method: EnsembleEGNN encodes each conformer via shared Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN) layers, then aggregates conformer representations using a Set Attention Block into a single ensemble embedding. The model is pretrained on the CREMP cyclic peptide ensemble dataset using a multi-task self-supervised objective: masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, and pairwise distance reconstruction. Downstream evaluation is performed on CREMP-CycPeptMPDB, with a hybrid variant co-trained end-to-end with a BERT sequence encoder.
AI.result: Training from scratch fails (R²=0.005). The pretrained EnsembleEGNN achieves R²=0.477 and Pearson r=0.699, outperforming the sequence-only BERT baseline (R²=0.439, r=0.667). The hybrid EnsembleEGNN+BERT model further improves to R²=0.538 and r=0.737.
AI.conclusion: Encoding conformational ensembles into a single thermodynamically informed embedding substantially improves cyclic-peptide property prediction. The synergy between ensemble-based structural encoding and sequence-based encoding in the hybrid model yields the best performance.

title: PATS: Policy-Aware Training Scaffolding for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: In long-horizon LLM agent reinforcement learning, weak policies often repeat similar failures, producing uninformative rollout trajectories and limiting effective policy optimization. Existing skill-centric methods improve exploration by optimizing, filtering, or internalizing reusable skills. However, they remain centered on the skills themselves rather than being designed as adaptive training-time support for the evolving policy. To address this, we propose a policy-centric training paradigm that reframes skills as a dynamic training scaffold. Our framework, Pats, converts rollout groups from the latest policy into evidence cards and uses task-specific evaluation to adjust the context used in subsequent rollouts. Concrete guidance helps weak policies to complete challenging tasks. As policy improves, redundant context is revised or removed to reduce reliance on explicit guidance while preserving useful rollout variation. The policy is optimized with environmental rewards using standard RLVR, and the training scaffold is discarded at deployment. On ALFWorld and WebShop, Pats improves over strong baselines by up to 18.6%. Across seven search-augmented QA benchmarks, it remains competitive while using 32.1% fewer prompt tokens than the baseline.

AI.tldr: Pats introduces a policy-centric training paradigm that dynamically adjusts skill-based guidance as a training scaffold for LLM agents, improving weak policies during training while discarding the scaffold at deployment. It achieves up to 18.6% improvement on ALFWorld/WebShop and maintains competitive QA performance with 32.1% fewer prompt tokens.
AI.motivation: In long-horizon LLM agent reinforcement learning, weak policies generate repetitive failures and uninformative rollouts, limiting optimization. Existing skill-centric methods focus on reusable skills rather than providing adaptive, training-time support tailored to the evolving policy's current capabilities.
AI.method: Pats (Policy-centric Adaptive Training Scaffold) converts rollout groups from the latest policy into "evidence cards" and uses task-specific evaluation to adjust the context injected into subsequent rollouts. As the policy improves, redundant context is revised or removed to reduce guidance dependence while retaining useful variation. The policy is optimized via standard RLVR with environmental rewards, and the scaffold is discarded at deployment.
AI.result: On ALFWorld and WebShop, Pats achieves up to 18.6% improvement over strong baselines. Across seven search-augmented QA benchmarks, it remains competitive while using 32.1% fewer prompt tokens compared to the baseline.
AI.conclusion: Reframing skills as a dynamic, policy-centric training scaffold — rather than static reusable modules — provides effective adaptive support during RL training, significantly boosting weak-policy performance while naturally fading guidance as the agent improves, yielding both strong results and token efficiency.

title: Beyond Sufficiency: Time Series Explanation with Counterfactual Necessity
summary: Faithful explanations of time-series classifiers should identify subsequences that are not only sufficient to preserve a black-box model's prediction, but also necessary for maintaining it. However, existing sufficiency-oriented methods can assign high importance to spurious subsequences that support the prediction without being essential to the model's decision. We introduce \textbf{TimePNS}, a necessity-aware framework for time-series explanation. Inspired by Pearl's counterfactual notion of necessity, TimePNS assesses whether a temporal factor is necessary by intervening on it and measuring whether the original prediction is disrupted. The framework adopts a two-stage design. Stage I learns an identifiable causal generative process together with a sufficiency-oriented explanation mask. Stage II performs counterfactual interventions on temporal factors to derive necessity signals, which supervise a temporal gate that refines the initial explanation by suppressing non-essential components and emphasizing counterfactually necessary ones. Experiments on synthetic and real-world time-series benchmarks show that TimePNS more accurately identifies decision-critical subsequences and consistently improves sufficiency-necessity trade-offs over strong baselines.

AI.tldr: TimePNS is a necessity-aware explanation framework for time-series classifiers that uses counterfactual interventions on identifiable causal factors to refine sufficiency-oriented explanations, suppressing non-essential subsequences and emphasizing those that are causally necessary for the model's prediction.
AI.motivation: Existing explanation methods for time-series classifiers focus on sufficiency — identifying subsequences that preserve the prediction. However, they can assign high importance to spurious subsequences that support but are not essential to the model's decision. There is a need for necessity-aware explanations that identify subsequences whose removal would disrupt the prediction.
AI.method: TimePNS employs a two-stage design: Stage I learns an identifiable causal generative process along with a sufficiency-oriented explanation mask. Stage II performs counterfactual interventions on temporal factors to derive necessity signals, which then supervise a temporal gate that refines the initial mask by suppressing non-essential components and emphasizing counterfactually necessary ones. The framework is inspired by Pearl's counterfactual notion of necessity.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world time-series benchmarks demonstrate that TimePNS more accurately identifies decision-critical subsequences and consistently improves sufficiency-necessity trade-offs over strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating causal necessity via counterfactual interventions significantly improves the faithfulness of time-series explanations, yielding better identification of truly decision-critical temporal subsequences compared to sufficiency-only approaches.

title: Bridging the Gap Between Plausibility and Admissibility: Constraint-Aware Flow Maps for Dynamic Graph Systems
summary: Generative models can support decision-making under uncertainty by producing ensembles of plausible future system trajectories, but statistical plausibility does not ensure structural feasibility. This study investigates whether post-sampling symbolic constraints can improve the reliability of generative trajectory modeling in dynamic graph-structured systems. A conditional diffusion model generates future graph-state trajectories from partial observations, while an external symbolic layer applies hard filtering, soft weighting, or projection-based repair. The framework is evaluated on two controlled synthetic regimes: a compact graph and a medium-complexity dependency graph, using metrics for structural validity, sample efficiency, diversity, robustness, and calibration. In the compact regime, the model produces an invalid probability mass of 0.002996, indicating an almost entirely admissible trajectory manifold. Under the same architecture and training protocol, invalid mass increases to 0.155929 in the medium-complexity regime. Hard filtering removes all invalid retained trajectories while preserving 84.4% of generated samples, whereas soft weighting preserves effective sample size but yields only limited validity gains. Family-level analysis shows that dependency constraints account for nearly all observed inadmissibility. These results indicate that statistical plausibility and structural admissibility are distinct reliability properties and that symbolic constraint handling becomes more valuable as graph-structural complexity increases.

AI.tldr: A conditional diffusion model generates graph-state trajectories, post-processed by symbolic constraints (hard filtering, soft weighting, projection-based repair). On a compact graph, only 0.3% of samples are invalid, but on a medium-complexity graph, 15.6% are invalid — nearly all due to dependency constraints. Hard filtering removes all invalid samples while retaining 84.4% of the generated set, demonstrating that symbolic post-hoc correction becomes increasingly valuable as graph-structural complexity grows.
AI.motivation: Generative models produce statistically plausible trajectories for decision-making under uncertainty, but statistical plausibility does not guarantee structural feasibility (e.g., adherence to dependency constraints in graph-structured systems). The authors aim to quantify and mitigate this gap through post-sampling symbolic constraint enforcement.
AI.method: A conditional diffusion model generates future graph-state trajectories from partial observations. An external symbolic layer applies one of three strategies: (1) hard filtering — discard samples violating constraints; (2) soft weighting — down-weight invalid samples while preserving effective sample size; (3) projection-based repair — map invalid trajectories onto the admissible manifold. Evaluation uses two synthetic regimes (compact vs. medium-complexity dependency graphs) and metrics covering structural validity, sample efficiency, diversity, robustness, and calibration.
AI.result: Invalid probability mass is 0.002996 in the compact regime versus 0.155929 in the medium-complexity regime. Hard filtering eliminates all invalid trajectories while retaining 84.4% of generated samples. Soft weighting preserves effective sample size but yields only limited validity improvements. Dependency constraints account for nearly all observed inadmissibility. Structural admissibility and statistical plausibility are shown to be distinct, decoupled reliability properties.
AI.conclusion: Statistical plausibility and structural admissibility are distinct reliability dimensions. Symbolic constraint handling becomes more valuable as graph-structural complexity increases. Hard filtering offers a practical, high-retention solution for enforcing structural constraints post hoc, though the growing invalid mass with complexity suggests that hybrid training-time integration of symbolic knowledge may be warranted for more complex regimes.

title: Expanding Flow Maps
summary: Flow-based generative models have enabled remarkable progress in fast and controllable generation across continuous and discrete state spaces, yet existing parameterizations are constrained to fixed dimensions or fixed sequence lengths. Here, we introduce Expanding Generative Flows (EFlows), which define flows between distributions of increasing dimensionality along an expanding interpolant that grows the state by augmenting it with conditional noise. Building on this construction, we propose Expanding Flow Maps (EFMs), a new class of flow maps that distill the expanding interpolant into efficient few-step generative models. Each EFM factors the map between any two timesteps into two learnable operations: an expand operator, which augments the state space with new coordinates or tokens conditioned on the current state, and a transport map, which pushes the expanded state forward along the interpolant. Composing these operators yields a single map that jointly expands and denoises the state, recovering existing fixed-canvas flows and flow maps as the special case in which the expand operator is the identity. We further extend the framework to the discrete simplex, enabling variable-size graph generation and variable-length sequence generation. Across both continuous and discrete modalities, we establish EFlows and EFMs as a principled framework for settings in which output size is itself a learned, controllable degree of freedom.

AI.tldr: EFlows introduces a flow-based generative framework where the state dimensionality grows during generation via an expanding interpolant. EFMs distill this into efficient few-step models by composing an expand operator (adds new coordinates/tokens) with a transport map (denoises). The framework unifies fixed-canvas flows as a special case and extends to discrete simplex for variable-size graphs and variable-length sequences.
AI.motivation: Existing flow-based generative models are constrained to fixed dimensions or fixed sequence lengths, limiting their applicability to tasks where output size is a variable, learned degree of freedom (e.g., graphs of varying node counts, sequences of varying length). The authors aim to remove this constraint by enabling flows between distributions of increasing dimensionality.
AI.method: The paper proposes Expanding Generative Flows (EFlows), which define flows between distributions of increasing dimensionality using an expanding interpolant that augments the state with conditional noise. Building on this, Expanding Flow Maps (EFMs) distill the interpolant into few-step generative models by factoring the map between any two timesteps into: (1) an expand operator that augments the state space with new coordinates/tokens conditioned on the current state, and (2) a transport map that pushes the expanded state forward along the interpolant. Composing these yields a single joint expand-and-denoise map. The framework extends to the discrete simplex for variable-size graph and variable-length sequence generation.
AI.result: EFlows and EFMs provide a principled, unified framework that recovers existing fixed-canvas flows and flow maps as the special case where the expand operator is the identity. The method is validated across both continuous and discrete modalities, demonstrating controllable generation where output size is a learned degree of freedom.
AI.conclusion: EFlows and EFMs establish a principled generative framework that removes the fixed-dimensionality constraint of prior flow-based models, enabling variable-size generation in both continuous and discrete domains. The compositional expand-then-transport design is simple, general, and subsumes prior fixed-canvas methods.

title: Agent-Guided Relational Concept Discovery: Toward Interpretable Surgical Margin Assessment
comment: This paper is accepted to MICCAI 2026, and this is the submission version, not the camera-ready version
summary: Deep learning models can effectively use Rapid Evaporative Ionization Mass Spectrometry (REIMS) data for surgical margin assessment. However, their clinical adoption remains challenging due to limited generalization to operating room conditions. This difficulty arises because models are typically trained on labeled spectra collected from resected tissue samples, while they must operate on noisy, unlabeled data acquired directly during surgery. In addition, the black-box nature of deep learning models makes it difficult to understand and systematically improve their behavior. Concept-based learning offers a promising way to address these challenges by mapping raw measurements to human-understandable concepts. However, supervised concept-based approaches rely on concept annotations, which are difficult to obtain in complex mass spectrometry workflows. We propose Agent-Guided Concept Discovery, a framework that learns meaningful concepts directly from data without requiring predefined concept labels. During training, a reasoning agent refines semantic descriptions of the learned concepts and adaptively adjusts their weight based on diagnostic relevance. These concepts are further grounded using a biochemical knowledge graph to ensure consistency with known metabolic relationships. Across Skin and Breast Cancer datasets, our model improves balanced accuracy and sensitivity over the baseline. In a representative intraoperative case, it shows fewer false positives, indicating better generalization to surgical conditions.

AI.tldr: A framework called Agent-Guided Concept Discovery learns interpretable concepts from REIMS mass spectrometry data without requiring manual annotations, using a reasoning agent and biochemical knowledge graph to improve surgical margin assessment accuracy and generalization.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models for REIMS-based surgical margin assessment suffer from poor generalization to noisy intraoperative data and lack interpretability. Supervised concept-based learning could help but requires costly concept annotations that are impractical in complex mass spectrometry workflows. The authors aim to overcome these barriers by enabling concept discovery directly from data without predefined labels.
AI.method: Agent-Guided Concept Discovery framework: (1) learns concepts directly from REIMS spectra without predefined concept labels; (2) employs a reasoning agent that iteratively refines semantic descriptions of learned concepts and adaptively weights them by diagnostic relevance; (3) grounds concepts using a biochemical knowledge graph to enforce consistency with known metabolic relationships.
AI.result: On Skin Cancer and Breast Cancer datasets, the model improved balanced accuracy and sensitivity over the baseline. In a representative intraoperative case, it produced fewer false positives, demonstrating better generalization to real surgical conditions.
AI.conclusion: Agent-Guided Concept Discovery enables interpretable, annotation-free concept learning for REIMS-based tissue classification, improving both performance and generalization to challenging intraoperative settings while maintaining biochemical plausibility.

title: Detecting LLM-Generated Tokens in Human--LLM Coauthored Text
summary: The rise of human-AI collaborative writing has created a growing need for fine-grained detection methods that support localizing likely LLM-generated content in mixed-authorship documents. Existing methods for detecting LLM-generated text mainly focus on document-level classification and cannot identify which parts of the text are generated by LLMs. This paper introduces a new method to address this urgent need. Our method operates at the token level, the natural unit of modern language models, and builds on existing token-level detection scores.
